#5627. 10-Acre Florida Ranch With NBA-Level Facility Is Listed for $38.9 Million in Celebrity Enclave Where Gisele Bündchen Lives

An enormous 9.69-acre Florida compound with a brand-new 10,500-square-foot entertainment facility "that can be transformed into anything you can imagine" and resort-inspired grounds has just hit the market in Southwest Ranches for an astonishing $38.9 million.

If it reels in anywhere near its asking price, the 23,442-square-foot estate could become one of the top sales in the ultrahigh net worth neighborhood that celebrities, professional athletes, and supermodel Gisele Bündchen call home.

"I have never seen a property done to this scale before," says Tommy Crivello of the Tommy Crivello Real Estate Group, who is co-listing the property with Angeline Earnest of Coldwell Banker Realty.

Once the home of Mexican singer Juan Gabriel, the luxury residence last traded hands for $9,000,000 in 2022. Its asking price of $1,659 per square foot is currently the highest-priced listing in the exclusive Sunshine Ranches enclave of Southwest Ranches.

"Everything has been completely redone with extensive remodeling," Earnest notes. "The landscaping, garage, pools, and the 10,000-square-foot recreational facility are all new. Every structure also has a new roof."

The sprawling property boasts a five-bedroom primary residence, a three-bedroom guesthouse with a catering-grade kitchen, a members-style clubhouse with a full bar and private theater, and a gym and spa wellness retreat with a massage room and cold plunge.

Private lakes, immersive art, koi ponds, "producing orchards," a Tiki pavilion, and two pools, including one with a custom 10-foot rock-jumping wall, can also be found on the enormous lot. An outdoor basketball court and hockey rink round out the property.

"There are 10 acres of walkable space," she adds. "It feels like the whole property is livable and is not overwhelming."

"We are seeing a lot of high-end celebrities coming here," Crivello says. "I see an entrepreneur, hedge fund person, athlete, or real big car collector buying this property. It could also be someone who is looking for a place for the entire family, as it is designed for multigenerational living."

A custom-engineered lighting system transforms the pathways into nocturnal works of art. For equestrians, the sale also includes plans for a seven-stall barn with oversized paddocks.

"The property is large enough that there is room for another outdoor facility, and it has direct access to miles of riding trails," he says. "Everything in Southwest Ranches has rural zoning, so you can have a garden and any kind of animal on property. It just flows effortlessly."

Created as a "fully integrated private campus," the serene property also features art installations and curated gathering spaces for entertaining.

“You can get to the beach in 30 minutes, Amerant Bank Arena in 15 minutes, Las Olas Boulevard for the nightlife, and Pembroke Gardens is just 10 minutes away,” Crivello says. “You can retreat to the country, or you can be in the limelight as much as you want to be.”

Built in 1964, the Chicago brick-clad main estate boasts a renovated interior with two guest suites, each with a private entrance and that “function as private apartments within the residence.”

A lavish upstairs primary wing has a breakfast bar, a refrigerator, a seating area, dual bathrooms, separate closets, and a private terrace.

Other highlights include an executive office, a chef’s kitchen, a built-in wine preservation system, a custom bar, and a wraparound covered balcony on the main level.

A detached garage pavilion spanning nearly 2,000 square feet is fully air-conditioned. The four-vehicle structure has lift capability to accommodate up to eight vehicles. It also has floor drains, integrated compressor and vacuum systems, EV-ready outlets, workstation walls, and extra storage space.

One of the most impressive features of the property is its enormous entertainment facility, “currently home to a nonprofit basketball program.”

The “NBA-level” structure features professional athletic flooring, locker rooms, conference spaces, a viewing balcony, and a smoothie bar.

Its flexible design could also be reimagined into a 50- to 100-vehicle auto showroom, a private museum, a production studio, or an event venue.

“The nice thing about the facility is that it has a second mezzanine where you can have spectators watch,” Crivello notes.

“You could also transform it into an indoor equestrian facility. It offers the peace of mind that upscale riders want. There has been a big shift for people who are car collectors, so the facility could also be transformed into an auto showroom. The building is huge and would be a focal point for an equestrian, athlete, or car collector.”

#5626. AMD beats expectations as agentic AI sparks its data center revenue growth engines

Shares of the chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc. rose more than 5% in late trading today after it delivered solid third-quarter earnings and revenue today, with data center sales almost doubling from a year ago.

The company reported earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.09 per share, easily beating Wall Street’s forecast of $1.95 per share. Revenue for the period jumped 45% from a year earlier, to $13.38 billion, ahead of the $13.09 billion analyst consensus estimate. All told, the company’s net income for the quarter came to $3.47 billion, up 77% from the previous year when it posted a profit of just $1.96 billion.

The star performer in the quarter was AMD’s data center business unit, which accounted for 64% of its overall revenue, up from just 47% one year ago. After spending years trying to compete with Nvidia Corp.’s graphics processing units for artificial intelligence market share, the company’s traditional central processing units or CPUs are suddenly back in vogue thanks to the emergence of agentic AI applications such as Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse. Autonomous AI agents can run much more efficiently on CPUs than they can on GPUs, boosting demand for the chips.

Looking ahead, AMD expects its server revenue to double year-over-year in fiscal 2027, with AI growth likely to accelerate even faster than the company projected just three months ago. “Adoption is just starting and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work,” AMD Chief Executive Lisa Su (pictured) said on a conference call with analysts.

AMD’s data center story isn’t all about CPUs, though. The company also sells GPUs, including bundles of them shipped inside data center-ready rack-scale systems called Helios, and that system’s popularity is growing fast.

Su said Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC, Microsoft Corp., Oracle Corp. and Meta are all using AMD Helios systems in their data centers. Last week, Meta said its first Helion racks are already up and running as it revealed that AMD invested $1 billion in its latest equity offering.

The chipmaker has also committed to a $5 billion investment in Anthropic, which last week revealed the long-awaited prospectus for its upcoming initial public offering.

AMD delivered its latest earnings report just days after its rival Intel Corp. did the same. Intel also posted strong data center revenue growth, but its stock fell more than 30% on Friday on weak guidance and concerns about its ability to meet demand for its products.

But Su said AMD had no such problems. Last month she made a high-profile visit to Taiwan, where she held meetings with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and a number of supply chain partners, and said after the trip that the company plans to substantially increase its supply in the coming year. “We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year,” Su added.

AMD’s results will go some way toward reassuring investors who have become increasingly nervous about the direction of the AI industry and whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on it each year is actually going to generate a return on their investments, said eMarketer analyst Jacob Bourne. “The results are a test of AMD’s own performance and the broader AI trade, and its data center and revenue beats will encourage investors after the recent semiconductor selloff,” he added.

Though AMD is far from immune to the recent volatility that has afflicted AI-related stocks, its future still looks increasingly rosy for now. “Demand for AI computing is not going to fall off a cliff, and AMD has the competitive products and major customer relationships to capitalize on that demand,” Bourne said.

Strength in the data center unit is helping AMD to ride out difficulties in its traditional market for personal computers, which is the reason for Intel’s poor outlook. During the second quarter, global PC shipments fell 4% from a year earlier, with buyers dissuaded by the rising cost of components such as memory chips, according to data from Counterpoint Research.

Along with Intel, AMD is a leading manufacturer of the x86 CPUs that power most of the world’s computers and laptops. The company reports PC chip revenue within a segment that also includes its chips for games consoles, and that unit saw its revenue decline 8% from a year earlier, to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue fell 40% from the previous year.

For the current quarter, AMD is targeting revenue of abouot $17 billion at the midpoint of its guidance range, ahead of the Street’s $16.2 billion consensus estimate. The company also sees its gross margins coming in at 55%, just below the Street’s forecast of 55.3%.

AMD was busy on the acquisition front during the quarter. In September it revealed it’s going to buy World Labs Inc. for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by the AI industry luminary Fei-Fei Li, has developed world models that can simulate 3D environments to support the training of intelligent robots and other physical AI applications.

The company also acquired a startup called Taalas Inc. that makes specialized model-specific integrated circuits, which are essentially chips that can be customized to run a specific AI model more efficiently. That acquisition should help to boost AMD’s position in AI inference. AMD also invested in the AI image generation model maker Stability AI Ltd., which raised $76 million in funding in August.

#5625. Tribeca Dominates Manhattan Luxury Sales This Week With Top 2 Penthouses on Same Street

Tribeca took the crown for the hottest neighborhood in Manhattan luxury sales last week, nabbing the top two priciest sales in the borough.

The lower West Side neighborhood, which John F. Kennedy Jr. and his bride, Carolyn Bessette, did much to make famous, has continued to push toward the Hudson River with new luxury residential skyscapers.

Last week's top two sales were coincidentally on the same street, with contracts signed at 111 Murray St. and 71 Murray St. Both were penthouse condos.

"I like to call it 'Tribeca lite,'" says Brown Harris Stevens agent Lisa K. Lippman, who not only represents real estate in the neighborhood, but also lives in it. "It's not prime Tribeca."

The broker says "prime" Tribeca would be around the the area of Duane and North Moore Street. (JFK Jr. and Carolyn lived in 20 North Moore St.)

But as prime Tribeca filled up, development spread east and west—with the western edge closer to sweeping river views, as well as the Hudson River Greenway bike path and all of the riverfront parks and piers.

"The area feels less residential," she tells Realtor.com of Murray Street and the surrounding streets, which are packed with glass skyscrapers. "There's always people who want to be on a higher floor, have a lot of amenities, but pay a little less."

The top sale for the week ending Nov. 1 was Penthouse One at 111 Murray St., with an asking price of $33.95 million. The penthouse, inside a 64-story tower built in 2018 and designed by architect David Mann, was a sponsor sale.

The sprawling, extra-large unit—at 7,675 square feet with five bedrooms and 6.5 bedrooms—was snapped up by Richard Saghian, the founder and chief executive of Fashion Nova, for $31 million, according to multiple reports.

According to Forbes, the 45-year-old fashion mogul is worth $2.1 billion and is the No. 1,900–ranked richest person in the world.

The penthouse will be added to his growing property portfolio, which includes a $141 million Bel-Air mansion and two Miami Beach properties: a $30 million double lot and a $32 million estate.

His latest acquisition offers 360-degree views of New York Harbor, as well as 233 square feet of private terraces with which to enjoy them.

The sweeping river views really helped move the property, says listing agent Emily Sertic of Douglas Elliman, who has headed up sales in the building since its launch.

"You'll capture a glimpse of Central Park, the Empire State Building, all the historic bridges, the rivers, and the harbor," she says. "From its view line only, it really encompasses an incredible experience of New York. Everywhere you turn, there are these astonishing view lines that just go on and on."

"The view line and the grandeur of the space for entertaining was really important," she says of what helped attract the billionaire buyer, who was represented by Ryan and Emilia Serhant of Serhant.

The great room alone is over 2,000 square feet, says the broker, and boasts an eat-in kitchen, butler's pantry, and private terrace.

"Whether it's for work, entertainment, guests, or family, the bedrooms were a huge draw to the space," she says.

Saghian, the college dropout son of Iranian immigrants, is reportedly single with no children.

The fast-fashion mogul appears to appreciate a real estate deal—creditors of his Bel-Air mansion originally wanted $295 million at auction and a judge had to approve the sale because of the relatively low price it ended up fetching. And the Tribeca penthouse originally asked for $50 million back in September 2025.

"It has all the features that any trophy buyer is looking for," says Sertic.

Some of those features fit for a billionaire include a chef's kitchen with Wolf, Miele, and Sub-Zero appliances, dual fridges and dishwashers, a 60-inch custom gas cooktop, multiple ovens, and a full-height wine refrigerator.

The full-service luxury building contains the usual array of amenities one would expect at this price point.

There is a 24/7 door attendant, concierge service, and valet team; a full-service wellness center and spa complete with hammam, treatment rooms, and a 75-foot lap pool with private cabanas; a fitness center; a children's playroom with splash pad, and a teen arcade room. There's also a private dining room, screening room, and landscaped garden.

The penthouse comes with a $36,000 monthly fee, including HOA dues and taxes.

The second top sale of last week was also on Murray Street. The glass-walled triplex penthouse at 71 Murray St. is a four-bedroom, 4.5-bath unit with a price tag of $18.5 million.

Listed by Jeremy V. Stein of Sotheby's International Realty, the sprawling 6,700-square-foot condo included an astonishing 3,148-square feet of terraces, including two roof terraces decked out for entertaining with a full Viking kitchen, fire pit, and dining area. There is also a floating glass staircase and 36-foot climbing wall.

Topping a boutique building with only 12 residences, the penthouse has monthly common charges and taxes totaling $17,232.

The two downtown top sales aren't that unusual—the former warehouse district has been trendy since the late Kennedy scion took up residence there in the early 1990s. (Actor Robert DeNiro—who moved there in 1981—can truly claim pioneer status.)

Sertic says the typical neighborhood buyers tend to be "youngish buyers and their families" who work in the surrounding neighborhoods, especially the Financial District.

"A lot of our buyers walk to work," she says. "They are high-performing and fast-moving, so convenience is huge."

Despite Tribeca nabbing the top two sales, it was the Upper East Side that pulled the most luxury (over $4 million) contracts again this week. Of the 34 contracts signed, the UES dominated with the highest amount of sales for the 10th time this year.

As is usual, condos outsold co-ops, 17 to 12. However, with only five sales between them, co-ops are holding their own.

The upward sales trajectory of co-ops—where buyers tend to be subject to a rigorous board approval process—is likely the effect of luxury inventory being so slim, say experts.

It also probably helps that co-ops often trade lower than condos, with an average ask of $6.48 million versus $10.44 million for condos, according to Olshan Realty.

The most expensive co-op of the week was a new build, constructed in 2023. The Lenox Hill penthouse at 200 East 75th St. had an asking price of $16.85 million.

#5624. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

A homeowner who isn't ready to accept a lower offer may be able to wait. But a builder with finished houses to sell has a different set of priorities. And that could work in your favor.If you're ready to buy, talk to a local agent about which builders have completed homes sitting on the market in your area see what they're willing to offer to get them sold.

#5623. Justin Baldoni Discreetly Sells Former Los Angeles Home for $2.1 Million After Making a ‘Fresh Start’ in Nashville

Actor Justin Baldoni discreetly offloaded his former Los Angeles home months after relocating to Nashville, TN, for a “fresh start.”

The three-bedroom, three-bathroom Culver City abode went for $2.1 million in an off-market transaction in August, according to Page Six. The 1,992-square-foot house was built in 1952 and sits on a 5,736-square-foot lot.

“He hasn’t lived there in years,” a People magazine source said. “The family has been living in Nashville for a bit now, but they moved to Ojai before that.”

The “It Ends With Us” director and his wife, Emily Baldoni, reportedly bought the home in 2017.

In an October 2020 People magazine interview, the couple opened up about life in the “urban farmhouse.”

The Baldonis said they invited loved ones to visit the home to write prayers and affirmations on its exposed wooden beams after completing a nine-month renovation.

“In the beams of the house is literally love,” Justin said.

The home had a host of interesting features, including a climbing wall in the garage for their children, Maiya and Maxwell.

There was also a built-in Wolf coffee machine and a top-of-the line Kohler toilet the actor compared to a “Transformer.”

While Emily shared that the plumbing feature “takes care of everything,” Justin noted that the family “didn’t panic as much as some others when all the toilet paper disappeared.”

The sale of the Los Angeles property isn’t the only quiet real estate move Justin, 42, has made this year.

Property records indicate that he listed his sprawling Ojai, CA, compound for $8.88 million on Feb. 5. The listing came just days after a rental listing for the same property—which was asking $40,000 a month—was taken down.

The estate, which the couple purchased for $2.2 million in 2020, has since been taken off the market.

The five-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom dwelling on a 10-acre lot in the picturesque neighborhood of Santa Paula was described by Emily as a “magical place” in a 2023 Architectural Digest interview.

Inspired by their trips abroad, the couple went to lengths to design “the whole house with feng shui in mind,” a practice inspired by his mother, “who’s done it for 30 years.”

“When we went to Tulum and parts of Mexico, we would take pictures of lamps or couches—just as inspiration—and then we started to put together a Pinterest board of things that we liked,” he said.

The couple made a series of upgrades to the home to create a “sanctuary.” According to the since-removed listing, the home was outfitted with “a state-of-the-art medical-grade air filtration system,” electromagnetic frequency shielding around the primary bedroom, a saltwater pool, and a “regenerative orchard.”

It also included a hot tub, sport court, custom-designed gym, LED-lit in-ground trampoline, koi pond with waterfall, fire pit, and walking paths.

Additional technological amenities included EV charging stations, a state-of-the-art security system, and fire mitigation systems.

The family packed their bags for Tennessee in December 2025, amid the highly publicized legal drama Justin was involved in after actress Blake Lively sued in 2024, claiming he had sexually harassed her during the filming of “It Ends with Us.”

“It’s obviously been an incredibly difficult time for the whole family, but Nashville has given them a fresh start,” a People magazine source previously shared.

After denying the allegations, Justin filed a $400 million countersuit against Lively and her husband, Ryan Reynolds, her publicist Leslie Sloane, and Sloane’s PR firm, citing defamation and breach of contract.

The suit was later dismissed by a judge, as were Lively’s sexual harassment claims. The actress later pursued allegations of retaliation against Justin, as well as his production company and publicity team.

Justin and Lively reached a private settlement days before the case was due to go to trial in May 2026.

However, the dispute continued when Lively sought $8 million in legal fees from Justin. She was awarded a total of $407,451.75 in an Aug. 26 order.

In July, when the dispute was still ongoing, the Baldonis posted an Instagram Reel to address the situation for the first time.

“We have not spoken publicly for the better part of the last two years, and it’s not because we haven’t had anything to say,” Justin said. “It just felt like every time we went to make a video like this, we wanted to speak, something was telling us not to. It just didn’t feel like the right time, and we were talking about it and feeling into it and praying about it.”

While Justin kept his statement fairly vague and never named Lively, the couple did share that they had experienced a lot of “trauma.”

"What I will say is that there have been so many painful things that have been spoken into existence over the last couple of years,” he said. “That created so much noise, and we didn’t want to add to the noise. So we just wanted to let the justice system run its course."

The couple noted that they had “so much more to say,” but that they were “going to focus on continuing the healing” and “hanging out” with their “kiddos and enjoying life.”

According to the New York Post, the family’s new Nashville home is a $3.4 million newly built abode. The six-bedroom, six-bathroom property spans 7,000 square feet and is situated on an acre lot.

#5622. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

#5621. Don Jr.’s Investor Business Partner Abruptly Resigns From Fannie Mae Board

Conservative businessman Omeed Malik, a close Trump ally and business partner of Donald Trump Jr., has stepped down from the board of Fannie Mae.

The government-sponsored mortgage giant said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday that Malik resigned from the board of directors, effective Oct. 30. Malik is president of the venture capital firm 1789 Capital as well as founder of investment bank Farvahar Partners. Trump Jr. joined 1789 as a partner in November 2024.

Malik "brings extensive experience in financial services and capital markets as well as a blend of legal, entrepreneurial, and strategic leadership expertise," Fannie said in its last annual report in February. He was paid $114,222 last year, that filing shows.

As a member of the eight-member board, Malik has been a part of Fannie Mae as it has enlarged its balance sheet at the behest of President Donald Trump, who pushed the GSE to buy mortgage-backed securities in a bid to lower mortgage rates.

Trump has also floated the idea of ending the conservatorship of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, potentially setting the stage for a $30 billion IPO. But the Trump administration has said little of those plans in recent months as Americans grapple with inflation and rising housing costs.

Malik joined the board in April 2025. At the time, Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte, who chairs the board, posted to X that "Omeed brings great capital markets, legal and investment experience as we Make Fannie and Freddie Great Again!"

Fannie Mae reported $4.2 billion in net income in the third quarter. This year it has provided about $344 billion in liquidity to 295,000 homebuyers. The company's overall net worth has swelled from $47.4 billion in 2021 to $119.6 billion in the third quarter.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5620. Don't Let the Fear of a Buyer Backing Out Scare You Away from Selling

There’s nothing quite like the excitement of getting an offer on your house. You’re one step closer to moving on to what’s next. But what happens if that buyer backs out or ghosts you before closing?

If you’ve been seeing headlines about more home sales falling through lately, that possibility may be keeping you up at night. And it’s true. According to Redfin and Cotality, canceled contracts have been on the rise.

But here’s what those headlines don’t always tell you…

Most sales still go through. Only 10-15% hit this snag. And even so, there are things you can do to help keep your sale from becoming one of them.

The key is knowing what tends to scare buyers away and getting ahead of those issues before they have a chance to derail your move.

Today’s buyers are being more cautious. Mortgage rates are stretching budgets, and with more homes to choose from, buyers have more freedom to walk away if something doesn’t feel right. As Redfin explains:

“That gives house hunters more options and makes them more likely to walk away if an inspection uncovers problems, an appraisal comes in low or the seller doesn’t agree to concessions.”

That’s why an accepted offer isn’t always a guaranteed sale. But it doesn’t mean you should be afraid to put your house on the market, either.

It just means getting ahead of potential problems matters more than ever.

A Redfin survey asked real estate agents why some buyers are backing out. And their answers give you a short of cheatsheet into what could go sideways and how you can get ahead of those headaches (see graph below):

This is the big one. And the good news? It’s also one of the areas where you can be the most proactive.

One simple way to head this off is by getting a pre-listing inspection before your house goes on the market. That way, if something needs attention, you can decide whether to fix it upfront (before you sell), adjust your price, or disclose it and come in already prepared for what’s likely to pop up in negotiations. It’s a lot better to find the skeletons in the closet before a buyer does.

Even buyers who are pre-approved can run into financing issues before closing. And with mortgage rates putting extra pressure on affordability, some buyers are finding it harder to make the numbers work.

While you can’t control whether a buyer’s loan goes through, you can work with your agent to look closely at their financing before accepting an offer. And if affordability is the concern, your agent can help you explore whether incentives like closing cost credits or a mortgage-rate buydown could make a difference.

Sometimes, your buyer needs to sell their house before they can buy yours. And if their sale falls through, yours could be affected too.

That’s why it’s important to understand any home-sale contingencies before accepting an offer. Your agent can help you look at where the buyer is in their own selling process and what protections you may want in place.

The goal isn’t to eliminate every possible risk. It’s to avoid being caught off guard by the ones you can plan for.

Just remember when you read headlines about canceled deals, they don’t give you the full picture. Most home sales still make it to closing.

And if a sale does fall through, that doesn’t automatically mean your house won’t sell. Sometimes a buyer’s circumstances change. Sometimes an issue comes up that can be addressed before the next offer.

What matters is having an agent who knows how to spot potential problems early, help you navigate negotiations, and keep your sale moving forward.

Because while you can’t control every twist and turn, you can control how prepared you are.

There's no need to let the fear of a buyer backing out hold you back. While no sale comes with guarantees, a little preparation upfront can go a long way toward making the whole process smoother.If you're ready to make a move, talk to a local agent about whether a pre-listing inspection makes sense for you.

#5619. Supermicro and Arista Networks crush expectations as AI infrastructure wins again

Growing nervousness about spending on the artificial intelligence boom has made technology stocks increasingly volatile this year, but all it takes is one good quarter to reignite investor confidence, as Super Micro Computer Inc. and Arista Networks Inc. both showed today.

The companies are still relatively small fry in terms of the bigger AI picture, but as key data center infrastructure providers, they have shown consistently strong revenue growth over the last couple of years, and neither looks to be slowing down.

Indeed, Supermicro’s sales shot up by an incredible 298% in its latest quarter as it powered its way to yet another impressive revenue beat. The server maker reported fiscal 2027 first-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $1.81 per share on sales of $19.95 billion, cruising past Wall Street’s guidance of $1.23 per share in earnings and $17.35 billion in sales. After-hours, the company’s stock gained more than 6%.

Meanwhile, Arista delivered third-quarter earnings of $1.20 per share on revenue of $3.66 billion, up 58% from a year earlier, surpassing the Street’s target of $1.08 per share in earnings and $3.33 billion in revenue. Its stock moved higher too, and rose more than 9% in the late-trading session. The company is a major supplier of networking equipment for AI data centers, helping to link together massive clusters of graphics processing units and other high-powered chips.

Supermicro Chief Executive Charles Liang (pictured) said his company continues to sell its servers and storage solutions as fast as it can build them. “Supermicro’s transformation into a total AI and IT data center solution provider continues to accelerate,” he added.

Investors were looking for signs that Supermicro may face headwinds in the coming months, with the impact of rising component costs being one of their major concerns. But the company’s results seem to have reassured doubters that supply issues could impact its profitability. Notably, Supermicro said its gross margin rose to 12.8% in the quarter, higher than the 9.3% margin recorded in the same quarter one year ago.

Supermicro’s guidance for the current quarter was impressive too. The company said it’s looking for earnings of between $1.66 and $1.90 per share on sales of between $19.5 billion and $21.5 billion in its second quarter. That’s much higher than the Street’s forecast, which calls for earnings of $1.14 per share and sales of $18.1 billion.

Arista’s 58% revenue growth was the biggest year-over-year jump since the company went public back in 2014, and it could well break that record again if its guidance holds true. The company said it’s looking for fourth-quarter earnings of between $1.26 and $1.30 per share on sales of $3.95 billion at the midpoint of its range. That would represent growth of 59%. The guidance was better than expected, with Wall Street looking for earnings of just $1.16 per share on sales of $3.65 billion.

Arista Chairperson and Chief Executive Jayshree Ullal told analysts that even she was surprised by how well the company did in the prior quarter. “This strong momentum across customer sectors highlights our increased relevance for the generative and agentic AI era,” she said.

#5618. Rhode Island Voters Back $120 Million Bond Measure To Support Affordable Housing

Rhode Island voters are projected to pass a ballot initiative to support increased housing through a massive bond issuance.

Rhode Island's Question 2 issues $120 million in general obligation bonds, which could then be used in various costs to increase the supply of affordable housing. The funding would go to pre-development work, new construction, property acquisition, and infrastructure improvements.

At 9 p.m. ET on Tuesday, an hour after polls closed, the measure had 61% support with 84% of the vote reported, according to the state's Board of Elections. The measure needs 50% support to pass.

Of the money from the bond issue, $25 million must go to increasing construction of for-sale homes and $10 million for public housing. The state expects construction on these projects to begin in 2028 and the new housing to come online from 2029 to 2032. That's according to the state's information on the ballot measure, which notes that the total cost of the bond will top out at around $192.5 million with interest.

The National Low Income Housing Coalition estimates that Rhode Island, with a population of about 1.1 million people, is short around 23,000 affordable rental homes for low-income renters. Around 30% the state's renters are considered extremely low income, with an average income of $31,970 for a household of four. According to NLIHC, renters need to make an annual household income of $70,617 to afford a two-bedroom rental home at HUD's fair market rent.

Many prospective buyers in Rhode Island are also being priced out.

Rhode Island's median listing price is $569,900, about $150,000 more than the median national listing price of $419,250.

Housing Works Rhode Island's 2026 Housing Fact Book found that purchasing a home in Rhode Island is out of reach for anyone making the median annual income and that housing costs continue to outpace wages.

Around a third of Rhode Island's homeowners are considered cost-burdened and spend more than 30% of their income on housing.

In the state's capital city, Providence, less than 4% of homes were considered affordable to middle-income buyers, showing a significant misalignment between available homes and local income level. In fact, Providence ranks among the most misaligned markets when it comes to incomes meeting the cost of housing, according to Realtor.com® research.

Former Gov. Dan McKee, who made housing reform a major focus of his administration, urged voters to support the bill. In September, he was defeated in the primary by Helena Foulkes, who is running against Republican gubernatorial candidate Aaron Guckian.

Guckian expressed opposition to the measure.

"Before we ask taxpayers to borrow another $120 million, plus interest, I think we owe them an accounting of the housing money we're already spending and what we're getting for it," Guckian wrote in an email to the Providence Journal.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5617. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. With the rules shifting and so many misconceptions out there, it's never too early to talk to a professional loan officer for advice on credit, budgeting, and what it would take to qualify for a mortgage.You may be closer to owning a home than you think.

#5616. Florida Voters Approve Landmark Measure To Reform Property Taxes

Florida voters are projected to approve a measure that would reform the state's property tax system, increasing the homestead property tax exemption and reducing the tax bill for some households.

Amendment 3, championed by outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis, aims to increase the homestead property tax exemption from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and to $250,000 in 2028. DeSantis, a Republican, estimated the latter threshold would eliminate property tax for 60% of Florida homeowners.

At 9:45 p.m. ET, with 98% of votes reported, The Associated Press reported the measure had 62% of votes in favor and 38% opposed. The measure, which would go into effect in 2027, needs 60% voter approval to pass.

"Big win on Amendment 3 for Florida homeowners," DeSantis posted on X.

The exemption would apply only to Floridians who established residency prior to December 2026. New residents would need to wait five years before being eligible for the exemptions.

The measure would also lower the annual cap on assessment increases for nonhomestead properties to 5%, down from the current 10%.

Byron Donalds, a GOP representative projected to win the election to replace the term-limited DeSantis, supported the measure. His opponent, Democrat David Jolly, did not. AP projects that Donalds will win the governor's race.

"In a state where homeowners insurance premiums are growing quickly due to climate concerns, which in turn drives HOA dues higher as well, any relief from the annual carrying costs of owning a home in Florida is welcome," says Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner.

Berner notes that the median listing price in Florida fell 3.5% year over year in September and the number of homes for sale fell 9.6% from last year.

"Buyers and sellers are opting out of participation in the market as affordability constraints keep deals from going the distance at prices both parties can agree upon," the economist says.

On Tuesday night, Florida Realtors® President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said the result proved "Florida homeowners chose property tax relief."

"At a time when families are paying more for housing, insurance, groceries and everyday necessities, voters seized the opportunity to keep more of their own hard-earned money, taking a meaningful step toward making Florida a more affordable place to buy, own and keep a home," he said in a statement to Realtor.com.

"Florida Realtors was proud to stand with homeowners in supporting Amendment 3. We have worked with state and local leaders for decades to reduce barriers to homeownership, and we look forward to building on that partnership as Florida puts this relief into place responsibly, without compromising the essential services our communities depend on.”

The MidFlorida Credit Union estimated in 2024 that the average homeowner in the state pays around $2,338 a year in property taxes. In more expensive areas like Miami-Dade County and Palm Beach County, taxes can be significantly higher.

DeSantis argued that the measure would provide much needed financial relief for homeowners. Opponents argued the reduction in property tax revenue would have a deleterious effect on local governments.

Florida does not have an individual income tax or estate taxes, creating a limited pool of money for local governments to fund with. State economists had argued that the measure would wipe out nearly a quarter of all funding for local governments and deprive schools of billions in local revenue, hitting smaller counties especially hard.

In August, a circuit court judge ruled that the bill's original title, "Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes," was "clearly and conclusively defective" and "more akin to a political slogan" than a neutral statement. The judge also dinged the bill for including "factually inaccurate" language and ordered that ballot language be amended prior to the midterm election.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier then changed the name of the proposed amendment to the "Homestead Tax Exemptions, Property Assessments, and Spending Restrictions Amendment" and revised the language that ultimately appeared on the ballot.

A model by the National Association of Realtors® found cutting property taxes by $200 a month lowered the income needed to afford the median-priced Florida home from about $133,800 to $125,200—a move that would put roughly 242,000 additional households above the affordability threshold.

NAR estimates that about 93,500 additional households under 45—including roughly 40,000 younger renters—could afford a starter home.

Florida homeowners might be thinking of more immediate relief, though. The state has some of the highest homeowners association fees in the country. It is also a center of the nation's property insurance crisis.

Florida Realtors' political action committee put $18 million into a "Vote Yes on 3" campaign, according to WPTV, significantly outraising its opponents. In a previously published op-ed to Realtor.com, Bonfiglio denied that the measure necessarily meant cuts to public services.

“Voting yes on Amendment 3 is Step 1, where Floridians decide that homeowners deserve this relief. But we can't forget about Step 2: implementation, where communities will work through how to deliver that relief while keeping public safety and core services first,” he wrote.

Meanwhile, opponents argue that such a measure would increase costs for public services, and that the measure privileges the desires of homeowners over non-homeowning citizens. An analysis published by the Florida Housing Coalition found that an estimated $1.61 billion in property taxes could be shifted to rental homes in 2028, growing to $2.19 billion by 2031.

"There's a small segment of homeowners that will benefit from this," Mike Weinstein, Jacksonville's chief administrative officer and a former state legislator, told NPR. "But the majority of people—renters, business owners, everyone else, and even many homeowners—won't see any benefit from this amendment at all."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5615. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5614. Tennessee Voters Opt To Ban State-Level Property Taxes

Voters in Tennessee are projected to approve Amendment 2, which bans any future statewide property tax and enshrines the prohibition in the state constitution.

Tennessee has not had a statewide property tax since 1949, though the state Legislature technically retained the constitutional authority to create one. Instead, property taxes are levied at the local level.

At 11 p.m. ET on Tuesday, the measure had 66.4% support with 82% of votes reporting, according to The Associated Press. An amendment to the Tennessee Constitution passes if it gets at least 50% support, and the number of “yes” votes is more than half of all votes cast for governor.

"It ensures that the state cannot impose property taxes again, putting taxpayers’ interests first and reinforcing local control," said Republican state Rep. Tandy Darby, who sponsored the amendment.

Amendment 2 would not prevent counties and municipal authorities from levying property taxes, but would prohibit the General Assembly from issuing property taxes now and in the future.

In order to change that, the state constitution would have to be amended once more, which would require a two-thirds vote in two legislative sessions and voter approval.

Republican Gov. Bill Lee came out in support of the initiative. It's supported by the National Federation of Independent Business as well as the Tennessee Realtors®.

Conservative nonprofit Tennessee Stands said the amendment "reinforces the principle that private property rights should never be subject to excessive government taxation or the threat of confiscation."

Some Democrats have opposed it on the grounds that the ban does not need to be written into the constitution and should remain a state statute.

#5612. Autonomous site reliability engineering startup Traversal bags $120M in funding at a $1B valuation

Traversal Inc., a startup that’s trying to automate site reliability engineering tasks with artificial intelligence agents, seems to be closing in on that goal after raising $120 million in fresh funding, bringing its valuation to $1 billion.

The newly minted unicorn’s round was led by Kleiner Perkins, Redpoint Ventures and Khosla Ventures, three of Silicon Valley’s highest-profile venture capital firms, whose names should give it the credibility it needs to accelerate its growth plans. Sequoia Capital – another big VC name – also participated in the round, alongside Battery Ventures and Amex Ventures.

AI might have made the job of software developers much easier than it used to be, but for the site reliability engineers tasked with maintaining the infrastructure to run that code, it has only made life much more difficult. The influx of AI-generated code has put infrastructure engineers under intense pressure, and they’re struggling to keep up.

According to a report earlier this year by Splunk Inc. and Oxford Economics, enterprise downtime costs have risen more than 50% in the last two years, draining up to $600 billion annually from businesses worldwide. That’s because software developers have increased their code output by around 180% over the same timeframe, which means those poor infrastructure engineers are forced to work harder than ever to match their growing output.

Enter Traversal, which is coming to the rescue with a highly promising autonomous site reliability engineer that’s designed to assist human specialists by diagnosing, remediating and preventing information technology infrastructure problems. Instead of just keeping watch and firing off alerts to human engineers when an outage occurs, Traversal actively investigates any issues that pop up and does its best to fix them so as to ease their ungodly workload.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Anish Agarwal said there’s an urgent need for a specialized AI site reliability engineer, because not even the best general-purpose large language models have been able to show they’re up to the task. He points to the ORCA-bench benchmark that his company co-developed alongside researchers from Cornell Tech and Columbia University. It reveals that even the most advanced frontier models barely achieve 25% accuracy on medium-difficulty SRE tasks, with their hallucination rates often exceeding 40%.

“Site reliability engineering is one of the hardest problems in applied AI because every company’s software environment is different, and with downtime costing companies as much as $600 billion a year, the stakes are clearly enormous,” Agarwal said.

Traversal’s AI far surpasses what the best frontier models can do. It’s designed to be deployed in enterprises’ IT environments, where it sits and analyzes massive volumes of operational telemetry, including logs, metrics and traces, so as to establish a baseline for normal behavior. When problems occur, it uses causal machine learning to identify the root cause of the issue, and then works out a solution so all the human engineer has to do is accept its recommendation to restore normal service.

Agarwal’s background in causal machine learning is the key to Traversal’s AI SRE’s much higher accuracy. It’s an AI discipline that combines causal inference with machine learning to identify cause-and-effect relationships, rather than relying on statistical correlations. In essence, it enables Traversal’s models to simulate the effects of various actions, interventions and policy changes have on IT infrastructure, so it can quickly work out what the likely cause of a problem is.

Agarwal said the company is striving to build a “superintelligent AI SRE” that can finally help enterprises to keep pace with the rapid velocity of their AI-enabled developer teams. And he believes it’s well on the way to achieving that goal. “After two years refining our technology, we’re seeing customers expand how they use Traversal across increasingly complex production environments,” he said.

In the last year, Traversal has grown its revenue more than nine-fold and its number of monthly active users has multiplied by 20. Some of its best-known customers include Pepsi Co., DigitalOcean Holdings Inc., Nubank and Harvey AI Corp.

Traversal’s momentum is impressive, but Agarwal said the company is only just getting started. With $120 million in the bank, it’s going to accelerate hiring within its engineering, go-to-market and research and development teams so it can get closer to its goal of building a superintelligent AI SRE.

Kleiner Perkins’ Aditya Naganath said Traversal is the first company he has seen that brings “real intelligence” into complex production environments, and he’s confident there’s going to be enormous demand for it. “As AI dramatically accelerates the pace at which software is written and shipped, the complexity of managing production will only grow,” he predicted. “Traversal gives engineering teams the intelligence they need to understand their systems, resolve incidents faster and operate with confidence at scales that simply weren’t possible before.”

#5611. Democrats Regain House and Senate in Midterms Defined by Affordability Concerns

Democrats rode affordability concerns to major wins on Tuesday night, retaking control of the House and Senate and flipping multiple districts.

Democrats flipped Senate seats in Texas, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina, and South Carolina and picked up a swath of seats in the House to win both chambers of Congress, according to The Associated Press projections. They've spent the year hammering Republicans on affordability and housing costs.

In the 2026 elections, voters decided all 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats, and numerous housing-related measures. Both Democrats and Republicans have listed priorities to improve housing affordability in coming years.

"Tonight’s Democratic sweep shuffles control of the legislative branch, but the economic impact, which is fundamental for the U.S. housing market, is far less clear," says Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel. "Democrats have a clear mandate to focus on pocketbook issues, but whether they can translate that into a legislative agenda that delivers on that mandate remains to be seen."

Housing issues have been a dominant note in 2026, as Americans struggle with affordability. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hit its highest level in three years last month before dipping back to 7.24% last week, according to Fannie Mae. The national average gas price is $4.14 a gallon compared to $3.03 a year ago, according to AAA. President Donald Trump has pledged to focus on affordability issues.

"President Trump has been laser-focused on making housing more affordable," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Realtor.com in a statement on Tuesday morning.

Ingle noted that Trump in his second term had signed an executive order prohibiting large Wall Street firms from purchasing single-family homes, directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to purchase $200 billion in mortgage bonds that helped drive rates to four-year lows, and "cut unnecessary red tape at a historic pace to boost supply, speed construction, and lower costs."

"The President will not stop fighting until the American Dream of homeownership is within reach for every American, which is why he continues to sign bold new executive orders and calls on Congress to pass further legislation," he said.

Congress passed a bipartisan housing package aimed at making it easier to build homes, the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, this summer. But it will take years for some of those changes to take effect in the market. And lawmakers expect states and local governments to implement some changes.

The Trump administration, meantime, has undertaken other changes such as encouraging more innovation in the homebuilding sector and reducing rules for some housing, like manufactured homes. It's also sought to limit the impact of institutional investors in the housing market.

"I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump posted on X late Tuesday, as major news outlets projected Democrats would take control of the House after flipping a half-dozen seats. Trump later told The New York Times he would accept the results of the election.

The economist Krimmel says that one "wild card" to keep an eye on is how the election outcome affects Trump's war with Iran.

"Many Democrats have been vocal critics of the conflict, which has sparked inflationary oil supply shortages," he says. "A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates. However, a lot of uncertainty remains. Wanting the conflict to end and finding terms that work for all involved are two different things."

Democrats marked the evening with several key wins in both the House and the Senate.

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews flipped the Senate seat formerly held by Republican Lindsey Graham. Andrews beat Graham's sister, Darlene Graham, who had been picked by Trump.

And Democrat James Talarico flipped a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat in almost a century to be elected to the Senate.

Democrats had several early victories. Democratic former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper flipped the state's Senate seat, replacing Republican Thom Tillis, who chairs the Senate's Financial Institutions and Consumer Protection Subcommittee. Democrat Jamie Ager also flipped a North Carolina House district.

"We knew that the chaos and corruption in Washington were hurting our people," Cooper said in a speech. "Today, you said, 'This has to stop.'"

Pennsylvania saw three formerly Republican seats picked up by Democrats Janelle Stelson, Paige Cognetti, and Bob Brooks. They ousted incumbents Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan Jr., and Scott Perry.

In New Jersey, Tom Kean Jr. lost reelection after an extended absence fueled national headlines. Meanwhile, in Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown returned to Congress after campaigning heavily against incumbent Jon Husted, attacking the Republication over his prior support of data centers.

"Politics should never, ever be about two private clubs who are more interested in beating up each other than they are in solving problems," said Josh Turek, who flipped a Senate seat in Iowa for Democrats.

On Truth Social, Trump posted a photo of a red hat with the word "veto." He has repeatedly criticized Democrats this year saying their policies drive up housing and other costs.

Trump told Fox News late on Tuesday night that he would not shy away from using presidential vetoes to block "crazy" measures advanced by Democrats in Congress.

"I have the power of veto, and the power of veto, you know, it's impervious," the president said.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, who won reelection in Louisiana, defended Republicans' economic actions in remarks before midnight. He said Americans would "suffer" if Democrats use control of Congress to enact "retribution" over the next two years.

"From the first day of this election we knew that to keep the House and sustain the majority, we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history," Johnson said. "It's very, very difficult to overcome."

But Johnson said an agenda of "common sense" would lead Republicans to take back the House in 2028.

"Republicans have much more work to do," he said. "The new Congress doesn't change that at all."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5610. Inside Legacy Hills’ Strategy for Reaching a Broad Range of Buyers

Developed by Centurion American, the Legacy Hills master-planned community (MPC) spans over 3,000 acres in Celina, Texas, and is planned for up to 7,000 homes at full buildout. The community opened in April 2024 and includes a diverse mix of builders, lot sizes, and floor plans. Pricing generally ranges from the $300,000s into the mid-$500,000s.

Importantly, Legacy Hills is not relying on a single buyer profile. Its product strategy creates multiple entry points into the community, with housing choices that can appeal to buyers at different price points and stages of life.

That product diversity is paired with a layered amenity program. Plans call for seven amenity centers throughout Legacy Hills, along with a 27-acre sports park and a 3-mile walking and biking trail. The planned 1876 Country Club adds a destination component with an 18-hole championship golf course, clubhouse, driving range, putting green, and short game facilities.

For families moving to Legacy Hills, children in the broader community attend Celina ISD, while future school sites are planned within the development. The community also broadens its reach further through Del Webb’s dedicated 55+ neighborhood, which adds to Legacy Hills’ family-oriented offerings with age-targeted homes and amenities.

The strategy is unfolding against a strong demographic backdrop. Celina’s population and household base are projected to more than double between 2020 and 2029, expanding the potential pool of buyers around the community.

At the same time, the broader housing environment remains competitive. The Zonda Market Ranking for MPCs characterized Dallas as slightly underperforming per August data, yet Legacy Hills stood out. In the Q2 2026 Master Plan Outlook report, the MPC recorded the largest year-over-year percentage increase in last 12-month sales among qualifying MPCs with at least 200 sales in the previous 12 months.

Legacy Hills illustrates the value of creating several paths into a large-scale community rather than building around a narrow customer profile. Differentiated housing, offerings for multiple life stages, and amenities ranging from everyday recreation to destination experiences give the development multiple ways to appeal to buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from a more in-depth case study in Zonda’s Master Plan Outlook subscription.

Eva Beeth is a data analyst within Zonda's economics department, where she supports housing market analysis through data modeling, forecasting, and market-level insights. She contributes to national and local research reports and analytical initiatives.

#5609. Realtors Predict These Nine Cities Will Be Unaffordable by 2027

Vibrant-Colored neon lights on a busy night at the bars and honky-tonks in the country music center, Broadway, the tourism center of Downtown Nashville, Tennessee

(TNS)–Home prices are climbing across the nation and some markets are hotter than others. According to a new report from Finance Buzz, nine U.S. cities are likely to become unaffordable by 2027, due to an influx of out-of-town buyers and tight inventory.

Here’s a look at the popular locales where housing costs are outpacing local incomes, as per Finance Buzz’s reporting:

Many areas in northern New Jersey are popular for people relocating out of New York City.

According to Daniel Smith, team lead at Smith Realty Team, homes in Montclair are expected to stay in high demand and continue commanding higher home prices.

“Retirees and pre-retirees are also targeting these towns because of their vibrant downtowns, access to health care, and cultural amenities, which makes competition even stronger,” he said.

Nashville attracted numerous new residents during the pandemic years, offering a lively city experience alongside lower taxes and a more affordable cost of living.

While home prices have come down slightly over the past year, the median sale price is currently $464,983 and real estate experts don’t expect a reduction any time soon.

Realtor Carla Gericke, with Porcupine Real Estate, said that “no income tax, easy access to Boston, and that elusive small-town feel with real community bones” is causing Nashua’s popularity to spike.

“Nashua’s median home price has soared to the $500,000 to $550,000 range, and demand keeps outpacing supply,” she said.

Gericke urged retirees looking to buy in the state to act quickly or venture outside the bigger cities to find better deals.

Arizona has long been a top destination for retirees hoping to escape the cold. Fred Loguidice, a real estate expert and founder of several home-buying companies in the area, said that home demand is outpacing supply, making it a market that is likely to stay competitive in the future.

“In markets like Phoenix, fewer homes are being built while demand persists, so prices consistently escalate,” he said.

Real estate expert Fred Loguidice also highlighted demand for Northeast hubs like the Buffalo metro area. While Zillow put the median home price at a moderate $261,300, home values in the area have been increasing.

“That momentum is a hard habit to break,” he said, noting its affordability and surging job opportunities make it a top choice for relocation for people in the region and beyond.

Athens is about 60 miles northeast of Atlanta and attracts many buyers and visitors alike with its lively college town atmosphere, excellent dining scene, and more.

While Georgia is often cited as a top spot to retire, thanks to the weather and lower cost of living, real estate trends indicate that home prices will continue to climb throughout the next year or so. Prices have gone up over the past year, with the median currently sitting at $353,333.

Florida boasts many affordable cities and tax incentives for retirees, but those considering Tampa may want to reassess.

Omer Reiner, realtor and president of Florida Cash Home Buyers, said home prices in the city are already high, and rising insurance costs are putting many popular areas out of reach.

“This is especially true for those nearing or at retirement, as higher costs of living when you are on any type of fixed income means you are spending more for less,” he said.

Iowa isn’t particularly known for its excessive home prices, but demand has been on the rise in Des Moines, according to real estate investor Jacob Naig, particularly for homes popular with retirees.

“Single-family homes, as well as small multi-family properties and single-level ranch-style homes that are particularly desirable to aging buyers, have seen a substantial rise in demand,” he said.

Many cities in the Pacific Northwest have seen rapidly rising home prices, and Ontario, which sits on the border of Oregon and Idaho, is no different. With stunning desert views, mountain ranges, and more, it’s a haven for outdoorsy types.

But recent real estate trends indicated it could be unaffordable in the coming years. Average home prices have risen steadily over the past year and currently sit at $307,769.

#5608. 8 Resilience Moves Builders Can Make Before Extreme Weather Hits

When extreme weather hits, small construction details can make a big difference in how well a home performs.

According to Fred Malik of the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS), research continually points to roofs, openings, and structural connections as potential failure points. Damage in these areas can allow wind and water into a home and trigger larger, cascading losses.

For builders, stronger construction can also help reduce disruption for homeowners, limit warranty-related costs, and protect a company’s reputation for delivering durable homes.

“Resilient, durable buildings are usually the result of making several intentional decisions,” Malik says.

Here are eight steps builders can take to improve resilience ahead of severe weather:

Rather than approaching roofing as a collection of individual products, Malik recommends treating the entire roof as one interconnected system. The goal is to keep the roof intact and prevent an initial failure from creating a pathway for additional wind or water damage.

A sealed roof deck creates an additional layer of protection beneath the primary roof covering. If shingles or other roofing materials are damaged or blown off during severe weather, this secondary layer can help limit water intrusion into the home.

Small details can have an outsized impact on performance. Builders should carefully install and inspect flashing at roof edges, roof-to-wall transitions, vents, chimneys, and other penetrations. These areas can become pathways for water if they aren’t properly protected.

Windows, entry doors, and other openings need to withstand both wind pressure and wind-driven rain. Following manufacturer installation instructions and properly installing flashing are critical to maintaining the home’s building envelope.

Garage doors represent a large opening in the building envelope and need to withstand pressures generated by high winds. Malik notes that this is important even in inland markets, where tornadoes can cause significant structural damage.

In areas exposed to more severe winds, builders should consider a professionally designed continuous load path connecting the roof to the walls and ultimately the foundation. Strong connections throughout the structure help transfer wind forces safely through the building instead of allowing individual components to fail.

In flood-prone areas, elevate or otherwise protect mechanical, electrical, and utility equipment. Keeping critical systems above anticipated flood levels can reduce damage and make it easier for homeowners to return to their homes after an event.

Programs such as IBHS’ FORTIFIED standards provide builders with a framework for putting resilience measures into practice. FORTIFIED goes beyond minimum code requirements with an emphasis on keeping the roof on, keeping water out, and tying the structure together.

The program also requires third-party documentation of critical resilience measures, including construction details that may no longer be visible once finishes and other materials are installed.

Overall, resilience isn’t dependent on a single product or construction technique. It’s the cumulative result of getting multiple details right, Malik says.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.
