#5587. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5586. Gina Hinojosa Ousts Greg Abbott in Texas Governor’s Race—What Her Win Means for Housing

Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa made history Tuesday night, becoming the first Latina elected as governor of Texas and the first Democrat to win the office in 36 years.

Her victory was a major upset that denied Republican Greg Abbott a record-setting fourth term—and could signal a change in direction for the state's housing policies.

Hinojosa campaigned on making homeownership more attainable by restricting corporate investors, cutting residential property taxes, and cracking down on predatory rental practices.

The proposals put her on a different path from Abbott, who emphasized removing barriers to home construction and expanding the state's existing property tax relief. The Lone Star state is already the nation's largest homebuilder, accounting for 14.6% of all building permits issued, and received an A- on its Affordability Report Card from Realtor.com® in June.

Speaking to supporters in Austin, Hinojosa framed her victory as a rebuke of wealthy corporate interests and their influence over state government.

“Tonight, Texas, we answered—and we didn’t whisper," she said. "We answered loud enough for every billionaire, every lobbyist, and every corrupt politician in Austin to hear: Texas belongs to us."

One of Hinojosa's central housing promises is to curb corporate investors' purchases of single-family homes, which she argues have made it harder for ordinary Texans to compete for homeownership.

It's an issue she's been advocating for since her time in the state House. In 2025, Hinojosa introduced House Bill 2910, which would have prohibited covered corporate owners from holding more than 10 single-family rental properties in Texas.

Another proposal, House Bill 2334, would have prevented investment firms from entering contracts to purchase newly listed single-family homes during their first 30 days on the market.

Neither bill became law, but the state could be particularly fertile ground for the proposals.

"Texas is where this type of policy would bite hardest, though I'd still expect a modest effect on affordability," says Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com.

Megainvestors accounted for 1.9% of all home purchases in Texas during the first half of 2026, the highest share of any state and roughly three times the national rate of 0.6%, according to Jones' research.

And in some markets, corporate buyers are even more concentrated. Investors accounted for 15.9% of home purchases in San Antonio, 15.6% in Dallas-Fort Worth, 13.5% in Houston, and 12.4% in Austin, according to research from Realtor.com.

In three of those four markets, investors purchased homes at prices substantially below the overall median, suggesting that competition remains concentrated in the more affordable segments of the housing market.

A federal law enacted in July will prohibit institutional investors controlling 350 or more single-family homes from purchasing additional properties beginning in January 2027, subject to certain exceptions—but "Hinojosa’s cap goes further than the federal law," according to Jones.

Still, she cautions that limiting corporate purchases would address only a fraction of the forces keeping homeownership out of reach.

"The effect on homeownership is limited because the policy only touches that segment, which is a small slice of total purchases," she explains, noting that housing supply, mortgage rates, insurance, and property taxes remain bigger drivers of affordability.

"Build-to-rent is the key question," Jones says, referring to developments constructed specifically as rental housing. The federal law exempts qualifying build-to-rent projects, but Hinojosa's proposal did not explicitly offer the same protection.

"Limiting investor [single-family rental] supply would more likely push rents up than down, which works against the affordability goal."

Hinojosa has also promised to address rental practices, including landlords' use of algorithmic pricing software and rent increases imposed during the application process.

Texas has been one of the nation's most welcoming markets for data centers, attracting tech giants with cheap land, abundant energy and generous tax incentives. The state accounts for an estimated quarter of U.S. data center capacity planned by 2030, according to Reuters.

But growing opposition over electricity costs, water consumption, and other neighborhood impacts has begun changing that equation. About 61% of National Association of Realtor members said their clients were concerned that data centers would raise energy costs, and 56% reported concerns about water usage, according to survey data released in September.

It was enough to make Abbott—once an enthusiastic supporter of the industry—halt new data center permits in September, pending an environmental and energy audit.

Now, Hinojosa has promised to go further, calling for a legislatively backed moratorium, greater local control over development, and protections against data center-driven utility increases.

Her victory heightened concerns that Texas could become a more difficult place to build. Shares of Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX fell Wednesday as investors weighed the prospect of tighter restrictions.

Hinojosa and Abbott both campaigned on cutting homeowners' property taxes, but differed over how to pay for that relief.

In 2025, Texas raised its school district homestead exemption from $100,000 to $140,000, saving homeowners hundreds of dollars annually—a measure that Hinojosa voted in favor of.

Now, she wants to go further by eliminating corporate subsidies and using the savings to reduce residential property taxes, with the eventual goal of eliminating them altogether.

Abbott, meanwhile, proposed eliminating school district property taxes on owner-occupied homes, using state surpluses to replace the lost revenue.

The proposals also reflect differences over public education. Abbott championed a $1 billion private-school voucher program in 2025, while also signing an $8.5 billion public school funding package. Hinojosa opposed the vouchers and has pledged to repeal the program while increasing support for public schools and teachers.

But her tax plan faces a substantial funding question: Replacing homeowners' school maintenance-and-operations property taxes alone would cost an estimated $8.6 billion annually. Hinojosa has yet to detail how eliminating corporate subsidies would cover that cost without reducing school funding.

Hinojosa will take office in January 2027, but many of her proposed housing reforms would require the approval of state lawmakers.

And while Tuesday's elections changed the political landscape in Austin, it didn't guarantee Hinojosa a friendly Legislature. Democrat Vikki Goodwin unseated Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, giving Democrats leadership of the state Senate. Republicans, however, are expected to retain their majority in that chamber.

Meanwhile, control of the Texas House remained undecided Wednesday morning. Democrats needed to flip 14 seats to take control for the first time since 2003, and were gaining ground in several Republican-held districts.

But even if Democrats capture the House, Hinojosa would still need Republican support in the Senate to advance her housing agenda.

The newly elected governor seemed undaunted Tuesday night, closing her victory speech by invoking her grandmother's advice: "No te dejes," she said, which loosely translates to "don't let yourself get pushed around."

Hinojosa's campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Realtor.com.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5585. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5584. A 1970s Hollywood Hills Home Was Reimagined With a ‘Floating’ Canyon Pool and Midcentury Soul

A sleek Nichols Canyon estate in Los Angeles, perched above the treetops, has recently hit the market for $4,994,000.

Built in 1978, the four-bedroom home has been entirely reimagined by an acclaimed design studio and now offers a timeless 2,798-square-foot floor plan.

“Ome Dezin acquired the property in 2025 with a clear vision to reimagine and resell it, completing the renovation in October 2026,” says listing agent Claire O’Connor of Compass. “What made this home compelling was its inherent architectural character.

"Rather than strip away its identity, they saw an opportunity to build upon it, creating something that feels distinctly contemporary while remaining rooted in its 1970s origins.”

Set on nearly half an acre, the hillside retreat has wood ceilings, exposed beams, marble, wood, and terrazzo floors, built-ins, and three fireplaces.

“Entertaining feels intrinsic to the architecture rather than an afterthought,” O’Connor said. “The interiors unfold naturally toward the outdoor spaces, culminating in a dramatic infinity pool suspended above the canyon. There’s an intimacy to the scale that makes it equally suited to a quiet evening or a gathering of friends. It’s a home that encourages connection without feeling performative.”

An expansive deck overlooks the infinity-edge pool, which is cantilevered over the hillside to create the illusion of floating above the canyon.

“I see this appealing to a buyer who values provenance and individuality over square footage,” she noted. “There’s a growing sophistication among luxury buyers in Los Angeles, with an increasing appreciation for homes that feel curated rather than manufactured. This is someone who recognizes that true luxury isn’t necessarily about having more, but about finding something that can’t easily be replicated.”

O’Connor notes that the home’s location in Nichols Canyon is “a particularly interesting position in Los Angeles."

"It offers an almost pastoral sense of seclusion within minutes of Hollywood and the Sunset Strip," she says.

"The winding roads, mature landscape, and dramatic topography create a sense of discovery that’s increasingly rare in the city. It’s that tension between urban proximity and natural isolation that makes it so desirable."

#5583. Midterm Takeaways: Democratic Subpoenas, State ‘Trifectas’ and Bi-Coastal Ballot Wins

A midterm election that saw both historic turnout and spending ended with big wins for the Democratic party nearly across the board. While voters clearly went to the ballot box seeking change, can real estate expect the landslide result to boost a sluggish housing market, bring down rates or spark more regulatory scrutiny into housing practices?

At this very early stage, the answer to most of these questions is, unsurprisingly, a big maybe.

While the mainstream focus is always on Congressional elections (where Democrats made historic gains), impactful federal legislation for real estate appears unlikely. President Donald Trump promised to leverage his veto powers if Democrats won, previewing even more gridlock in Washington, but also told the Wall Street Journal on election night that he would work with Democrats.

Realtor.com® Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said in a statement that relief for the housing market at large “relies on a calmer geopolitical environment,” saying that it was unclear whether Democratic control of Congress could deliver this.

Real estate professionals understand well, though, housing is a local issue, and the results most likely to be impactful for practitioners are coming in lower-profile state elections. At the same time, though, a strongly Democratic congress in D.C. offers potential new wrinkles to high-profile real estate controversies and investigations.

As the dust settles on ballot initiatives, and new lawmakers set agendas for 2027, here are the biggest takeaways from the midterms:

Florida and California voters back major housing changes

Two of the most populous states in the country—which also have faced some of the most acute issues with housing supply and affordability in the past few years—overwhelmingly approved two unique initiatives that proponents say will offer some immediate benefits to buyers and homeowners.

In California, Proposition 37 was on track to be approved by around two-thirds of voters. The initiative, designed to simultaneously address the state’s long-running housing affordability and supply issues, creates a special “secondary mortgage” loan for down payments, and hopes to incentivize the construction of around 200,000 new homes at (relatively) attainable price points.

Speaking to RISMedia before the election, housing experts were cautiously optimistic the initiative could move the needle in the medium-term, though critics note the extra down payment loan means higher monthly costs for borrowers.

In a statement after the election, one of the initiative’s architects, Bob Hertzberg, thanked the California Association of Realtors®, among other supporters, for “a decisive first step to create generational homeownership opportunities in California.”

Simultaneously in the Sunshine State, voters strongly backed Amendment 3, which creates new tax relief for many property owners. The initiative makes several changes to how taxes are calculated, aiming to lower—or even eliminate—property tax bills for many homeowners.

The change has sparked some controversy, with concerns that it would deprive local governments of significant revenue. Supporters say it provides vital relief for homeowners struggling with rising homeownership costs, and opens up homeownership to more buyers (though notably, only people who establish state residency before December 2026 will be eligible for the exemption).

Both the Florida and California initiatives were supported by state Realtor® associations.

The result of another housing-focused ballot initiative in Massachusetts that would reduce minimum lot sizes for single-family homes was too close to call at press time Wednesday morning (Realtor® associations have supported that initiative as well).

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has demanded investigations into real estate practices—focused on Compass’s acquisitions, and role in building off-MLS “private” inventory.

With Democrats taking control of the Senate, Warren is now the highest-ranking member on the powerful Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee, which wields the power to issue subpoenas and hold high-profile hearings.

Whether Democratic control of Congress results in any new pressure on Compass or its policies remains to be seen. But back in February, Warren signed a letter with 17 other Democratic lawmakers that called the process by which Compass received approval for its acquisition of Anywhere “corruption,” citing media reports that the brokerage had bypassed antitrust concerns with back-channel lobbying.

Another signatory to that letter, Democratic Senator Ron Wyden, simply posted the word “Subpoenas” on social media as election results poured in last night. Wyden is currently the ranking member on the Senate Finance Committee.

Two Democrats (and one Republican) in the house also penned letters to the FTC this year focusing on “lead diversion” practices used by portals like Zillow, which they called deceptive. Lawmakers largely framed these practices as harming consumers amid larger affordability struggles.

With a significant focus on housing, it appears possible that Democratic oversight could very well shift more scrutiny onto real estate, even though enforcement power largely still rests with the executive branch.

State houses flip amid focus on ‘private’ listings, affordability

At least six state governments (Nevada, Wisconsin, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Minnesota) appear on track to flip to a Democrat “trifecta” this year—meaning the party controls both the lower and upper legislative chambers, and the governor’s office. Other states saw significant Democratic gains, rebalancing legislative power that (often) has more of an impact on real estate issues.

Notably, a handful of (mostly) Democratic states passed laws over the last year or so restricting “private” marketing, though at least some of those bills had bipartisan support.

A trifecta, at least on paper, allows more legislation overall to move through state governments, and can result in previous shelved legislation getting another shot at becoming law. Governors also have significant executive power to regulate issues that impact housing in those states.

Among the many regulatory and legislative issues previously or currently being considered in these now-Democrat controlled states are rent control (Nevada), denser housing in suburbs (Arizona), state-wide accessory dwelling units (Pennsylvania), zoning reform for starter homes (Minnesota) and property tax cuts or refunds (Michigan and Wisconsin).

None of these issues are guaranteed to remain in the spotlight once lawmakers are seated and legislative sessions ramp up, but real estate advocates have pointed out that housing issues remain top-of-mind for many voters, who will likely expect substantive action and reforms in places where Democrats are newly empowered.

Jesse Williams is content director for RISMedia Premier.

#5582. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.

#5581. Oumi’s Frontier AI Engineer now builds AI agents and retrains the models behind them

Enterprise artificial intelligence platform company Oumi PBC today extended its Frontier AI Engineer agent so it can build AI agents for customers and retrain the models those agents run on.

The release goes after a problem that tends to surface once agents leave the demo stage. A failing agent might have a bad prompt, a broken tool or a weak underlying model.

Oumi says enterprises have traditionally tried to fix it with prompt and harness engineering because retraining a model’s weights has required skills normally found at frontier AI labs. That approach often stalls before the agent is reliable enough to put to work.

Oumi’s Frontier AI Engineer already sets objectives, designs evaluations and runs training experiments for custom models on its platform. With today’s update, a team can describe in plain language what it wants an agent to accomplish, and FAiE helps define the tools and environments that agent needs before moving on to evaluation and training. Whatever goes wrong once the agent is in production is turned into evaluation sets and training data for the next round.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Manos Koukoumidis said better prompts and bigger generic models will only take agents so far. The ones that succeed will improve “by training the weights of the models powering them, learning from their own work,” he said, pointing to failed tasks and user preferences as the signals that count.

Companies that already run agents elsewhere can keep them there. Under a feature Oumi calls Bring Your Own Harness, the customer’s orchestration, tools and memory stay put and connect to Oumi for evaluation and model training. Models end up tuned in the same environment the agent works in every day.

Oumi is also adding direct preference optimization to the supervised fine-tuning it already supported, so a model can be trained on examples of the behavior users preferred. Reinforcement learning arrives through group relative policy optimization, which grades a model on task outcomes. Several methods can be chained together in a single multistage training run, and FAiE helps choose the strategy, set up rewards and diagnose problems along the way.

The training work feeds Oumi’s broader argument about model ownership. Most enterprise agents run on general-purpose models from frontier AI providers that aren’t optimized for a particular customer’s work. The company’s pitch since launching a commercial platform for custom models in March has been that a specialized model the customer owns outright can do better work at lower cost.

Group relative policy optimization is launching in private preview, and the Seattle company is taking requests for access. Oumi is a venture capital-backed startup that raised a $10 million seed round led by Venrock Management and Obvious Management Services in January 2025. The founding team includes former engineering leaders from Google LLC’s Gemini group.

#5580. DC Mayor-Elect Janeese Lewis George Promises 72,000 New Housing Units

Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George has been elected the first new mayor of Washington, DC, in 12 years after breezing past a crowded field to cap off a campaign focused on affordability.

The Associated Press called the election for Lewis George before 7 p.m. on Tuesday, reflecting her commanding lead over Rhonda Hamilton, a community advocate running as an independent; Robert L. Gross, representing the D.C. Statehood Green Party, and 11 write-in candidates. That race did not include a Republican contender.

The win potentially places Lewis George, a 38-year-old D.C. Council member, on a collision course with President Donald Trump, who previously labeled her a "communist" and suggested that she was a threat to the safety and prosperity of the nation's capital.

"The people of D.C. elect the mayor of D.C., and I am willing to work with this administration to the benefit of D.C. residents," Lewis George told FOX 5 DC after her victory. "And I'm also willing to stand up to this administration when it comes to doing just that."

Lewis George will replace outgoing Democratic Mayor Muriel Bowser, who decided last year not to seek re-election for a fourth term.

"Congratulations to Mayor-Elect Janeese Lewis George," Bowser wrote on X Wednesday morning. "I’ll run through the tape and support a seamless transition. I love you, DC."

When she is sworn in on Jan. 2, Lewis George will become D.C.'s first democratic socialist mayor, joining the ranks of New York City's Zohran Mamdani, Seattle's Katie Wilson, and Mayor-elect David Morales, of Providence, RI.

The cornerstone of Lewis George’s platform is her "Homes for All" plan, which includes provisions for rent stabilization, a coordinated affordable housing development system, stricter code enforcement, and expanded down-payment assistance.

Her long-term goal is to add 72,000 new housing units throughout D.C. within five years.

Additional housing-related planks in the mayor-elect's platform include amending the city’s zoning restrictions to add more homes and mixed-income housing, especially closer to transit lines.

"Increasing supply, paired with policies to protect residents, really is critical to stopping further displacement and making housing more affordable for all," she wrote in an op-ed.

The latest American Community Survey numbers from the U.S. Census Bureau reflect the urgent need for change. Buyers in D.C. have to contend with a 25% gap between earned income and the minimum required income to afford a home.

On the broader affordability front, Lewis-George campaigned on lowering utility bills for the district's 700,000 residents and pushing through universal affordable child care.

Lewis George easily won the Democratic primary in June, but President Trump does not count himself among her supporters.

Trump said after her victory that he "wouldn’t like" having Lewis George as mayor and threatened to carry out a federal takeover of D.C. if she won.

"Maybe we’ll take back Washington, run it on a federal basis," he said. "We won’t put up with it. We’re not going to lose our businesses."

Lewis George responded at the time that threatening the revocation of the city's home rule "because you do not like how residents vote is an attack on democracy itself."

However, now that the Democrats reclaimed control of the House and Senate, D.C. is expected to be shielded from Trump's potential efforts to encourch on its autonomy, since it is the Congress, not the president, that has legislative power over the district, according to the Associated Press.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5579. Mortgage Rates Dip as AI Jitters Boost Bonds Ahead of Fed Decision, GDP Data

In A Nutshell: Rates have mellowed a bit coming into a big week with a Fed meeting and the first read of Q3 GDP data.

Last Week’s Highlights: Oil prices continued to increase last week, but rates came down, as doubts about the AI narrative battered stocks, sending money into the bond market. On the housing front, the increase in mortgage rates has sent builder confidence down to its lowest level in 14 years. Permits for single-family homes also fell to a multiyear low.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest event of the week is the Fed decision and press conference Wednesday afternoon. The committee is not scheduled to update its forecast (the “dot plot”) this time. Markets believe the Fed will hold and then hike on December 9th for an every-other-meeting hike cadence, so the attention will be on clues for the next meeting rather than the outcome of this one. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will hold a press conference but is likely to stick to his usual practice of not foreshadowing upcoming decisions. Fed watchers may get more color out of SF Fed President Daly and St. Louis Fed President Musalem’s remarks on Friday.

Apart from the Fed, there are also a couple of important data releases this week. The first look at Q3 GDP is coming on Thursday morning. Part of the thesis for rates increasing so much these last few months is a belief that the economy is growing faster. At one point, estimates had Q3 GDP growing as fast as a 5% annual rate. Forecasters are expecting this advance estimate to land around 3.2%, which would be a meaningful pick-up from 2.2% in Q2. And finally, the September durable goods report will be released on Tuesday with forecasters expecting a solid reading of 2.0% month-over-month growth. This report tracks new orders, shipments, and inventories of long-lasting manufactured products, which is a signal of how confident businesses and consumers are about the future.

#5578. Inside Joe Rogan’s Incredible $14.4 Million Austin Mansion—and Home to His Very Controversial Podcast

Podcaster Joe Rogan has once again found himself at the center of controversy after he was confronted about his past political views.

Rogan, 59, was on the receiving end of scrutiny when comedian Sam Tallent called Rogan out for voting for President Donald Trump in the 2024 election.

"Dude it's weird, cuz like, I talk to people a lot who I don't share like, the exact ideals with, like, I don't like that you f—n' endorsed Trump, but like, I have a lot of friends who voted for Trump," Tallent said.

Tallent added, "No, it's fine. Listen, it used to be that people used to be able to differ in their opinions and have conversations. But today we have become so divided, and I think a big factor is social media, echo chambers, propaganda, bots, gaslighting. And it seems like there's so much riding on everything constantly, because you're looking at your phone all the time.

"And everything on the phone is, 'This is the end. This is the end, this is the beginning of the end, this is a signal of the end, the only hope is to stop this,' and on both sides. People are addicted to their phones, so like, the information you're getting almost all day long is very bleak and very dire."

Rogan's podcast has long been known as a hotspot for the internet personality to share his outspoken opinions on everything from from celebrity gossip to political policy.

"The Joe Rogan Experience," which he records largely at his $14.4 million home in Austin, TX, is widely regarded as one of the most successful podcasts in the world, but it seems listeners on Apple have a different opinion.

Rogan, who drew a gargantuan audience with his three-hour-long interview with Trump during his campaign for president, has seen his podcast tumble down the Apple rankings of most popular shows—falling to third place, behind the New York Times' "The Daily" and a true-crime hit called "Crime Junkie."

The news came shortly before Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko accused the podcaster of "pushing Russian propaganda on his podcast," amid the war in Ukraine. Klitschko slammed Rogan's comments about President Joe Biden's decision to provide U.S.-made missiles to Ukrainian forces.

In a previous episode with music producer Scott Storch, the two discussed their relief that Trump had won the election, and then criticized the Biden administration for providing Ukraine with long-range missiles for use in its war with Russia.

“I feel safer knowing that Trump is in office,” Storch told Rogan.

“What I don’t feel safer about is that now they’re launching missiles into Russia,” Rogan replied. “How are you allowed to do that when you’re on the way out? [There] should be, like, some sort of, like, a pause for, like, significant actions that could potentially start World War III.

“Yeah, [Vladimir] Putin should not have invaded Ukraine, yes, 100%, but don’t start World War III,” Rogan added.

In a video response, Klitschko addressed Rogan directly: “You talk about these American weapons being sent to Ukraine, which you believe will lead to the third World War.

“So, let me tell you that you’re repeating Russian propaganda. Putin’s Russia is in trouble, so they want to scare you and people like you.”

He added, “Putin’s Russia wants to destroy Ukraine quietly, they want America to stay quiet. Not great, but quiet. A great America is not an America that abandons countries that defend freedom with their lives.”

Klitschko offered to come on Rogan's podcast so they could further discuss the topic as "free men."

Rogan is no stranger to provoking outrage and controversy with his comments, and his show retains the top spot in Spotify's rankings. However, his lackluster showing in the Apple charts will no doubt come as something of a surprise to the podcaster.

Indeed, Rogan's show has proven so popular that even Vice President Kamala Harris reportedly considered an appearance on "The Joe Rogan Experience." She ultimately opted for the more female-focused "Call Her Daddy" with host Alexandra Cooper.

Still, the podcaster has managed to lure dozens of A-list celebrities to his new $14.4 million home on Lake Austin in Texas, where he moved to from California in 2020, and where he has built a custom studio to record his show.

Rogan, a former comedian, previously provided UFC color commentary before launching his podcast in 2009. By 2015, he was one of the most popular podcasters.

Rogan interviewed everyone from Edward Snowden to Neil deGrasse Tyson, J.D. Vance, and Bernie Sanders. (After Sanders appeared on his show in 2020, Rogan endorsed the Democratic Party candidate in the 2020 presidential race.)

In 2020, Rogan moved from Southern California to Austin after reportedly agreeing to an estimated $100 million deal to broadcast exclusively with Spotify.

In February 2024, Rogan reportedly signed a new $250 million agreement with Spotify that allowed him to broadcast on other platforms, including YouTube and Apple.

That same year, Rogan opened up about his decision to relocate to Texas, explaining that California's strict COVID-19 restrictions were partly to blame.

"Everything’s shut down, everything’s staying shut down," he recalled of the pandemic in California. "All my friends that were in the restaurant industry were struggling.

"I started looking out here in May [of that year], and I went to a restaurant with my kids, and they were like, 'We don’t have to wear a mask? We could eat at a restaurant?' Then we went to the lake, and people are playing music and jumping in the water, and [my children] were like, 'We want to live here!

"That was it. Two months later I lived here."

In 2022, he explained that he believed he would find "more freedom" in Texas than he was able to enjoy on the West Coast.

Since his Texas move, he seems to be recording shows in a studio built inside his sleek mansion, which sits right on Lake Austin.

Rogan's 4-acre property comes with 300 feet of Lake Austin frontage, according to the original listing. The 11,000-square-foot mansion was built in 2008 and offers eight bedrooms and 10 baths.

The parklike surroundings include “views of the lake and the undeveloped preserve land on the opposite side.” There are three docks, a pool, and terraces.

The mansion features a formal dining room with built-ins, a dual-island kitchen with a casual eating area, a living area with floor-to-ceiling windows, and an office. A gym can also be found on the grounds.

Rogan's Instagram account reveals several upgrades he made in addition to his studio, including a cold plunge tub and a sauna.

The locale, not far from downtown Austin but seemingly a world away, was a draw for Hollywood A-lister Sandra Bullock, who reportedly owns a home in the area.

Claudine Zap has been a writer and editor at Realtor.com since 2015, covering celebrity real estate, unique homes, and real estate trends. She also contributed to the site’s “House Party” podcast. She was previously a writer and editor at Yahoo, where she covered entertainment, culture, fashion, food, travel, and web trends. Claudine earned a B.A. in government and anthropology at Smith College and a master’s in journalism at the University of California, Berkeley, where she won the McClatchy Prize for In-Depth Reporting. #5577. 12 housing bills that could shape affordability after the midterms

Concerns over housing supply and affordability have reached a fever pitch and become a major issue for voters in this year’s midterms.

With the midterm elections just days away, housing affordability remains a pressing issue for voters — and a growing legislative priority for lawmakers in Washington.

Congress has spent much of the past two years considering proposals aimed at lowering housing costs, helping first-time buyers, unlocking existing inventory and encouraging new construction. But despite growing bipartisan interest in housing policy, many of those proposals remain stalled in committee as voters prepare to decide which party will control Congress.

Lawmakers scored a significant bipartisan victory in July with the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a sweeping package aimed at boosting housing supply and addressing barriers to development. Yet much of the broader housing agenda remains unfinished, including proposals to expand homebuyer assistance, increase affordable housing investment and raise the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Some bills have continued attracting additional congressional support in recent weeks, but none of the proposals highlighted in September has advanced since. With both chambers largely out of session until after Election Day on Nov. 3, further legislative action will likely have to wait until lawmakers return to Washington.

Inman revisited the most consequential housing bills that could help shape the federal government’s approach to supply, affordability and homeownership in the next Congress.

What it does: The bipartisan legislation would double the capital gains exclusion on the sale of a primary residence, from $250,000 to $500,000 for individuals and from $500,000 to $1 million for married couples, and automatically adjust those limits over time to account for inflation. Why it matters: Supporters argue that the limits, which have remained unchanged since 1997, discourage longtime owners with substantial equity from selling and effectively lock inventory off the market. NAR has made the proposal a major 2026 priority and is currently framing it as one of the fastest ways to increase existing-home supply. Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means and the Senate bill before Finance, and neither has advanced beyond referral. Support has continued growing, however, with 159 House cosponsors and 25 Senate cosponsors as of late October, including lawmakers from both parties. With Congress largely out of session until after the election, inclusion in a broader tax package during the lame-duck session or next Congress remains one possible path forward.

What it does: This legislation would establish a refundable federal tax credit equal to 10 percent of a first home’s purchase price, capped at $15,000. Eligibility and the size of the credit would be subject to income and local home-price limits.

Why it matters: Unlike proposals intended to increase supply over time, the bill would directly reduce the cost of purchasing a first home for qualifying households. The tradeoff is that giving buyers more purchasing power does not add more homes to the market, and in a supply-constrained market, it can also put upward pressure on prices.

Status: Both versions were introduced in July 2025 and remain before the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees, respectively. Neither chamber has taken action beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., the bill would increase the mandatory share of Federal Home Loan Bank earnings devoted to the system’s Affordable Housing Program. The Consumer Federation of America estimates the change would generate roughly $300 million in additional annual funding for affordable housing development, down payment assistance and home repair programs, without requiring additional taxpayer funding.

Why it matters: The 11 Federal Home Loan Banks provide liquidity to more than 6,500 member institutions, including banks, credit unions and community development financial institutions. Housing advocates have argued that the system should devote more of its earnings to its public mission. In a broader reform proposal, the Coalition for Federal Home Loan Bank Reform has called for doubling the mandatory Affordable Housing Program contribution from 10 percent to 20 percent, which it estimates would add about $600 million annually for affordable housing.

Status: The House Financial Services Committee considered H.R. 10325 on Sept. 16, but a motion to report the amended bill favorably failed 21–28. That leaves the measure facing a significant setback in the House, even as housing and consumer groups continue pushing for broader FHLBank reform.

What it does: Designed to make it easier to pull together a down payment, this bill would raise the amount first-time buyers can withdraw from an IRA without paying the usual 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty from $10,000 to $50,000.

Why it matters: The proposal targets a major barrier for many prospective first-time buyers: saving enough cash for a home’s down payment and covering closing costs. It would expand access to buyers’ existing retirement savings rather than create a new federal subsidy. NAR lists the bill among its current legislative priorities.

Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate companion, introduced by Sens. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., and Todd Young, R-Ind., is before Finance. Neither has advanced beyond committee, though the Senate bill’s bipartisan sponsorship distinguishes it from some other first-time buyer proposals.

What it does: Seeking to make homebuilding and rehabilitation more feasible in distressed neighborhoods, this legislation would create a federal tax credit to support the construction and rehabilitation of owner-occupied homes where development costs exceed what finished properties can command on the market. The credit is designed to help close that gap and make projects financially viable.

Why it matters: The credit is intended to make starter-home projects possible in communities where builders currently cannot make the numbers work, with a particular focus on for-sale housing rather than rental development.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance. In May, the bipartisan sponsors released planned revisions, including more flexibility for state housing finance agencies and a shorter four-year authorization, that they intend to carry into the next version of the bill, whether in a year-end package or the next Congress.

What it does: This proposal would establish a federal investment tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying costs to convert nonresidential buildings into housing, increasing to 30 percent in certain areas where development is particularly challenging. At least 20 percent of the resulting units would need to remain affordable to households earning no more than 80 percent of area median income for 30 years.

Why it matters: The bill targets two persistent real estate problems at once — underutilized commercial buildings and the shortage of housing. Office-to-residential conversions have attracted substantial interest, but challenging layouts, financing hurdles and construction costs can make projects difficult to pencil out. A tax credit is intended to help close that feasibility gap. NAR also lists this bill among its 2026 legislative priorities.

Status: Introduced in March 2025, the bipartisan bill has attracted 57 cosponsors, including lawmakers from both parties, but remains before the House Ways and Means Committee without advancing beyond referral.

What it does: Focused on expanding and modernizing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, the proposal includes a broad series of changes involving tenant eligibility, project financing and credit administration.

Why it matters: LIHTC is a central federal financing tool that helps drive the construction of affordable rental housing across the country. Congress already adopted two pieces of the broader proposal in 2025, permanently increasing annual Housing Credit authority by 12 percent and lowering the bond-financing threshold from 50 percent to 25 percent. According to the National Council of State Housing Agencies, roughly two dozen other provisions remain unenacted.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance, with both measures drawing broad bipartisan support. Advocates continue pushing the remaining provisions either through the standalone bills or as part of future tax legislation.

What it does: The bill would update federal rules for mortgage revenue bonds and mortgage credit certificates used by state housing finance agencies, including increasing limits on certain home improvement loans and changing refinancing and recapture provisions.

Why it matters: Those programs can help lower- and moderate-income households access lower-cost mortgage financing, giving this technical tax legislation a direct connection to homeownership affordability.

Status: The House version, introduced in February 2026, remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate bill remains before Finance. The Senate measure was discussed during an Oct. 21, 2025, Senate Banking housing subcommittee hearing, but neither version has advanced beyond committee.

What it does: Seeking to open underused land owned by churches and other religious organizations to new housing development, this bill would preempt certain state and local laws that block affordable housing on those properties.

Why it matters: Religious institutions collectively control substantial amounts of land, including parcels in expensive housing markets where zoning can constrain redevelopment. The bill is notable because it tackles supply by asserting federal authority over certain local land-use restrictions, rather than relying primarily on grants or tax incentives.

Status: Introduced by Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., and Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., in September 2025, the bipartisan legislation remains before the House Financial Services Committee. Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes, D-Ohio, joined as a cosponsor in October, but the bill has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: This measure would amend the Fair Housing Act to prohibit discrimination based on a person’s source of income, veteran status or military status.

Why it matters: The change would expand federal fair-housing protections for veterans, service members and renters who rely on housing vouchers or other lawful sources of income. It could also create new federal compliance obligations for landlords, property managers and real estate professionals.

Status: Both versions remain in committee, with the House bill before Judiciary and the Senate measure before Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs. The House proposal has continued attracting support, reaching 23 cosponsors following the addition of Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, on Oct. 22. Neither chamber has advanced the legislation beyond referral.

What it does: Rather than establishing a tax credit or housing-production program, the Saving the American Dream Act would require HUD, Treasury, Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and the Federal Housing Finance Agency to coordinate housing research and market data and submit a joint report to Congress identifying opportunities to improve housing affordability.

Why it matters: Federal housing policy is currently divided among HUD, Treasury and other agencies. Supporters of the effort argue that greater coordination could reduce conflicting policies and give Washington a more coherent strategy for addressing affordability.

Status: Introduced in September 2025, the bipartisan bill remains before the House Financial Services Committee and the Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity. It has attracted 40 cosponsors, including two who joined on Oct. 1, but has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Norma Torres, D-Calif., on Oct. 22, the legislation would establish a new HUD grant program to help states streamline financing and administrative processes for affordable housing development. The proposal would authorize $90 million annually from fiscal 2027 through 2029, including funding to consolidate state financing programs, simplify applications for builders and improve access to development assistance.

Why it matters: Affordable housing developers often navigate multiple state agencies, financing programs and administrative requirements to move projects forward. By simplifying those processes, the proposal aims to reduce administrative barriers that can delay projects and increase development costs. States that meet the bill’s initial requirements could also use funding to streamline zoning, permitting and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit administration.

Status: Torres introduced the bill without cosponsors on Oct. 22, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee. It has not advanced beyond committee referral.

NAR’s current legislative agenda is centered heavily on housing supply, with the trade group estimating the country is short 4.7 million homes. Following the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July, NAR has continued pressing lawmakers on housing supply, with its latest advocacy materials putting particular emphasis on unlocking existing inventory through the More Homes on the Market Act and proposed changes to the capital gains exclusion for longtime homeowners.

The organization is also pushing lawmakers to fully fund several HUD programs, including fair housing enforcement and housing counseling services, while calling for long-term reauthorization of the National Flood Insurance Program. NAR says the flood program supports roughly 500,000 home sales each year and argues that lapses or uncertainty around coverage can disrupt transactions in flood-prone communities.

The flood insurance program’s current authorization expires Dec. 11, the same day a temporary spending measure funding federal agencies, including HUD, is set to expire. The deadlines leave Congress facing another round of funding and insurance negotiations during its post-election lame-duck session.

Passage of ROAD has not ended NAR’s work on the legislation itself. Many of the law’s new grants and housing programs still depend on future congressional appropriations and HUD rulemaking, including incentives for local housing production, zoning and permitting reforms, commercial-to-residential conversions and home-repair programs. NAR is now encouraging states and local governments to prepare for those programs, while pressing Congress to provide the funding needed to put them into effect.

Implementation of the law is also underway. On Oct. 22, the Treasury Department proposed regulations clarifying restrictions on large institutional investors purchasing single-family homes. Under the law, beginning Jan. 7, 2027, investors controlling at least 350 single-family homes will generally be prohibited from purchasing additional properties, subject to exceptions for activities including build-to-rent and renovate-to-rent programs.

For qualifying programs designed to help renters become homeowners, the proposal also establishes a framework for a 30-day first-look period and a right of first refusal before investors sell the properties to other buyers.

Reporter’s note: This story was originally published on Sept. 24, 2026, and has been updated to reflect the latest available information.

Additional note: AI tools were utilized in reviewing and verifying current federal housing bills, legislative priorities and related reporting for this story. All substantive details were checked against congressional records, primary-source materials and prior reporting before publication.

#5576. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Asad Khan studies housing market trends and the forces behind them as a senior economist at Redfin. Previously, he was an economic consultant at Analysis Group where he worked on antitrust and valuation matters. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5575. Carolyn Fugere Named President and CEO for William Pitt – Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty

Paul Breunich, executive chairman of William Pitt – Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty, announced that Carolyn Fugere has been appointed president and Chief Executive Officer.

According to a release, Fugere will lead the real estate company serving Connecticut, Westchester County and the Hudson Valley in New York, and the Berkshires in Massachusetts.

During her service as co-president and chief sales officer—where she was responsible for overseeing 31 offices and 1,100 sales advisors—the company posted the highest total closed dollar volume for any five-year period in the company’s history, the release states.

Fugere will become the fourth CEO in the company’s 77-year history, and the first-ever woman to hold the position. The release notes that in 2026, William Pitt – Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty rose to the rank of the top-producing, independently-owned Sotheby’s International Realty affiliate by sales volume and closed units worldwide for the global brand, which encompasses nearly 1,075 offices throughout 81 countries and territories on six continents.

Fugere commented that this No. 1 ranking serves as an opportunity and a responsibility to continue raising the standard of professional real estate advisory services.

“I’ve always believed that the measure of our success is the positive impact we have on the people around us,” Fugere said. “Whether we’re helping our advisors grow, supporting our colleagues, guiding our clients through important moments in their lives, or contributing to the communities we serve, we have an opportunity every day to make a difference. We have an extraordinary organization, and I believe we have both the opportunity and the responsibility to continue raising the standard of our profession.”

Fugere’s tenure in residential real estate spans 25 years in total and 16 with William Pitt – Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty, where she has grown in her career through multiple roles.

She embarked in the industry as a sales advisor, marketing and selling in suburban, urban and rural markets, and then advanced into brokerage management, leading eight sales offices across Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York.

Fugere was honored twice as a Manager of the Year, and she oversaw the firm’s expansion in a brand-new territory in the Berkshires. She also restructured and headed the company’s training department, leading training initiatives for agents and staff before stepping into the co-president role.

From his initial recruitment meeting with Fugere in her days as a brokerage manager with her prior firm, Breunich recalled recognizing her talent.

“I told her she could stay at her old company and be a soldier, or she could come to our company and become a generaI. I got the general,” he said.

As executive chairman and owner, Breunich will continue to be actively involved. His own tenure with the firm spans 38 years including 30 years as CEO, the release states.

“Rather than a change in direction, this appointment is an exciting evolution in the leadership of our firm, and a natural progression of Carolyn’s work and commitment to the organization,” Breunich added. “She has been deeply involved in shaping the company’s culture, vision and strategy for many years.”

“Real estate is more than a profession to me. It is a lifelong passion centered entirely on the success of our agents,” Fugere said. “I am honored to step into this role and lead an organization I care so deeply about. Backed by an extraordinary team, my focus remains on supporting our advisors, strengthening the relationships that drive our business and continuing to build on what makes our organization so special.”

For more information, visit https://www.williampitt.com/.

#5574. Milwaukee Brewers Captain Christian Yelich Lists Newly Built Malibu Mansion for $30 Million

Milwaukee Brewers captain Christian Yelich is looking to shed his contemporary Malibu mansion, listing the hillside estate for $30 million.

The World Series champion purchased the 1-acre property for $5.55 million in 2020. At the time, the lot included “fully approved plans” from architect Michael Kovac of KOVAC Design Studio.

The 5,300-square-foot residence was completed this year, according to Architectural Digest. A KOVAC representative told the publication that Yelich plans to move his family to Wisconsin.

The 34-year-old baseball star has been romantically linked to professional soccer player, Paige Noel Almendariz, although it is not clear if the couple live together.

“Set in the heart of Malibu, this one-of-a-kind coastal retreat has been thoughtfully rebuilt from the ground up with an unwavering commitment to quality, design, and comfort,”reads the listing, which is held by Yelich’s mother, Alecia Yelich with Compass.

Her bio notes that professional athlete relocation is her speciality.

“Offering sweeping views of the Queen’s Necklace, Surfrider Beach, Pacific Coast Highway and Nobu, this is the kind of property that rarely comes to market,” the listing continues. “Every inch of the home has been carefully curated, blending sophisticated finishes with cutting-edge technology to create a living experience that is both luxurious and effortless.”

The home boasts four bedrooms, four full bathrooms, a powder room, a dedicated pool bathroom, and an outdoor shower.

Nestled in a light-flooded corner of the home with retractable glass walls that let in fresh air, the primary suite is truly astonishing. Even the soaking tub and walk-in shower have killer views.

The five additional bathrooms are impressive, as well, offering expansive windows and closets equipped with refrigerators in each room.

Custom hardwood floors imported from France run throughout the home for a touch of warmth, both aesthetically and through the radiant-heated flooring that complements them.

Floor-to-ceiling windows can also be found across the home, making the idyllic Malibu surroundings feel like part of the decor.

The chef’s kitchen offers sprawling counter space, chic modern fixtures, and plenty of storage for snacks, supplies, and cooking gadgets.

The kitchen sink faces the home’s breathtaking ocean views, while automated pocket doors seamlessly connect the room to the picturesque outdoor living space.

The home has a number of standout spaces to use for entertaining guests or to enjoy on a quiet night in, including the custom wet bar and a private cinema with a dedicated concession room, an LED video wall, luxury seating, immersive surround sound, and professional acoustic treatments.

Technology has been carefully incorporated into the dwelling, which the listing describes as a “fully integrated smart home,” which gives residents the opportunity to “effortless control lighting, climate, entertainment, shades, security, and access from a single platform.”

A custom two-car carage and newly-constructed sealed driveway provide a safe space for residents’ vehicles.

Outdoor living was considered as thoughtfully as the interiors, with the backyard anchored by a resort-style infinity-edge pool.

There’s no shortage of lounge space, with multiple entertaining spaces spread among the area’s various decks and patios, and fire features and outdoors amenities to be enjoyed. An outdoor kitchen and barbecue area are also perfectly-suited for hosting.

Fully-automated Tuuci umbrellas leverage integrated heaters to provide shade from the sun or warmth during a chilly night.

There is even an oversized fully-enclosed outdoor television; a state-of-the-art addition that’s designed to provide “a remarkable viewing experience even in the brightest Malibu sunshine.”

Prospective buyers with pets will also be thrilled to learn there’s also a custom dog run.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.
