#5573. Open Real Estate: We’re almost there, but not quite

OPINION: The Open Real Estate options give sellers just two choices: market or participant view. Darryl Davis makes the case for a third door.

Picture a homeowner at the kitchen table. She likes you. She trusts you. And she says something agents hear every week: “I want you to sell my house. Just you. I don’t want a parade of strangers walking through my bedroom with agents I have never met. But I don’t want to hide it either. Advertise it. Get the word out. I want the best price.”

That is not a strange request. Some homeowners would happily give up a few dollars on the sale price for less stress, more convenience, and the peace of working with one agent and one office. And right now, the newest system in real estate has no way to say yes to it.

On October 26, Keller Williams, AGNT (the parent of eXp and NextHome), HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group launched Open Real Estate (ORE). Four competitors came together to stop listings from disappearing into company silos. They deserve real credit. But read the FAQ, and you will see the system gives a seller only two doors.

Now go back to our homeowner. Door one sends strangers through her bedroom. Door two gives her one agent but forbids anyone to advertise her house, the last thing she asked for. She wants one agent and full marketing. ORE makes her pick one.

That is not seller choice. That is a choice between two things she did not ask for.

Here is the option that is missing, and it is simple.

I can already hear the objection. “Darryl, isn’t this just a pocket listing with a nicer name?”

No. A pocket listing is hidden. A Coming Soon tease builds buzz while keeping other agents out, and nobody, not even the listing agent, can show it. The true exclusive is the opposite of both. The house is actively marketed to the public, and every member company knows it is available. The only thing exclusive is who walks through her front door.

Think of a restaurant that only takes reservations. Everybody sees the menu and knows where it is. You call first, and the owner decides who gets a table. Nobody calls that a secret restaurant.

Let’s say it out loud. In a true exclusive, the listing agent may well sell the house to their own buyer and get paid on both sides. For some sellers, that is exactly why they choose it. They understand that one cook in the kitchen managing the whole process beats two, especially when the second one is an untrained buyer’s agent.

ORE already has what it needs to offer this, and technology can make the fiduciary piece stronger than ever.

CCP had the right intentions. NAR wanted to stop listings from disappearing. But it was the wrong strategy, and it did the opposite. Once a listing is publicly marketed, it must go into the MLS within one business day.

Keep it quiet, though, and it falls under the office exclusive exemption. That does not tell agents to share. It tells them to stop advertising and keep the listing inside their own company. The brokerage itself became the pocket.

A rule meant to bring listings into the open pushed many further underground. As I wrote earlier this year, a Redfin analysis found pocket listings rose 67 percent after CCP passed. NAR leaves enforcement to local MLSs, and in a lot of markets, they have quietly stopped enforcing it or issuing penalties. A rule on the books but not enforced protects no one. It only confuses the agents trying to follow it.

For newer agents: Before CCP, a seller could hire one brokerage to market and show her home exclusively. But those exclusives usually stayed out of the MLS, so other agents often never knew the house existed. The true exclusive keeps what sellers liked about the old way and adds what was always missing: every agent knowing the house is for sale. That is the replacement.

Let’s give our homeowner the third door: one agent, full marketing and a way for the right buyer to find her. That is real seller choice.

Until a model like this is in place, we are still hurting buyers and sellers. Period.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Darryl Davis is the CEO of Darryl Davis Seminars. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5572. Descope launches Envoy to let consumer apps accept personal AI agents as users

Customer and agentic identity platform company Descope Inc. today launched Envoy, a service that lets consumer websites and apps accept personal artificial intelligence agents acting for their customers without rebuilding how people sign in.

Agents arriving through Envoy get an identity of their own, separate from the customer’s. The launch goes after a choice consumer businesses have been stuck with since agents such as Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse started shopping and paying for things on people’s behalf.

Amazon.com Inc. blocked Muse from its store in September, saying the agent did not identify itself as one when placing orders, and JPMorgan Chase & Co. moved a month later to keep outside agents away from customer bank accounts. Descope expects blocking will get harder to maintain as more customers do their shopping through an agent.

The alternative, in Descope’s telling, is an agent that signs in as the customer with the person’s own password and one-time code. Nothing in that session shows software was involved, so when a fraud rule fires the logs point at the person. The business ends up absorbing the cost in disputed orders and returns.

Envoy is built around a proposed standard that offers a third option. Meta and Sierra Technologies Inc. published a 0.1 draft of the Personal Agent Protocol in October to set rules for how an agent signs in for someone without posing as them. Under Poppy, as the draft is known, a business publishes the endpoints agents should use and verifies which agent is calling. The business then issues a session bound cryptographically to that agent until the interaction ends.

Developers who adopt Envoy do not have to implement Poppy themselves or keep pace with revisions to it. Descope runs discovery and agent identification, and agents need no advance registration because each one presents a published client metadata document. Session tokens are tied to a key the agent holds through the Demonstrating Proof of Possession standard. Envoy supports all three of the draft’s sign-in types.

Inside Envoy, businesses spell out what an agent is allowed to do on a customer’s account through the Rich Authorization Requests extension to OAuth. In the example Descope gives, a retailer could let a shopping agent place orders for a customer and still keep it away from the payment methods on file. How long any elevated access lasts is left to the retailer as well.

Sensitive actions can go back to the customer for approval on a separate channel, using Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication. Another example from Descope has an agent booking travel hold a fare it found overnight and send the details to the customer’s phone for approval the next morning.

Every token and log entry records the customer and the agent as separate parties, so a company can revoke an agent’s access without signing the customer out. Envoy runs alongside whatever customer identity system a business already has.

Descope co-founder and Chief Executive Slavik Markovich said every login page on the internet was built for a person on the other side, and “that assumption no longer holds true.” In his view, the Personal Agent Protocol is doing for consumer agents what the Model Context Protocol did for enterprise tools.

GoFundMe Inc. and GoodRx Holdings Inc. are among the launch and design partners working with Descope on Envoy over the coming months. Each donation on GoFundMe is “an act of trust,” according to Arnie Katz, the fundraising platform’s chief product and technology officer. He said Envoy will keep the donor and the agent distinct in every session and ask users to approve donations from their phones.

At GoodRx, Chief Technology Officer Nitin Shingate expects people to send agents out to compare pharmacies and find the lowest price on a prescription before they reach the counter. Agents there will get limited permissions covering pricing information.

Agent builders get a tool of their own. A Poppy software development kit, released alongside Envoy, lets any agent work with the protocol, with Descope handling discovery and session management behind it. The kit is written in TypeScript and has no external dependencies.

Envoy sits on top of Descope’s Agentic Identity Hub, which the company updated last month with controls aimed at agents employees build or adopt inside their own organizations. The hub now handles authentication and access control for more than 1,000 MCP servers and millions of agent transactions each month, according to Descope.

Descope is a venture capital-backed startup whose investors include Lightspeed Venture Partners, Notable Capital and Dell Technologies Capital. The company has raised $88 million to date, including a $35 million seed extension in September 2025.

#5571. Fed Holds Rates Steady, But Sets Up a December Hike

Takeaway: The Fed skipped hiking rates at today’s meeting, as expected. But they set up a hike at the December 9th meeting.

The Fed’s main message: Future hikes may be necessary because the economy is strong and inflation is too high. But they’re also patient, willing to skip hiking at some meetings in the interest of waiting for more data.

Chairman Warsh also announced a big change for Fed meetings starting next year, setting aside one meeting for big picture deliberation.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5570. Katy Perry’s Proposed Youth Summer Camp Sparks Wildfire Concern From Santa Barbara Residents

Katy Perry’s Firework Foundation has proposed a youth summer camp just outside of her hometown of Santa Barbara, CA, but nearly 400 residents are opposing the plan, citing a laundry list of concerns from wildfire risk to traffic and noise.

According to the project’s website, Gratitude Canyon “would provide a permanent home for Camp Firework” at a Goleta property that formerly operated as the headquarters of Bragg Live Food Products—the company that popularized apple cider vinegar.

Gratitude Canyon explains that the pop star and her sister, Angela Lerche—the foundation’s president—spent “significant time” at the proposed site of the camp growing up, noting a “close friendship” with Patricia Bragg, the company’s former CEO who died in 2023 at the age of 94.

The foundation estimates that “approximately 97% of the roughly 110-acre property would remain open space, agriculture or landscaping,” and that the camp’s activity would be “concentrated on about 16 acres,” leaving “much” of the existing apple orchard to remain.

The County of Santa Barbara's Major Condition Use Permit Application Project Description supports those claims.

The program has operated for seven years across more than a dozen camp sites, and serves children ages 11 through 13, combining “art, nature, leadership, and relationship-building for young people who may not otherwise have access to immersive camp experiences.”

A petition under the name “Neighbors Against Gratitude Canyon” has garnered 396 signatures from concerned residents in response to the way the project is “currently proposed.”

“The Firework Foundation is seeking County approval to rezone 183 Winchester Canyon with a General Plan Amendment and build a youth camp/event center, bringing 8,000+ visitors a year into a quiet, residential canyon, with amplified noise permitted 9am-9pm, 400-person events, and one way in or out of a high fire-risk, debris-flow zone,” the petition states.

Neighbors Against Gratitude Canyon has organized the neighbors’ “top concerns.” The first on the list is that they believe the camp is a “Trojan Horse” and is a “year-round event center” designed “under the guise of a summer camp for underserved kids.”

However, Gratitude Canyon has stated that the proposal is not intended to serve as “a wedding or concert venue,” and plans to keep limited use outside of summer camp to schools, nonprofits, and “occasional retreats,” as well as “no more than four special events per year.”

Additionally, the petition raises concerns about fire safety, claiming “a formal fire protection plan and independent county-reviewed evacuation analysis still haven’t been completed,” and that evacuation capacity for the camp’s children and staff should be established prior to changing the property’s zoning.

However, Gratitude Canyon’s frequently asked questions page notes “fire prevention has been incorporated into the project form the earliest planning stages” and claim “measures include defensible space, vegetation management, emergency access, onsite water, hardened structures, evacuation planning, emergency communications, and 24-hour staffing while campers are onsite.”

The Gratitude Canyon website also explains that the Firework Foundation is engaging “directly with neighbors” and that the project “remains an evolving proposal.”

The summer camp proposal is not the first time Perry has been involved in a dispute centered around property in Santa Barbara.

The “California Gurls” singer and her former fiance, Orlando Bloom, were involved in a yearslong courtroom battle regarding a $15 million Montecito mansion.

The legal drama began in 2020, when the couple purchased the home from 1-800-Flowers founder, Carl Westcott, who rescinded the deal days later.

Westcott had reportedly purchased the estate for $11 million just two months prior, and sued Perry’s long-time business manager, Bernie Gudvi, who handled the purchase. Westcott claimed he “lacked capacity” to sell his home because he was suffering from a brain disorder and was under the influence of painkillers.

After years of legal back-and-forth, a 2023 ruling concluded that the original sale contract should be upheld. Perry countersued Westcott, seeking nearly $6 million in damages from the veteran, including $3.5 million in lost rental income and more than $2 million in repairs due to his alleged “lack of maintenance” of the property. The damages were later revised to $4.8 million.

Perry was awarded $1.94 million in damages, which was deducted from the $6 million that remained outstanding on the property’s original purchase price, leaving Perry and her representatives responsible for paying just over $4 million.

In October of this year, Westcott alleged he had only received a fraction of the amount owed, leaving Perry and Bloom susceptible to another legal confrontation.

#5569. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5568. Beyond the Zero Down Payment: The Best States for Homebuyers Using VA Loans in 2026

VA loans can help veterans and active-duty service members turn their dream of homeownership into a reality.

Partly guaranteed by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, they don’t require down payments or charge monthly mortgage insurance, unlike many other loan programs.

If you or a loved one are eligible for a VA loan, you may be wondering where to buy a home. According to Military.com, Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Virginia, and Tennessee are all solid options.

“What makes these states attractive isn't necessarily one standout benefit. It's the combination of things that can make life after the military a little easier, whether that's keeping more of your retirement income, finding a good civilian job, or living somewhere with a strong veteran community,” says Chris Birk, vice president of mortgage insight at Veterans United Home Loans in Columbia, MO.

By becoming familiar with what each state has to offer, you could narrow down your home search and find a property that aligns with your lifestyle budget.

From no property taxes and lower housing costs to veteran-specific tax breaks, these military-friendly states can make homeownership more accessible and affordable.

According to data from the VA, Virginia is one of the leading states for VA-backed loans, likely due to its large military population and steady real estate market growth.

“Northern Virginia’s proximity to government facilities like the Pentagon, Fort Belvoir, and Marine Corps Base Quantico allows many veterans to transition into federal or defense-related employment without uprooting their families,” says Dell Jeanty, real estate agent at Dell Residential in Arlington, VA.

The state offers real estate tax exemption for qualifying veterans with a 100% service-connected, permanent and total disability. Additionally, due to the major military installations and frequent military relocations, Virginia has a high concentration of assumable loans.

“This means you could potentially take over a seller's lower, locked-in historical interest rate and further your savings as a veteran,” Jeanty adds.

Many markets in North Carolina, including Charlotte, offer opportunities for veterans at different stages of life, whether you’re transitioning to a civilian career or retiring.

“There’s an established veteran community and plenty of ways to build new connections through work, recreation, and shared interests. You can choose city living or quieter settings with more land while enjoying professional sports, outdoor activities, and travel access,” says Ashley Horton, global real estate adviser at Premier Sotheby's International Realty in Charlotte.

Also, military installations across the Carolinas like Fort Liberty and Camp Lejeune are within driving distance, and highway connections and a major airport keep you connected to other markets. Plus, North Carolina lets qualifying military retirees deduct military retirement pay from state taxable income.

“Compared with markets in other states, those in North Carolina can give you more home, more space, and more options for the same budget. If you’re relocating from higher-cost cities, the equity from your previous home can stretch further here,” adds Horton.

Florida is one of those states where you’ll never run out of things to do.

You can enjoy country living with land and wide-open spaces, a coastal environment with beautiful beaches and waterways, or a neighborhood close to shopping, restaurants, and entertainment. And of course, you can’t beat being able to enjoy the outdoors almost year-round.

“I live and sell in the Orlando area, which is most well known for the Disney and Universal theme parks. In fact, Universal Studios Orlando just opened the Epic Universe park—fun for the whole family,” says Christina Rordam, a real estate agent at Florida Realty Investments in Orlando.

Also, since there are fewer homebuyers to compete with in Florida, you may have more leverage to negotiate ideal terms.

According to Rordam, there are currently two groups of sellers: the motivated and the unrealistic.

“The motivated home sellers are moving for job transfers, divorcing, having kids, and needing more space. These types of life events really encourage sellers to take a long, hard look at the current market and cut buyers a good deal,” Rordam explains.

In the past, it was almost unthinkable to negotiate price, repairs, and closing costs. Now, it's much more likely.

Rordam has a cash buyer for whom she negotiated $1,600 in repairs and $20,000 off the purchase price on a home that had been on the market less than a week.

In addition, Florida has no state individual income tax and some valuable property tax benefits for qualifying veterans.

“For example, certain veterans with service-connected disabilities may qualify for additional homestead property tax exemptions, and veterans with qualifying total and permanent service–connected disabilities may be eligible for a full exemption from property taxes on their homestead. Those savings can make a real difference in the overall cost of owning a home,” says Sheena Haney, broker and owner at Haney Signature Realty in St. Augustine, FL.

To Haney, Florida is more than just a place to buy a home.

“It’s a place where you can really enjoy the lifestyle, raise a family, retire, and make lasting memories,” adds Haney.

Texas gives veteran buyers something incredibly valuable: options.

In Central Texas, for example, you’ll find everything from established neighborhoods to new construction, where builders may offer incentives to make homeownership more affordable.

“San Antonio is especially attractive because of its relatively low cost of living, allowing many military families to stretch their housing budgets further,” says April Guerra, real estate agent at LPT Realty in Leander, TX.

Put simply, the Lone Star State doesn’t force you to sacrifice space, amenities, or lifestyle to find a home within your budget.

“If you’re a veteran looking to establish roots after military service, that flexibility can make a meaningful difference,” Guerra explains.

Texas also has a long-standing connection to the military.

“I grew up in San Antonio, proudly known as Military City, USA, home to Joint Base San Antonio, including Fort Sam Houston, Lackland, and Randolph. Now, working in the Austin area, I'm also near Camp Mabry and Fort Hood. Military families are an important part of these communities,” says Guerra.

There’s an established VA healthcare system as well.

“For example, in the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex, Dallas has a full-service VA hospital.  Fort Worth has a large VA outpatient clinic,” says Elizabeth Lane, real estate agent at HomeSmart Realty in Dallas.

Additionally, Texas offers no state individual income tax, potential property tax exemptions for qualifying disabled veterans, and access to military and veteran support networks.

There's also a strong sense of community and diverse employment opportunities.

“Companies like Lockheed Martin and Bell Textron have a large presence in North Texas and like to recruit veterans,” adds Lane.

Tennessee offers a unique mix of benefits for military homebuyers.

First and foremost, there’s no state income tax.

“On top of that, Tennessee has some of the lowest property taxes in the U.S., ranking roughly eighth to 10th lowest, depending on the specific index,” says Wendy Monday, real estate agent at Broker Onward Real Estate in Nashville, TN.

By contrast, states such as New Jersey and Illinois have significantly higher tax rates, which add considerably to the cost of homeownership.

Also, Nashville is one of the premier healthcare hubs in the country, making top-quality medical care exceptionally accessible locally.

It boasts an incredibly high density of Level 1 Trauma Centers, top-tier children's hospitals, and specialized emergency rooms right in the metro area.

“You won't have to travel to another city or state if you or a family member ever face a complex diagnosis or require a rare medical specialist,” Monday explains.

#5567. Share of Adjustable Rate Mortgages Hits Highest Level Since September 2025

A house key sitting on mortgage application.To see more of my financial images click on the link below:

Mortgage rates ticked down a bit this past week but landing at 7.3%, it wasn’t enough to move the needle for buyers submitting loan applications for 30-year-fixed rate mortgages. Sitting almost a full percentage point lower, adjustable rate mortgages (ARMs) however continue to be attractive for buyers looking to start out with a lower monthly payment.

The latest Market Composite Index from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)—its measure of mortgage loan activity volume and includes purchases and refinances—shows mortgage application activity decreasing 1.2% on a seasonally adjusted basis after last week’s 3.4% increase. On an unadjusted basis, the Index decreased 2% compared with the previous week.

This week’s decline follows weeks of fluctuations as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate still lingers around 7.29%, according to Freddie Mac and this week currently sits at 7.25%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Freddie Mac’s next rate report will be released Thursday.

“Mortgage rates drifted down to their lowest level since September 2026 last week in the wake of the Federal Reserve’s decision to hold on additional rate hikes at its October meeting,” said Mike Fratantoni, MBA’s SVP and chief economist. “While the 30-year rate declined to 7.3 percent, activity is still quite slow, with purchase application volume down for the week and refinance volume effectively flat at a very low level.”

MBA once again pointed to increased activity in the ARM share of total mortgage applications as a sign that buyers are ready to move on lower rates. According to the report, the average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs decreased to 6.29% from 6.41%, with points decreasing to 1.00 from 1.20 (including the origination fee) for 80 percent LTV loans. The adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) share of activity increased to 11.4 percent of total applications, MBA reported.

“As we have highlighted in recent weeks, more borrowers are choosing ARMs in this environment to lower their initial payments, with the ARM share at its highest level since September 2025,” Fratantoni said.

An ARM loan is where the interest rate is fixed for an initial period, typically five years, and then changes annually for the life of the loan, based on market conditions.

MBA’s Refinance Index increased 0.1% from the previous week and was 60% lower than the same week one year ago. MBA’s seasonally adjusted Purchase Index–its weekly measurement of nationwide home loan applications based on a sample of about 75% of U.S. mortgage activity–decreased 2% from one week earlier. The unadjusted Purchase Index decreased 4% compared with the previous week and was 19% lower than the same week one year ago, according to the report.

The refinance share of mortgage activity saw an increase this week–to 39.8% from 38.9% the previous week, MBA reported.

A look at government-backed loans this week shows the FHA share of total applications decreased to 16.0% from 16.6% the week prior. The VA share of total applications increased to 11.2% from 11.0% the week prior, and the USDA share of total applications increased to 0.6% from 0.5% the week prior.

#5565. EXCLUSIVE: ‘The Wolves of Real Estate’ Director Reveals the Unanswered Questions Behind the Alexander Brothers’ Downfall

Before their names became synonymous with a federal sex-trafficking case, Tal and Oren Alexander built careers selling some of the country’s most expensive homes.

Now, a documentary examining the brothers and their crimes is raising questions about the role wealth, professional prestige, and exclusive social circles played in giving them access to women.

Peacock’s three-part series, “The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers,” examines the rise and downfall of Tal, Oren, and their brother Alon, tracing a story that stretched from luxury properties and lavish parties to a Manhattan courtroom.

All three were convicted of federal sex offenses, including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking, on March 9. On Oct. 27, each was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York.

Speaking exclusively to Realtor.com®, Emma Schwartz, director of “The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers,” says the brothers’ status helped draw women into their orbit, while cautioning against assuming that every allegation involved their professional lives.

“Testimony at trial made clear that the brothers’ wealth and status was one of the reasons they were able to attract so many women,” Schwartz says.

“But many of the allegations we heard about did not involve their jobs or work.”

Tal and Oren rose to prominence at Douglas Elliman before leaving in 2022 to co-found luxury brokerage Official.

Their résumés included the $238 million Manhattan penthouse transaction at 220 Central Park South in 2019, which set a U.S. residential sale record at the time. Alon, Oren’s twin, worked in the family’s private security business.

Prosecutors described a scheme in which the brothers used their money and connections, including Tal and Oren’s standing in ultraluxury real estate, to facilitate sexual assaults.

Women were enticed with trips, accommodations, and exclusive experiences, according to the government’s account of the evidence.

Yet the criminal proceedings were not primarily an examination of the brokerage business, Schwartz explains.

“One of the interesting things about the criminal trial was how little it focused on the brothers’ professional lives,” Schwartz says.

Only one Douglas Elliman agent testified, according to the interview responses, with the government seeking information about a summer lease in the Hamptons.

Nevertheless, some testimony revealed an overlap between the properties associated with the brothers’ business image and the places where women said they were assaulted.

“For instance, the house that two women testified at trial that they were raped and trafficked to, was featured in a business video for the brothers,” Schwartz says.

Another woman testified that the possibility of making a professional connection had interested her in attending a party to which the brothers had invited her friend, according to Schwartz.

Those accounts illustrate how professional opportunity and social access could intersect. They do not, on their own, establish that the brothers systematically used access to clients’ listings to commit crimes.

Questions about what others knew also remain central to the story.

“One of the biggest questions so many have is who knew what about the brothers’ behavior?” Schwartz says.

The interview responses point to an email from an Elliman official, discussed in the documentary and presented at trial, as evidence that at least some people knew about the brothers’ playboy lifestyle.

But Schwartz distinguishes that awareness from knowledge of sexual violence.

“We also know from reporters at The Real Deal that there had been rumors about the brothers’ alleged behavior circulating in the industry for years before the lawsuits came out,” Schwartz says.

Rumors, awareness of partying, and evidence that a particular person knew about a crime are different matters. The responses do not establish criminal wrongdoing by the brokerage or its other employees.

For Schwartz, another striking aspect of the trial was the difficulty women described in acknowledging and reporting their experiences.

“One of the striking things about the trial was how so many of the women said they had been ashamed and too afraid to report what happened to them,” Schwartz says.

Some took months or years to describe what happened as rape or sexual assault, according to the interview responses.

That hesitation is a significant part of the documentary’s larger story: the barriers women faced in coming forward, even as the brothers maintained wealth and social standing.

“This all raises an important issue about sexual assault cases: women often take a long time, sometimes years, before they are ready to speak about what happened,” Schwartz says.

The civil justice system also played a role. New York’s Adult Survivors Act created a temporary window allowing adults to bring certain sexual-assault claims that would otherwise have been barred by expired filing deadlines. That window ran from Nov. 24, 2022 through Nov. 24, 2023.

Schwartz credits that law with allowing the first two women to file their civil claims, helping set in motion the public scrutiny that followed.

“This is a story about why speaking up matters,” Schwartz says.

“It took just two women filing lawsuits, amplified by the media to open the floodgates for dozens of women to come forward.”

Asked whether the case reveals something broader about luxury brokerages, Schwartz resists drawing a sweeping conclusion about the entire industry.

“It’s really hard to know how much anyone can generalize from the brothers to the industry more broadly.”

The hope, instead, is that the women’s accounts will help others feel able to share their own experiences.

“The women and people who spoke for our documentary did so in hopes that sharing their experience would encourage others to speak up and not feel the shame they did.”

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. #5564. Tencent releases Hy4, a powerful frontier AI model introducing visual understanding and computer use

Tencent Holdings Ltd. today introduced Hy4, a new large language model that adds computer-use capabilities for the first time, using advanced visual understanding, reasoning and tool-calling to deliver long-horizon agentic performance.

The company said the model marks a significant leap in performance over its Hy4 Preview, which arrived Aug. 28, weighing in at 770 billion parameters with 49 billion active parameters. Both provide a 1 million-token context window, putting it in the same range as current open-weights frontier models from European and Chinese developers, including Mistral AI SAS, Beijing Moonshot Technology Co. Ltd. and Z.AI Co. Ltd.

The company said it substantially scaled up both pre-training and post-training, reporting gains over the preview version in instruction following, long-context understanding, agentic long-horizon tasks and deep research. Tencent also identified excessive reasoning and over-verification during the previous version’s “thinking” processes.

The new model focuses heavily on real-world productivity for workplace collaboration, human experience and professional work. The company said it optimized long-context learning capabilities to understand complex information, including web development, document summarization, visual creative tasks, document presentation, and more.

The company added that it also enhanced its capability for front-end and game development, high-complexity tasks that include intricate business logic, state management and orchestration. Some models struggle with producing stateful, elegant and beautiful user interfaces that are visually polished and also fully functional.

It is not uncommon for professional game developers, industry engineers and amateur vibe coders to use AI models as part of their work. However, a recent spate has had coders begin to reproduce, reverse-engineer and clone older and semi-recent video games. That prompted Anthropic PBC to block Claude Code and its underlying Opus 5.5 model from assisting in these tasks.

The company said it integrated deeply with major engines such as Unreal Engine, Unity and Godot, giving it the capability to support complex game logic and multiplayer implementations. Compared wit the preview, Tencent said, Hy4 improved by 19.1 percent in the GameDev bench and 9.8 percent in GameLogic benchmarks, although the actual baseline numbers remain internal and weren’t released.

To advance scientific reasoning, Tencent advanced the next stage of Recursive Self-Improvement to enhance research and development capabilities. Using the Hyra 2.0 harness, an autonomous AI research agent system, the model optimized the pre-training infrastructure for smaller models sharing the same architecture.

The model is currently available on Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, CodeBuddy, Yuanbao, WeCom’s AI Assistant, Ima and more. It can also be accessed via third-party sources such as OpenRouter, Hermes and OpenCode. The company added that, despite its significant enhancements over Hy4 Preview, it kept costs low, maintaining the same pricing at around 90 cents per million input tokens, $2.70 per million output tokens and 4.5 cents per million cached input tokens.

The Flash version of the model is scheduled for release soon to deliver greater cost efficiency for users. The company also said it intends to release the model weights and system cards in coming days.

#5563. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.

#5562. JD Vance Blames Iran War for GOP Rout as Mortgage Rates Soared

Vice President JD Vance is blaming Republicans' election losses on the Iran conflict and rising prices.

"The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance said in a post on X, hours after Democrats shellacked Republicans in the midterm elections, flipping almost three dozen seats in the House and Senate to win control of both chambers.

Vance noted that polling found the war in Iran and cost of living and inflation concerns were the top items on voters' minds heading into Election Day.

Those were among the top reasons that many of the voters who helped propel President Donald Trump to a second term in 2024, with majorities in both chambers of Congress, voted in Democrats on Tuesday, Vance said.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance said in the post. "The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

"But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," Vance said.

Indeed, Americans were broadly concerned about affordability in the months leading up to the election. While Trump said he remained focused on it, he spent the run-up to the election detailing projects in Washington, DC, such as a botched effort to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Both Democrats and Republicans have promised their own affordability agendas for the coming months. But in swing states that turned against Trump, including Iowa, Ohio, Texas, and Maine, housing affordability was at the top of voters' minds. So, too, have many young voters worried that homeownership is rising out of reach.

Most markers of inflation show many costs have risen sharply this year. Gas prices often embody Americans' concerns, and AAA reports the national average price for gas is $4.12 a gallon, compared to $3.05 a year ago.

Trump, for his part, continued defending his economic record on Tuesday, telling media outlets that night that he would accept the election results and might seek common ground with Democrats.

But then he also posted an image of a red hat with the word "veto" on it, before celebrating the rise of the Dow the next morning following the results.

"Stock Market just hit another Record High—91 Days in just a short period of time—Less than two years," he posted to Truth Social on Wednesday. "Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All!"

And yet, the war in Iran and its resultant rise in oil prices and other costs hamstrung efforts to improve affordability. The Federal Reserve hiked interest rates earlier this year, and kept them steady in its most recent meeting. Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee in recent months show that leaders are worried that inflation is stickier than expected and that the conflict with Iran will continue to drive up costs.

Vance said in his post that it was "sound" political advice to call for a diplomatic solution to the Iran conflict. He also indicated that he could be open for change to the controversial immigration enforcement policies that have deeply affected the housing market and home construction.

"I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance," Vance said in the post. "But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you."

Meanwhile, Democratic leaders said in a press conference on Wednesday that they would focus on affordability in the coming term.

New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is likely to become the new Speaker of the House, repeatedly avoided discussing Trump. Instead, he said his focus was on "affordability and accountability."

"We know we have to undertake, with the seriousness of purpose, a relentless effort to make life more affordable for everyday Americans," Jeffries said. Later he added, "We have been focused, relentlessly, on dealing with the affordability crisis and driving down the high cost of living."

Massachusetts Rep. Katherine Clark, who is currently minority whip but stands as a contender to become House majority leader, said that could include efforts to roll back the president's tariffs, which have driven up the cost of many homebuilding materials and household goods.

Jeffries said the House Democratic Caucus will convene next week and lay out a clear plan for what to do next. But neither he nor Sen. Chuck Schumer had heard directly from Trump on Wednesday.

The National Association of Realtors®, in a Wednesday statement, called for more progress on housing.

“Regardless of which party controls Congress, NAR’s priorities remain the same: increasing housing supply, improving affordability, protecting property rights and expanding access to homeownership," NAR said. "Our research shows that 85% of Americans believe homeownership is part of the American Dream, underscoring why housing must remain a priority for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle."

RPAC-supported candidates won in at least 325 races, and a number of ballot initiatives this year involved housing-related issues. NAR also noted the bipartisanship of the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, the housing package aimed at making it easier to build homes. Congress passed it this summer with large majorities from both parties.

"We will continue building on that momentum, working with REALTOR® champions and real estate allies in both parties to advance commonsense solutions that bring more homes to the market and help more Americans achieve the dream of homeownership," NAR said.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5561. Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home

From today, Redfin is celebrating America’s 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America.

With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide.

Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027.

“America’s story isn’t just written in history books. It’s written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.”

Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America’s founding.

The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades.

The home’s remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning.

Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms.

Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923.

Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa.

The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south.

Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition.

#5560. I analyzed 1,133 Instagram posts with Meta’s new AI

Meta Muse for Small Business connects to your Instagram analytics. Here are five prompts to analyze your past posts before asking AI to create more.

Meta quietly released something at the end of September that I think a lot of real estate agents are going to want to play with.

It’s called Meta Muse for Small Business, and while there are plenty of AI tools that can help you brainstorm a Reel or write a caption, what is massive about Muse is that it can connect directly to your Instagram professional account analytics, along with your Facebook Pages, Meta ad accounts and other business tools.

I connected mine and started playing with it, but instead of asking it to make more content, which is how I use AI most of the time, I wanted to see what would happen if I used it to understand all the content I had already made.

Eventually, we analyzed 1,133 of my Instagram posts. It helped me understand why my rolling views had fallen from roughly 4 million to 2.46 million, showed me that at least 27 of my 98 newest followers were real estate professionals, and identified patterns in the topics and formats that have historically performed best for me.

That was when I realized I had probably been using AI backward. If you have been consistently creating content for a few years, you already have your own data set of what works and what doesn’t, so before asking AI for another 10 Reel ideas, there may be more value in asking it to help you understand what your audience has already told you.

Here are five prompts I’m using to do that.

“Analyze my Instagram performance over the past 90 days. Don’t give me content recommendations yet. First tell me where the biggest weakness is between reach, engagement, profile visits, follower growth and conversion, and show me the data that led you to that conclusion.”

A few months ago, my Instagram analytics showed roughly 4 million views in a 30-day window, and more recently that number had fallen to about 2.46 million, so naturally my first reaction was that something wasn’t working.

The story was a little different once I dug into the data. Some of my biggest posts, including videos with more than 1 million views, had simply aged out of the rolling reporting period. I would love to tell you I publish a million-view video every week, and I’m working on it, but I don’t.

My views were down, but roughly 84 percent were still coming from non-followers, and my content had reached more than 1.4 million accounts. The point wasn’t to ignore the decline; it was to understand what was causing it before changing a strategy that might not actually be broken.

“Analyze my most recent followers, and group them into the most common audience types you can identify. Don’t assume who my target audience is. Tell me what the data shows.”

We pulled roughly 100 of my newest followers, and of the 98 we could analyze, at least 27 had Realtor, real estate, broker or realty directly in their name or username.

Initially, I wondered whether that was a problem because I sell houses and still want consumers seeing my content, but last year we closed roughly $12 million in sales volume from referrals, and relationships with other agents have also created speaking opportunities, partnerships and other revenue. Trying to get rid of an audience already producing real business made very little sense.

Instead, I’m leaning into it while becoming more intentional about building consumer-focused lead pillars through my local Dana Point Daddy page and YouTube.

I’m also still making consumer-focused and humorous content on my main account because my past clients, database, sphere, friends and family are seeing and engaging with it. We’re still marketing directly to our database, hosting client events and doing the things that generate real estate business outside social media.

Your unexpected audience might be completely different from mine, but you probably shouldn’t decide whether the audience you’re building is good or bad until you know who is in it and what that audience is worth to your business.

“Analyze my highest-performing posts from the last year and group them by topic, format and hook. Tell me what patterns repeat among my winners and which patterns I seem to be underusing.”

I spend an embarrassing amount of time studying other creators, saving their posts and trying to understand why something went viral, while apparently not spending nearly enough time studying the years of content I already had telling me what my own audience responds to.

We analyzed 447 of my carousel and single graphic posts and isolated 103 that used headline-style hooks. The winners repeatedly included income statistics that create sticker shock, local rankings people want to agree or disagree with, surprising changes in the Southern California housing market and California housing policies translated into something useful for homeowners.

This October, Inman turns its focus to AI and its rapid rise in real estate. During Artificial Intelligence Month, we’re digging into the startups shaking things up and the established players folding AI into their offerings.

I don’t need to make variations of those posts forever, but I can look for new topics that share the DNA of things my own audience has already told me it wants instead of constantly trying to recreate somebody else’s viral post.

“Compare how frequently I publish each content format with how those formats actually perform. Where is my time allocation inconsistent with my results?”

At the time of the analysis, I had published 66 times over 28 days, and Reels were the format I was publishing most frequently even though they weren’t my best-performing format. Carousels were.

I’m not going to stop making Reels because different content has different jobs, but if I’m deciding where to spend another hour this week, I should probably know whether the format consuming most of my time is producing my best results.

“Based only on the patterns you identified in my historically best-performing content, give me 10 new content ideas. For each one, tell me which past pattern it is based on and why you think it fits my audience.”

This is where the first four prompts become useful instead of just interesting because I can ask any AI tool for 10 content ideas and it will happily give them to me, but without context it is essentially making an educated guess.

Once it understands what my audience has historically responded to, I can ask a much better question: What should I make next based on what has already worked for me?

I’m still going to experiment, tell personal stories and make something weird because I think it’s funny, but now my own history gets a vote.

Meta Muse for Small Business has only been out for about a month, so I am sure I’m barely scratching the surface of what I can do with it, but this experiment has already changed the way I’m using AI.

If you’ve been consistently posting for a few years, you may already have hundreds or thousands of experiments sitting inside your Instagram, so before asking AI for another hook, caption or content idea, ask it to help you understand those experiments first.

For me, the most interesting thing AI has done for my content lately isn’t helping me create more of it. It’s helping me make better decisions about what I create next.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5559. The Renovation Cool-Off Is Here, but Delaying Certain Repairs Could Cost You More Than You Save

Spending on home improvements and repairs is only expected to grow by 1.5% by the third quarter of 2027, according to Harvard University Joint Center for Housing Studies. Given the high cost of labor and materials these days, this is no surprise.

But if you’re trying to cut back on home projects to save some cash, it's important to understand which ones are truly optional and which ones actually need immediate attention.

“Not every project needs to happen right away. Your home doesn't have to look brand-new to be safe, comfortable, and in good shape,” says Jeri Goodkin Dausey, president and certified general contractor at SBC in Miami Beach, FL.

By knowing how to prioritze your budget, you can protect your home’s condition and value without draining your savings.

There are quite a few projects you can delay without hurting your home, as long as everything is safe and working properly.

“Sometimes, waiting can save you quite a bit of money in the short term,” Dausey explains.

Here’s what you can put on the back burner until you have more funds at your disposal.

If your cabinets, countertops, and fixtures are still in decent shape and everything works, there's no need to rush into a complete remodel.

“Let's say you were planning to spend $25,000 on a renovation but could take care of the immediate issue with a $500 repair instead. That's $24,500 you can hold onto for now,” says Dausey.

A fresh coat of paint or new trim can make a significant difference in your home’s aestehtics, but these are usually things that can wait if the walls and surfaces are in good shape.

“If you put off a $4,000 paint job and just spend $200 on a few touch-ups, you've kept another $3,800 in your budget,” Dausey explains.

Dmitri Popescu, general manager at Olympic Decks in Seattle, echoes Dausey’s thoughts.

“Repainting a room because you dislike the color or replacing an undamaged backsplash can generally wait. There’s no need to spend your money on a temporary makeover,” Popescu explains.

Not loving the look of your floors doesn't necessarily mean you need to replace them. If they're safe, stable, and free of water damage, you may be able to live with them a little longer.

“Putting off an $8,000 replacement and spending $300 on maintenance leaves you with $7,700. Just be sure to check out loose tiles, soft spots or areas that are lifting,” says Dausey.

An outdoor kitchen, new landscaping, or a bigger patio might be nice to have, but they're not necessities. If everything outside is safe and in good shape, these projects can wait.

“Delaying a $15,000 cosmetic upgrade in your backyard frees up a lot of money for other things. Just don't overlook problems like poor drainage, hazardous trees, or an unsafe deck,” advises Dausey.

These expert tips can help you decide whether a project can wait:

Ask yourself, does this project actually protect my home, or is it simply for aesthetics?

“Cosmetic upgrades can wait, but projects that protect the structural integrity and long-term value of your property can't,” says Roxanne Conrad, chief operating officer at Premium Service Brands in Charlottesville, VA.

Clogged gutters and unstable exterior surfaces like missing shingles and unsealed windows, for example, can be an issue.

“They can lead to much larger problems down the road if neglected for too long,” Conrad says.

If you’ve noticed the issue a while ago and it’s worsening, it likely deserves your time and money.

“Catching problems early is almost always easier and cheaper than repairing them as they fail,” Conrad explains.

Take care of what keeps your home safe, dry, and in good shape, and don't feel pressured to tackle every cosmetic project right away.

Keith Ostendorf, project developer at Next Stage Design + Build in San Jose, CA, recommends phasing.

“Some homeowners move forward in phases, which spreads out the spending and can cut the costs of moving out, since work in one part of the house can happen while the family lives in the rest,” he adds.

#5558. VMware gets simpler AI deployment and low-cost version for basic private clouds

Broadcom Inc. is expanding its VMware portfolio with new capabilities that simplify artificial intelligence workload deployment, strengthen infrastructure security and simplify disaster recovery.

The company is also introducing a lower-cost virtualization platform aimed at smaller customers that don’t need a full private cloud platform.

Today’s updates span VMware Cloud Foundation, the company’s flagship private cloud platform, and a collection of optional advanced services. Several capabilities are already available in VCF 9.1.1, which was released in September, while others are scheduled for the first quarter of Broadcom’s 2027 fiscal year, which began on Monday.

The changes are part of a broader Broadcom effort to position VCF as a common infrastructure platform for traditional virtual machines, containers and increasingly demanding AI workloads.

More than 2,600 customers had deployed VCF 9 as of September, representing more than 24 million allocated cores, according to Prashanth Shenoy (pictured), Broadcom’s chief marketing officer and vice president of marketing for cloud platform, infrastructure and solutions.

Broadcom is introducing AI Infrastructure Quickstart, an automated deployment capability designed to simplify the initial configuration of private AI environments.

It combines vCenter cluster deployment, vSphere Supervisor activation and VMware Kubernetes Service cluster provisioning into a single workflow, replacing multiple manual configuration processes. “We have consolidated all of that, made a quick start workflow and streamlined the workflow completely so they can get it up and running day zero in a matter of minutes,” Shenoy said.

Broadcom is also adding native S3-compatible object storage through VMware vSAN. The feature, expected to become generally available in the upcoming VCF release, supports AI applications that depend heavily on unstructured data and lets developers provision storage through self-service interfaces.

On the security front, Broadcom is incorporating additional capabilities directly into VCF rather than requiring customers to purchase them separately. These include confidential computing support for Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. processors, which was already available in VCF 9.1.1, as well as planned policy-based virtual private cloud connectivity and automated infrastructure configuration compliance.

Broadcom said the compliance features will continuously monitor infrastructure settings against industry benchmarks, identify configuration drift and provide remediation guidance.

The virtualization maker is also moving disaster recovery functionality into the core VCF and VMware vSphere Foundation platforms. The capability will provide orchestrated recovery across thousands of workloads, including recovery from outages, equipment failures and natural disasters.

Additional protection will be available through VMware HyperArmor, a previously announced service that provides hypervisor-level defenses including virtual patching, continuous monitoring and multifactor authentication.

Two other advanced services, VMware Live Recovery and VMware Compliance and Configuration Management, address cyber recovery and continuous compliance enforcement for virtual machines and containers.

The company is also broadening its portfolio at the lower end with VMware vSphere Express, a new offering for environments containing up to 128 processor cores. Based on vSphere 9, Express includes live virtual machine migration, high availability, distributed networking, security and simplified patching.

Shenoy said the product is intended for customers that need basic virtualization without purchasing the more comprehensive and costly VMware vSphere Foundation or VCF platforms. “They don’t need a whole cloud in their two-server environment,” he said.

Customers can upgrade to the larger platforms as their requirements grow. Broadcom didn’t disclose pricing, although Shenoy indicated Express would be substantially less expensive than its higher-end offerings.

#5556. Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom

In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down.

The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected.

The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back.

It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027.

Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data.

Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5555. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.
