#5554. Meghan Trainor Lists $18 Million Encino Mansion Formerly Owned by Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner

Meghan Trainor is saying goodbye to her sprawling Encino, CA, mansion, and has listed it for $17,995,000.

Although the manse is only 6 years old, it's already been home to a number of celebrity residents.

The “All About That Bass” singer and her husband, “Spy Kids” actor Daryl Sabara, purchased the abode in 2024 for $17,125,000. Previously, the dwelling belonged to music producer Zedd, who had listed the home for just under $19 million in January of that year.

The “Clarity” producer snapped up the six-bedroom, 12-bathroom property for $15.2 million in September 2021 from Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner.

The Jonas Brothers rocker and “Game of Thrones” star were the original owners, having bought the home for $14.1 million when it was built in 2019.

Spanning about 14,779 square feet, the home was designed by "distinguished” architect Jae Omar and sits on a near-acre of land in the exclusive Royal Oaks enclave.

A lavish two-story entrance creates an “incredible indoor/outdoor feel,” according to the listing, which notes that the compound is “for the most discerning buyer.”

With an impressive scale and an open-concept flow, the home is well-suited for hosting large gatherings as well as intimate dinners.

A generously sized great room with wall-to-wall sliding doors opens the home to an idyllic courtyard, while a built-in bar and a soothing fireplace keep things cozy.

The chef's kitchen has a sleek aesthetic, with modern cabinetry and countertops and a picture-frame window located above one of the two sinks. It’s also equipped with Miele appliances and a discreet refrigerator.

An oversized island seats seven, creating a perfect spot for families to spend quality time together.

There’s even a separate catering kitchen for more involved occasions.

Young children—like Trainor and Sabara’s three little ones, Riley Thomas, Barry Bruce, and Mikey Moon—could never be bored here. A one-of-a-kind playroom boasts a foam pit, slide, art station, and hidden reading nook. In fact, the entire home caters to readers, with floor-to-ceiling bookcases found throughout.

The property also includes an office space, a professional music studio with a vocal booth, and a fitness center with a steam shower.

The second floor includes yet another family room and five en suite bedrooms.

In its own wing, the primary suite has a sitting area, wet bar, and multiple patios. The spalike bathroom is impossibly luxurious, with an oversized walk-in shower and a soaking tub.

According to the listing, the primary suite’s two walk-in closets are “reminiscent of a luxury boutique.”

The backyard is yet another destination for a young family to enjoy, with “park-like” grounds that can be used for lounging, entertaining, and play.

Outdoor amenities include a kitchen and barbecue, a putting green, a fire pit, and a projection screen. “Enchanting” lighting and a robust sound system add to the magic.

The sparkling pool has a spa and runs alongside a separate guest structure that has a pub with a billiard room and fish tank. On the second floor is a fully decked-out screening room.

The property comes with a four-car garage, a security room with high-tech cameras throughout, and a Control4 smart home system.

This is the second Encino property Trainor has had on the market this year.

In April, she sold a $6.8 million property in the affluent neighborhood, hours before announcing she had canceled “The Get In Girl Tour” to prioritize time at home with her family.

The seven-bedroom, 7.5-bathroom dwelling was listed for $11.99 million in June 2024, with the price steadily decreasing over the following 21 months before falling to $6.99 million in March 2026.

Trainor and Sabara purchased the home in 2020 for $6.5 million and completed a full renovation, including a recording studio.

#5553. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5552. Democrats Eye Tougher Data Center Regulations as They Regain Control of Congress

Democrats who rode data center discontent to victory in the midterms are expected to pursue strict new regulations on data centers when they take control of Congress in January.

The Democratic sweep flipped dozens of House and Senate seats, and a number of those races hinged on broadsides against Republicans for their purported support of the industry. Meanwhile, voters considered more than 40 local measures to constrain data center development, and almost all of them passed.

The results are likely to bring new life into Democrats' efforts to add guardrails to the artificial intelligence buildout. But their majority does not go far enough to override a veto from President Donald Trump, who has sought to aggressively promote data centers in the United States, in the pursuit of what he dubs "super intelligence."

Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs, raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com® research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas.

"If the Democrats take control of Congress, it could be a major problem for data center developers," Balaji Tammabattula, CEO of BaRupOn LLC, which develops energy infrastructure for data center companies, recently told Realtor.com.

Data center companies, he said, are already reconsidering future investments. In Texas, Senate winner James Talarico released a blueprint for data center regulation with more enforcement. The state has a temporary moratorium on data centers in place, which Democratic Gov.-Elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to extend.

Just a few hours before polls closed, The Hill reported that Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google, and other tech companies were considering a more formal framework for data center development.

"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X shortly after the results came in.

Congress' one effort to rein in the impacts of data centers fell short just before the midterms. Several weeks ago, the House passed a bill to encourage utilities to shield ratepayers from the costs associated with data center buildouts, the Ratepayer Protection Act.

That followed widespread backlash against data center buildouts. But Senate Democrats tanked the bill because it didn't go far enough. They've coalesced around a few competing ideas for how to regulate data centers at the federal level.

In the meantime, Democrats put forth their own bill, the Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers (GRID) Act, with more enforcement power and penalties. Among its powers, it would require data center developers to provide their own energy, so they don't pull from the local power grid. It would also require more disclosure about data center developments and give the government the power to issue fines.

Also, 20 Democrats signed on to a bill that would create a total moratorium on data center development. But the president has veto power, and he has opposed such a harsh move.

Trump has advocated for data center development in the United States to prevent the technology being developed abroad. In the face of public backlash, he convened technology leaders in Washington in September and asked them to self-police the build-out of super intelligence.

The White House also released an accord signed by those major companies committing to developing the technology safely. Trump called it "morally binding."

While data centers affect property taxes, the exact impact on homeowners' tax burden is complicated. And the study found no impact on property values from large facilities in the two years after they open.

Democrats may find an opening to create more rules around data center construction. Although Democrats also took control of governor's offices in many major states with data center developments, Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel says that doesn't necessarily mean they will lead to sharp constraints on data centers.

"Utilities costs, rather than home values, are probably the biggest immediate change voters are feeling or fearing," Krimmel says. "Our analysis of data center impacts on the housing market found essentially no effect on inventory or sales behavior so far."

The Urban Institute suggested a few levers to help data centers support housing affordability. It suggested tax relief or energy cost offsets for communities that host many data centers. Otherwise, they risk straining local housing markets due to rising electricity costs, especially in high-growth regions.

Meanwhile, Brookings suggested an electricity tax on data centers or some kind of offset to local governments. But it warned that regulation of the sector could encourage developers to build more centers overseas.

It's unlikely the currently divided Congress will use the remainder of its term to pass rules around data centers. But when the new one comes in, it can reintroduce the GRID Act or other bills. The GRID Act’s 20-megawatt threshold would cover essentially the entire pipeline, more than 99% of planned capacity, Krimmel says.

"That would give homeowners the most direct protection on rates," Krimmel explains. "Requiring new projects to bring their own power could also slow data center development, and the jury is also still out on the local economic and labor market impacts of data centers on localities."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5551. Smartsheet AI-powered platform bridges gap between planning and results

Smartsheet Inc. today introduced an artificial intelligence-powered planning and execution platform designed to help enterprises identify when projects are veering off course and take corrective action before delays and cost overruns become serious problems.

Announced at the company’s Engage 2026 conference, the new vsActual platform — pronounced “versus actual” — uses AI agents to continuously monitor work across multiple enterprise systems, compare progress against strategic objectives and recommend adjustments. The company also announced new agentic workflow capabilities, integrations and security controls for its existing work management platform.

The centerpiece of vsActual is what Smartsheet calls Execution Graph, a knowledge graph built from what the company said are two decades of workflow data encompassing millions of projects and nine petabytes of information. The graph maps relationships between tasks, projects, programs and strategic objectives to help AI agents understand how changes in one part of an organization affect others.

The company’s goal is to address a growing disconnect between individual productivity improvements enabled by AI and measurable organizational results, said Pratima Arora, Smartsheet’s chief product and technology officer.

“We were seeing a lot of intelligence and productivity gains getting stuck at an individual level and not translating to a team and organization level,” she said.

VsActual is designed to operate across existing enterprise applications rather than require organizations to consolidate work onto a single platform. It can connect to applications from Oracle Corp., SAP SE, Workday Inc., Atlassian Corp. PLC and ServiceNow Inc. to gather information about budgets, schedules, staffing and project dependencies.

Smartsheet said AI agents can turn strategy documents, spreadsheets and budget proposals into structured plans, model alternative scenarios and monitor execution against those plans. A drift-detection agent (pictured) continuously searches for emerging problems, while other agents generate executive reports and recommend changes as business priorities evolve.

The system can also trace the consequences of disruptions across organizational hierarchies. “If there is a delay in a Jira ticket that has impact five levels up, we can detect it and tell you what is happening,” Arora said.

Smartsheet said its historical workflow data provides an advantage over competing planning and work management products. Execution Graph builds on an existing Amazon Web Services Inc. Neptune knowledge graph containing approximately 100 million nodes and incorporates information about workflow patterns, dependencies and collaboration, Arora said.

The company uses multiple foundation models, selecting them based on workload requirements and cost. AWS and Databricks Inc. are its major underlying technology providers. Arora said Smartsheet isn’t training its own large language models.

The announcements also expand Smartsheet’s existing AI capabilities. New Agentic Workflows allow users to schedule recurring activities such as status reports and risk assessments. Specialized creation and data-quality agents can generate project structures, dashboards and reports or identify problems in underlying data.

New integrations include native connections to ServiceNow, Microsoft Corp. Dynamics 365, HubSpot Inc. customer relationship management, Workday Inc. human resources software and Intuit Inc.’s QuickBooks. Conversational integrations with GitHub, Zendesk Inc., Airtable and Monday.com Ltd. are entering early access, with additional AI-assisted integrations planned for early 2027.

Arora emphasized that agentic workflows combine conventional automation with AI rather than relying exclusively on large language models. “This industry overuses LLMs sometimes where it is just simple deterministic action,” she said.

Although some agents can execute scheduled tasks automatically, Arora said human approval remains the default approach for consequential actions. “Our default stance is human in the loop,” she said.

The compay also announced International Organization for Standardization/International Electrotechnical Commission 42001 certification, security event streaming and data classification capabilities intended to strengthen oversight of AI operations.

Smartsheet developed vsActual with about a dozen enterprise design partners. The company publishes pricing on its website.

#5550. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5549. Absolute Home Mortgage targets growth through First Option strategic transaction

Absolute Home Mortgage Corp. announced a strategic transaction with First Option Mortgage in a deal that will combine the lenders, along with Mortgage Equity Partners, into a platform positioned to originate about $4 billion annually after regulatory approval. First Option’s team will move to Absolute and operate as a DBA unit, keeping its leadership and local relationships.   AI Summary

Absolute Home Mortgage Corp. on Wednesday announced a strategic transaction with First Option Mortgage that positions the combined independent mortgage bank to grow its originations volume. The move was not considered to be a merger or acquisition.

New Jersey-based Absolute said in its announcement that Georgia-based First Option will migrate onto Absolute’s platform and continue to operate as a DBA unit after regulatory approval. The deal also brings First Option executives into Absolute’s ownership and governance structure, a move aimed at building out a dedicated growth engine in a consolidating market.

As part of the transaction, First Option leaders Alvin Shah and Kurt Nikolai will join Absolute’s ownership group and board of directors, pending regulatory approval. Shah will become chief strategy officer, with responsibility for strategic expansion and additional acquisitions that are actively pursuing, according to the announcement.

Combined with Absolute’s wholly owned subsidiary Mortgage Equity Partners, the platform is “positioned to originate approximately $4 billion annually” once approvals are complete, the company said. That level of volume would give the lender additional operating leverage at a time when many independent mortgage banks (IMBs) are looking to scale up or sell.

“This partnership is exciting. We have proven what we can do together in the face of adversity and tough market conditions,” Matthew VanFossen, CEO of Absolute Home Mortgage Corp, said in a statement. “Now we are 100% confident that we are strategically positioned to scale. There is no better time to capitalize on the foundation we have built.”

Data from Modex shows that Absolute Home Mortgage has closed roughly 3,000 loans and $1.13 billion in volume over the past 12 months, with 250 producing loan officers across 33 branches. First Option has produced $398 million across 1,300-plus units and has 91 producing LOs across 11 branches. Massachusetts-based Mortgage Equity Partners has 81 producing LOs across 19 branches, with total volume of $613 million on nearly 1,600 loans in the past year.

Absolute said Shah, Nikolai and VanFossen have worked in “close strategic alignment” for years, operating separate IMBs but maintaining similar approaches to operating models, culture and growth. Bringing these businesses and teams under one platform formalizes the relationship.

“We have been building toward this for years, on the operating model, on the culture and on the vision,” Nikolai said in a statement. “We have been strategically aligned for years, and we have seen firsthand how well our teams work together. Bringing our two lenders together makes natural sense.”

The First Option team will keep its existing leadership and sales culture while continuing to serve borrowers and referral partners in local markets under a DBA structure. That approach mirrors how some companies are structuring IMB rollups — centralized capital, compliance and operations paired with local branding and relationships.

Absolute framed the deal as another step in a longer-term consolidation strategy. The company said it intends to continue acquiring and partnering with independent mortgage companies that want to gain scale while retaining their brands and leadership teams.

Shah said the combined platform is designed to be attractive to other IMBs facing higher costs, thinner margins and increasing compliance demands.

“I am excited about the combined resources of this team and the scaling opportunity it brings to the market,” Shah said. “Scale creates opportunities for other mortgage companies to join our platform and become more profitable. We have the people, the capital alignment and the platform to grow aggressively, and we intend to.”

VanFossen said he expects scale and customer retention to be critical in the next cycle.

“The IMBs that win the next cycle will be the ones that operate at scale, retain their customers, and move decisively when the market opens up,” he said. “That is exactly what we are building. First Option is a major step, and we are not done. We intend to be the platform of choice for independent lenders who want to grow.”

#5548. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5547. United Wholesale Mortgage Pushes Through Q3 Amid Headwinds, Predicts Steady Q4

Despite having lower margins for the third quarter, United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) Chairman, President and CEO Mat Ishbia stated that he feels prepared to handle “headwinds in the industry” during the company’s third quarter earnings call.

On the call, Ishbia referenced the challenges the mortgage market has faced within the past five years, saying that the market is “showing a lot of warts on a lot of different companies.”

“Everyone’s got some issue,” he stated. “A lot of other people are operating holes where they don’t have enough business. They don’t have enough opportunity to get loans, they can’t keep up production and they can’t invest in AI.”

Interest rates have weighed on the housing market heavily as of late, leaving mortgage lenders with lower demand. For UWM’s earnings however, Ishbia attributes the company’s success to the recent Oaktree partnership, which came together after an ugly bidding war with CrossCountry Mortgage.

“The best way to hedge is to do a lot more loans when rates drop, as long as you can stomach the Mortgage Servicing Right (MSR) values going down because rates drop,” Ishbia added. “We have a great hedging policy and process. We partnered with Oaktree on that and Vandy Fartaj. We feel really good about the process of how we’re hedging and how much to hedge, versus how much not to hedge.”

The latest Federal Reserve meeting in October concluded with no changes to rates, but mortgage rates have slowly begun to inch downward to the lower 7% range—around 7.24% according to Freddie Mac—after spiking dramatically from the September meeting’s rate hike.

“I think the natural hedge is the best way to do it, and we’re not back to the natural hedge yet,” he said.

Although the quarter’s loan origination volume came in at $33.4 billion—down from Q2 which was $39.7 billion, and the first quarter at $44.9 billion—Ishbia mentioned that expenses were down substantially, specifically tied into investments with AI technology.

“Those (expenses) are really just tied to the investments we’ve made in AI and technology over the last couple years when everyone thought our expenses were higher,” he noted. “And so we’re starting to see the fruits of our labor.”

In total, Q3 revenue clocked in around $811.1 million, which is down from last quarter’s $888 million and slightly down from last year’s revenue of around $843 million.

Adjusted EBITDA came in at $178.3 million, less than last quarter and last year’s estimates ($185.9 million and $211.1 million, respectively).

UWM’s stock grew following the earnings call, as the earnings report beat out expectations. The company’s stock jumped nearly 13%, but is still down about 59% year to date.

Net loss was down quarterly in Q3, to $212.6 million compared to Q2 at $451.9 million. It was significantly higher than last year’s Q3 net loss however ($12.1 million). As an improvement from the previous quarter, Ishbia again credits the lower expenses to the company’s AI investments now panning out.

“AI can definitely help you cut costs and expenses, and you’re seeing some of that benefit, but you have to make a massive investment in it to do that. As you can see, it helps you do more loans, grow your business and drive the top line revenue,” he commented.

As for market share, Ishbia emphasizes the power and role brokers play in UWM’s success. He described brokers as the “growing channel” and states that they are the “winners right now.”

“UWM’s market share is fantastic. We’re strong, we’re dominant, and we’re going to continue to grow. If we lose market share, I hope that happens because that means the broker market has gotten so big and it’s going to keep growing, that’s my focus,” he continued. “My focus is growing the broker channel, helping every loan officer do a little bit more loans, helping every real estate agent that works with brokers do more business, and helping them all win.”

With 2026 winding down, Ishbia sees the upcoming year as a time of “optimization” but said he expected the mortgage market to remain tough for some time. He also notes that UWM focuses primarily on purchase mortgages, and acknowledges the challenges that refinance mortgage loans could face with current rates.

“Since we’re mostly purchase, I’m not as concerned about the volume going down as much as a lot of refinance shops will,” he concluded. “Traditionally, the fourth quarter and first quarter are always the tougher times in the mortgage market. But once again, expenses are down, AI is winning and brokers are growing. We feel like we’re in the best position of anybody to capitalize on opportunity.”

#5546. NAR advances strategic plan with new tools, MLS outreach and housing initiatives

The National Association of Realtors released its third-quarter 2026 update on its 2026–2028 strategic plan, highlighting expanded engagement with nearly 500 MLS executives, early implementation work on the new 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, and the launch of a fraud-prevention hub and AI-focused training.   AI Summary

The National Association of Realtors (NAR) is moving from policy wins to implementation as it rolls out fraud-prevention tools, MLS engagement and housing supply efforts tied to its 2026–2028 strategic plan, according to a third-quarter progress report released Wednesday.

The update, covering the quarter ended Sept. 30, outlines how NAR is trying to convert advocacy wins and market research into practical support for agents, brokers and MLSs as the industry adjusts to commission lawsuits, changing rules and tighter housing affordability.

NAR said its work in the third quarter focused on five areas: MLS engagement, executing new federal housing-supply law, fraud prevention, commercial market intelligence and broker support. The association also highlighted technology and data initiatives, as well as developments in ongoing antitrust litigation.

NAR said it has now “expanded MLS executive engagement” to nearly 500 MLS leaders and formed a new MLS work group made up of industry experts. The group is publishing resources focused on maintaining a “pro-competitive, transparent marketplace,” according to the association’s update.

The outreach sits on top of an ongoing feedback effort that includes surveys, focus groups and in-person meetings with members, NAR said.

Why it matters: MLSs are reassessing rules, data access and listing practices in light of settlement-driven policy changes and regulatory scrutiny. More structured engagement between NAR and MLSs could influence how quickly and consistently local marketplaces adapt and how much operational risk brokers face during the transition.

NAR’s report puts significant emphasis on follow-through after the passage of the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law July 11. The association said it “spearheaded” the push for the bill and is now working with state and local associations to turn the federal statute into local supply and affordability gains.

Beyond the ROAD to Housing Act, NAR said it continued advocacy for the More Homes on the Market Act and secured another “credit score modernization” change at the Federal Housing Administration. Details on the FHA move were not included in the high-level summary.

Why it matters: With mortgage rates still elevated and inventory tight in many markets, the near-term impact of any federal housing law will depend on how quickly local governments change zoning, permitting and infrastructure processes. Lenders, builders and brokers should watch how NAR and its state partners translate the law into specific local reforms and incentives.

NAR launched a central fraud-prevention hub and a consumer-facing guide aimed at helping members, associations and buyers and sellers spot red flags, protect sensitive information and safeguard transactions. The association also rolled out new fraud- and AI-focused education, including NAR NXT conference sessions and a Broker Power Hour on AI voice cloning and deepfake scams.

Why it matters: Wire fraud, business email compromise and emerging AI-enabled scams are driving higher operational and reputational risk on transactions. Centralized resources and training from NAR could influence how brokerages standardize verification, identity and communication protocols at the office level.

For commercial practitioners, NAR launched the Commercial Real Estate Demand Index and expanded the members-only Metro Market Dashboard. The association also released six local market assessment reports intended to give commercial Realtors a clearer view of where demand is growing across major property types.

Why it matters: With office valuations under pressure and higher rates reshaping cap rates, local demand data can help investors, lenders and brokers price risk, underwrite deals and identify resilient sectors within each metro.

NAR said it connected with more than 5,000 brokers in the quarter to discuss business challenges and share broker-focused resources. It also expanded broker programming and peer engagement, including a national broker networking session and planning for the first Broker Innovation Forum, scheduled for the NAR NXT conference.

The association said it is also building out data, technology and security resources, including expanded AI and emerging technology programming and new member research via the 2026 Realtors Technology Report, which tracks how agents are using tools in their businesses.

Additional third-quarter highlights cited by NAR include:

Why it matters: For brokerage leaders and MLS executives, NAR’s education and technology agenda will shape what agents are trained on — from AI usage to compliance — and may influence which tools and workflows firms prioritize heading into the 2027 market cycle.

NAR’s third-quarter update is part of a standing reporting cadence on its 2026–2028 strategic plan, which is organized around expanding housing opportunity, protecting market integrity and delivering business-building resources for members. The full update is available on NAR’s website.

#5545. Kylie Kelce Reveals the One Thing That Makes Someone the Perfect Houseguest

Kylie Kelce has revealed what a visitor needs to do to be the perfect guest in their home—and it has to do with impressing her and her NFL-star husband Jason Kelce's daughters.

On a recent episode of her podcast, "Not Gonna Lie," the mom of four revealed that their daughters— Finnley, 18 months, Bennett, 3, Elliotte, 5, and Wyatt, 7—love having guests read to them.

“I know one way to my girls’ hearts, and really kids, I always tell people you don’t need to bring gifts when you come to our house. If you come in, you sit down, you offer to read our girls a book, they will be like forever," she revealed.

Kelce added, “Like genuinely, we have obviously family [that] will come and they’ll bring this and they’ll bring that, but if when you come and you sit down, you read a book, I think it’s one of the best ways to connect with kids.”

The glimpse of her houseguest request came just days after she defended her and her spouse's decision to snap up multiple Philadelphia properties right next to each other.

In an episode of her podcast, which featured guest Nikki Glaser, Kelce, 34, and the comedian chatted about hate comments.

"Do you ever get in the comments? Do you ever get feisty?” Glaser asked.

In her reply, Kelce detailed an Instagram account that frequently posts information about their real estate.

“One of the ones that I did it—which was not to a person so it doesn’t really feel as aggressive—was like ‘Celeb Homes.’ They put a bird’s-eye view of where we live with our children, and they were trying to give details of our property," she said.

The account then revealed that the Kelce family had also purchased the home "next door."

She then told the comedian, "I think I typed ‘get f---ed.’ And then when I tried to post it, it wouldn’t let me. Why? I want to tell people to get f---ed."

Her admission came after she offered a glimpse of the family's childcare arrangements during an appearance on an episode of "IMO with Michelle Obama and Craig Robinson." She explained that she and the former Philadelphia Eagles star prefer to keep their relatives closely involved in raising their children.

The couple have built a support system that allows them to balance their professional commitments with family life.

A major part of that arrangement involves Kelce's parents, Lisa and Ed McDevitt, who live just 15 minutes from the family's Philadelphia-area home.

Kelce explained that her parents regularly help care for the girls, making it possible for her and Jason to navigate their busy schedules without relying on round-the-clock childcare.

Although the couple do employ a nanny, Kelce revealed that the arrangement is limited to traditional working hours rather than having someone live in their home.

“My husband and I have very busy schedules. We don’t necessarily want a live-in nanny or someone who’s going to be raising our kids void of us. That feels weird. So we do a lot with my parents every chance we get. We do things with Jason’s parents. We find that those are the values that we were raised with that we want our kids to have, not just because we tell them that, but because we live it," she explained.

The decision, she explained, reflects their desire to remain actively involved in their daughters' everyday lives.

Rather than bringing in someone to provide full-time care, the Kelces turn to their extended family for additional support.

Kelce said maintaining those close family relationships is particularly important because she wants her daughters to grow up with the same values that shaped her and Jason's childhoods.

She also emphasized how grateful she is for the nanny who helps the family during the workday, acknowledging that the additional support is essential to managing their responsibilities.

However, the couple's approach to childcare goes beyond convenience.

For Kelce, living close to her parents has been a priority, and she admitted that the thought of settling somewhere far from her family has never appealed to her.

“We couldn’t do it without my parents. My parents live 15 minutes from us, and they have helped us in every way imaginable," she said.

The Pennsylvania native explained that remaining in the area where she grew up has allowed her to preserve those relationships while raising her own family.

That connection to her hometown has also influenced the kind of upbringing she hopes to provide her daughters.

Kelce wants the girls to become familiar with the places that shaped her childhood, from local businesses to the community organizations that continue to play a role in her life.

She believes that growing up with those personal connections can help children develop a stronger sense of responsibility toward the communities around them.

Her own involvement with the Eagles Autism Foundation is one example of how she has maintained those local ties.

For Kelce, the opportunity to contribute to the community where she was raised is another benefit of remaining close to home.

“Now, granted, we do have a nanny. I always give a shoutout because we couldn’t do it without her, but we have her during regular work hours and really nothing outside of that," she added.

#5543. University AI’s biggest challenge? Scaling research without losing control

The push for sovereign AI is reaching university research labs, where control over data, models and compute now shapes what science gets done.

Universities sit at an unusual crossroads in the current technological shift, as their work spans open education and tightly controlled federal research. Learning sits at the heart of both missions, making AI a core supporting technology for expanding research and education alike, according to Vince Kellen (pictured, center), chief information officer of the Texas A&M University System.

“AI is a platform for thought. It’s a platform for discovery,” Kellen noted. “AI kind of undergirds all of what we’re going to be doing in the future — certainly what we’re doing in the present now.”

Kellen and Casey Bryan (right), chief information officer of the Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station, spoke with Krista Case (left) during theCUBE’s coverage of the AI Cybersecurity & Resilience Summit. They discussed how Texas A&M is building a secure, controlled foundation for AI-driven research. (* Disclosure below.)

The foundation of Texas A&M’s approach is IGNITE, short for Innovative Growth in Next Generation AI Technology Ecosystem. It is a state-funded AI and high-performance computing platform led by TEES, as the experiment station is known. Dell Technologies Inc. is building the system with Advanced Micro Devices Inc. graphics processing units inside an Equinix Inc. data center in Dallas. That investment will give research teams the computing power their existing systems lack, Bryan noted.

“Part of our current challenge is that existing resources, while they are performing some of that work, are severely underpowered,” he said. “Research is getting done but could be helped by capacity and scale, which I think IGNITE’s going to bring to the table.”

But the economics matter as much as the capability. Public attention has centered on neoclouds and cloud providers, yet on-premises data centers are growing significantly because of both security controls and cost, according to Kellen. High retail prices for AI computing resources are now limiting the ability of institutions to conduct scientific research.

“There’s no way we could take the science to your classic neocloud provider today and conduct the same thing,” Kellen said. “It’s 5 to 10x the cost.”

Controlling those assets significantly reduces costs and strengthens security, Kellen said. Sovereignty spans four pillars — data, infrastructure, capability and model, and governance — with Equinix supplying physical protection for the compute itself, Bryan added. As a state agency, TEES follows National Institute of Standards and Technology frameworks 800-53 and 800-171, as well as Texas Administrative Code 202, and it wants IGNITE to be ready for Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification Level 2.

“There’s a lot of controls we have to inherit, but our researchers shouldn’t have to think about all those,” Bryan said. “It should be absolutely seamless when they go to use the capabilities.”

That principle shaped the IGNITE build. When TEES sat down with Dell’s implementation team to schedule workshops, security came first, and the project’s architecture review board has since affirmed that direction, according to Bryan. For institutions starting their own sovereign AI projects, that sequencing is the lesson.

“The idea was to build that security foundation with which all of the other operational components could be built and referenced back to,” Bryan said. “At its core, start with security early — get it embedded in the process earlier on — and it’s much easier to keep it baked in at the beginning than have to worry about adding that at the end.”

#5542. Nationwide Equities debuts ReverseReach tool for mortgage broker lead generation help

Nationwide Equities has launched ReverseReach, a tool and help desk program that lets mortgage brokers and loan officers screen their existing customer databases for reverse mortgage opportunities without deep product expertise. The platform pairs a simple scenario runner with access to full-time underwriters, aiming to lower barriers to reverse lending and give originators a way to generate new business from past clients amid a challenging forward mortgage market.  AI Summary

Nationwide Equities Corp. has launched ReverseReach, a new tool and support program aimed at helping mortgage brokers and loan officers uncover reverse mortgage opportunities in their existing customer databases and referral networks, the company announced Tuesday.

The New Jersey-based wholesale reverse mortgage lender said ReverseReach is designed for originators who may not specialize in reverse products but have years of past customers who are now older, equity rich and potential candidates for reverse mortgages.

“Mortgage brokers may be sitting on substantial untapped business opportunities without even realizing it,” Paul Lamparillo, CEO of Nationwide Equities, said in a statement. “Over the years, brokers have built relationships with thousands of homeowners, many of whom may now qualify for reverse mortgage products.

“We created ReverseReach to make uncovering those highly lucrative opportunities simple, efficient and accessible — even for brokers who have never closed a reverse mortgage before — so they can confidently and comfortably begin originating them.”

The company has largely pivoted to proprietary reverse mortgage production, mirroring recent changes in the broader industry. Modex data shows that Nationwide Equities has originated 111 reverse mortgages for $216 million in volume over the past 12 months, while data compiled by Reverse Market Insight shows that it has endorsed 26 Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) through the first nine months of this year.

In 2020, Nationwide Equities launched its private-label reverse mortgage, EquityPower, which was built to offer higher loan proceeds than HECM products.

ReverseReach allows mortgage professionals to enter a borrower’s financial and property scenario and quickly gauge whether a reverse mortgage is worth pursuing. The program is positioned as a preliminary opportunity identification tool rather than a full underwriting engine.

Regardless of the initial result, brokers can connect with a live underwriter to discuss the file and potential structures, according to the company.

Nationwide Equities is pairing the technology with a help desk staffed by full-time Direct Endorsement (DE) underwriters who answer eligibility questions, help structure loans and walk brokers through complex borrower situations.

“One of the biggest obstacles to broader reverse mortgage adoption is simply recognizing when a borrower may be a good candidate,” Philip Parziale, president of Nationwide Equities said in a statement. “ReverseReach bridges that gap. Brokers don’t need to become reverse mortgage experts to identify a potential transaction. They need a simple way to recognize the opportunity and a knowledgeable lending partner to help them execute it.”

Parziale added that direct access to underwriters is a central part of the offering. “Regardless of how good your technology is, there is something special about being able to speak to a live person on the phone and walk you through a scenario and respond to follow ups,” he said.

The launch comes as volume in the broader forward mortgage market remains under pressure from higher rates, tighter affordability and intense competition for a smaller pool of qualified borrowers. Many retail and broker shops are looking to diversify into reverse mortgages, home equity products or nonqualified mortgages (non-QM) to stabilize production.

For brokers, the reverse space has historically been constrained by product complexity, reputation concerns and training requirements. ReverseReach aims to lower that barrier by giving originators a simple screening workflow across their existing loan origination system and past client lists, backed by lender-side expertise.

Lenders are investing in education and simple tools to capture aging-in-place demand from older homeowners with significant home equity. Brokers who have closed thousands of loans over the past decade may find that a meaningful share of these clients now meet age and equity thresholds for reverse products.

Nationwide Equities positions ReverseReach as a business development strategy focused on reengaging existing borrowers rather than purchasing new leads or ramping up paid marketing. Potential applications include:

#5540. NYC Votes to Cut Construction Red Tape in Bid to Spur More Homebuilding

New York City voters overwhelmingly approved a plan to overhaul the city's notoriously complicated construction permitting process Tuesday, handing Mayor Zohran Mamdani a victory in his effort to accelerate housing development.

Question 4, one of five ballot measures approved in the Nov. 3 election, received roughly 68% support, according to preliminary election results.

The measure promises to simplify construction by bringing 40 types of permits and approvals currently handled by 18 separate government offices and agencies into one centralized digital system.

"New Yorkers voted for a government that moves as fast as they do," Mamdani said in a statement Tuesday night, adding that the reforms would "directly address the affordability crisis and help New Yorkers stay in the city they love."

However, the new system isn't required to launch until 2030. Even when it does, faster permitting will address only one of the many obstacles making housing so difficult and expensive to build in New York.

"No single reform will be a silver bullet for housing supply and affordability, especially in a city like New York," explains Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com®. "Instead, each pro-supply policy change is a baby step in the right direction. And these marginal gains will add up."

The Big Apple needs approximately 700,000 additional homes over the next decade to meet existing and future demand, according to an August 2026 draft assessment from the city's housing and planning departments.

Yet developers filed plans for just 8,064 multifamily units in the second quarter of 2026, in a stunning 52% decline from the previous quarter, according to the Real Estate Board of New York.

That amounts to less than half the 17,500 new homes the city needs to add each quarter—and they're only proposed units, not completed homes.

Centralizing permits could help close that gap by cutting down the time and cost builders are forced to spend navigating city bureaucracy.

"Streamlining approvals can make a huge difference," Krimmel says. "It might not be the flashiest reform, but when it comes to new construction, time is money."

And permitting takes a very, very long time in New York City.

Of the nearly five years it takes to build a typical 20-unit apartment building in the Big Apple, roughly 1.5 years are spent securing permits alone, according to a September 2026 study examining construction timelines across 60 U.S. cities.

Now compare that to similar projects in Raleigh, NC, or Phoenix, AZ, where it takes roughly two years from application to completion.

"In a city like New York City with high land acquisition costs and a complex regulatory environment, predictability in timelines and financing can be critical for ensuring new construction can pencil," Krimmel says.

And research suggests those time savings could translate into more homes.

Cutting approval times by 25% could have increased multifamily housing production in Los Angeles, CA by 12.7% between 2010 and 2022, according to a 2026 study published in the Journal of Urban Economics.

When researchers accounted for additional development that faster approvals might encourage, the estimated increase reached 23.7%.

The question for New Yorkers, though, is when those reforms might translate into more housing options and lower rents. The median asking rent hit $3,785 in October—up 4.5% from a year ago.

Under the new rules, applicants would have one digital portal to submit documents, track applications, and obtain approvals, rather than navigating separate systems across multiple agencies.

But streamlining applications doesn't necessarily mean they'll be reviewed any faster.

In fact, the average time required to approve applications through the Department of Buildings' existing digital portal climbed from 8.3 days in 2020 to 20.3 days in 2025, according to a July report from New York State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli.

And its hardly the only challenge. Krimmel says the overhaul won't address other barriers to construction, including zoning restrictions and the complexity of financing multifamily developments.

Still, he sees the reform as one step toward untangling a much larger problem.

"In the same way that a complex web of red tape and veto points is extremely good at creating barriers to new construction, real solutions will require the city untangles that web bit by bit," he says.

With the new system potentially four years away, the first test will be whether it actually shortens permitting timelines. Any corresponding increase in housing construction—and relief for renters—could take considerably longer.

As Mamdani acknowledged Tuesday night, "Now comes the work of turning these votes into results."
