#5539. LGI Homes Q3 2026 earnings reveal leadership test in downturn

LGI Homes posted higher Q3 2026 revenue and improved gross margin while cutting SG&A dollars. Demand weakened materially, with orders down 61.2% and cancellations up, putting focus on leadership, culture, and capital discipline.  AI Summary

A peculiar phenomenon in homebuilding has fascinated me for much of the past two-plus decades.

In virtually every market, across almost every customer segment and price point, a handful of homebuilders consistently outperform competitors facing essentially the same business conditions.

They face the same mortgage rates, land and development costs, labor constraints, household purchasing-power challenges and regulatory obstacles. They work with essentially the same raw materials, including people, capital, building products, subcontractors and operating processes. Yet their results can differ dramatically, especially when business conditions turn difficult.

A decade or so ago, a highly regarded homebuilding business strategist mused aloud to me about this phenomenon. He was struck by how companies dealt with essentially the same competitive hand, yet a few outlier leaders figured out how to produce better results than the rest.

I’ve thought about that observation often, particularly during periods when the industry’s cyclical pressures expose the difference between companies that can withstand adversity and those that can turn adversity into an opportunity to strengthen their businesses.

The distinction is especially relevant now. U.S. homebuilders are facing an unforgiving mix of weak selling conditions, elevated capital costs, stubbornly high land and development expenses, and households whose purchasing power has failed to keep pace with the cost of homeownership. These pressures have persisted long enough to strain business plans based on more favorable assumptions, and little is certain about when conditions will improve.

Which brings us to LGI Homes, its Q3 2026 earnings report, and a question that extends well beyond a single company’s quarterly performance:

What distinguishes homebuilding enterprises whose leaders and organizations can emerge from a prolonged downturn stronger than they entered it?

LGI Homes’ November 3 earnings report is a useful case study because its operating results show both encouraging evidence of management’s execution and unmistakable signs that the business faces tough sledding ahead.

The Woodlands, Texas-based builder reported 1,222 home closings in the third quarter, including 33 currently or previously leased homes, a 10.4% increase from the year-earlier quarter. Homebuilding revenues rose 10.3% to $437.5 million, and net income increased to $24.6 million, or $1.05 per diluted share, compared with $19.7 million, or $0.85 per share, in the year-earlier quarter.

Profitability and expense management emerged as clear strengths. Homebuilding gross margin reached 20.2%, and adjusted homebuilding gross margin was 23.7%, both up 40 basis points sequentially. Selling, general and administrative expenses declined 2.5% in absolute dollars, while SG&A as a percentage of total revenue improved 180 basis points year over year, reflecting operational rigor and executional excellence.

The company also reduced its net debt-to-capital ratio to 40.6%, up 420 basis points from a year earlier, and ended September with $447.7 million in liquidity. Its active community count increased by 7.1% year over year to 151.

Yet a forward-looking lens tells a far less rosy story. Net orders plunged 61.2% to 609 homes, down from 1,570 a year earlier, while the cancellation rate rose to 53.8% from 33.6%. Backlog declined 47.5% to 685 homes. Management narrowed its full-year closing guidance to 4,600 to 4,800 homes, reflecting weaker sales activity and ongoing affordability pressures.

These results speak of the vulnerability of LGI’s business model at a time when the company’s core customer is among the most financially constrained in the housing market.

LGI has built much of its business around helping renters become homeowners through a direct-to-consumer sales model, speculative construction, and a value proposition that emphasizes attainable monthly payments. These capabilities have helped distinguish the company for years. They also leave its sales performance especially vulnerable to turbulent headwinds, such as mortgage-rate movements and changes in buyer qualification.

The third-quarter numbers make it clear that LGI’s operational strengths have not shielded it from those pressures. Will the capabilities that helped the company develop its distinctive business model now enable it to adapt more effectively than competitors under the same conditions?

Wolfe Research’s November 3 assessment of LGI serves as an important counterweight to any temptation to interpret the company’s earnings performance as evidence that it has already mastered the current downturn.

Analyst Trevor Allinson and his team credited LGI’s Q3 operating performance, namely its gross-margin strength and SG&A expense reductions, while maintaining a Peer Perform rating. Wolfe noted that LGI’s predominantly self-developed land position supports margins at a time when several competitors have sustained hits to sequential margins.

Wolf Research’s analysis also explicitly recognizes LGI’s process-driven organization as a competitive strength, citing the company’s ability to pare back operating errors in land acquisition, construction efficiency and warranty management.

This is not to say that Wall Street exactly overlooks the value of management execution or organizational capability. Wolfe’s analysis shows that analysts recognize those strengths and attempt to account for their financial impact. What’s hard to quantify is how much those muscle-memory operational capabilities can influence future results when demand remains both tepid and unpredictable.

Wolfe’s assessment highlights that LGI’s order decline creates a difficult trade-off between sales pace and profitability. With third-quarter net order absorption averaging about 1.3 homes per community per month, the company faces pressure to accelerate sales, potentially through additional incentives that would erode margins.

The firm reduced its 2027 earnings-per-share estimate by 30.1%, from $3.42 to $2.39, reflecting its expectation that weaker demand and the need to balance price against sales volume will constrain profitability. Its concerns also extend to LGI’s leverage, its comparatively high SG&A expense ratio, and its substantial owned-land position, all of which can weigh on returns when inventory turnover slows.

Those financial risks aren’t merely temporary obstacles that a strong corporate culture can surmount through resolve.

LGI’s net debt-to-capital ratio of 40.6% remains elevated relative to many competitors, despite recent improvements. Its 50,270 owned lots represent a substantial capital commitment, especially given current sales rates.

The company therefore enters the next phase of this downturn with meaningful strengths, but also with structural exposures that could constrain its flexibility if weak demand persists.

In a conversation earlier this week, Tony Avila, founder of Builder Advisor Group and Avila Real Estate Capital, offered a useful framework for identifying homebuilders best positioned to weather and grow stronger in the current environment.

Avila cited stronger margins, lower leverage, attractive finished-lot positions, higher returns on capital, and the ability to serve a broader range of buyers as key indicators of financial strength. Geographic diversification can provide additional protection, although builders operating in individual markets with favorable supply-and-demand dynamics may also be well positioned.

His observations reflect a reality that homebuilding’s financial fundamentals become especially important when market conditions deteriorate and access to capital becomes more expensive or more restrictive. Builders with stronger balance sheets and favorable land positions can preserve liquidity, maintain operational flexibility, and pursue opportunities that weaker competitors may be forced to abandon.

Avila also cautioned that the industry’s current difficulties could persist into 2028, suggesting that the ability to withstand a prolonged period of weak demand may become an increasingly important competitive distinction.

These characteristics provide an essential foundation for evaluating resilience. They identify which companies have the financial capacity to withstand adversity and retain strategic options while competitors face mounting constraints.

I would argue that they represent the table stakes of resilience rather than its full measure.

Financial strength can give an enterprise room to maneuver, but it does not necessarily indicate whether management will recognize changing opportunities, make the right adjustments, or mobilize its organization to perform better.

By the same token, a company that falls short of some of these financial criteria may possess organizational capabilities that enable it to improve its position over time, provided its financial constraints do not undermine those efforts.

For LGI, its land holdings and leverage are sources of financial risk, yet its operating history and recent management decisions suggest an organization actively attempting to adapt rather than simply waiting for market conditions to improve.

At the recent HousingWire Homebuilder Summit in Dallas, I introduced a framework for evaluating the organizational qualities that distinguish homebuilding enterprises capable of sustained improvement.

I described five interdependent characteristics: Character. Capability. Collaboration. Competitive fire. And customer-first culture.

Together, they form what I think of as a leadership stack, analogous to the technology stack, the capital stack, or a coordinated network of subcontractors that supports other essential elements of a homebuilding business.

Character builds the trust that enables leaders and teams to confront difficult realities and make decisions that serve the enterprise’s long-term interests. Capability reflects the organization’s accumulated knowledge, skills, and ability to execute, while collaboration enables people across functions and markets to learn from one another and solve problems more effectively.

Competitive fire fuels the determination to improve performance rather than accept prevailing conditions as an excuse for disappointing results. A customer-first culture keeps the entire organization focused on delivering homes and experiences that people genuinely need, value, and can afford.

These qualities are not substitutes for sound financial management. Their value lies in how they influence the decisions, processes and behaviors that ultimately drive financial results.

Nor can they be established simply through executive declarations about corporate culture. More convincing evidence comes from what leaders and their organizations actually do when prior assumptions break apart.

LGI’s predominantly owned and self-developed land position has long been central to its operating model. By keeping much of the land development process in-house, the company has sought to manage lot costs, maintain product consistency, and preserve margins that might otherwise be surrendered to third-party developers.

During the earnings call, Chairman and CEO Eric Lipar emphasized the importance of the strategy.

“Our on-balance sheet predominantly owned land strategy, together with our in-house development capabilities reflects the long-term decisions we’ve made to set LGI apart from much of the industry. It remains a competitive advantage, generating strong margins while giving us flexibility to adapt to changing market conditions.”

LGI’s Q3 margin performance reflects these advantages. However, the risks of tying up capital in land become more pronounced when demand slows and projected absorption rates prove overly optimistic.

Management has reduced its owned-lot position for six consecutive quarters, from a peak of 61,893 lots in the second quarter of 2022 to 50,270 as of September 30, 2026. Meanwhile, controlled lots increased 18.1% sequentially to 8,130, reflecting opportunities to pursue finished-lot takedowns and smaller projects that meet the company’s current underwriting requirements.

These adjustments do not transform LGI into an asset-light builder, nor do they eliminate the financial consequences of its current land investments. They do, however, demonstrate a willingness to adjust capital commitments while preserving the capabilities that have historically differentiated its business.

CFO Charles Merdian offered another example during the earnings call, explaining that the company has adjusted the size and timing of future development sections to reflect slower absorption assumptions.

Those tactics involve altering project execution, even after initial land acquisitions and infrastructure investments. Management cannot recover all previously committed capital, but it can adjust the timing and amount of additional investment required to bring future lots to market.

This is organizational adaptability expressed through capital allocation and operational execution. It reflects the capacity to revisit assumptions, coordinate decisions across land development and construction functions, and change course without necessarily abandoning the underlying strategy.

LGI’s speculative construction and direct-to-consumer sales model offers another example of the distinction between adapting an operating strategy and abandoning its core customer proposition.

The company has historically focused on renters and first-time buyers whose purchasing decisions depend heavily on affordable monthly payments and the ability to move into a completed home on a relatively predictable schedule.

That positioning has become more challenging as mortgage rates and household expenses have tightened qualification standards. LGI’s elevated cancellation rate and sharp decline in orders indicate that its core customers are struggling to convert interest in homeownership into completed transactions.

Yet Lipar’s comments suggest management views the company’s customer knowledge and operating specialization as reasons to maintain its basic approach while modifying the supporting processes.

“We continue to see interest in homeownership, and our job is to remain disciplined while adapting our sales and financing strategies, production plans and product offering to current conditions.”

The company has expanded its sales process to accommodate buyers who need more time to qualify, while using closing-cost assistance, mortgage-rate buydowns and forward rate commitments to improve payment affordability. Management has also emphasized the need to adjust production plans and product offerings without sacrificing the features and customer experience that support the company’s value proposition.

These measures cannot eliminate the underlying affordability problem. Their effectiveness will depend on whether enough prospective customers can ultimately qualify and close at prices that maintain acceptable returns.

But they illustrate the strategic value of an organization that understands its customers well enough to adapt how it serves them while remaining committed to the needs that originally shaped its business model.

In this context, a customer-first culture becomes more than a statement of corporate values. It becomes a source of operating intelligence that informs decisions on financing, product, inventory, and the allocation of sales resources.

Of the five characteristics in the leadership stack, competitive fire may be the hardest to measure and the easiest to misunderstand or even overlook.

It is not merely optimism about an eventual market recovery, an appetite for expansion, or an unwillingness to acknowledge deteriorating conditions. Competitive fire becomes a meaningful organizational advantage when it fosters a persistent determination to improve performance while maintaining the discipline needed to protect the enterprise.

Founded in 2003, the company gained much of its early operating experience during the period surrounding the Great Financial Crisis, when collapsing housing demand, restricted credit and widespread industry failures forced homebuilders to reconsider fundamental assumptions about their businesses.

LGI emerged from that period and later expanded into a national homebuilder operating in 36 markets across 21 states. The company reports that it has earned a profit every year since its founding, a record that spans both the financial crisis and the industry’s more recent cycles of disruption.

That history does not establish that LGI will outperform during the current downturn. The industry’s competitive environment, capital structures, and affordability challenges have changed substantially since the GFC.

It does, however, suggest the company has developed institutional familiarity with adversity and a management culture shaped by operating without favorable market conditions. Its current community expansion strategy will be a significant test of that culture.

LGI expects to end 2027 with more than 180 active communities, approximately 20% above its third-quarter 2026 count. Management says much of the capital needed to support those openings has already been invested, allowing the company to expand its selling capacity without taking on incremental debt specifically to fund the openings.

At the same time, management expects the new communities to achieve absorption rates and margins similar to those currently seen, rather than assuming an imminent recovery in buyer demand. LGI is positioning itself for greater market reach while attempting to underwrite growth against the difficult conditions it observes, not the more favorable conditions it might prefer.

The strategy carries substantial execution risk. Expanding into more communities does not automatically translate into stronger earnings or higher returns when the pool of qualified buyers is constrained, and additional operating capacity can become a financial burden if sales productivity remains weak.

Still, the decision reflects an effort to preserve future growth opportunities while aligning investment and production plans with current market realities. Whether competitive fire becomes a genuine advantage will depend on how effectively LGI’s leadership and team execute those plans, learn from setbacks, and improve results in the coming quarters.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s concept of antifragility offers a useful way to frame the distinction between companies that merely survive adversity and those that become stronger because of it.

Resilience is the ability to absorb shocks, withstand disruption, and recover. Antifragility goes further, describing systems that benefit from volatility, stress, and uncertainty rather than merely enduring them.

Now, homebuilding is inherently cyclical, capital-intensive, and exposed to forces beyond the control of even its most capable executives. A resilient homebuilder may retain enough financial strength to weather a prolonged downturn and resume growth when demand improves. An antifragile homebuilder would use that same period to improve its processes, strengthen its people, sharpen its understanding of customers, and develop competitive advantages that leave it better positioned than before.

A single quarter of improved margins or successful cost reductions cannot establish the difference. It requires evidence that the organization has turned difficult experience into durable improvements in performance and competitive capability.

LGI has not yet demonstrated that outcome in the current cycle, but it has shown a willingness to adapt key elements of its operating model while preserving the strategic capabilities that management believes distinguish the company. Its land development adjustments, inventory management, sales-process changes and disciplined approach to balancing margins against volume provide observable evidence of that effort.

The next several quarters will show whether those decisions can improve absorption rates, cash generation, returns on capital, and competitive position, particularly if the industry’s difficult demand conditions persist through 2027 and beyond.

The industry’s current challenges are likely to produce meaningful differences in performance among homebuilders that appear superficially similar in their geographic exposure, customer segments and product offerings.

Homebuilding’s outliers are not necessarily the companies that begin a downturn with the strongest balance sheets, the most favorable markets, or the fewest obstacles. Those advantages matter enormously, but they do not fully explain why certain competitors consistently outperform.

The more elusive advantage lies in how organizations use their resources, learn from changing conditions, and translate leadership into sustained operational improvement.

That is where competitive fire – the determination that drives an organization to keep finding ways to improve when headwinds make improvement hardest – plays a role in homebuilding business outcomes that’s all too unappreciated.

#5538. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5537. North Carolina Passes New Limits on Property Tax Levies

On Tuesday, North Carolina voters narrowly approved House Bill 1089, which proposed a limit on property tax increases. The amendment needed 60% of voters to support it in order to pass. It received 60.4% support.

The amendment does not specify the terms of those limits. Instead, that will be up to the North Carolina General Assembly to decide.

Proponents, including North Caroline House Speaker Destin Hall, contended that surging property assessments have enabled local governments to impose excessive tax burdens on residents without delivering proportional public services. Last year, Hall formed the House Select Committee on Property Tax Reduction and Reform, a 23-member committee to examine property taxes in the state.

“Families are getting ripped off as some, but by no means all, local governments rake in billions more than inflation and population growth warrant,” Hall said in a press release earlier this year.

Support for the amendment fell across party lines. Conservatives and commercial organizations supported the measure, arguing that the amendment would help curb local government spending and protect property owners.

Political pundits theorized that the ballot measures were meant to entice Republican voters to the polls during an off-election year. But Western Carolina University Professor Chris Cooper told NPR's All Things Considered the theory didn't hold much weight to him.

"The notion that North Carolinians were not going to show up and vote from the Republican persuasion, but now they are because of a constitutional amendment, is on there, frankly that stretches credibility for me a little bit."

But critics of the proposal said that creating a property tax cap would hobble local governments. Further, the North Carolina Housing Coalition argued that the proposal would most benefit larger corporate property owners while providing little benefit to owners of single-family homes.

Tamika Walker Kelly, president of the North Carolina Association of Educators, criticized the bill for favoring “tax breaks over classrooms.”

“When local revenue is constrained, schools feel it immediately with overcrowded classrooms, aging school buildings and educators stretched too thin,” Walker Kelly told NC Newsline. “A constitutional cap does not protect struggling families, it protects the largest landowners in the state, while the families who depend on public schools are left with less.”

In the U.S., property tax rates are determined at the local level and vary widely. The average effective property tax rate on owner-occupied housing in North Carolina is .66%, which is relatively low compared with states like New Jersey and Illinois, where the effective tax rate is 1.88%, according to Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan tax policy nonprofit.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5536. Ballot roulette: Florida voters pick property tax break over local services

Florida voters approved a homestead exemption expansion with 62% support, with increases to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Opponents warned of public safety and service impacts, and state analysts projected nearly $5 billion in lost local revenue in 2027-28.  AI Summary

With the cost of living on the ballot, Florida voters approved a major tax break for homeowners.

The amendment to increase the Sunshine State’s homestead exemption won the 60% it needed on election night. Voters weren’t swayed by warnings that the higher exemption would devastate municipal coffers and services.

The ballot measure was given little chance of winning. But current economic conditions proved an insurmountable obstacle for the argument against the measure.

Unofficial returns showed it finishing with 62% of the vote. The changes take effect in phases starting in 2027.

“An incredible victory for Florida homeowners!” the Florida Republican Party wrote on social media. “More money stays in your pocket.”

Neil Schiller, managing partner at Government Law Group, told HousingWire TBD the result will change how cities weigh development.

“Projects that generate jobs, economic activity, and alternative tax revenues may become more attractive, while developments that require significant public services and infrastructure will face greater financial scrutiny,” Schiller said. “Amendment 3 may be remembered as the moment Florida cities had to fundamentally reinvent how they do business.”

The vote shows how important affordability has become, Andrew Hellinger, co-principal at Urban-X Group, developer of River Landing Shops & Residences in Miami, said in an e-mail to HousingWire TBD.

Hellinger added, “However, people still need roads, public transportation and essential community services, and those have to be paid for.”

The amendment replaces the $50,000 homestead exemption with a phased increase. It rises to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Only primary residences qualify, so second-home and investment-property owners get nothing.

Homeowners must establish Florida residency by Dec. 31, 2026, to get the full benefit. Later arrivals get the $50,000 exemption for four years before qualifying. The school board levy is excluded.

The measure also cuts the annual assessment cap on non-homestead commercial property from 10% to 5%. That change starts Jan. 1, 2027. Renters, who occupy about a third of Florida’s housing units, get no relief.

Gov. Ron DeSantis called a special session to put the amendment on the ballot. Lawmakers approved it with changes protecting school funding. DeSantis had sought a broader exemption.

DeSantis cast the measure as a fix for tax bills inflated by pandemic-era migration. Newcomers, led by New Yorkers, overwhelmed the housing supply and lifted values and tax burdens for longtime residents. Florida home prices rose more than 50% between 2020 and 2022.

Prices have since stalled, and the average home value fell 3.7% over the past year. Assessments haven’t followed: under the Save Our Homes recapture rule, they keep rising until they meet market value. The annual increase is capped at 3% or inflation, whichever is less.

Most counties held millage rates steady or cut them, yet bills still climbed. City tax bills statewide rose about 50% on average over several years.

The Florida Sheriffs Association said in August it was “significantly concerned.” By mid-September, it was running ads featuring sheriffs from four counties. One said, “We want a tax cut too, but Amendment 3 is the wrong way to do it.”

Association President Billy Woods warned of fewer deputies, slower 911 response and more crime. Opponents also included the Florida State Fraternal Order of Police, Florida Professional Firefighters and Florida Fire Chiefs Association. The Florida League of Cities and Florida Association of Counties opposed it, citing too much uncertainty.

According to the legislature’s economic research office, estimated local governments would lose nearly $5 billion in 2027-28.

The Florida Policy Institute, a progressive think tank, created Floridians for Shared Prosperity, which sponsored a campaign urging a no vote.

“Amendment 3 will leave working families and seniors with a lose-lose choice: pay more through new fees and higher taxes or face major cuts to the services you depend on,” the campaign’s website stated.

Voters approved the amendment anyway, with encouragement from the Florida Realtors and others in real estate.

“This is your one shot at real property tax relief,” apartment owner and investor Grant Washington wrote on social media Monday. “Vote Yes on Amendment 3 and put your money back where it belongs. In your pocket!”

#5535. Oracle urges database customers to prepare for quantum security risks

Attackers can copy encrypted traffic today and decrypt it once quantum computers mature, making quantum-resistant cryptography a present-day concern.

Oracle Corp. is applying the philosophy behind its security controls beneath AI agents to encryption across database fleets, according to Vipin Samar (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering, database security, at Oracle.

“Even though we don’t have quantum computers which are sufficiently powerful today, when they come, that can create a risk because people can make a copy of your encrypted data today,” Samar said. “Your TLS 1.2 traffic, 1.3 traffic, I can make a copy of it. And then when quantum becomes available, I can figure out the session key and decrypt … your entire sensitive data.”

Samar spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed security concerns related to quantum-resistant cryptography. (* Disclosure below.)

Oracle’s new Cryptographic Posture Assessment in Oracle Data Safe assesses cryptographic configurations across database fleets, flagging weak spots such as lingering TLS 1.0 and 1.1 support. Agentic AI-driven remediation is in preview, Samar noted.

“It doesn’t help if network encryption is strong, but other parts are actually on the weaker side. And this becomes a challenge, especially when PQC or the quantum computers come along because they can attempt to hack into any of those systems,” Samar said.

Deep Data Security, which enforces row- and column-level access in Oracle AI Database 26ai, uses signed OAuth2 tokens to identify the end user behind an AI agent’s query. Oracle treats AI as one more application accessing the same data.

“We said instead of sprinkling this dust everywhere, why don’t we secure at the source?” Samar said. “When you move something inside the database, you get great security because there are no ways to bypass it.”

#5534. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5533. What housing market headlines can’t tell your clients

National housing demand is showing signs of stabilizing, but local market conditions tell a more nuanced story. HousingWire Data shows diverging trends between Houston and its broader metro, rising inventory and pricing pressure in Phoenix, and changing inventory patterns in Tampa. Interactive HousingWire Intelligence charts help housing professionals identify emerging shifts and translate market data into actionable guidance for buyers and sellers.  AI Summary

Mortgage rates are moving closer to 7%, and housing demand is showing signs of stabilizing. But what does that mean for a homeowner preparing to list, a buyer wondering whether to wait or an agent trying to set realistic expectations?

In his latest Housing Market Tracker, HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami explains why a path to sub-7% mortgage rates is back on the table. While weekly pending home sales have recently stabilized, that doesn’t yet signal a sustained recovery.

For housing professionals, the opportunity is to translate those national trends into what clients are experiencing in their own markets.

HousingWire Data from Houston, Phoenix and Tampa reveals three things worth watching:

A client sees that housing demand is stabilizing and asks whether it’s finally a good time to sell.

Houston demonstrates why the answer requires more local context.

Across the Houston metro, the ratio of new pending sales to new listings improved during October, but not because buyer activity increased. New listings declined faster than pending sales, making the ratio look stronger even as fewer homes went under contract.

Within Houston city limits, the opposite happened. Pending sales declined faster than new listings, pushing the ratio lower.

Even inventory told a different story. Active inventory was higher than a year ago across the metro but lower within the city.

Neither market showed growing pending activity, yet the conditions affecting buyers and sellers were different.

For a homeowner, that distinction matters more than whether a regional headline describes the market as improving.

The takeaway: Use broader housing trends to start the conversation, then show clients what’s happening among the homes they’re actually competing with. A seller needs to understand current competition and buyer activity, not simply whether the overall market appears stronger.

A homeowner considering whether to wait for lower mortgage rates might assume that more affordable financing will bring more buyers.

But lower rates could also encourage more sellers to list, making the relationship between supply and demand especially important.

Phoenix illustrates what happens when several indicators point in the same direction.

Over the latest four-week period, new pending sales declined faster than new listings. Compared with a year ago, pending activity was down nearly 17%, while new listings were slightly higher.

Meanwhile, active inventory continued to grow, and more than half of active listings had experienced a price reduction.

Together, those indicators suggest increasing competition among sellers. Fewer homes are moving into pending status, more inventory is available and price reductions are becoming more prevalent.

That doesn’t guarantee prices will fall, but it identifies conditions that could create additional pricing pressure if the trend continues.

The takeaway: Don’t evaluate pending sales, inventory or price reductions in isolation. When several indicators reinforce one another, they provide stronger evidence of where conditions may be headed. That can help sellers evaluate pricing and timing, while giving buyers a clearer picture of their negotiating position.

A seller points out that inventory is still lower than last year. Does that mean competition remains limited?

Tampa shows why the direction of recent activity matters just as much as the year-over-year comparison.

Within Tampa city limits, new listings and pending sales were essentially unchanged over the latest four weeks. Active inventory remained below last year’s level, and the share of listings with price reductions had declined.

But inventory was also beginning to increase compared with the preceding four weeks.

That doesn’t establish a market shift. Recent pending activity has been relatively steady, and price-cut share continues to ease. Still, the inventory increase is worth monitoring.

If inventory continues building while pending activity remains weak, sellers could face greater competition even before the year-over-year inventory comparison turns positive.

Try it yourself: Switch the chart above between 6M and YoY. The six-month view shows how inventory has been building recently, while the year-over-year comparison reveals that inventory remains below last year’s levels. Both are true, but each tells you something different about the market.The takeaway: A favorable market statistic doesn’t mean conditions are standing still. Track recent changes alongside year-over-year trends, and revisit pricing or buying strategies when the evidence begins to shift.

Logan’s Housing Market Tracker provides the national context. HousingWire Intelligence helps professionals connect that context to the markets where their clients are making decisions.

Use HousingWire Intelligence to chart new listings, pending sales, active inventory and price reductions in your city. Look at how the indicators move together over time, compare recent changes with the same period last year and consider what those patterns mean for the properties your clients are buying or selling.

Your clients can find national headlines and AI-generated market summaries on their own. What they need from you is the expertise to explain what those trends mean for their home, their competition and their next decision.

Methodology: HousingWire Data analysis of single-family homes across all price quartiles for the four weeks ending Oct. 30, 2026, compared with the preceding four weeks and the equivalent period in 2025. City-level figures are used for Houston, Phoenix and Tampa, with Houston metro data included for comparison. New listings and pending sales are four-week totals; inventory and price-cut shares are averages of weekly snapshots. Price-cut share represents active listings that have experienced a reduction, not reductions made during the reporting period.

#5531. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5530. Bright turns on Ocusell integration so agents enter listings once

Bright MLS launched a live integration with Ocusell’s network, letting agents enter and edit listings once and syndicate to Bright and other MLSs. Ocusell says it can cut listing creation time up to 75% and prevent over 85% of compliance errors.  AI Summary

Bright MLS has turned on its live integration with Ocusell’s listing network, allowing brokers and agents who work across multiple MLSs in the Mid-Atlantic to enter and edit listings once and syndicate them into Bright and other participating MLSs without double data entry, the companies announced Tuesday.

The operational launch marks the first major product milestone from the joint venture Bright and Ocusell formed in 2025 and introduces OneList, a co-developed listing input platform built on the Ocusell Network that is designed to give brokerages and MLSs a single, connected listing interface nationwide.

“We entered into this joint venture to remove friction from the daily work of our brokers and agents,” said Bright MLS President and CEO Brian Donnellan, who is also a HousingWire Vanguard award winner. “Our role as an MLS is to adapt to how real estate pros operate and to help them succeed. This partnership with Ocusell is a clear example of that.”

The launch comes as the Open Real Estate (ORE) initiative is running a national request for proposal search for a vendor that can deliver “input once, distribute everywhere” listing entry across markets. Ocusell says it is already live across 30 MLSs, and with OneList now operating at Bright, one of the nation’s largest MLSs, the company is positioning its network as a scalable solution for multi-MLS entry.

For brokers, the integration is aimed at reducing staff time and compliance risk tied to re-keying listing data into separate MLS systems. Agents can enter listing specifics, photos and disclosures once; the platform then auto-validates those fields against each local MLS’s rules while maintaining existing access and display policies. According to Ocusell, its infrastructure can cut listing creation time by up to 75% and prevent more than 85% of compliance errors.

On top of cross-market sync, according to the announcement, the forthcoming OneList interface layers in real-time AI-driven compliance and Fair Housing screening, intelligent media management with automated photo tagging and organization, and integrated listing promotion that lets agents launch targeted marketing campaigns from the listing input workflow.

“This is a total game changer for agents, brokers, and home buyers and sellers,” said Steve Mapes, executive in charge of growth strategy at Bright MLS. “When agents aren’t stuck doing double data entry because they belong to multiple MLSs, they have more time to serve their clients and do what they do best. Technology should make things better, faster and more efficient, and we’re excited to get this up and running.”

“Now is the time for MLSs to help shape what comes next for their brokers,” Hayden Rieveschl, the CEO of Ocusell and a 2026 HousingWire Insider, said in a statement. “Bright and Ocusell are demonstrating what’s possible when you listen to brokers and turn their needs into action. As more brokerages operate across markets, MLSs have an opportunity to remove barriers and make doing business easier.”

The move reflects a broader shift in organized real estate as large regional brokerages, teams and franchises increasingly span multiple MLS territories while regulators and plaintiffs’ attorneys scrutinize how listing data is shared and displayed.

For brokers and agents, multi-MLS input has historically meant duplicate work, inconsistent data, higher error rates and delays getting listings in front of buyers across markets. A centralized entry layer like OneList, if widely adopted, could streamline operations for multi-market firms, tighten compliance controls and create more standardized listing data for downstream tools, portals and valuation models.

For MLS organizations, the Bright-Ocusell rollout is a signal that listing input may increasingly be handled through connected, vendor-operated platforms rather than bespoke MLS-only interfaces, potentially reshaping how MLSs think about technology procurement, interoperability and data licensing.

Ocusell said the integration is live now for active Bright MLS brokerages that manage listings across multiple markets, according to the announcement. Bright said rollout timelines and early-access details for the broader OneList platform will be shared in future communications.

#5529. Oracle rethinks the lakehouse as AI agents become data consumers

A shared semantic layer is fast becoming the dividing line between lakehouses built for reporting and those built for artificial intelligence.

As AI agents join human analysts in querying corporate data, enterprises need platforms that make sense of information scattered across clouds, formats and rival systems. Oracle Corp. has spent the past year rebuilding its data stack around that shift, part of a broader database modernization push. The company now pitches its Autonomous AI Lakehouse as an open layer that sits across an enterprise’s existing data estate rather than replacing it, according to Nipun Agarwal (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering, Oracle Database, at Oracle.

“Lakehouses were the platform which customers use for running analytics,” Agarwal said. “Now, lakehouses have become the decision backbone for AI.”

Agarwal spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Oracle’s Autonomous AI Lakehouse combines a shared semantic layer with fast, real-time access to data across platforms to support AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

Oracle’s approach rests on a catalog that can mount other catalogs, such as Databricks Inc.’s Unity Catalog, along with Postgres and MySQL databases, so data is queried in place rather than copied. The company announced a business semantic layer and broader Apache Iceberg support at the October event, with table and column descriptions the system generates applying to non-Oracle sources as well, according to Agarwal. Crucially, Oracle does not see the offering as competing with other lakehouses, he added.

“We really believe that for any enterprise, they’re gonna have a choice,” he said. “They’re gonna be using multiple data sources. They’ll have multiple lakehouses.”

Oracle’s Lake Cache speeds up queries by moving the most-used Iceberg tables into Exadata’s flash cache. Real-time access is also becoming essential as software agents become the main consumers of the data: Scheduled refreshes of copied data can fall short when agents request it on demand, according to Agarwal.

“With AI that’s no longer the case, because for AI, the consumer is not a human necessarily,” Agarwal said. “The need for real-time access is a lot more with AI.”
