#5528. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5527. Zillow pushes Preferred agent program toward 100% of buyer connections

Zillow reported Q3 2026 traffic down 3% to 215 million monthly users and a $158 million net loss. It highlighted AI mode expansion, Preferred growth and gains in mortgage and rentals revenue.  AI Summary

Zillow may be facing calls for investigations into some of its practices by consumer advocacy organizations and federal lawmakers, but the real estate listing portal giant is doubling down on its belief that it is “building the faster, easier and more affordable moving experience.”

“As more consumers and professionals use Zillow to move from dreaming to transacting, the old real estate experience will feel slow, difficult and expensive by comparison,”  Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman and Zillow COO and CFO Jeremy Hofmann wrote in a letter to shareholders published on Wednesday.

Despite this confidence, Zillow may be facing some headwinds. The company said that in the third quarter of 2026, visitor traffic to its apps and sites was down 3% during the quarter to 215 million average monthly unique users, while overall visits were down 5% annually to 2.3 billion according to Comscore data. Despite the declines, Comscore data shows that Zillow attracted 77% of average monthly unique visitors in the real estate category in Q3. In addition to this, the company said it has found that its AI search mode is deepening engagement, with visitors who use this option spending nearly three times as long as those who don’t on the site.

Zillow said that AI mode is now available to 100% of its signed-in users. The company said it was also exploring ways to use AI to make real estate professionals more productive and to help its internal engineers, who are using AI to ship 60% more changes to production than they did in 2024, according to Zillow.

“Buyers spend an average of two to three hours a week with us over about five months — and then for most, Zillow software and services power their transaction: the majority of residential real estate transactions in the U.S. run through our professional software,” the executives wrote. “Because of Zillow’s transaction infrastructure, our agentic AI does more than guide the shopping experience people love; it assists consumers and professionals throughout the transaction itself.

In addition to the decline in traffic, Zillow also reported a net loss of $158 million for the quarter, down from a $10 million net income generated in Q3 2025. This decline came even as revenue rose 7% annually to $724 million.

Zillow’s Preferred lead referral program is one of cornerstones of its revenue generation engine. The company reported that in Q3, two-thirds of buyer connections came to a Preferred agent partner in the integrated experience, roughly double what it was a year ago. Zillow said it was on track for Preferred to represent over three-quarters of connections by the end of the year, with it anticipating reaching 100% of connections in the first half of 2027. Zillow also noted that Preferred connections generate 35% more revenue per connection that its previous lead generation model.

Even with the growth of the Preferred program, Zillow’s for-sale revenue was flat year-over-year at $489 million. In addition to this, its residential segment recorded a 4% annual decline in revenue to $419 million, which the company attributed to higher-than-expected mortgage rates putting downward pressure on housing transaction volume.

Bright spots in Zillow’s Q3 earnings report occurred in its mortgage and rentals segments. Zillow’s mortgage rose 32% annually to $70 million, due to a 55% increase in purchase loan origination volume to $2.0 billion.

In markets where Zillow has integrated its mortgage product with its Preferred program the longest, Zillow said adoption rates of Zillow Home Loans is around 20%.

“We are also making Zillow Home Loans a trusted lender for Preferred agent partners’ entire book of business, not just for clients they connect with through Zillow,” Wacksman and Hofmann wrote.

Rentals revenue was up 26% year-over-year to $220 million, which the company attributed to multifamily revenue growing 35% year over year. Zillow said its rentals segment now accounts for roughly 30% of its total revenue, up from 21% two years ago. Additionally, the company noted that 81,000 multifamily properties were advertised on Zillow at the end of the third quarter, a 17% annual increase.

“Diversifying into this space has brought us a large growth opportunity and made our business more robust,” the executives wrote. “Our rentals strategy is to offer the broadest, most comprehensive inventory from single-family homes to large apartment buildings, and to streamline the transaction experience for consumers and housing providers.”

Executives added that they believe Zillow is still just scratching the surface of the opportunity presented by the rentals sector.

“We see a clear path to more than $1 billion in annual rentals revenue and a substantial opportunity to keep growing across both multifamily and longtail rentals well beyond that milestone,” Wacksman and Hofmann wrote.

The company also highlighted the performance of some of its other offerings, noting that its CRM product, Follow Up Boss, recorded roughly 141,000 monthly active users in Q3, up 16% annually. In addition to this, Zillow said over 800 brokerages had signed up for its pre-marketing product Zillow Preview and its listing enhancement product, Zillow Showcase, was on 5.4% of all new U.S. listings.

“Even as housing conditions deteriorated sharply, Zillow kept growing and outperforming, powered by our brand, audience, value to partners, disciplined cost management and strong growth levers across our well-diversified business,” Hofmann and Wacksman wrote. “These advantages are driving our performance through an exceptionally difficult macro environment today and position us to accelerate when conditions improve.”

#5525. HECM broker rankings for August stay steady as shift to proprietary products rolls on

August HECM endorsements kept Atlantic Avenue Mortgage, loanDepot and Caliver Beach atop 12-month broker rankings. RMI data later showed September endorsements fell 6.7% to 1,790, the lowest since April 2020.  AI Summary

Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) endorsements for August show that Atlantic Avenue Mortgage, loanDepot and Caliver Beach Mortgage remain the top brokers on a 12-month rolling basis, according to a report published Wednesday by HECMWorld.com based on data compiled by Reverse Market Insight (RMI).

The three leading brokers have remained intact for much of 2026, with Atlantic Avenue now at a rolling total of 1,002 endorsements, down slightly from 1,009 in July. loanDepot endorsed 43 loans in August, upping its rolling total to 476, while Caliver Beach produced 19 loans, dropping its rolling total slightly to 352.

The rest of the top 10 on a rolling basis includes West Capital Lending (194), C2 Financial Corp. (191), Barrett Financial Group (155), NEXA Lending (140), Carrington Mortgage Services (122), Senior Lending Corp. (115) and Integrity 1st Mortgage (107).

West Capital Lending had a strong month and jumped ahead of C2 Financial for #4, 194 to 191, after adding 15 loans in August. Caliver Beach Mortgage stays at #3 with 352.

HECMWorld.com noted in an email that it’s still waiting for data from the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to compile its HECM direct lender rankings for October. The data for the prior month is typically released in the first few days of each month.

September data published by RMI showed that HECM endorsements were down 6.7% from August, with the 1,790 loans in September representing the lowest total for any month since April 2020.

Last month, New View Advisors released the newest edition of its Proprietary Reverse Mortgage Production Index, which shows that private-label products are driving overall growth for reverse mortgage originations even as HECM production wanes. The company said that prop loans represented more than 60% of reverse mortgage volume in September — a share that is likely to rise further.

“Rising interest rates may challenge the reverse mortgage industry in the fourth quarter, but proprietary loans could still propel reverse mortgage industry totals to over $8 billion in 2026, versus $7.3 billion in total new originations of reverse mortgages in 2025,” New View explained.

In his weekly “Ribler on Rates” video series, Dan Ribler of Longbridge Financial said Wednesday that the 10-year Treasury yield, which closely connects with long-term mortgage rates, has offered some relief to capital markets and borrowers in recent weeks.

“In the last 30 days, the 10-year Treasury yield is down about 35 basis points at the same time as the S&P 500 is down about 2.5% to 3%. This is not a structural, massive repricing of anything,” Ribler said.

“This is just a 30-day cycle of risk-off — currencies, dollars moving out of riskier assets, whether it’s stocks, whether it’s AI infrastructure, into safer assets and Treasurys. As more dollars move into Treasurys, the price goes up and the yield comes down, and we get a little bit of rate love on our rate sheets.”

HousingWire‘s Mortgage Rates Center on Wednesday showed that 30-year fixed rates averaged 7.34%, although rates for reverse mortgage products typically run higher than that figure. Higher rates impact reverse mortgages differently than traditional forward mortgages as they eat into available proceeds for borrowers.

As lenders look to keep business flowing through the end of the year and beyond, they’re looking to technology as a potential spark plug.

On Wednesday, Nationwide Equities Corp. announced the launch of ReverseReach, which aims to help traditional mortgage brokers with lead generation efforts through their databases of past clients.

“We created ReverseReach to make uncovering those highly lucrative opportunities simple, efficient and accessible — even for brokers who have never closed a reverse mortgage before — so they can confidently and comfortably begin originating them,” CEO Paul Lamparillo said.

#5523. As AI takes over coding, Oracle rethinks how applications are built

As vibe coding moves from novelty to everyday practice, enterprises face a new problem: Machine-generated software still has to be maintained, governed and understood by people.

Low-code platforms were built to speed up application development, and AI is now rewriting that mission. Oracle Corp. previewed its answer ahead of its annual conference, and the tipping point for software development has already arrived, according to Mike Hichwa (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering at Oracle.

“In 2025, the majority of code was human-authored, and in 2026 and forever afterwards, the majority of code is going to be machine-generated,” Hichwa said. “We’re probably not going back. What we’ve done to address this change is we invented our own language. We call it APEXlang.”

Hichwa spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed vibe coding and the need to maintain and govern AI-generated code. (* Disclosure below.)

APEXlang is a highly abstracted application definition language that captures intent rather than implementation. Oracle introduced it with the APEX AI Application Generator and is publishing its grammar, skills and documentation in the public domain so coding agents such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex can generate it. Oracle is also working with OpenAI to train models to generate the language more efficiently, Hichwa explained.

“What you’re generating actually matters, because once you generate it, and you generate it 100 times or 1,000 times within your enterprise, then you’re going to need to maintain it. You’re going to need to look after it,” Hichwa said. “What people want with their portfolio of applications, they want consistency, they want governance, they want ease of understanding.”

Governance comes from the runtime, too. Generated APEXlang is interpreted by the APEX engine, which Oracle patches and updates monthly, so customers don’t have to revisit what they built. The same design is meant to curb AI slop, since a compact definition is easier to read than sprawling generated code, according to Hichwa.

“What we’re generating is much, much smaller, much more human understandable, so it is less sloppy because it is more abstracted,” Hichwa said. “It’s like a CliffsNotes. It’s not the full book.”

#5522. Mortgage policy faces tight runway in split Washington

Democrats now control both chambers of Congress while President Trump retains the White House and agency leadership. Trade groups including the MBA and ALTA are pushing for cost relief, FHA premium cuts and stronger consumer protections, while analysts warn that geopolitical tensions, looming debt ceiling fights and tougher confirmations at agencies like the CFPB will keep rates and regulatory timelines uncertain.  AI Summary

Housing and mortgage industry leaders say there is room for housing policy to move in Congress even as Washington, D.C., divides power between a Democratic-controlled House and Senate and a Republican-led White House.

Democrats captured both chambers on Tuesday night, but any housing bills under the new leadership will need support from President Donald Trump and enough Republican votes to clear the Senate. “Voters made it clear that affordability is a central concern, and housing is the biggest line item in most family budgets,” said Isaac Boltansky, head of public policy at Pennymac. “The ROAD to Housing Act laid a solid foundation, and we believe lawmakers on both sides of the aisle should work on a ROAD to Housing 2.0 package that builds on it and helps more families buy and keep a home.”

Asked what should be included in a 2.0 package, Boltansky cited the lock-in effect created by capital gains taxes, which can discourage homeowners from selling, and the Neighborhood Homes Investment Act as a “good starting point.”

The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) said in a statement that housing remains a bipartisan issue and it will “work with new and returning lawmakers as well as the Trump administration to advance common sense proposals to lower costs.”

The trade group in October released a policy road map to reduce closing costs, expand credit access and lower rental housing financing costs. Its proposals include easing tri-merge credit report use, aligning loan-level price adjustments (LLPAs) and lowering the annual mortgage insurance premium for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans.

Scott Norman, CEO of the Texas Mortgage Bankers Association, told HousingWire that the election shifts power but also creates opportunity for policy changes.

“It was a surprising night, but every election brings opportunity,” Norman said. “In Austin and in Washington, a gavel is something you borrow, and last night voters took a few back. That’s the system working as designed. No chairmanship belongs to the person holding it, and no majority is permanent. In much of the world, a change in power signals a crisis. Here, it simply means new leadership and a fresh look at policy.”

The American Land Title Association (ALTA) said that as policymakers continue addressing housing affordability challenges, consumer protection must remain part of the conversation.

“Fraud is unaffordable, and increasingly sophisticated schemes are putting American homeowners and their property rights at risk,” ALTA said.

Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said many Democratic campaigns emphasized economic issues, but the impact of the elections on the broader economy and mortgage rates is still unclear.

“Democrats have a clear mandate to focus on pocketbook issues, but whether they can translate that into a legislative agenda that delivers on that mandate remains to be seen,” Krimmel said.

Krimmel pointed to the conflict in the Middle East as a key variable. He said uncertainty remains around how the election outcome will affect the Iran war, which has been a source of inflation pressure. Democrats have been vocal critics of the conflict, and a resolution that improves oil supply would likely ease inflation and “potentially provide relief for mortgage rates.”

“Wanting the conflict to end, and finding terms that work for all involved are two different things,” Krimmel said.

On fiscal policy, Boltansky said another debt ceiling confrontation is likely in 2027: “Any focus on addressing the country’s harrowing fiscal trajectory would be welcome for the bond market, which obviously has a direct impact on rates,” he said.

While Congress can set agendas and control oversight, executive branch leadership will still drive most regulatory implementation for housing and mortgage markets.

Tim Rood, founder and CEO of Washington, D.C.-based advisory and technology firm Impact Capitol, said in his newsletter that Democratic majorities can control the agendas for the House financial services and Senate banking committees, investigate agencies, shape spending negotiations and withhold Senate confirmation of nominees when the new Congress convenes in January.

But he pointed out that Trump retains executive authority and leadership at agencies “does not change automatically with Congress.”

Rood said that for mortgage executives, the new alignment means more hearings, tougher confirmations and a more contested implementation calendar, “not an overnight rewrite of the rules.”

“The real fight will be over which existing policies can still be executed, funded and defended,” he said.

One closely watched appointment is Brian Johnson’s nomination to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). An attorney told HousingWire the confirmation is now at risk as Democrats may demand additional representation across financial agencies as part of broader negotiations.

The same attorney said one of the industry’s top regulatory priorities — changes to the loan originator compensation rule — remains unresolved.

“There are things that both sides of the aisle could help, like increase the availability of credit to borrowers by allowing lenders to claw back compensation in certain situations or compete. Maybe something will happen that is coordinated, but I think it’s kind of open in the air at the moment,” the attorney said.

Editor’s note: Sarah Wheeler contributed reporting to this story.

Important Information About Our Operating and Non-GAAP Financial Measures

Non-GAAP Financial MeasuresWe provide supplemental non-GAAP financial measures to our financial results. We use these non-GAAP financial measures, and we believe that they assist our investors, to make period-to-period comparisons of our operating performance because they provide a view of our operating results without items that are not, in our view, indicative of our operating results. These non-GAAP financial measures should not be construed as an alternative to GAAP results as the items excluded from the non-GAAP financial measures often have a material impact on our operating results, certain of those items are recurring, and others often recur. Management uses, and investors should consider, our non-GAAP financial measures only in conjunction with our GAAP results.

Non-GAAP operating expense, non-GAAP operating margin, non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP gross margin, non-GAAP net income and non-GAAP EPS exclude the effect of the following items: stock-based compensation; amortization of acquired intangible assets; acquisition and transaction-related charges included in general and administrative expenses; impairment and other charges (credits), net; non-operating charges (credits), net shown in the reconciliation provided; and income tax adjustments. Additional information about the items we exclude from our non-GAAP financial measures and the reasons we exclude them can be found in "Non-GAAP Financial Measures" in our Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2025.

Free Cash Flow: We provide information on free cash flow to enable investors to assess our ability to generate cash without incurring additional external financings and to evaluate our performance against our announced long-term goals and intent to return excess cash to shareholders via stock repurchases. Free cash flow is cash provided by (used in) operations net of capital expenditures. Free cash flow is not a measure of cash available for discretionary expenditures.

Constant Currency (CC): We present CC information to provide a framework for assessing how our underlying business performed excluding the effects of foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations. To present CC information, FY'26 and comparative prior period results for entities reporting in currencies other than United States dollars are converted into United States dollars using the foreign exchange rate as of September 30, 2025, rather than the actual exchange rates in effect during that period.

Operating MeasureARR: ARR (Annual Run Rate) represents the annualized value of our portfolio of active subscription software, SaaS, hosting, and support contracts as of the end of the reporting period. We calculate ARR as follows:

We believe ARR is a valuable operating measure to assess the health of a subscription business because it is aligned with the amount that we invoice the customer on an annual basis. We generally invoice customers annually for the current year of the contract. A customer with a one-year contract will typically be invoiced for the total value of the contract at the beginning of the contractual term, while a customer with a multi-year contract will be invoiced for each annual period at the beginning of each year of the contract.

ARR increases by the annualized value of active contracts that commence in a reporting period and decreases by the annualized value of contracts that expire in the reporting period.

As ARR is not annualized recurring revenue, it is not calculated based on recognized or unearned revenue and is not affected by variability in the timing of revenue under ASC 606, particularly for on-premises license subscriptions where a substantial portion of the total value of the contract is recognized as revenue at a point in time upon the later of when the software is made available, or the subscription term commences.

ARR should be viewed independently of recognized and unearned revenue and is not intended to be combined with, or to replace, either of those items. Investors should consider our ARR operating measure only in conjunction with our GAAP financial results.

#5520. Seattle farmworker payroll startup Ganaz acquired as CEO Hannah Freeman steps away

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:38 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 1:47 pm

Seattle startup Ganaz, which provides payroll and HR tech for agricultural workers and employers, has been acquired by Beacon Holdings.

Ganaz co-founder and CEO Hannah Freeman announced the deal Wednesday on LinkedIn, saying the public benefit corporation “is in great hands” at Beacon, which “is building momentum for our next exciting season.”

Freeman indicated she is stepping away from the company to “catch my breath, spend more time with my daughter, and dream about what’s next,” she wrote. “I’ll miss our team & customers, but will be cheering you on from the sidelines.”

Ganaz launched in 2017 and has raised more than $10 million, with its last disclosed funding round in June 2021. That financing valued the company at $26 million, according to PitchBook. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Beacon, based in Toronto, buys software businesses serving traditional industries and provides shared technology and operational resources. The company said in September that its portfolio included 45 software businesses.

Ganaz’s platform provides employee onboarding, training, communication and analytics tools. It also offers a Mastercard payroll card that gives unbanked workers access to digital banking. Employers save time and money by skipping paper checks, while workers keep more of their pay by avoiding check-cashing and high remittance fees.

Ganaz received GeekWire’s 2023 Geeks Give Back Award. “We founded Ganaz to make life better for farm workers, and we do that by building technology that agricultural employers love and can’t live without,” Freeman told GeekWire in 2023. “We build our tools to help both workers and employers prosper, and that kicks off a virtuous cycle that helps agricultural communities prosper as well.”

At that time, the startup was serving more than 250,000 agricultural workers in the U.S. and Mexico and 100 employers in the sector.

The company has about 17 employees, according to LinkedIn. Freeman did not say in her post whether Ganaz will continue as a subsidiary or whether its employees will receive job offers from Beacon. GeekWire has reached out to Freeman for comment and will update the story with any reply.

#5519. Microsoft Azure revenue surges 48% to $33.2B, beating expectations as cloud and AI demand grows

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:47 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:30 pm

Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations.

The growth suggests that Microsoft is selling cloud and AI computing about as fast as it can install it. Azure revenue rose $10.8 billion from a year earlier, driven by demand for services across the platform, Microsoft said in its quarterly filing. That came even as some new data center capacity arrived late.

For investors worried about Microsoft’s record capital spending, it’s a sign that the company’s massive AI and cloud infrastructure buildout is turning into sales. Microsoft’s shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading following the earnings report.

Overall, Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, up 19% and above the $90.75 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance. Earnings were $4.89 per share excluding the impact of its OpenAI investment, compared with expectations of $4.72.

It’s the first time Microsoft has reported Azure’s quarterly revenue figure, not just its growth. The disclosure is part of a new financial structure that took effect this quarter, splitting the company into two segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.

Capital spending came in below Microsoft’s forecast. The company spent $45.2 billion, including finance leases, short of the more than $50 billion it expected. Some data center capacity that third parties were supposed to deliver in the quarter was delayed, the company said.

Google Cloud, which includes Google’s Workspace productivity apps, brought in $30.7 billion in revenue in the quarter, up 103% from a year earlier, Alphabet reported Wednesday afternoon.

Amazon reports earnings Thursday afternoon, including AWS results.

Update, 3:05 p.m.:Microsoft expects Azure growth to accelerate again this quarter, to 49% to 50% excluding currency changes, CFO Amy Hood said on the earnings call. “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” she said.

Hood said Azure’s growth came from Foundry, Microsoft’s service for building AI apps and agents, and from engineering work that let Microsoft sell unused capacity on its existing servers. That helped make up for delays in new data center capacity that outside providers were supposed to deliver.

Those delays pushed some spending later into the fiscal year. Microsoft now expects to spend about $170 billion on capital expenditures in calendar 2026, down from about $175 billion. It expects to spend more than $50 billion this quarter, and Hood said spending will accelerate in the first half of calendar 2027.

Hood also said Microsoft may tap additional sources of financing to help pay for the buildout, “when we believe it is attractive to do so.” The company still expects to bring in more cash than it spends this fiscal year.

Microsoft’s expense forecast for the December quarter includes an estimate for the buyout offer it announced Monday, Hood said, though she didn’t give the amount.

The company expects total revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion for the December quarter, above the $95.7 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance.

#5518. MATSON, INC. ANNOUNCES THIRD QUARTER 2026 RESULTS AND RAISES FULL YEAR OUTLOOK

HONOLULU, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Matson, Inc. ("Matson" or the "Company") (NYSE: MATX), a leading U.S. carrier in the Pacific, today reported net income of $209.4 million, or $6.96 per diluted share, for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.  Net income for the quarter ended September 30, 2025 was $134.7 million, or $4.24 per diluted share.  Consolidated revenue for the third quarter 2026 was $1,113.5 million, compared with $880.1 million for the third quarter 2025.

Matt Cox, Matson's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, commented, "Matson had a stronger-than-expected third quarter.  Our China service performed well, with its speed and reliability serving as important differentiators amid continued pressure on global shipping networks and congestion at key Asia ports.  Strong demand and elevated freight rates in our China service drove a substantial year-over-year increase in Ocean Transportation operating income, particularly compared with last year's muted peak season.  In our domestic ocean tradelanes and logistics, we saw stable performance."

Mr. Cox continued, "Looking ahead, we expect the strong demand and elevated freight rates we experienced in our China service in the third quarter to continue through year end and into early 2027.  As a result, we expect Ocean Transportation operating income in the fourth quarter 2026 to be approximately 50 percent higher than the result achieved in the year ago period.  We also expect Logistics operating income in the fourth quarter 2026 to be modestly higher year-over-year.  Taken together, we expect consolidated operating income in the fourth quarter 2026 to be approximately 50 percent higher than fourth quarter 2025."

Third Quarter 2026 Discussion and Outlook for 2026

Ocean Transportation:  The Company's container volume in the Hawaii service in the third quarter 2026 was 0.3 percent lower year-over-year primarily due to lower general demand.  Hawaii's economy has slowed as continued strength in construction has been offset by softer tourism and higher energy-related inflation.  The Company expects volume in full year 2026 to be modestly lower than the level achieved in 2025, based on the Company's expectation of similar economic conditions and stable market share.

In the China service, the Company's container volume in the third quarter 2026 increased 16.0 percent year-over-year.  The China service performed well, with its speed and reliability serving as important differentiators amid continued pressure on global shipping networks and congestion at key Asia ports.  Strong demand and elevated freight rates in the China service drove a substantial year-over-year increase in Ocean Transportation operating income, particularly compared with last year's muted peak season.  The Company expects similar operating conditions to continue through year end and into early 2027.  As such, the Company expects volume in full year 2026 to be higher than the level achieved in 2025.

In the Guam service, the Company's container volume in the third quarter 2026 increased 4.3 percent year-over-year.  In the near term, the Company expects Guam's economy to remain stable.  For full year 2026, the Company expects volume to be modestly higher than the level achieved last year.

In the Alaska service, the Company's container volume in the third quarter 2026 decreased 4.8 percent year-over-year primarily due to lower southbound seafood volume and an additional northbound sailing in the year ago period.  In the near term, the Company expects Alaska's economy to remain stable supported by a low unemployment rate, steady job market and continued oil and gas exploration and production activity.  For full year 2026, the Company expects volume to be modestly lower than the level achieved last year.

The contribution from the Company's SSAT joint venture investment was $7.4 million in the third quarter 2026, or $1.9 million lower than third quarter 2025.  The decrease was primarily due to lower lift volume.  For full year 2026, the Company expects the contribution from SSAT to be lower than the $32.5 million achieved in full year 2025.

Based on the outlook trends noted above, the Company expects Ocean Transportation operating income in the fourth quarter 2026 to be approximately 50 percent higher than the $136.0 million achieved in the fourth quarter 2025.

Logistics:  Operating income for the Company's Logistics segment was $16.1 million in the third quarter 2026, or $2.5 million higher compared to the level achieved in the third quarter 2025.  The increase was primarily due to higher contributions from transportation brokerage and freight forwarding, partially offset by a lower contribution from warehousing.  For the fourth quarter 2026, the Company expects Logistics operating income to be modestly higher than the $7.7 million achieved in the fourth quarter 2025.

Consolidated Operating Income:  For the fourth quarter 2026, the Company expects consolidated operating income to be approximately 50 percent higher than the $143.7 million achieved in the fourth quarter 2025.

Depreciation and Amortization:  For full year 2026, the Company expects depreciation and amortization expense to be approximately $205 million, inclusive of dry-docking amortization of approximately $35 million.

Interest Income:  The Company expects interest income for the full year 2026 to be approximately $20 million.

Interest Expense, Net:  The Company expects interest expense, net for the full year 2026 to be approximately $6 million.

Other Income (Expense), Net:  The Company expects full year 2026 other income (expense), net to be approximately $10 million in income, which is attributable to the amortization of certain components of net periodic benefit costs or gains related to the Company's pension and post-retirement plans.

Income Taxes:  For the third quarter 2026, the Company's effective tax rate was 20.5 percent.  For the fourth quarter 2026, the Company expects its effective tax rate to be approximately 20.0 percent compared to last year's 5.2 percent, which benefited from a one-time tax adjustment of $18.5 million, or $0.59 per share, related to the Company's deferred tax assets and liabilities.

Capital and Vessel Dry-docking Expenditures:  For the third quarter 2026, the Company made capital expenditure payments excluding vessel construction expenditures of $41.8 million, vessel construction expenditures (including capitalized interest and owner's items) of $52.5 million, and dry-docking payments of $15.9 million.  For the full year 2026, the Company expects to make capital expenditure payments, including maintenance capital expenditures, of approximately $130 million, vessel construction expenditures (including capitalized interest and owner's items) of approximately $375 million, and dry-docking payments of approximately $45 million.

Matson's Cash and cash equivalents increased by $80.0 million from $141.9 million at December 31, 2025 to $221.9 million at September 30, 2026.  As of September 30, 2026, there was $298.6 million of cash and cash equivalents and investments in fixed-rate U.S. Treasuries in the Capital Construction Fund.  Matson generated net cash from operating activities of $460.6 million during the nine months ended September 30, 2026, compared to $370.2 million during the nine months ended September 30, 2025.  Capital expenditures (including capitalized vessel construction expenditures) totaled $349.8 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, compared with $258.7 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2025.  Total debt decreased by $30.0 million during the nine months to $331.2 million as of September 30, 2026, of which $291.5 million was classified as long-term debt.1  As of September 30, 2026, Matson had available borrowings under its revolving credit facility of $544.2 million.

#5517. Oracle connects AI-driven testing with a new approach to database security

Frontier AI models that uncover software flaws by the hundreds are forcing database providers into larger, faster patch cycles, and real application testing is becoming the safeguard that keeps those fixes from breaking production systems. The same AI wave is also undermining security rules written into applications.

Oracle Corp. has responded on two fronts, hardening its code against outside attackers while moving agent controls down to the data layer. The first effort began when the company turned an early-access frontier model on its own software, according to Juan Loaiza (pictured), executive vice president of Oracle Database Technologies at Oracle.

“Back in March, we got early access to the Mythos model and we ran it against our code and it started finding all these security vulnerabilities,” Loaiza said. “It’s turning up some very serious security issues. And so we said, ‘Hey, this is a code red moment. The house is on fire.'”

Loaiza spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why AI-discovered vulnerabilities, AI-generated code and AI agents require enterprises to treat security as a data problem. (* Disclosure below.)

Most of Oracle’s response to AI-discovered vulnerabilities is landing in its regular quarterly patches, which have grown much larger as a result, Loaiza explained. A quarterly security update earlier this year addressed more than 1,400 vulnerabilities across the company’s portfolio. Customers must automate patching and stay current, but every large patch raises fears of regression in systems that cannot fail.

“We have something called Real Application Testing where we can capture real workload and run it to make sure that your workload is not affected by these patches,” Loaiza said. “It’s not quite as simple as just apply because the applications that people run are extraordinarily complex. They run entire countries, entire industries.”

Patching handles outside attackers. Internal AI use is a separate threat, because applications have traditionally enforced end-user security, and AI now writes much of that code or goes straight to the data. Oracle’s answer is Deep Data Security, which began shipping in April and passes an authenticated user’s identity as an encrypted token through to the database. The company has since extended those authorization controls across remote databases, lakehouse data and related tables.

“The new world as I see it is all these end-user security rules have to be enforced where AI can’t bypass them, which means all the way down in the data,” Loaiza said. “The AI agent has to get your identity. It’s acting on behalf of you. It can’t leak the data if it can’t see the data.”

Business rules follow the same logic. Application code has always blocked a credit card charge above the customer’s limit, but an AI agent told to enforce that rule may not comply, Loaiza noted. Oracle is providing declarative ways to define such rules, along with SQL Assertions that check whether changes made through SQL are valid.

“There’s credit limits, there’s all sorts of things that are business rules that can’t be violated. And again, if we move those all the way down into the data, then no matter how you access the data, what mechanism you use, how AI is used, it cannot violate those rules,” Loaiza said.

#5516. 8 winter workouts and how many calories they burn

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These winter workouts that burn calories range from skiing and ice skating to shoveling snow, with AccuWeather's calorie estimates for each of the eight activities

Cold weather changes where people exercise more than whether they can. Snow, ice and short days close off some routines, but they open up others. Many of the activities that define winter in northern climates ask a lot of the body, from gliding across a frozen pond to clearing a driveway after a storm.

This guide covers eight winter workouts that burn calories, drawn from a longer list of cold-weather activities published by AccuWeather. The eight include sports such as skiing, snowboarding and hockey. They also include snowshoeing and ice skating, along with running, hiking and walking. The final entry covers outdoor chores that AccuWeather also counts as exercise: shoveling snow, chopping wood and raking leaves.

For each activity, this article gives AccuWeather's calorie estimate. Most of those figures are expressed per hour. Raking is the exception. The source gives that range without a time unit. The estimates cover a wide spread. Walking starts at 200 calories an hour, the low end of AccuWeather's range for it. Running reaches as high as 1,200 calories an hour at the top of its range. For cross-country skiing, the source notes that dedicated skiers sometimes pass 1,000 calories an hour.

These numbers are estimates, not fixed values. AccuWeather does not state the body weight, intensity or method behind any of them. The calories a person burns will vary with factors the source does not spell out. The figures offer a rough basis for comparing activities, not a precise count for any single workout.

The slides follow the order in which AccuWeather presents the activities. That order is not a ranking. Each slide stands on its own. Readers can go straight to the activity that fits their location, budget or schedule. Some entries, such as hockey, revolve around a rink. Others fit into daily life, such as walking the dog or running errands on foot.

AccuWeather also offers one general caution. It warns that anyone exercising outdoors in winter should dress for the weather to avoid hypothermia and frostbite.

Skiing of any kind, whether downhill or cross-country, can burn 500 or more calories in an hour, according to AccuWeather. That one estimate covers both forms of the sport.

The figure climbs for the most committed athletes. AccuWeather reports that dedicated cross-country skiers sometimes go past 1,000 calories per hour. The outlet presents that as a high-end figure for serious devotees of cross-country skiing.

Neither number is fixed. AccuWeather does not give the body weight, pace or effort level behind its skiing estimates, so an individual skier's burn will differ.

Cross-country skiing has two main methods. CBC describes the classic method as the traditional style of the sport. A classic skier glides along parallel tracks with a rhythmic motion that resembles running or walking.

The second method is skate skiing. Skate skiers push off their skis at an angle instead of gliding straight ahead. CBC compares that motion to the stride a hockey player uses on the ice.

Snowboarding burns an estimated 300 to 450 calories per hour, according to AccuWeather. That range falls below the outlet's estimate for skiing, which it puts at 500 or more calories an hour for both downhill and cross-country skiing.

Even the top of the snowboarding range, 450 calories an hour, sits under the 500-calorie floor AccuWeather gives for skiing.

AccuWeather describes snowboarding as less intense than skiing. It also presents the sport as more oriented toward fun than skiing is.

Ice hockey burns an estimated 400 to 600 calories an hour, according to AccuWeather. The source sets hockey apart from the other winter workouts it lists as the one built around a team.

The estimate spans 200 calories from its low end to its high end. AccuWeather gives the same 400 to 600 range for snowshoeing.

AccuWeather points to two ways to get into a game. The first is to join a team that plays at a rink. That route connects a player with an existing group and a place to play.

The second route is less formal. A player rounds up friends who have their own gear and organizes a game with them.

Both routes depend on other people to make a game happen. AccuWeather does not say how many players a game needs, how often rink teams play or what joining one costs.

Snowshoeing burns an estimated 400 to 600 calories an hour, according to AccuWeather. The forecaster presents it as a beginner-friendly alternative to skiing that costs less.

The equipment is simple to put on. Snowshoes go on over a regular pair of winter boots.

AccuWeather's estimate for snowshoeing is the same 400-to-600 range it gives for ice hockey.

Snow depth changes the workload. The National Park Service notes that snowshoeing a trail can take far more effort than walking the same trail on foot without snow. How much more depends on how deep the snow lies.

Particularly deep snow calls for a different technique. The park service recommends the kick-step for those conditions. The snowshoer kicks the foot while lifting it. That motion shakes extra snow off the front of the snowshoe.

The basic walking motion also changes on snowshoes. They force a wider stride than a normal walk. The park service warns that this wider gait can lead to achy hips.

Snow builds up on the gear itself, too. The agency advises stopping now and then to clear clumps stuck in the snowshoe's spikes. A trekking pole can help with that task, according to the park service.

Running burns an estimated 600 to 1,200 calories per hour, according to AccuWeather. The weather company treats running as a year-round workout. A routine built in spring or summer does not have to stop when temperatures fall.

The top of that range is double the bottom. The low end, 600 calories, matches the upper limit of the 400 to 600 calories an hour AccuWeather estimates for both hockey and snowshoeing.

Running's range overlaps with AccuWeather's hiking estimate of 430 to 650 calories an hour only between 600 and 650. Its low end also sits above the 470-calorie ceiling AccuWeather gives for walking. Ice skating, which AccuWeather puts at up to 700 calories an hour with real effort, tops out near the bottom of running's range.

Winter changes the ground underfoot. AccuWeather advises runners to plan their routes with icy patches in mind before heading out.

Timing is its second point. Temperature and visibility both shift over the course of a day. AccuWeather suggests weighing both when choosing a time to run.

Clothing is the third consideration. AccuWeather recommends breathable layers for cold-weather runs. AccuWeather's three tips for winter runners cover the route, the hour and the clothing.

Footwear matters on slick surfaces too. The National Institute on Aging recommends nonskid, rubber-soled shoes with low heels for people exercising outdoors in snow and ice. That kind of shoe makes a slip less likely.

The institute also lists precautions for anyone exercising outside in the cold. It recommends learning the signs of hypothermia. It also advises telling others where you will be and carrying a fully charged mobile phone.

The National Institute on Aging suggests considering an indoor workout when it is very windy, cold, icy or wet outside. An online workout video or a person's own routine can fill in on those days.

Ice skating can burn up to 700 calories an hour, according to AccuWeather. That estimate applies when the skater puts real effort into the session.

That condition shapes how to read the number. AccuWeather presents 700 calories as a ceiling for hard skating, not as the typical result of a trip to the rink. The source gives no figure for a slow, casual loop around the ice. That kind of outing falls outside what the estimate describes.

The way AccuWeather states the figure also sets skating apart from most of the activities in this article. Snowboarding, snowshoeing, running, hiking and walking each come with both a low and a high estimate. Skating has only an upper limit. The one other activity here described the same way is vigorous snow shoveling, covered with the other winter chores.

Without a stated floor, the skating figure is most useful for comparing upper limits. On that basis, the ceiling for hard skating sits above the top of AccuWeather's ranges for snowboarding and snowshoeing. A skater who wants to approach that ceiling has to keep the effort high for the full hour.

Winter hiking burns an estimated 430 to 650 calories an hour, and walking burns an estimated 200 to 470 calories an hour, according to AccuWeather. Of the two, hiking has the higher range.

The two ranges do not sit apart. They share a band from 430 to 470 calories an hour. Near the top of its range, walking matches the low end of the hiking range. The activity's name alone does not settle which outing burns more on a given day.

Walking also needs no special trip. AccuWeather counts walking the dog and running errands on foot toward this activity. A walk to the store or a loop around the block with a pet fits that description. Those examples fold the exercise into routine outings rather than setting it apart as a separate workout.

AccuWeather gives less detail on hiking. It does not describe the terrain, pace or distance behind its hiking range. It also gives no separate figure for hiking through snow. That leaves the hiking estimate as a general guide, not a figure for any particular trail or condition.

Shoveling snow, chopping wood and raking leaves can each burn hundreds of calories, according to estimates from AccuWeather. It puts vigorous snow shoveling at up to 500 calories per hour and chopping wood at 400 to 500 calories per hour.

The shoveling number is an upper limit. AccuWeather attaches it to vigorous shoveling, not to shoveling in general. The source gives no figure for shoveling at an easier pace.

Chopping wood comes with a range rather than a single ceiling. The bottom of that range is 400 calories per hour. The top, 500 calories per hour, matches the most AccuWeather gives for hard shoveling.

Those chore figures sit near several of the sports on AccuWeather's list. The wood-chopping range falls inside the 400 to 600 calories an hour the source gives for ice hockey and for snowshoeing. The shoveling ceiling equals the floor of its estimate for skiing, which starts at 500 calories an hour.

Raking leaves carries an estimate of 250 to 400 calories. AccuWeather does not attach a time frame to that range. Without one, the raking figure cannot be lined up against the hourly numbers for shoveling and wood chopping.

AccuWeather groups these three tasks as winter chores alongside sports such as skiing, hockey and ice skating. Unlike hockey or skating, none of the chores requires a rink or a team. The source does not say how much snow, wood or leaf cover its estimates assume.

#5515. CertiK Verified 40.68M TPS for Sui, Here Is What It Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The biggest throughput figure a blockchain security firm has ever signed off on is sitting on CertiK's homepage right now: 40.68 million transactions per second.

It isn't CertiK's own number, and it isn't an on-chain number either. If you read the 2,000-word report behind it, you'll come to become more interested in what CertiK chose not to verify than in what it did.

Scroll past the client logos and media mentions on CertiK and you'll find it in the "Latest Research And Market Insights" strip. One card says CertiK independently verified Sui's Mainnet Tunnel performance campaign, which recorded more than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions across 7,680 tunnels at a peak of 40.68 million TPS.

Most readers will see "CertiK" next to "40.68 million TPS" and stop there. Crypto social media mostly did the same. Sui's own post described the figure as set live on stage at Sui Basecamp 2026 and certified by CertiK, and added that the network now clears in under 20 seconds what Visa processes in a day.Walking through CertiK's verification method when the report first came out. Now that the number has been promoted to CertiK's front page, it's worth looking at exactly what it represents.

According to CertiK's announcement, Sui ran a live Mainnet performance campaign on October 7, 2026, during Sui Basecamp Day. It recorded 15,241,348,297 tunnel transactions across 7,680 tunnels, and every tunnel was opened and settled on chain.

A Sui Tunnel works roughly like a private room. A small group of participants carries out many application actions without sending each one to the blockchain. Sui records the starting terms when the tunnel opens and the final result when it closes. Everything in between happens off-chain as signed receipts. CertiK compares the design to Bitcoin's Lightning Network but notes that tunnels can handle more than payments.

The test was more varied than a single payment loop. The campaign ran 10 runs across five workload types: simple payments, flash, blackjack, tic-tac-toe and battleship. Payments still made up most of the activity. Its 6,144 tunnels committed more than 12 billion transactions, or 78.98% of the total.

This is the part of the report I respect most. The peak came from the busiest complete second, between 08:46:17 and 08:46:18 UTC, when 40,682,328 qualifying tunnel transactions were committed. The highest 60-second rolling average was 40,339,143.65 TPS.

Doing the math on the gap between those two figures. It's about 343,000 transactions, or roughly 0.84%. In other words, the network held near-peak throughput for a full minute rather than spiking for one second.

CertiK also avoided the easiest way to inflate a number like this. For concurrent tunnels sharing the same time window, it added up their transaction counts once and divided by a single shared duration. It did not add individual per-tunnel rates together or multiply one tunnel's rate by the number of tunnels.

The checking itself was thorough. All 7,680 executions and all 960 slots reached VERIFIED status, and the 15.24 billion committed transactions matched the full-history admitted receipts exactly. The work ran on dedicated AWS infrastructure with 128 vCPUs and 247 GiB of RAM.

There's also a small correction in the story. Sui's first announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS. CertiK's audited peak came in about 68,000 higher, a 0.17% difference. A verifier landing slightly above the project's own claim is unusual, and I think it reflects well on the method.

The homepage card doesn't mention any of this, but the full report is clear about its limits.

First, this isn't on-chain throughput. CertiK states that Tunnel TPS measures off-chain tunnel transactions and is not a measurement of Sui's on-chain capacity.

Second, the data came from the project being tested. The Sui team supplied the campaign data and executed all test scenarios, and CertiK examined the retained evidence and recalculated the totals.

Third, the cryptographic checks were not exhaustive. CertiK reconciled the arithmetic, receipt counts and timestamps, but it did not re-run individual signatures or do a fresh cryptographic replay of every receipt.

Fourth, the report can't speak to how the system would behave in normal use. The records don't establish clock accuracy, failure rates, latency percentiles or results across repeated runs. The sustained figure is the best 60-second window observed, not a guaranteed minimum.

Put simply, CertiK verified that the accounting is correct. It did not verify that Sui can handle 40 million real users' actions every second.

The number that's most telling isn't the TPS figure. More than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions were anchored to Sui through just 1,920 on-chain lifecycle transactions: 960 openings and 960 settlements.

By simple calculation, that's about 7.9 million off-chain actions for every on-chain transaction. That ratio is what the tunnel design is built to achieve. It's an impressive engineering result, but it measures how well Sui compresses activity, not how fast its base layer runs.

This isn't the first speed record CertiK has signed off on, and the earlier ones show why comparisons are tricky. In its earlier TON verification, CertiK worked from per-minute transaction count data and arrived at 104,715 TPS for TON's testnet. In April 2025, Qubic announced 15.52 million TPS verified by CertiK, measured over 10 peak ticks on its Layer 1 mainnet.

On paper, Sui's tunnel figure is about 2.6 times Qubic's and nearly 390 times TON's. But these were three different kinds of tests: a sharded testnet, a base-layer burst and an off-chain channel network. They don't belong on the same leaderboard.

My view is that the 40.68 million figure is real, well documented and carefully bounded. It's also a measure of what an off-chain system can process, not what Sui's blockchain itself handles. CertiK's report is honest about that, even if the one-line homepage card isn't.

#5514. Bigger than Bing or Xbox: Microsoft’s OpenAI haul reaches $10B in quarterly revenue

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 4:28 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:33 pm

OpenAI generated $10 billion in revenue for Microsoft in the quarter ended Sept. 30, about 11% of the Redmond company’s total revenue, according to its quarterly filing Wednesday.

The amount is up sharply. In the fiscal year that ended in June, Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion in revenue from its business with OpenAI, or about $6 billion a quarter on average.

That $10 billion surpasses some of Microsoft’s longest-running businesses. Xbox brought in $5.4 billion in the quarter. Search and advertising, which includes its Bing search engine, generated $6.6 billion. Windows licenses sold through PC makers, along with Surface and other Microsoft devices, brought in $3.6 billion.

The total covers revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI, as well as other business between the companies, such as OpenAI’s use of Azure to train and run its AI models. Microsoft didn’t say how much came from each, or how much of Azure’s growth came from OpenAI.

Azure revenue rose 48% to $33.2 billion in the quarter, beating Wall Street’s expectations and the company’s own forecast of 44% to 45% growth.

Microsoft has begun disclosing its revenue from OpenAI because its stake of about 24% makes OpenAI a “related party” under accounting rules, requiring it to report the business they do with each other.

Microsoft first reported the number in its annual report in July, as a full-year total. This is the first time it has given a quarterly figure.

The original AI alliance: Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, eventually committing $13 billion, and became its exclusive cloud provider. ChatGPT ran on Azure when it launched in late 2022.

The companies have loosened their ties since then. OpenAI restructured as a public benefit corporation in October 2025, and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal to supply OpenAI’s computing capacity. OpenAI committed to buy an additional $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement gave OpenAI broader freedom to use other cloud providers.

OpenAI has also agreed to keep sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030.

In addition, Microsoft sells access to OpenAI’s models to business customers through its Azure OpenAI Service, and the models became the foundation for its Copilot products, putting Microsoft at the front of the generative AI boom. That revenue comes from Microsoft’s own customers, so it isn’t part of the $10 billion.

Microsoft, for its part, now builds its own AI models and offers models from Anthropic and others.

Many customers, not a few: Asked by Bernstein Research analyst Mark Moerdler whether AI growth on Azure was coming from big businesses or AI-native companies, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t mention OpenAI.

He said he doesn’t want Azure’s AI business to depend on a few big customers, and that broad adoption by businesses is just getting started.

Nadella described it as “a decade-long thing,” and contrasted it with relying on “four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you” to show a few quarters of growth. That, he said, is “not a business as far as I’m concerned.”

He added that Microsoft has large customers who want to buy capacity, “and as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient.”

Later in the call, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges brought up the fact that OpenAI made up 11% of revenue. Nadella didn’t address the number but praised OpenAI’s latest models and said customers are increasingly mixing models from different companies, or training their own.

He cited Microsoft’s tools for routing each task to whichever AI model handles it best. If you use AI coding agents, Nadella said, you want Anthropic and OpenAI “to compete for your workload, not like once a quarter, but for every task.”

New risk language: Microsoft also expanded a warning in its quarterly filing about the risks of depending on outside AI providers. The company builds products such as Copilot on AI models from outside companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. It now says it has “limited visibility into or control over” how those models are designed, trained, secured and tested.

Without naming OpenAI or Anthropic, the same section notes that some of these AI partners are also “significant customers of Azure,” and that the benefits Microsoft expects from those relationships “may not be realized or sustained.” It says those partners could change how much they buy, and that Microsoft itself may change how it allocates scarce data center capacity or prices it.

Microsoft is an investor in both companies. According to its latest filing, it owns about 24% of OpenAI, down from about 25% in June and about 27% after OpenAI’s restructuring a year ago, and has put $12.0 billion of a promised $13.0 billion into the company.

In addition, Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, and its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment. Microsoft hasn’t disclosed the size of its Anthropic stake, and Anthropic’s IPO filing earlier this week didn’t specify it either.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.
