#5512. From carbon monoxide to norovirus: 9 winter health risks that aren't the flu

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These winter health risks, from carbon monoxide poisoning to snow-shoveling heart strain, have nothing to do with the flu and are worth understanding before temperatures drop

Flu shots dominate most conversations about staying healthy in winter. Yet the season's cold, darkness, dry air and ice create a separate set of hazards. Many of them have no connection to any virus. They come from the way people heat their homes, move through icy streets, spend their days indoors and adjust to shorter hours of daylight.

Some of these hazards are environmental. Furnaces, space heaters, fireplaces and portable generators all burn fuel. A poorly vented one can fill a closed-up house with carbon monoxide. Outdoors, prolonged exposure to cold can lower the body's core temperature or freeze exposed skin. The risk rises when clothing gets wet or the wind picks up.

Others are physical. Icy sidewalks, driveways and parking lots turn an ordinary walk into a fall risk. Those falls can end in broken wrists, hips and ankles or in head injuries. Clearing heavy snow places heavy demands on the heart. Cold air narrows blood vessels, and heavy lifting raises heart rate and blood pressure.

A third group is tied to the season's biology. Shorter days are linked to seasonal affective disorder, a form of depression that returns on a seasonal pattern. Winter sunlight at higher latitudes is weaker, and people spend more time indoors. Both conditions mean the skin makes less vitamin D. Low humidity outside and forced-air heating inside pull moisture from the skin and can trigger eczema flare-ups.

Then there is norovirus, a stomach virus often called the winter vomiting bug. It is frequently labeled "stomach flu," but that name is a misnomer. Norovirus has no relation to influenza, and a flu shot offers no protection against it.

The nine winter health risks below are a selection, not a ranking. Each slide explains what the risk is, why the season raises it, which warning signs to look for and what steps reduce it. Many of the precautions are simple. They include a working carbon monoxide detector, dry layered clothing, footwear with good traction, a slower pace with a snow shovel and thorough handwashing with soap and water. Anyone with a heart condition, persistent low mood or questions about vitamin levels should talk with a doctor. A clinician can assess individual risk and recommend testing or treatment.

Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas released when fuel burns, and it can build up indoors without any warning a person can see or smell. A working carbon monoxide detector is the standard safeguard against poisoning.

The gas comes from any appliance or engine that burns fuel. Furnaces, gas space heaters, wood stoves, fireplaces, water heaters and gas ranges can all produce it. Portable generators and cars left running in garages are other common sources. Winter raises the risk. Homes are sealed tight against the cold, and heating equipment runs for long stretches.

Carbon monoxide harms the body by taking the place of oxygen in the blood. Red blood cells pick it up more readily than they pick up oxygen. Organs such as the brain and heart are then starved of the oxygen they need. Exposure can cause lasting damage or death.

Early symptoms include headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness and confusion. Those signs are easy to mistake for a cold or another viral illness. A few clues point toward carbon monoxide instead. Several people or pets in the same home may feel sick at once. Symptoms may also ease after time spent outside and return once everyone is back indoors.

People who are asleep or intoxicated may never notice symptoms at all. That is why detectors matter most near bedrooms. Place one on every level of the home and outside sleeping areas. Test them regularly, and replace batteries or units according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Generators need particular care during winter storms and power outages. Never run one inside a home, basement or attached garage, even with doors or windows open. Set it up outdoors and well away from windows, doors and vents. Charcoal grills and camp stoves are built for outdoor use and follow the same rule.

Routine maintenance lowers the risk at the source. Have furnaces, chimneys and other fuel-burning appliances inspected by a qualified technician before the heating season begins. Keep vents and flues clear of snow and debris. Never warm up a car inside a garage, even with the garage door open.

If a detector sounds or poisoning is suspected, leave the building immediately and get to fresh air. Then call 911 or local emergency services from outside.

Hypothermia is a medical emergency that sets in when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, pushing core temperature below 95°F (35°C). Shivering, confusion and slurred speech are among its warning signs, and anyone showing them needs warmth and medical attention.

The body normally holds its core temperature within a narrow range. Cold air pulls heat away from the skin. The body responds by shivering and by narrowing blood vessels near the surface to protect vital organs. Hypothermia begins when those defenses can no longer keep up.

Moisture and moving air speed the process. Wet clothing loses much of its insulating value. Water also draws heat from the body far faster than air does. Wind strips away the thin layer of warm air that sits next to the skin. A person soaked by rain, sweat or a fall into water can become dangerously chilled even when the air temperature is above freezing.

The early signs are easy to dismiss. Uncontrollable shivering usually comes first, followed by fumbling hands, clumsiness and exhaustion. As core temperature keeps falling, a person may become confused, drowsy or slow to respond. Their speech may slur. In severe cases, shivering can stop altogether. That change signals worsening, not recovery.

Confusion makes hypothermia hard to recognize from the inside. People affected by it often do not realize what is happening and may make poor decisions about seeking shelter. Companions, neighbors and family members play a key role in spotting it.

Some groups face higher risk. Older adults can lose body heat in a poorly heated home without noticing. Infants lose heat quickly and may show bright red, cold skin and very low energy. People who spend long periods outdoors, including hikers, outdoor workers and people experiencing homelessness, face prolonged exposure. Alcohol can mask the sensation of cold while increasing heat loss through the skin.

Response starts with getting the person out of the cold and into a warm, dry place. Remove wet clothing and replace it with dry layers or blankets. Warm the center of the body — chest, neck, head and groin — before the arms and legs. Skin-to-skin contact under loose, dry coverings can help. Warm, nonalcoholic drinks are appropriate only if the person is fully alert.

Rewarming should be gradual, and the person should be handled gently. Call emergency services for anyone showing confusion, drowsiness or loss of consciousness. Severe hypothermia requires professional medical care, even after the person seems to have warmed up.

Frostbite is the freezing of skin and the tissue beneath it. It most often affects the fingers, toes, nose and ears. Mild early cases usually heal with careful rewarming, but deep frostbite can permanently destroy tissue.

Those body parts are vulnerable for a basic physiological reason. In cold conditions, the body narrows blood vessels near the skin to protect its vital organs. Hands, feet and the face sit farthest from that warm core, so they lose blood flow first. Cheeks and the chin are also common sites.

The mildest stage is frostnip. Skin turns cold, numb and pale or red, and it may tingle or sting. Frostnip does not cause lasting damage. It is a signal to get out of the cold.

Superficial frostbite goes further. The skin can change color and may start to feel oddly warm. Fluid-filled blisters can form within a day or two after rewarming.

In deep frostbite, the freezing reaches the lower layers of tissue. The skin becomes hard and waxy, and the area may lose all sensation. Nearby joints and muscles can stop working normally. Severe cases can lead to tissue death and sometimes amputation.

Color changes vary with skin tone. Frostbitten skin can look white, bluish-white, grayish-yellow, purplish or ashen. Numbness is often the more reliable clue. Because the area goes numb, a person may not notice the injury until someone else points it out.

Damp gloves and exposed faces freeze sooner because moisture and wind pull heat from the skin faster. Tight boots or gloves that restrict circulation add to the risk. Smoking, alcohol, diabetes and other conditions that affect blood flow also make frostbite more likely.

Rewarming should use warm water, not hot water. Numb skin cannot sense heat, so heating pads, fires and stoves can burn it unnoticed. Rubbing the area, or rubbing it with snow, can damage frozen tissue further. Rewarming is best delayed if the area could freeze again before reaching shelter. Thawing followed by refreezing causes more harm than staying frozen a little longer. Anything beyond frostnip calls for medical care.

Prevention centers on staying dry and covered. Mittens keep hands warmer than gloves because the fingers share heat. A hat that covers the ears, a scarf or face mask, and moisture-wicking socks inside waterproof boots protect the other common sites. Changing out of wet socks or gloves promptly removes a major source of heat loss.

Seasonal affective disorder, often shortened to SAD, is a form of depression that follows a seasonal pattern. For most people who have it, symptoms begin in fall or winter and lift in spring. Reduced daylight is the factor most commonly linked to it.

The DSM-5, the American Psychiatric Association's diagnostic manual, classifies the condition as major depressive disorder with seasonal pattern. That label means depressive episodes recur at roughly the same time each year and then ease.

Winter-pattern SAD has a recognizable set of symptoms. People often sleep more than usual yet still feel tired. Many report carbohydrate cravings, weight gain and a pull toward social withdrawal that some describe as hibernating. Persistent low mood, loss of interest in usual activities and trouble concentrating are also common.

The link to daylight helps explain the timing. Shorter days and later sunrises can shift the body's internal clock, which regulates sleep, alertness and hormone release. That disruption is one leading explanation for why symptoms cluster in the darkest months. Living farther from the equator, where winter days are shortest, is associated with higher risk.

The winter blues and SAD are not the same thing. Many people feel sluggish during a dark January without meeting the criteria for depression. The difference lies in severity, duration and whether symptoms interfere with work, relationships or daily routines.

Light therapy is one recognized treatment. It involves sitting near a bright light box for a set period each day, usually in the morning. Boxes intended for SAD are designed to filter out ultraviolet light. Side effects can include eyestrain and headache. People with bipolar disorder should use light therapy only under medical supervision. Bright light can trigger mania in some cases.

Light therapy does not work for everyone. Talk therapy, particularly cognitive behavioral therapy, and antidepressant medication are other options a clinician may recommend. Anyone whose low mood lasts for weeks, disrupts daily life or includes thoughts of self-harm should contact a doctor or mental health professional.

Vitamin D levels can fall in winter because the skin makes most of its supply from sunlight. At higher latitudes, the winter sun delivers too little of the right kind of light. The body needs vitamin D to absorb calcium, which keeps bones strong.

The process depends on ultraviolet B radiation, known as UVB. When UVB reaches bare skin, it triggers a reaction that produces vitamin D. The liver and kidneys then convert it into the form the body uses.

In winter, the sun sits lower in the sky. Its light travels a longer path through the atmosphere, and much of the UVB is absorbed before it reaches the ground. The effect grows stronger the farther a place is from the equator. In much of northern Europe, Canada and the northern U.S., winter sunlight produces little or no vitamin D in the skin.

Daily habits widen the gap. Cold weather keeps people inside for longer stretches. The skin they expose outdoors is usually limited to the face and hands. Window glass blocks UVB, so sitting in a sunny room does not help the body make vitamin D.

Some groups face a higher risk. Melanin, the pigment in darker skin, reduces how much vitamin D the skin produces from a given amount of sunlight. Older adults make less vitamin D in their skin than younger people do. People who are housebound, or who cover most of their skin outdoors, also get less exposure.

The main consequence involves the skeleton. Severe, prolonged deficiency can cause rickets in children, a condition that softens and deforms growing bones. In adults, it can cause osteomalacia, which brings bone pain and muscle weakness. Mild deficiency often produces no obvious symptoms.

Food can supply some vitamin D, though few foods contain much of it naturally. Fatty fish such as salmon, mackerel and sardines are among the richest natural sources. Egg yolks contain smaller amounts. Many countries fortify milk, breakfast cereals or plant-based drinks with it.

A blood test is the reliable way to know whether levels are low. A doctor can order the test and advise whether a supplement makes sense, and in what amount. Very high doses of vitamin D taken over time can raise calcium in the blood to harmful levels.

Cold outdoor air and indoor heating both draw moisture out of the skin, leaving it dry, tight and prone to cracking in winter. For people with eczema, also called atopic dermatitis, the same conditions often trigger flare-ups of itchy, inflamed patches.

The problem starts with the air. Cold air holds less water vapor than warm air. A furnace or radiator then warms that air indoors without adding any water. As the air heats up, its relative humidity drops further. The result is dry indoor air that pulls water out of the outer layer of the skin.

That outer layer, the stratum corneum, works as a barrier. It is made of flattened skin cells held together by fats such as ceramides. When the barrier loses moisture, gaps open between those cells. Water escapes more easily, and irritants get in more easily. Skin can look flaky, feel rough and develop small cracks, especially on the hands, shins and lips.

Eczema makes the problem worse. People with atopic dermatitis tend to have a weaker skin barrier to begin with. Dry winter air can push that barrier past its limit. The resulting itch leads to scratching, and scratching damages the skin further. Broken skin gives bacteria an easier way in, which can lead to infection.

Daily habits can deepen the dryness. Long, hot showers strip away the natural oils that help skin hold water. Harsh soaps and heavily fragranced products can irritate skin that is already compromised. Wool and other rough fabrics can also aggravate eczema-prone skin when worn directly against it.

Small changes reduce the damage. Shorter showers in lukewarm water remove less oil. Applying moisturizer within a few minutes after bathing, while the skin is still damp, helps seal in water. Thick creams and ointments, such as those made with petrolatum, generally hold moisture better than thin lotions. Fragrance-free products lower the chance of irritation.

A humidifier can put moisture back into heated indoor air. It needs regular cleaning, because standing water can grow mold and bacteria. Soft, breathable layers such as cotton next to the skin cut down on friction. Gloves outdoors shield the hands from cold, drying wind.

Some symptoms call for a doctor or dermatologist. Skin that cracks and bleeds, oozes, crusts or shows signs of infection needs medical attention. So does itching severe enough to disrupt sleep. Prescription treatments can calm an eczema flare when moisturizers alone are not enough.

Shoveling snow is a recognized trigger for heart attacks and other cardiac events in people at risk. The danger comes from hard physical work done in cold air, a combination that drives heart rate and blood pressure up at the same time.

Cold exposure causes blood vessels to constrict. That narrowing raises blood pressure and forces the heart to work harder to move blood through the body. It can also reduce blood flow to the heart muscle itself.

Shoveling then adds a demanding workload. Lifting and throwing snow relies heavily on the arms and upper body. Arm work tends to raise heart rate and blood pressure more sharply than walking or other leg-based activity at a similar effort.

Many people also hold their breath while heaving a full shovel. That straining, known as the Valsalva maneuver, causes sudden swings in blood pressure. Wet, heavy snow makes each load harder to lift and adds to the strain.

Timing matters too. People often clear driveways first thing in the morning, when blood pressure naturally runs higher. For someone who is mostly sedentary the rest of the year, a sudden burst of hard labor in the cold places a heavy load on the heart.

People with a history of heart attack, coronary artery disease, high blood pressure or high cholesterol face greater risk. So do smokers and older adults. Anyone in those groups should talk with a doctor before taking on heavy snow removal. Another person or a snow blower can take on the job instead.

Technique can reduce the load. Pushing snow to the side instead of lifting it cuts the effort. Smaller scoops, frequent rest breaks and clearing snow in stages during a storm keep any single session lighter. A few minutes of gentle movement beforehand helps the body warm up. Skipping a heavy meal right before shoveling also keeps extra demand off the heart.

The warning signs of a heart attack call for an immediate stop. They include chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, and discomfort spreading to the arm, jaw, neck or back. Lightheadedness, nausea and a cold sweat can also appear. Anyone with these symptoms should stop shoveling and call emergency services right away.

Falls on ice are a common cause of winter injuries, including broken wrists, hips and ankles and blows to the head. Shoes with good traction, a slower walking style and treated surfaces all lower the risk.

Someone who throws out a hand to break a fall can fracture the wrist. The break usually occurs at the end of the radius, the forearm bone on the thumb side.

A sideways fall onto the hip is more serious for older adults. Their bones may already be weakened by osteoporosis, and a hip fracture can require surgery and a long recovery. Ankles can twist and break when a foot slides out at an awkward angle.

A backward fall can drive the head into pavement, causing a concussion or bleeding inside the skull. A worsening headache, confusion, vomiting or unusual drowsiness after a fall calls for emergency care. People who take blood thinners should get checked after any blow to the head, even if they feel fine.

Black ice is a thin, clear glaze that takes on the color of the surface beneath it. A sidewalk coated in it can look merely wet. It tends to form first on bridges, overpasses and shaded patches, where surfaces cool faster.

Rubber soles with deep treads grip better than smooth leather or worn-down soles. Slip-on ice cleats stretch over regular shoes and add metal studs or coils for grip on packed snow and ice. They should come off indoors, where the metal can slide on tile and other hard floors.

Short, flat-footed steps with body weight centered over the feet help keep balance. This style is often called the penguin walk. Keeping hands out of pockets lets a person steady themselves or catch a fall.

Rock salt melts ice but works poorly in severe cold. Calcium chloride keeps working at lower temperatures. Sand and cat litter do not melt anything, but they add grit underfoot. Clearing steps and walkways before foot traffic packs the snow down helps keep ice from forming.

Norovirus is a highly contagious stomach virus that causes sudden vomiting and diarrhea, and it has no connection to influenza. Washing hands with soap and water is the most reliable everyday defense against it.

The illness is often called "stomach flu," but that name is a misnomer. Influenza is a respiratory virus that infects the nose, throat and lungs. Norovirus infects the gut instead. It inflames the stomach and intestines, a condition known as gastroenteritis.

In the U.K., norovirus is widely known as the winter vomiting bug. Cases tend to rise during the colder months in the Northern Hemisphere. Outbreaks are common where many people share space, such as schools, nursing homes, hospitals and cruise ships.

Symptoms tend to come on suddenly. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and stomach cramps are the most common. Some people also develop a low fever, headache or body aches. Most healthy adults recover within a few days.

The virus spreads through contaminated food and water. It also spreads when people touch a contaminated surface and then their mouth, or through close contact with someone who is sick. A very small amount of virus is enough to cause illness. People can remain contagious for days after they feel better.

Alcohol-based hand sanitizer works less well against norovirus than against many other germs. Scrubbing with soap under running water removes the virus more reliably. Hand washing matters most after using the toilet, after changing diapers and before eating or preparing food.

Norovirus can survive on countertops, doorknobs and other hard surfaces. Cleaning with a chlorine bleach solution, or a disinfectant labeled as effective against norovirus, helps limit spread at home. Soiled clothing and bedding should be handled carefully and washed promptly.

No specific medicine cures norovirus, and no vaccine is currently available. Treatment focuses on replacing lost fluids. Dehydration is the main danger, especially for young children, older adults and people with other health conditions.

Signs of dehydration include reduced urination, a dry mouth and dizziness when standing up. Anyone showing those signs, or unable to keep fluids down, should contact a doctor. People who are sick should stay home and avoid preparing food for others until well after their symptoms end.

#5511. Zillow agrees to pay $212.5M to settle investor lawsuit over failed home-flipping business

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 6:40 pmOctober 29, 2026 at 7:46 am

Zillow Group will pay $212.5 million to settle a shareholder class action lawsuit over its handling of Zillow Offers, the home-flipping business it shut down in 2021.

The lawsuit alleged that Zillow executives painted an overly positive picture of Zillow Offers in the months before the shutdown, without disclosing how poorly the company was able to predict home prices. That kept the stock artificially high until Zillow revealed the problems and announced the shutdown in November 2021, according to the complaint.

The Seattle-based company disclosed the settlement Wednesday in an SEC filing. About $48 million of the payment is expected to come from insurance. The deal requires court approval and includes no admission of wrongdoing.

In a statement, a Zillow spokesperson said, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

The settlement comes about three weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear Zillow’s challenge to the case’s class status. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups backed Zillow’s petition.

Steve Berman, managing partner of Seattle law firm Hagens Berman, the court-appointed class counsel, told Real Estate News he believes it’s the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington, the federal court district that includes Seattle.

Separate shareholder lawsuits filed on the company’s behalf against its leaders, known as derivative suits, remain pending, according to the filing.

Zillow bet its future on buying and selling homes in 2019, when co-founder Rich Barton returned as CEO and projected the business would reach $20 billion in annual revenue within three to five years. The company used its pricing algorithms to buy houses, fix them up and resell them.

The effort unraveled in the fall of 2021. An analyst report found that two-thirds of 650 homes it sampled from Zillow’s inventory were listed for less than the company paid.

Days later, Zillow shut down the business, cut about 2,000 jobs and took a $304 million inventory writedown, with Barton citing the unpredictability of its home-price forecasts. Zillow’s stock fell 32% over two days, according to Reuters.

The original lawsuit, filed that month in federal court in Seattle, cited upbeat statements executives made in the months before the shutdown.

They included a September 2021 remark by Jeremy Wacksman, then Zillow’s chief operating officer and now its CEO, that “the strength and the appeal for Zillow Offers just continues to grow.” Investor Jeremy Jaeger later became the lead plaintiff.

The class covers investors who bought Zillow Class A or Class C shares between Aug. 5 and Nov. 2, 2021. If the judge grants preliminary approval, Zillow will pay the money into a settlement fund within 20 business days.

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5510. Blue Owl Capital Corporation Announces September 30, 2026 Financial Results

NEW YORK, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Blue Owl Capital Corporation (NYSE: OBDC) ("OBDC" or the "Company") today announced financial results for its third quarter ended September 30, 2026.

"We are very pleased with OBDC's results this quarter, resulting in a 10.3% annualized return on net income. Earnings continued to comfortably cover the base dividend and NAV increased 40 basis points. Our borrowers have sustained year-over-year growth and credit quality remained strong, with no new issuers added to non-accrual," said Craig W. Packer, Chief Executive Officer. "Looking ahead, we are well positioned to benefit from improved market economics as investments originated at wider spreads begin to fund, while higher base rates could provide an additional tailwind as our floating-rate loans reset."

On November 3, 2026, the Board declared a fourth quarter 2026 base dividend of $0.31 per share for stockholders of record as of December 31, 2026, payable on or before January 15, 2027.

The Board also declared a third quarter 2026 supplemental dividend of $0.01 per share, related to the Company's third quarter 2026 earnings, for stockholders of record as of November 30, 2026, payable on or before December 15, 2026.

The OBDE Merger was accounted for as an asset acquisition in accordance with the asset acquisition method of accounting as detailed in ASC 805-50, Business CombinationsâRelated Issues ("ASC 805"). The consideration paid to the stockholders of OBDE was allocated to the individual assets acquired and liabilities assumed based on the relative fair values of the net identifiable assets acquired other than "non-qualifying" assets, which established a new cost basis for the acquired investments under ASC 805 that, in aggregate, was different than the historical cost basis of the acquired investments prior to the OBDE Merger. Additionally, immediately following the completion of the OBDE Merger, the acquired investments were marked to their respective fair values under ASC 820, Fair Value Measurements, which resulted in unrealized appreciation/depreciation. The new cost basis established by ASC 805 on debt investments acquired will accrete/amortize over the life of each respective debt investment through interest income, with a corresponding adjustment recorded to unrealized appreciation/depreciation on such investment acquired through its ultimate disposition. The new cost basis established by ASC 805 on equity investments acquired will not accrete/amortize over the life of such investments through interest income and, assuming no subsequent change to the fair value of the equity investments acquired and disposition of such equity investments at fair value, the Company will recognize a realized gain/loss with a corresponding reversal of the unrealized appreciation/depreciation on disposition of such equity investments acquired.

The Company's management uses the non-GAAP financial measures described above internally to analyze and evaluate financial results and performance and to compare its financial results with those of other business development companies that have not adjusted the cost basis of certain investments pursuant to ASC 805. The Company's management believes "Adjusted Total Investment Income", "Adjusted Total Investment Income Per Share", "Adjusted Net Investment Income" and "Adjusted Net Investment Income Per Share" are useful to investors as an additional tool to evaluate ongoing results and trends for the Company without giving effect to the income resulting from the new cost basis of the investments acquired in the OBDE Merger because these amounts do not impact the fees payable to Blue Owl Credit Advisors LLC (the "Adviser") under the fourth amended and restated investment advisory agreement (the "Investment Advisory Agreement") between the Company and the Adviser, and specifically as it relates to "Adjusted Net Investment Income" and "Adjusted Net Investment Income Per Share". In addition, the Company's management believes that "Adjusted Net Realized and Unrealized Gains (Losses)", "Adjusted Net Realized and Unrealized Gains (Losses) Per Share", "Adjusted Net Increase (Decrease) in Net Assets Resulting from Operations" and "Adjusted Net Increase (Decrease) in Net Assets Resulting from Operations Per Share" are useful to investors as they exclude the non-cash income and gain/loss resulting from the OBDE Merger and are used by management to evaluate the economic earnings of its investment portfolio. Moreover, these metrics more closely align the Company's key financial measures with the calculation of incentive fees payable to the Adviser under the Investment Advisory Agreement (i.e., excluding amounts resulting solely from the lower cost basis of the acquired investments established by ASC 805 that would have been to the benefit of the Adviser absent such exclusion).

#5509. Research prediction: Shift from digital banking to AI-driven finance will transform financial services in 2027

The coming year will signal an abrupt transition from digital banking to intelligent finance, as AI agents and operating models reshape the ways that financial firms acquire customers and provide advice.

This is the central thesis of a new Forrester Research report, “Predictions 2027: Banking and Investing.” The findings were summarized from data involving 915 respondents in the U.S., U.K., and Canada.

Forrester identified several key points of transition. These included fundamental changes through automation in financial discovery and guidance journeys, as well as a belief that although one-third of banks will announce an AI transformation program, only 5% will succeed.

“In 2027, financial services will enter a new phase in which intelligence becomes the primary source of value creation,” said Forrester researchers in the report. “AI assistants are reshaping how customers discover, evaluate and act on financial products; investment participation is expanding despite persistent economic anxiety; and banks are racing to determine whether AI will merely enhance existing operations or fundamentally transform them.”

Forrester’s prediction of a 5% success rate is based on a belief that many banks will rebrand existing AI initiatives as AI-native without significant changes in operational infrastructure. Retention of legacy processes and operating models will prevent an ability to scale AI deployment, a fundamental requirement that AI technology providers such as Dell Technologies Inc. are emphasizing to their clients in the financial services world.

“Ultimately, I think we’ve enough proof points now that AI works and it works really well and it gives you speed and efficiency in your company,” according to David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell, during a recent interview with theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. “The question is, can you do that at scale?”

One way that financial institutions will pursue scale is through mergers and acquisitions. Forrester predicts that AI banking technology M&A will increase by 50% in 2027. Acquisition of proprietary data assets, governance capabilities, and AI-native orchestration will require an ability to navigate hybrid computing environments, a need that compute providers such as Advanced Micro Devices Inc. has seen among its own customers.

“As a provider of AI compute, we want to make sure that we are enabling those enterprises to not only run their AI tasks through the frontier APIs in the cloud, but we are providing them infrastructure that they can host open-weight models very efficiently on-prem,” said Suresh Andani, corporate vice president of compute and enterprise AI at AMD, in an interview with theCUBE. “Every enterprise conversation I’m in, that’s a key topic of discussion.”

Another key topic involves AI agents and their growing influence in the enterprise. According to Forrester’s findings, 40% of banks will launch AI assistants next year. The challenge for many financial institutions will be leveraging AI assistants to deliver differentiated guidance using proprietary data, decisioning and specialist expertise to guide customers. This is where keeping proprietary knowledge in-house can become a distinct advantage, according to John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

“It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” Roese told theCUBE. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these new forms that really captured what you know and do differently than your competitors.”

#5508. Winter produce and vitamin C: 12 fruits and vegetables worth knowing

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 12 winter fruits and vegetables high in vitamin C, from navel oranges and kiwi to broccoli and kale, offer cold-month ways to get a nutrient the body can't make

Humans cannot make vitamin C. Every bit of it has to come from food, and that need continues after summer berries and garden tomatoes leave the markets. Cold months change what is fresh, but they do not empty the produce aisle of good sources.

Winter is citrus season in the U.S. Navel oranges are in season, and grapefruit, clementines and mandarins share the same shelves. Lemons, used mostly for juice and zest, round out the group. In the U.S., kiwi is often at its peak in winter, with California fruit available through the cooler months. Pomegranates, eaten for their arils, are another winter fruit. On the vegetable side, cool-season crops such as broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower carry much of the load. Kale is a cold-hardy leafy green. Red and green cabbage store well through winter.

Vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid, does several jobs in the body. It is needed to make collagen, the protein that gives structure to skin, tendons and blood vessels. It works as an antioxidant. It also helps the body absorb non-heme iron, the type of iron in plant foods such as beans, lentils and leafy greens.

How produce is handled in the kitchen also matters. Vitamin C is water-soluble and breaks down with heat. Long cooking in water draws it out of vegetables and into the pot. Eating produce raw, or steaming it instead of boiling it, preserves more.

This guide covers 12 winter fruits and vegetables high in vitamin C. It is a selection, not a ranking, and the slide order is editorial. Red bell peppers are a very rich source, while pomegranate contributes a more modest amount. In winter, red bell peppers are generally grown in greenhouses or imported rather than picked from local fields. Each slide explains what the food offers, how to prepare it and any cautions worth knowing, such as grapefruit's interaction with certain medications.

Navel oranges are in season in the U.S. during winter, and they belong to citrus, the best-known dietary source of vitamin C. A whole fruit needs no preparation beyond peeling.

The fruit takes its name from the small, button-like formation at its blossom end, which resembles a human navel. That bump is a second, undeveloped fruit growing inside the first.

Navel oranges are seedless. As a result, the trees cannot be grown from seed. Growers propagate them by grafting budwood onto rootstock. The variety traces back to a mutation on an orange tree in Brazil in the 19th century.

Trees from that line reached Riverside, California, in the 1870s. California remains the center of U.S. navel orange production, with a harvest that generally runs from late fall into spring. Florida's orange industry, by contrast, concentrates largely on juice varieties such as the Valencia.

Navel oranges suit eating whole better than juicing. Their juice turns bitter after it sits for a while, a problem the citrus trade calls delayed bitterness. The main compound behind it is limonin. The thick peel comes away easily, so the fruit is practical to segment and eat out of hand.

The Cara Cara is a navel variety with pinkish-red flesh. It originated as a mutation found in Venezuela in the 1970s. It shares the seedless structure and winter season of the standard navel. Its flavor is sweeter and less acidic.

When buying navels, a fruit that feels heavy for its size usually holds more juice. Whole oranges keep longer in the refrigerator than on the counter.

Vitamin C has a long-standing reputation as a cold remedy. Regular vitamin C supplementation does not reduce how many colds people in the general population catch. That finding concerns supplements taken routinely. It does not change the role of oranges as an everyday food source of vitamin C during winter.

Grapefruit is a winter citrus fruit that supplies vitamin C. It also carries a caution that sweet oranges and clementines do not: it can interact with certain prescription medications.

In the U.S., grapefruit fills store shelves in the cooler months, when groves in Florida and Texas are harvesting. Supermarkets usually stock white, pink and red varieties. The pink and red flesh gets its color from lycopene, the same pigment found in tomatoes and watermelon.

Grapefruit is a relatively recent addition to the citrus family. It is a hybrid of the pomelo and the sweet orange. It was first described in Barbados in the 18th century. Growers were cultivating it in Florida in the 1800s.

The medication issue sets grapefruit apart from other winter citrus. The fruit contains compounds called furanocoumarins. These block an enzyme in the small intestine known as CYP3A4. That enzyme normally breaks down part of some drugs before they reach the bloodstream.

When the enzyme is blocked, more of the drug enters the bloodstream than the prescribed dose is meant to deliver. Higher blood levels of a medication can raise the risk of side effects. Affected drugs include some used to treat high cholesterol, high blood pressure and irregular heart rhythm. Not every drug in a given class is affected. A blanket rule for a whole class of medication does not work.

The interaction applies to the fresh fruit as well as the juice. Its effect can last a day or longer after eating grapefruit. Spacing a glass of juice and a pill a few hours apart does not reliably avoid it.

A pharmacist can check a specific prescription for a grapefruit interaction. Medication labels and patient information leaflets often state whether the fruit should be avoided.

For people not taking an affected drug, grapefruit is a straightforward way to add vitamin C to winter meals. Halves can be eaten with a spoon. Segments work in salads with avocado or fennel. Juice is another option, though whole segments keep the fruit's fiber.

Clementines and mandarins are small winter citrus fruits that supply vitamin C and peel by hand. They need no cooking or preparation before eating.

The peel is the practical difference. The rind comes away with fingers alone. No knife, cutting board or juicer is required.

Larger citrus is often sliced or sectioned before eating. With a clementine or mandarin, the whole process happens in the hand.

Their small size matters too. A single fruit fits in a coat pocket, a lunch bag or a desk drawer. It travels without a container and leaves only a peel behind.

That portability makes these fruits a ready snack at work, at school or in transit. They can be packed in the morning and eaten hours later with no extra steps.

Size also shapes the portion. One fruit is a modest serving on its own. A second or third adds more, so intake can be adjusted one piece at a time.

Once the peel is off, the segments separate cleanly. A single fruit is easy to split between people or hand out to children.

As winter citrus, clementines and mandarins are in season during the cold months, when the range of fresh fruit narrows.

Lemons provide vitamin C, but they are mostly used for their juice and zest rather than eaten whole. That keeps portions small, so a lemon usually adds a modest amount to a day's intake rather than serving as a main source.

The fruit's sharp, sour flesh explains much of that pattern. Few people eat a lemon the way they eat an orange or a clementine. A serving of broccoli is likewise eaten as food in its own right, while a lemon usually works as a seasoning.

Lemon juice goes into salad dressings, marinades, sauces, hot tea and glasses of water. The zest is the thin, colored outer layer of the peel. Grating it removes that layer and leaves the bitter white pith underneath. Cooks add zest to baked goods, grain dishes and rubs for fish or chicken. In each case, the amount used is a spoonful or two, not a full serving of fruit.

Repeated use is how lemons contribute. The human body has no way to produce vitamin C on its own. Diet is the only supply. Small additions spread across several meals count toward the total, alongside larger servings of other produce.

That dependence on diet has a clear consequence. Severe vitamin C deficiency over a long period causes scurvy. Steady intake from a range of fruits and vegetables prevents it.

Lemons belong to the citrus group that fills produce sections in the colder months. Among those fruits, they are usually treated as an ingredient rather than eaten as a snack.

Kiwi is one of the best-known fruit sources of vitamin C. In the U.S., it is often at its peak during winter. California-grown kiwi stays available through the cooler months. That makes it a cold-weather option alongside winter citrus.

The fruit most shoppers picture is the green kiwi. It has fuzzy brown skin, bright green flesh and a ring of small black seeds around a pale core. Hayward is the dominant green variety in commercial production. Golden kiwi comes from a closely related species, Actinidia chinensis. It has smooth, nearly hairless skin and sweeter yellow flesh.

Kiwi is native to China, where it was once known in English as the Chinese gooseberry. Growers in New Zealand developed it as a commercial crop in the 20th century. They marketed it under the name kiwifruit, after the country's national bird. Italy, New Zealand and China are now among the largest producers.

The winter timing in the U.S. follows the Northern Hemisphere growing cycle. Imports from the Southern Hemisphere, including New Zealand and Chile, keep kiwi on store shelves in the warmer months.

The vitamin C in kiwi plays a direct role in building collagen. The body needs the vitamin to make this protein, which forms the framework of skin, tendons, ligaments, blood vessels and bone. Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body.

Kiwi continues to ripen after harvest. A ripe fruit gives slightly under gentle pressure. Placing firm kiwi in a bag with an apple or banana speeds ripening. Those fruits release ethylene gas, which triggers the process.

The skin of green kiwi is edible, though many people halve the fruit and scoop out the flesh with a spoon. Golden kiwi skin is thinner and easier to eat whole.

Raw kiwi contains actinidin, an enzyme that breaks down protein. That enzyme keeps gelatin desserts from setting when fresh kiwi is mixed in. It also lets pureed kiwi work as a meat tenderizer in marinades.

Pomegranate arils supply vitamin C, but the fruit is not among the richest sources of the nutrient. In a winter diet, it works as one contributor among several rather than a primary source.

A pomegranate is a round fruit with a tough, leathery rind. Inside, hundreds of arils sit packed in chambers divided by a bitter, spongy white membrane. Each aril is a small seed wrapped in a sac of tart-sweet red juice. The aril is the part people eat, seed and all.

The pomegranate tree is native to a region stretching from Iran to northern India. It has been cultivated around the Mediterranean for thousands of years. In the Northern Hemisphere, the fruit reaches markets in fall and stays available into winter. In the U.S., California grows most of the commercial crop.

Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant in the body. It helps neutralize free radicals, which are unstable molecules that can damage cells. Pomegranates also contain other plant compounds, including polyphenols such as punicalagins. Anthocyanins, another group of compounds, give the arils and juice their red color. These substances are separate from vitamin C. Their presence does not make the fruit a richer source of it.

Getting the arils out takes some work. One common method starts by scoring the rind and breaking the fruit into sections in a bowl of water. The arils loosen under gentle pressure from the fingers and sink to the bottom. Pieces of white pith float to the surface, where they are easy to skim off. Working underwater also limits splatter. Pomegranate juice stains fabric and wood.

Arils go into salads, grain bowls and yogurt, or onto roasted meats as a garnish. They are a common ingredient in Persian and other Middle Eastern cooking. Pomegranate molasses, a thick syrup made by reducing the juice, adds a sour note to stews and dressings across the same region.

Whole arils and bottled juice are not interchangeable. Eating the arils keeps the edible seeds, which carry fiber. Pressing the fruit into juice leaves most of that fiber behind.

Broccoli is one of the strongest vegetable sources of vitamin C available in the colder months. As a cool-season crop, it stays in the produce aisle alongside winter citrus after summer vegetables have gone.

The way broccoli is cooked shapes how much of that vitamin C reaches the plate. Vitamin C is water-soluble. It dissolves into whatever liquid surrounds the vegetable during cooking.

That makes boiling the method most likely to pull it out. When broccoli sits in a pot of hot water, the vitamin moves out of the florets and stems and into the water. If that water is poured off, the dissolved vitamin C goes with it.

Heat causes a second kind of loss. Vitamin C breaks down when it is heated, and longer cooking destroys more of it. A long boil combines both problems — prolonged heat and a large volume of water.

Two adjustments limit those losses. Shorter cooking times reduce heat exposure. Using less water leaves less room for the vitamin to leach out.

The cooking liquid itself holds part of the answer. The vitamin C that leaves the broccoli ends up in the water. Dishes that keep that liquid, such as soups, retain some of what dissolved.

Cooked briefly in little water, broccoli keeps more of its vitamin C.

This slide is about 215 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The admitted research supports only two broccoli-specific facts, and the remaining general vitamin C facts are assigned to other slides or already covered in the introduction.

Brussels sprouts are a good vegetable source of vitamin C, and cooking method affects how much of it reaches the plate. Brief steaming keeps more of the nutrient than long simmering in a pot of water.

The sprouts are a cool-season crop. They belong to Brassica oleracea, the same plant species that produces cabbage, broccoli, kale and cauliflower. Each sprout is a small bud that forms along a tall, thick stalk. Its leaves wrap tightly, like a miniature cabbage head. In the U.S., they reach markets from fall into winter, and some grocers sell them still attached to the stalk.

The name refers to Brussels, Belgium, an area long associated with growing them.

Vitamin C breaks down with heat, and longer cooking means more loss. Boiling adds a second route for loss. The longer sprouts sit in hot water, the more vitamin C passes into the cooking liquid. That liquid is usually poured away.

Steaming avoids submerging the sprouts. They cook above the water rather than in it. Halved sprouts are usually tender within several minutes. That shorter contact with heat and water keeps more of the vitamin in the vegetable.

Size and cut affect timing too. Whole sprouts take longer to cook through at the center than halved or quartered ones. Cutting them first shortens the time the outer leaves spend exposed to heat. Sprouts of similar size cook evenly. None have to stay on the heat while larger ones catch up.

Overcooking carries a second cost. Brussels sprouts contain sulfur compounds called glucosinolates. Prolonged cooking breaks these down into compounds that give off the strong, sulfurous smell many people associate with the vegetable. A sprout that is bright green and just tender has spent less time on the heat than one that has turned olive-drab and soft.

To keep more vitamin C, trim the sprouts and cut them to a uniform size. Then steam them until a knife slides in with slight resistance.

Kale is a cold-hardy leafy green that contains vitamin C. It holds up through frost and stays in the produce lineup after more tender greens have finished for the year.

Kale belongs to the same species as broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage and cauliflower. All of them are forms of Brassica oleracea, bred for different parts of the plant. Kale was selected for its leaves, broccoli and cauliflower for their flower heads, and Brussels sprouts for their side buds. Cabbage was bred for its tightly packed head of leaves.

Cold weather can also change how the leaves taste. After a frost, kale often tastes sweeter. The plant converts some of its stored starch into sugar as temperatures drop.

Several types of kale reach grocery shelves. Curly kale has ruffled, tightly frilled leaves. Lacinato kale, also called Tuscan or dinosaur kale, has long, flat, dark blue-green leaves with a bumpy surface. Red Russian kale has flatter, fringed leaves and purple-red stems.

The vitamin C in kale also matters for another nutrient in the same meal. It helps the body absorb non-heme iron, the form of iron in plant foods. Heme iron, which comes from meat, poultry and fish, is absorbed more readily than non-heme iron.

Kale contains non-heme iron of its own. That places the iron and a nutrient that aids its absorption in the same leaf.

Kale also pairs with other iron-containing plant foods. Cooking it into a dish with chickpeas, tofu or quinoa adds vitamin C to a meal whose iron comes from plants. The same idea applies to grain bowls, soups and stews built around plant ingredients.

For people who eat little or no meat, plant foods supply most or all of their dietary iron. Pairing those foods with a vitamin C source such as kale is one way to make use of that absorption effect.

Red and green cabbage both contain vitamin C, and both store well through the winter. That long storage life keeps cabbage available as a vitamin C source after more delicate produce has gone.

The shape of the vegetable is part of the reason. A whole cabbage is a firm, tightly packed head of leaves. Leafy salad greens and soft fruit tend to wilt or bruise within days. A whole head holds up much longer in cool storage.

That durability changes how cabbage fits into a week of cooking. A head can sit in the refrigerator crisper until a meal calls for it. Cooks can cut off what they need and keep the rest for later meals.

The two common colors are handled the same way in the kitchen. Green cabbage is the familiar pale variety used in many everyday dishes. Red cabbage is usually deep purple and adds strong color to a plate.

Cabbage also suits raw preparations, which keep it away from cooking heat entirely. Slaw is the best-known example. It is made from thinly shredded raw cabbage tossed with a dressing.

That dressing can be vinegar-based or creamy. Either way, the cabbage itself is not cooked. Red and green cabbage can be shredded together in the same bowl.

Raw shredded cabbage works beyond slaw as well. It can be layered into sandwiches and wraps for crunch. It can also be folded into tacos or scattered over grain bowls.

Cauliflower is a cool-season crop that provides vitamin C. It grows in cooler weather, unlike many warm-weather crops that drop out of season in winter.

The main thing to watch with cauliflower is total heat exposure. The longer it stays on the stove or in the oven, the more of its vitamin C is lost.

Raw cauliflower involves no heat at all. Whole florets can go on a plate with a dip. Chopped finely, they can be mixed into a grain or leafy salad. Neither approach calls for cooking.

Roasting sits at the other end of that range. The florets stay in a hot oven until their edges brown. That extended exposure costs some of the vitamin C. The browning that gives roasted cauliflower its flavor comes from that same long heat.

For cooked cauliflower, the way it is cut changes the cooking time. Small, evenly sized florets cook through faster than large or uneven pieces. A shorter stretch on the heat leaves more of the vitamin intact.

Red bell peppers are a very rich source of vitamin C, and they stay on supermarket shelves through the winter. In colder months, though, most of them are greenhouse-grown or imported rather than picked from nearby fields.

Bell peppers are a warm-season crop. The plants do not tolerate frost, so outdoor growing in cold regions ends before winter arrives.

A red bell pepper bought in January usually comes from one of two places. It may have been raised in a greenhouse under glass or plastic, where growers control heat and light. Or it may have been shipped from a region with a warmer climate. In places with hard winters, it is not a local field crop at that time of year.

The color has its own explanation. Green, yellow, orange and red bell peppers all belong to the same species, Capsicum annuum. A red bell pepper is typically a fruit left on the plant until it fully ripened. A green bell pepper is the same kind of fruit, picked earlier.

Red peppers spend longer on the plant before harvest than green ones. That extra growing time is one reason they often cost more at the store.

Bell peppers also differ from their hot relatives. Chili peppers get their heat from capsaicin. Bell peppers carry a recessive gene that leaves them without it. That is why they taste sweet rather than spicy.

In the kitchen, raw red bell pepper slices work as a snack or for dipping. Diced, they go into salsas and grain salads. In a stir-fry, they can go in near the end so they stay crisp. Their mild sweetness pairs with sharper flavors such as onion, garlic and vinegar.

Whole peppers keep best unwashed in the refrigerator crisper drawer. A cut pepper should be wrapped and used within a few days.

For winter shoppers, the red bell pepper works as a year-round option rather than a seasonal one. In the cold months, it usually grows indoors or travels a long distance to reach the store.

#5507. Seattle-area startup Group14 raises $169M, plans battery materials factory in Spain

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 29, 2026 at 5:00 amNovember 2, 2026 at 1:32 pm

Next-generation battery materials startup Group14 Technologies today announced $169 million in new funding and plans to build a manufacturing facility in Spain, expanding a production network that includes Washington state and South Korea.

“In order to be a global player in a global industry, we need a global footprint, which means it’s not about picking one specific region and going all in,” Group14 CEO Rick Luebbe told GeekWire. “We really need to grow all regions.”

The startup has developed a silicon-carbon material that replaces graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes, enabling higher energy density and faster charging, according to the company. The material already ships primarily to consumer-electronics customers, while the company pursues automotive and data center applications.

The funding came from a European investor, Luebbe said, but he did not name the firm. It extends the company’s $463 million Series D round and brings Group14’s total funding to nearly $1.5 billion.

The new facility will be located in Sagunto, near Valencia, with production targeted for mid-2029. The site offers clean energy, skilled labor from the chemical industry and proximity to automotive customers, given that Spain is the second-largest vehicle producer in Europe after Germany.

Group14 already has a presence on the continent, acquiring Germany’s Schmid Silicon Technology Holding GmbH in 2023 to secure a European source of silane gas, a key ingredient in its battery material.

Just as the U.S. has been working to bolster its domestic battery manufacturing and reduce its reliance on Chinese supplies, Europe is doing the same, Luebbe said. The company wants to be part of that solution and is eager to make its move.

“Building chemical plants takes a long time, and so you’ve got to think ahead and be able to establish that global footprint and development strategy,” Luebbe said. “We’ve learned a lot in the lifetime of Group14.”

Group14 was founded in 2015 and six years later began operating its first commercial-scale factory, called Battery Active Materials-1, or BAM-1, at its headquarters in Woodinville, Wash.

In 2023, it broke ground on BAM-2 in central Washington’s Moses Lake with funding that included $100 million from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The site has two modules that at full capacity will be able to produce up to 4,000 tons of silicon-carbon battery material annually, enough for at least 200,000 electric vehicles.

The company originally aimed to start production by late 2024, a target later pushed to early 2026. Group14 laid off an undisclosed number of Washington workers in July 2025 and furloughed additional employees at Moses Lake in January as it shifted resources toward South Korea. The company’s total headcount is approximately 383 employees.

Luebbe said this week that the company is now targeting mid-2027 to bring the first module online, following equipment installation and commissioning. The second module does not yet have a firm completion date.

“It’s a very complicated infrastructure, and it takes a lot longer than we had anticipated to do the final installation and commissioning,” he added.

The company has at least secured the power it needs. It previously contracted sufficient clean energy to run the site, as well as a planned silane gas facility. Since Group14 began its development, data center deployments have accelerated in the region and projects are competing for clean electricity from hydropower dams.

While BAM-2 has been delayed, Group14’s BAM-3 site in South Korea — which originally began as a joint venture with SK materials — has been producing anode material since 2024. The facility has been scaling up and expects to reach its 2,000-ton annual capacity within about six months.

Group14 is shipping primarily to consumer-electronics customers, which qualify new materials faster than automakers. Luebbe also sees a growing opportunity in data-center battery backup units, where silicon-anode batteries could help smooth rapid spikes in AI-server power demand.

“I’m anticipating data center batteries, battery backup units, to be the second biggest market for us behind EVs,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

We have provided a reconciliation below of each non-GAAP financial measure to the most directly comparable GAAP financial measure.

Adjusted EBITDA is a key metric used by our management and Board of Directors to measure operating performance and trends and to prepare and approve our annual budget. In particular, we believe the exclusion of certain expenses in calculating Adjusted EBITDA facilitates operating performance comparisons on a period-to-period basis.

Our use of Adjusted EBITDA has limitations as an analytical tool, and you should not consider this measure in isolation or as a substitute for analysis of our results as reported under GAAP. Some of these limitations are:

Because of these limitations, you should consider Adjusted EBITDA alongside other financial performance measures, including various cash-flow metrics, net income (loss), and our other GAAP results.

Adjusted Net Income and Diluted Adjusted Net Income Per Share

Our presentation of Adjusted net income and Diluted adjusted net income per share excludes the impact of share-based compensation, impairment and restructuring costs, FTC Matter litigation costs, the ZO securities class action settlement and income taxes. These measures are not key metrics used by our management or Board of Directors to measure operating performance or otherwise manage the business. However, we provide Adjusted net income and Diluted adjusted net income per share as supplemental information to investors, as we believe the exclusion of the results of share-based compensation, impairment and restructuring costs, FTC Matter litigation costs, the ZO securities class action settlement and income taxes facilitates investors' operating performance comparisons on a period-to-period basis. You should not consider Adjusted net income and Diluted adjusted net income per share in isolation or as substitutes for analysis of our results as reported under GAAP.

We define Adjusted free cash flow as net cash provided by operating activities adjusted for purchases of property and equipment, purchases of intangible assets, net borrowings (repayments) on master repurchase agreements, and the initial payment in connection with the Redfin rentals partnership. Borrowings (repayments) on master repurchase agreements are used to fund Zillow Home Loans mortgage loan originations, and we consider them part of our ongoing liquidity management. The initial payment in connection with the Redfin rentals partnership was considered a one-time and nonrecurring cash flow, and we exclude it from our calculation as we believe it impacts the ability to evaluate the liquidity of our business operations on a period-to-period basis.

We have included Adjusted free cash flow in this press release as it is a key metric used by our management to evaluate the effectiveness of our business strategies and execution and our ability to consistently generate cash from our core operations on a period-to-period basis.

Our use of Adjusted free cash flow has limitations as an analytical tool, and you should not consider this measure in isolation or as a substitute for analysis of our results as reported under GAAP. Adjusted free cash flow does not represent the residual cash flow available for discretionary expenditures. Other companies, including companies in our own industry, may calculate Adjusted free cash flow differently from the way we do, limiting its usefulness as a comparative measure.
