#5505. 10 ways to train indoors this winter, and what changes calorie burn in each

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These indoor winter workouts, from rowing to jump rope, keep you training through the cold, with a clear look at what drives calorie burn for each one

No workout has a single true calorie count. Two people can finish the same 30-minute session on a rowing machine and burn very different amounts of energy. The number on a cardio machine's display is an estimate, built on assumptions about the person using it.

That matters in winter, when more training moves indoors. Short days, icy pavements and cold wind make outdoor runs and rides harder to schedule and riskier to attempt. Gyms, pools and living rooms fill the gap. The choice of what to do inside often comes down to a practical question: how much work does this session do?

A standard reference for answering it is the Compendium of Physical Activities. It assigns each activity a MET value, short for metabolic equivalent of task. One MET represents the energy a person uses while sitting quietly at rest. An activity with a higher MET value demands proportionally more energy than rest.

To turn that into an estimate, multiply the MET value by body weight in kilograms, then by the number of hours spent on the activity. The result is an approximate calorie figure. It is a starting point, not a measurement.

Four variables shape the real result. Body weight comes first: a heavier person burns more calories than a lighter person doing the same activity at the same intensity. Intensity is the second. It is the one a person controls most directly, through pace, resistance, load or rest. Duration is the third. Fitness level is the fourth. A trained athlete can often hold a higher intensity for longer than a beginner, which changes how much work a session does.

The 10 indoor winter workouts below are a selection, not a ranking. They run in alphabetical order, and none is presented as the top calorie burner. Each slide explains what the workout involves, which muscles it uses and what equipment it needs. Each also covers which adjustments raise or lower its calorie burn, and why it suits a season that keeps training inside.

The list spans machines found in most gyms, classes offered at studios and routines that need nothing more than floor space. That range lets a reader match a workout to the room, budget and joints they have.

A bodyweight circuit strings together push-ups, squats, lunges, burpees and planks with short rests, using the body as the only resistance. It needs nothing more than a patch of floor. That makes it a practical way to keep training at home when winter weather rules out exercising outside.

The structure is simple. Each exercise runs for a set number of repetitions or a fixed stretch of time, and the next one follows straight away. Rest comes after a full round of every move rather than between individual exercises. A common format is three to five rounds, adjusted for fitness level and the time available.

Each move covers a different part of the body. Push-ups load the chest, shoulders and triceps, while the core holds the torso in a straight line. Squats work the quadriceps, glutes and hamstrings. Lunges train the same muscles one leg at a time, which adds a balance challenge. Burpees combine a squat, a plank and a jump into a single movement. Planks build endurance in the abdominal and lower-back muscles that stabilize the spine.

The order of exercises shapes how the circuit flows. Alternating upper-body and lower-body moves lets one muscle group recover while another works. That keeps the session moving without forcing long pauses.

Progression comes from changing leverage and speed instead of adding weight. Incline push-ups, with the hands on a kitchen counter or sturdy chair, reduce the load for beginners. Decline push-ups, with the feet raised on a step or couch, shift more of the work onto the shoulders and upper chest. Jump squats add an explosive phase to a standard squat. A side plank moves the demand onto the obliques.

Rest length is a major lever on calorie burn in this workout. Shorter breaks keep the heart rate elevated across the session. As a result, the circuit works as cardio as well as strength training. Adding rounds raises the total. Swapping in explosive variations such as jump squats or full burpees raises it as well.

The format suits small winter living spaces. A floor area about the size of a yoga mat covers every move in the circuit. In an apartment, jump squats and burpees can be loud for neighbors below. Step-back burpees, which replace the hop with a step, keep the noise down. Standard squats in place of jump squats do the same. A few minutes of marching in place and arm circles before the first round warm up the joints. A non-slip surface keeps hands and feet from sliding during push-ups and lunges.

Dance cardio turns continuous, choreographed movement set to music into an aerobic workout. Its calorie burn depends less on any single step than on how fast the routine moves, how big the movements are and how long the dancer keeps going without stopping.

Zumba is one of the most widely recognized versions of the format. Alberto "Beto" Perez, a dancer and fitness instructor, created it in Colombia in the 1990s. Classes draw on Latin rhythms such as salsa, merengue, cumbia and reggaeton, layered over simple aerobic patterns. Instructors tend to lead by demonstration and hand signals rather than long verbal breakdowns. Participants follow along in real time.

Zumba is one option among many. Jazzercise, founded by Judi Sheppard Missett in 1969, blends jazz dance with aerobic exercise. Studios and streaming platforms offer hip-hop cardio, Bollywood-style sessions and other music-led routines. Ubisoft's Just Dance video game series scores players on how closely they match the choreography on screen.

Tempo is the first lever on calorie burn. A faster song demands quicker footwork and more steps per minute. Range of motion is the second. Deep knee bends, high knees, full arm sweeps and small jumps move the body through more distance than a shuffle in place. The third lever is rest. A dancer who stops to drink water or wait between every track lets the heart rate settle. Moving straight from one song into the next keeps it elevated.

The format also trains coordination. Routines pair footwork with arm patterns, turns and changes of direction. That challenges balance and rhythm alongside the cardiovascular system. Beginners can learn the footwork first. The arm patterns can be layered on once the steps feel familiar.

Group classes add a social structure. A live session supplies a fixed schedule and an instructor who sets the pace. A solo workout at home has neither unless the dancer builds them in.

At home, dance cardio needs very little: a cleared patch of floor, a screen and supportive shoes. Footwear deserves attention. Running shoes with deep tread can grip the floor during pivots and strain the knees. Cross-trainers or dance-fitness sneakers with smoother soles turn more easily. People in apartments can swap jumps for low-impact steps to limit noise for downstairs neighbors.

That flexibility suits winter. A session can start the moment the music does, with no drive to a gym and no warm-up in freezing air. It fits into a dark evening after work.

High-intensity interval training, or HIIT, alternates short bursts of near-maximal effort with brief recovery periods. It is defined by the timed pattern of work and rest, not by any single exercise.

The best-known format is the Tabata protocol. It comes from research led by Izumi Tabata at Japan's National Institute of Fitness and Sports, published in 1996. The protocol calls for 20 seconds of maximal-intensity work followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated for eight rounds. The full set lasts four minutes. The original study used a stationary cycle ergometer. The effort was meant to be close to exhausting by the final rounds.

Most gym and home HIIT sessions are less extreme than the original Tabata format. A common structure pairs 30 seconds of hard work with 30 seconds of easy movement. Another uses 40 seconds on and 20 seconds off. Beginners often flip that pattern, working for 20 seconds and resting for 40.

The work-to-rest ratio is the main dial on intensity. Shorter rest leaves less recovery before the next burst. Heart rate then stays higher across the session, and that sustained effort drives calorie burn in an interval workout. Very short rests at a truly maximal effort usually lead to a drop in output in the later rounds. Slightly longer work periods at a hard but repeatable pace can keep the total workload high.

Interval timing works with almost any movement. Sprints on a spin bike, hard pulls on a rowing machine and fast treadmill efforts all fit the format. So do floor moves such as mountain climbers or high knees.

The efforts are demanding, so HIIT is usually spaced through the week rather than done daily. Training plans commonly place an easier day or a strength session between interval days to allow recovery.

Beginners can scale the format in three ways. They can lengthen the rest periods or cut the number of rounds. They can also swap jumping moves for low-impact ones, such as step-backs in place of burpees. Several minutes of easy movement before the first interval prepares the muscles and joints for the hard efforts.

For winter training, the appeal is time. A complete interval session, including a warm-up and cool-down, can fit into 20 to 30 minutes. That suits short days and dark evenings, when a long outdoor run is harder to schedule.

Indoor cycling is low-impact cardio that works mainly the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes and calves. Its two main controls, resistance and cadence, let a rider set the effort precisely without leaving the house.

Cadence $CDNS is pedal speed, measured in revolutions per minute, or RPM. Resistance is how hard the pedals push back. On most spin bikes, a knob or lever sets it. Raising either one, while holding the other steady, increases calorie burn. A rider spinning fast against almost no resistance does less work than the speed suggests. Pushing heavy resistance at low cadence builds leg strength, but it can be hard to sustain. Structured sessions often move between the two, pairing faster seated spins with slower, heavier climbs.

Equipment shapes the experience. A spin bike has a heavy flywheel at the front and a riding position close to that of a road bike. An upright stationary bike seats the rider more vertically. A recumbent bike adds a backrest and places the pedals forward. That layout supports the lower back. Outdoor cyclists can also mount their own bike on a smart trainer and ride virtual courses in apps such as Zwift.

Bike setup affects both comfort and efficiency. A common starting point is to set the saddle level with the hip bone while standing beside the bike. At the bottom of the pedal stroke, the knee should stay slightly bent rather than locked straight. A saddle set too low pushes stress onto the front of the knee. A saddle set too high makes the hips rock from side to side.

Studio classes and home riding suit different needs. Instructor-led classes add music, coaching cues and a group pace that can push effort higher. SoulCycle built its studio business on that format. Peloton streams live and on-demand classes to its connected bikes at home. Riding solo offers more control over timing and session length.

The low impact sets indoor cycling apart from running. The feet never leave the pedals. That spares the knees, hips and ankles the landing forces of each running stride. It also makes cycling a common option for people easing back from injury. For road cyclists, an indoor bike is a way to hold on to fitness through months of ice, snow and early darkness.

Jumping rope is a compact, low-cost cardio workout that builds footwork, coordination and calf endurance. It needs little more than a rope, a patch of sturdy floor and enough headroom for the rope to pass overhead.

Rope length shapes the whole session. A common check is to stand on the middle of the rope with one foot and pull the handles up along the body. For beginners, handle tips that reach about armpit height are a typical starting point. Experienced jumpers often shorten the rope toward chest height to speed up each turn. A rope that is too long slaps the floor ahead and slows the rhythm. One that is too short catches the toes.

Space matters in three directions: above, in front and behind. The rope sweeps a full arc over the head on every turn. Ceiling height, hanging lights and ceiling fans count as much as floor area. A garage, basement or wide hallway often works better than a furnished living room.

The type of rope changes how the workout feels. Beaded and PVC ropes turn more slowly and are easier to time. That makes them a common pick for beginners. Speed ropes made of thin coated steel cable spin faster and are the usual choice for advanced footwork. Weighted ropes put more load on the shoulders and forearms, adding upper-body effort to the session.

Good form keeps each jump low, just high enough to clear the rope. Landings come on the balls of the feet with the knees slightly soft. The elbows stay close to the ribs, and the wrists do the turning rather than the whole arm. Common progressions run from the basic two-foot bounce to the alternate-foot step, high knees and side-to-side skier.

Calorie burn depends mostly on skip speed and how long a person keeps the rope moving without a miss. Frequent trips break the rhythm and lower the effort. Double-unders, where the rope passes under the feet twice in a single jump, demand a higher jump and quicker wrists. That raises the work involved in each repetition.

Every session involves a long run of small landings, which load the ankles, calves and Achilles tendons. A wooden floor or rubber gym mat absorbs more of that impact than bare concrete or tile. Cushioned cross-training shoes help too. In an apartment, a mat also cuts the noise that reaches neighbors below.

Boxers have long used the rope for footwork and conditioning, often skipping in timed rounds that mirror a fight. Beginners can borrow that structure with short rounds of skipping separated by rest. Each round can grow longer as misses become rarer. For winter, the rope folds into a bag and needs no power, machine or gym membership.

The kettlebell swing is a hip-hinge movement that trains the glutes, hamstrings and core while driving the heart rate up. Paired with a few other kettlebell lifts in a circuit, a single bell can serve as both a strength session and a cardio workout.

The swing starts with the bell on the floor between the feet. The lifter pushes the hips back, keeps the spine neutral and hikes the bell back between the legs. A sharp drive of the hips forward then sends it out in front of the body. The arms act as connectors. The power comes from the hips, not the shoulders.

Two versions are common in gyms. The Russian swing stops the bell at about chest height, with the arms roughly parallel to the floor. The American swing carries it all the way overhead. That overhead finish lengthens the path of the bell. It also demands more shoulder mobility and makes it harder to keep the lower back neutral at the top of each rep.

A circuit adds movements the swing leaves out. The goblet squat, with the bell held by its horns at chest height, trains the quads and an upright torso. The clean brings the bell from the floor to the rack position, resting against the forearm and the front of the shoulder. The Turkish get-up takes a lifter from lying on the floor to standing with the bell locked out overhead, then back down again. It is slow and deliberate, and it tests shoulder stability and coordination more than conditioning.

Bell weight and pace set the calorie burn. A heavier bell moved for the same number of reps asks more of the working muscles. A faster pace with shorter breaks keeps the heart rate elevated across the whole session. Long pauses between rounds pull the workload down.

Lower-back safety comes down to technique. The swing should be a hinge rather than a squat, with the shins staying close to vertical. Each rep should finish with the lifter standing tall and the glutes contracted, not leaning backward. Rounding the spine to chase the bell on the backswing is a common error, and it shifts strain onto the lower back.

For winter training at home, a single kettlebell fits in a closet corner. Bells were traditionally sized in a Russian unit called the pood, equal to about 16 kilograms. Modern bells come in a range of lighter and heavier sizes, sold in kilograms or pounds.

A rowing machine works the legs, core and upper body in one linked stroke. Calorie burn on an indoor erg follows the power a rower puts into each drive. That power appears directly on the machine's monitor.

Erg is short for ergometer, a device that measures work done. Competitive crews have long used ergs to keep training through winter, when rivers and lakes are too cold or frozen to row on. Home and gym models come in air, magnetic, water and hydraulic designs. Concept2's air-resistance rowers are a common sight in gyms and at indoor rowing competitions. The rower stays seated throughout. That keeps impact on the knees and ankles low.

Each stroke follows a fixed order. The drive starts at the catch, with shins close to vertical and arms straight. The legs push first. The torso then swings back from the hips, and the arms finish by drawing the handle toward the lower ribs. The recovery reverses that sequence: arms extend, the body tips forward and the knees bend to slide the seat back to the catch. Pulling with the arms before the legs have finished is a common error. It shifts work away from the large leg muscles and onto the smaller muscles of the arms and shoulders.

The damper lever on an air rower is often mistaken for a resistance dial. On a Concept2 machine, it runs from one to 10 and controls how much air flows into the flywheel housing. A higher setting makes each stroke feel heavier and slower to accelerate, much like rowing a larger, slower boat. It does not by itself make the workout harder. Resistance on an air rower comes from how hard the rower pulls. A faster-spinning flywheel pushes back with more force.

Stroke rate and power are separate measures. Stroke rate counts strokes per minute. Power reflects how hard and how fast each drive moves the handle. A high rate with weak strokes can produce less work than a slower rate with strong leg drive.

The monitor reports that work as watts, as a pace per 500 meters or as a running calorie estimate. Raising the wattage, holding a faster split or extending the session all increase the energy a workout demands.

Stair climbing lifts your full body weight upward with every step. That puts sustained work on the glutes, quadriceps and calves. It can be done on a gym stepmill or in an ordinary building stairwell. Both options keep training going when sidewalks are icy.

Each step works like a small single-leg press. One leg drives the body up while the other swings through to the next stair. The hamstrings help extend the hip, and the core holds the torso upright. The body works against gravity the whole time. Heart rate climbs quickly as a result, even at a modest pace.

Gym machines come in two main styles. A stepmill, such as the StairMaster StepMill, has a revolving set of stairs that rolls downward like a short escalator. The user keeps climbing to stay in place. A stepper uses two pedals that move up and down without a full step cycle. The stepmill more closely copies the motion of a real staircase. Both let the user set a step speed and hold it for an entire session.

A building stairwell costs nothing and is common in apartment blocks and office towers. It offers real stairs with landings, which break up the climb with brief turns. It has no speed setting, so the climber controls pace alone. Check building rules first. Some stairwell doors lock from the stairwell side, and some are fitted with alarms.

Posture has a direct effect on calorie burn. Leaning on the side rails of a machine shifts part of body weight onto the arms. The legs then lift less, and the workout gets easier. Standing tall with only a light touch on the rails for balance keeps the full load on the legs.

Pace and step pattern are the other levers. A faster step rate raises effort. Taking two stairs at a time lengthens each stride and works the glutes and hips through a deeper range of motion. Alternating single and double steps adds variety within one session.

The way down needs attention in a real stairwell. Descending puts braking force through the knees and the front of the thigh, which can strain sensitive joints. Riding the elevator down and then repeating the climb spares the knees that load. A stepmill avoids the descent entirely.

Lap swimming in an indoor pool is a full-body, low-impact workout. Water supports most of a swimmer's body weight. The arms, legs, back and core can work hard without the pounding of running or jumping.

That buoyancy makes swimming an option for people with sore knees, hips or ankles. Each stroke pulls against the resistance of the water rather than against gravity. The shoulders, lats and chest drive the pull. The hips, glutes and legs supply the kick. The core holds the body in a long, flat line, which reduces drag as the swimmer moves through the water.

Lap swimmers usually rotate among four strokes. Freestyle, also called front crawl, is the fastest and the one most people use for continuous laps. Backstroke uses a similar alternating arm pattern on the back. It keeps the face out of the water and makes breathing simple. Breaststroke combines a simultaneous arm sweep with a frog-style kick, and it is the slowest of the four in competition. Butterfly moves both arms together over the water with an undulating dolphin kick. It is the most technically and physically demanding of the four. Most recreational swimmers use it only in short bursts.

Stroke choice is one of three main levers on calorie burn. The other two are pace and the time spent resting at the wall. A swimmer who glides through easy breaststroke and pauses after every length uses far less energy than one holding a steady freestyle pace. Shortening rest between lengths keeps effort high across the session. Swimming sets on a fixed send-off time, where each repeat starts at a set point on the clock, does the same. Technique also matters. A swimmer with inefficient form can tire quickly while covering little distance.

Two common pieces of pool equipment let swimmers target one part of the body. A kickboard is held out in front of the swimmer. The arms stay still and the legs do the work. A pull buoy is a foam float squeezed between the thighs. It keeps the legs afloat without kicking and shifts the load to the arms, shoulders and back. Fins and hand paddles add speed or resistance. They also change stroke mechanics, and swimmers tend to use them in limited doses.

Pool length shapes how a workout is counted. Many U.S. pools are 25 yards long, while long-course competition pools measure 50 meters. Swimmers often plan sets by distance rather than minutes. A pace clock on the wall helps them track intervals and rest.

The winter case for swimming rests on heated indoor pools at gyms, YMCAs, community recreation centers and universities. The water temperature stays steady regardless of snow or ice outside. The main seasonal adjustment comes after the swim. Wet hair and damp skin lose heat quickly in cold air. Drying off fully and covering the head before leaving the building limits that heat loss on the way home.

A treadmill lets runners and walkers set an exact speed and incline. Those two settings are the main ways to change how many calories a session burns.

The machine moves a motorized belt beneath the user at a chosen pace. In the U.S., consoles usually show speed in miles per hour, while most other markets use kilometers per hour. Incline is shown as a percentage grade, and raising it tilts the front of the deck upward. With no wind, ice, traffic lights or uneven pavement, a runner can hold a target pace for an entire session. That precision suits training plans built around specific paces.

Speed is the first lever. A faster pace covers more ground each minute, and heart rate and breathing climb to match. The jump from walking to running also changes the movement itself. Running includes a moment when both feet leave the belt. That raises both the effort and the impact on each landing.

Incline is the second lever. Each step on a raised deck lifts the body upward as well as forward. That shifts more of the work onto the glutes, hamstrings and calves than flat walking does. Heart rate can climb to a demanding level even at a walking pace. For people who want to avoid the pounding of running, incline walking offers a lower-impact way to raise the intensity.

How a person holds on matters too. Gripping the handrails, especially on a steep incline, lets the arms carry part of the body's weight and often shortens the stride. The legs do less work, and the calorie burn drops. The console calculates its calorie readout from settings such as speed, incline and any body weight entered. It has no way to detect someone leaning on the rails. A light touch for balance keeps most of the effort on the legs.

Safety starts before the belt moves. Most treadmills have a safety key that clips to clothing. If the user drifts too far back or falls, the key pulls free and the belt stops. A safe start means standing on the side rails, starting the belt at a slow speed and then stepping on. Clear space behind the machine reduces the risk if someone slips off the back.

In winter, a treadmill at home or in a gym supports steady runs, interval sessions and long incline walks after dark or during a snowstorm.

#5504. Coding Dojo co-founder unveils ‘Idea to Launch,’ a 30-day program to help aspiring founders build with AI

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 29, 2026 at 8:00 amOctober 29, 2026 at 7:47 am

Richard Wang, co-founder and former CEO of coding bootcamp Coding Dojo, is launching Idea to Launch, a 30-day program that helps would-be founders turn a startup idea into a working product using AI coding tools and hands-on engineering help.

Nearly four years after selling Coding Dojo to Perdoceo for $70 million, Wang was looking for a way to keep doing work that had a measurable impact on people’s lives. He found it in mentoring aspiring founders.

Wang thinks AI is about to do for software what smartphones did for video. Cheap cameras and cloud platforms gave rise to the influencer economy, and he believes AI will push the cost of building a product close to zero.

“We’re going to create this whole new builder economy that’s about to come in the next three to five years,” he said. “Baby boomers are gifted with cheap housing. I think Gen Z is going to be gifted with a cheap price to build.”

He sees plenty of demand. Citing a Shopify-Gallup study and a Zapier/Harris poll, Idea to Launch says 60% of Americans have a business idea but only 9% launch one. Wang said the reasons people hold back include fear of failure, not knowing how to get started, and not wanting to give up a paycheck or benefits.

Unlike accelerators such as Techstars or Y Combinator, Idea to Launch doesn’t take equity, and participants don’t have to quit their jobs. Over 10 evening sessions, founders get coaching, run customer interviews, build a product with AI tools such as Lovable, Replit and Cursor, and plan a launch. Each founder also gets 10 hours of one-on-one help from professional engineers.

Wang said people without technical backgrounds can now vibe-code 80% to 90% of a product on their own. The hard part, he said, is connecting it to other services, setting up the database correctly and making it secure.

“We’ll provide that type of knowledge with real engineering support,” he said. For engineers who have never done customer discovery or marketing, the program fills in the business side.

Security researchers have found serious vulnerabilities in apps built on vibe-coding platforms. A 2025 scan found 170 of 1,645 apps built with Lovable exposing user data, and another case this year exposed nearly 19,000 user records. Wang said the program’s engineers will make sure security holes are fixed “before they launch or before they get onto the first customer.”

The first cohort starts Jan. 11, followed by three more through April. Each is capped at 15 to 20 founders. Tuition is $3,500 for the inaugural cohort, down from the normal $5,000. Sessions will be held in person in Seattle or Bellevue, and Wang said he expects to pick a space within the next month. He is self-funding the venture.

Wang, who immigrated from China at 13 and was the first in his family to attend college, became Coding Dojo’s CEO in 2015. He left in 2017 for Trupanion and returned in 2019. The company grew to $50 million in peak annual revenue, according to Wang, and had 194 employees at the time of the sale, according to GeekWire’s earlier reporting. It operated campuses in several states before shifting online during the pandemic.

Wang sees Idea to Launch expanding to other tech hubs, then online, and eventually licensing the program globally, much as Coding Dojo grew to multiple campuses. If the first cohorts go well, he can envision a follow-up program, Launch to Traction, to help founders find more customers.

He doesn’t plan to invest in participants’ companies. Having spent years building and selling Coding Dojo, Wang said he knows how hard that road is and would rather “cheer them on from the sidelines.” He said taking VC money at Coding Dojo created pressure to grow 100% a year, something he calls “startup steroids.”

For Wang, the point isn’t to find the next unicorn. It’s to give more people a shot at building something now that AI has made it cheaper and easier.

“I think everyone should try at least once just to bring their idea to reality,” he said.

Track all of GeekWire’s startup coverage: Sign up for the weekly startup email newsletter; check out the funding tracker and VC directory; and follow our startup news headlines.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5503. What Solana’s Alpenglow Switch Actually Changes at Slot 459,653,000

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

For about 400 milliseconds this afternoon, Solana will stop landing user transactions. That isn't a failure.

It's the scheduled handoff between two consensus systems, and it's probably the only "400 ms" figure that matters today.

Many people heading into the Alpenglow launch still treat 400 ms block times and 12.8-second finality as the bar to beat. Those are the old chain's numbers. They describe TowerBFT, the system Alpenglow is replacing, so Alpenglow shouldn't be checked against them. If you go through Solana's own documentation, you'll find the right benchmarks before the first post-launch numbers arrive.

According to Solana's official Alpenglow page, the upgrade's feature gate activates at the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, October 21, at about 13:20 UTC. The Solana Foundation says to treat that time as an estimate and to watch the epoch instead.

The new consensus doesn't take over the moment the epoch begins. TowerBFT keeps running for the first 5,000 slots, and Alpenglow takes control at slot 459,653,000. Anza, the team behind the main Agave client, put that switch at around 14:00 UTC.

That time isn't fixed. Solana Compass calculated that with about 375,000 slots left before the switch, each millisecond of drift in average slot time moves the boundary by roughly six minutes. Using epoch 1062's pace, it estimated the switch at about 14:02 UTC.

The transition itself has a cost. Solana Compass reports a gap of roughly two slots, about 400 ms, during which blocks carry only votes and user transactions don't land. So the 400 ms everyone is watching for will turn up, just as a pause rather than a block time.

This is where much of today's coverage gets it wrong.

Block time first. Solana's page says slots moved from 400 ms to 200 ms in a separate "reduced slot times" upgrade, which finished this month. That change isn't part of Alpenglow. It was already running before today. Solana Compass measured epoch 1062 averaging 217.7 ms per slot over 26.1 hours. Checking Alpenglow against 400 ms would mean grading it against a number the network had already beaten before the switch.

Then finality. The 12.8 seconds is TowerBFT's figure. Under that system, a block became final only after enough votes built up over 32 slots. Alpenglow's stated target is about 150 ms, which Solana describes as 99% faster than TowerBFT.

Solana is careful about that 150 ms figure, and I think readers should be too. The Foundation calls it an expectation, not a constant, and says one-round finality comes in lower. Galaxy's engineers, quoted by Solana Compass, call it a design target rather than a measured result. As I noted when looking at how CertiK verifies a TPS claim, a target is a claim until someone measures it on the live network.

Alpenglow is Solana's first replacement of its core consensus since TowerBFT, and today's launch only covers part of it.

The first phase, Votor, ships in Agave 4.3. Validators now send votes directly to each other and combine them into certificates, instead of submitting votes as on-chain transactions. Per Solana's page, votes are no longer transactions and no longer appear in blocks. A block can finalize in one round if at least 80% of stake notarizes it. Otherwise, a second round uses 60% thresholds.

Proof of History no longer paces block production. Execution stays the same: the SVM, programs, transactions and fees don't change.

The second phase, Rotor, will replace Turbine, Solana's block propagation layer. Solana lists it as "not yet scheduled." If someone credits today's numbers to "Alpenglow" as a whole, half of the design hasn't shipped yet.

The security trade-off is also worth knowing. TowerBFT needed more than two-thirds of stake for confirmation. Alpenglow tolerates 20% malicious stake plus 20% offline stake. Solana Compass notes that slashing for double voting is defined but not enabled in this first version.

Validators also pay differently. TowerBFT voting cost about 1 SOL per epoch in vote transaction fees. Alpenglow replaces that with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch Validator Admission Ticket (SIMD-0357), which is burned. A validator that can't pay doesn't vote or produce blocks in the next epoch.

In my view, this is the detail most likely to affect today's real numbers.

Alpenglow's fastest finality depends on the one-round fast path, which needs at least 80% of stake to notarize a block. On the morning of October 20, a tracker run by Pumpkin's Pool, cited by SolanaFloor and reported by Solana Compass, flagged 151 validators holding 20.3% of stake as unprepared. The day before, that figure was 45%.

The math is uncomfortable. If 20.3% of stake really couldn't vote, only 79.7% would be left, which is just short of the fast-path threshold. In that case, blocks would need the slower second round, and finality would land above the headline figure.

I expect that number to drop before the switch, since operators have been upgrading quickly. But it's the main reason I wouldn't trust any finality figure from the first hour without also checking how much stake is actually voting. Validators without a registered BLS key, or that miss the required client version, stop voting entirely. Their delegators also stop earning inflation rewards.

There's already one public reference point. Solana's page links to a community cluster explorer run by Valid Blocks, where Alpenglow has been running on Agave 4.3.2.

When I checked this morning, it showed an average finalization time of 131 ms over the past hour, ranging from 111 ms to 156 ms. Average slot time was 215 ms. That's inside Solana's target range.

That cluster had 62 active validators and about 10.2 million SOL staked. Mainnet is far larger, more spread out geographically, and runs under real load. Test-cluster results are a strong sign, but they aren't proof of how mainnet will perform.

You don't need to wait for a press release to know whether the switch happened. Solana's getAgGenesisCert RPC method returns null while the cluster is still on TowerBFT and returns a genesis certificate once Alpenglow is live. Nodes older than Agave 4.3 return a "Method not found" error, which shouldn't be confused with null.

Once the certificate shows up, here's what I'll be watching over the first few epochs:

One caveat for developers: according to Anza's operator notes, the Clock sysvar's unix_timestamp now estimates when the parent block ended, not when the current block began, and should be treated as approximate. Any timing tool that reads block timestamps may need adjusting.

If Alpenglow delivers, Solana goes from finality you wait for to finality you'd barely notice. I'll believe the 150 ms figure once mainnet consistently shows it.

#5502. Laza Medical Raises Up to $160 Million in Series B Financing Led by GE HealthCare to Advance Intelligent Imaging for Transforming the Cath Lab

Company's first-of-a-kind intelligent imaging system aims to expand patient access, streamline high-quality cardiac care, and establish the foundation for future robotic interventions

LOS GATOS, Calif., Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Laza Medical, Inc., a Shifamed portfolio company pioneering AI-powered robotic imaging solutions for cardiac interventions, today announced it has raised up to $160 million in Series B structured financing. GE HealthCare led the round, with participation from returning investors Unorthodox Ventures, PA MedTech, and AMED. The financing will support the company's mission to transform the cardiac catheterization laboratory through intelligent imaging technology designed to simplify procedures, increase autonomy, alleviate resource constraints, and unlock the possibilities for future robotic-enabled interventions.

"The future of cardiac intervention must be one where access, consistency, and quality of care are no longer barriers to better outcomes," stated Jyoti Gera, CEO of Cardiovascular and Interventional Solutions, Advanced Imaging Solutions at GE HealthCare. "Integrating imaging modalities so they work seamlessly together has the potential to redefine the cath lab, enabling more efficient workflows today and paving the way for smarter, robotic procedures tomorrow. We're excited to expand our collaboration with Laza and work together toward this shared vision."

As cardiovascular procedures become increasingly complex, care teams need more intuitive and consistent image guidance amid growing demands for specialized imaging expertise. By combining AI and robotics, Laza has the potential to simplify procedural imaging, extend the reach of specialized imaging expertise, and help care teams navigate and guide complex cardiac interventions with greater confidence.

"High-quality imaging is foundational to all successful cases," said Dr. Firas Zahr, Head of Interventional Cardiology at Oregon Health Sciences University Hospital, who had experience with the software during the first-in-human clinical study last year. "Consistent anatomic and spatial context simplifies procedures and helps clinicians navigate the anatomy with confidence and precision."

"The cath lab is poised for a fundamental evolution, and intelligent imaging powered by AI will play a defining role in what comes next," said Amr Salahieh, Founder and Board Chairman at Laza Medical. "As we reimagine the role of imaging in interventional care, we are grateful for the strong support from our investors, which validates our approach and reinforces our conviction that this solution will streamline processes, reduce variability, and ultimately improve the quality and reach of cardiac procedures."

The Laza Medical System is under development and is not approved for commercial sale in any geography.

Laza Medical is a privately held portfolio company of Shifamed, LLC. The company focuses on developing a high-quality, AI-powered robotic imaging solution for cardiovascular interventions. For more information, visit www.lazamedical.com.

Founded by serial entrepreneur Amr Salahieh, Shifamed is a highly specialized medical innovation hub focused on developing solutions that accelerate time to market, reduce risk, increase impact, and forge a path toward a world where patients are able to lead longer, healthier lives.

Shifamed's goal is to lead the way in next generation of cardiac cath lab innovation, bringing together breakthroughs in advanced imaging, artificial intelligence (AI), and robotics to transform how interventional cardiovascular procedures are performed.

#5501. OpenAI to acquire developer tooling startup Pierre Computer

OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to acquire Pierre Computer Company Inc., a low-profile developer tooling startup.

The terms of the deal were not disclosed. Observers pegged it as a shot at Microsoft Corp.’s open-source software repository GitHub for the age of artificial intelligence agents.

Pierre operates a cloud service that AI agents can use to store the code they generate. It can also store related files such as software licenses and interface design elements. According to Pierre, the service provides significantly better performance than competing technologies. It helped one customer, AI startup Lovable Inc., cut code retrieval latency by about 70%.

Pierre also develops a collection of popular open-source libraries. Two of those libraries, Trees and Diffs, underpin the interface of OpenAI’s Codex programming tool.

Large software projects contain upwards of hundreds of code files that are organized in dozens of folders. Many programming tools include a sidebar specifically designed to help developers navigate those folders. Trees, the first Pierre-developed library used by Codex, marks it easier to implement such sidebars.

Trees can equip a folder navigation sidebar with a search feature and drag-and-drop controls for moving subfolders. Additionally, it flags code files that have been recently added or updated. Developers review those files first when performing tasks such as troubleshooting an outage.

Diffs, the other Pierre library that OpenAI has integrated into Codex, is also designed to power programming tool interfaces. In particular, it can be used to implement the main interface that shows the code the user is currently editing.

When a code file is updated, Diffs points out the specific lines of code that changed to spare developers the hassle of manually finding them. It can show changes in a separate interface section or in-line.

OpenAI will continue to offer Trees and Diffs under an open-source license after the acquisition closes. Additionally, it plans to integrate the features of Pierre’s paid code hosting service into Codex. In the longer term, the Pierre team will help OpenAI “ship new products and platforms.”

The effort will place an emphasis on building software that can optimize coding agents. In particular, OpenAI hopes to streamline agent workflows that involve Git. That’s an open-source tool developers use to manage code files. Trees, Diffs and Pierre’s paid storage service all provide built-in support for Git.

OpenAI makes extensive use of the tool internally. On Monday, the company revealed that it has built a software engine called Pando to boost the performance of its internal Git environment. The engine reduces the amount of time it takes OpenAI engineers’ coding agents to create and read code files.

#5500. How cold is too cold to exercise outside? 10 things to weigh before a winter workout

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How cold is too cold to exercise outside depends on wind, wetness, clothing and health — these 10 cold-weather factors help you judge whether a winter workout makes sense

The thermometer gives only part of the answer. A calm, dry morning and a windy, wet one can share the same reading. They still pull heat from the body at very different rates. Moving air strips away the thin layer of warmth that sits next to the skin. Water conducts heat away from the body far faster than still air does. That is why the question of how cold is too cold to exercise outside has no single number attached to it.

Exercise complicates the picture in both directions. Working muscles produce heat. A runner can feel comfortable in conditions that would chill someone standing at a bus stop. That same effort produces sweat. Damp clothing, especially cotton, insulates poorly. The heat that kept a person warm mid-workout disappears quickly once the pace drops or the session ends. A cold-weather workout can feel fine for the first stretch and turn risky later, especially on a long outing far from shelter.

The exerciser matters too. Clothing choices, time spent outdoors and the condition of the heart, lungs and circulation all shape how well someone handles the cold. Someone with asthma may react to cold, dry air. Someone with Raynaud's phenomenon may find their fingers turning white and numb while a training partner feels little discomfort. Icy pavement and early darkness add hazards that have nothing to do with body temperature at all.

The U.S. National Weather Service publishes a wind chill index. It estimates how cold the air feels on exposed skin when temperature and wind speed are combined. It is a starting point for reading a forecast. It cannot account for wet gear, a skipped warm-up or an underlying health condition.

The 10 factors below offer a practical way to judge whether a winter run, ride or walk makes sense on a given day. They are a selection, not a complete checklist. They cover two cold-related injuries, frostbite and hypothermia, along with the clothing and gear choices that lower the risk of both. They also address the warm-up, breathing cold air, footing and visibility, and medical conditions that call for extra care. The last one covers what to do once the workout ends. Each can be read on its own.

Wind chill measures how quickly moving air pulls heat away from exposed skin. On a windy day, outdoor exercise can carry much more cold-weather risk than the air temperature alone suggests. The wind forecast deserves as much attention as the thermometer reading.

Wind speed drives the effect. The faster the wind blows, the faster bare skin loses heat. Gusty conditions can also swing between tolerable and harsh within a single workout. A calm start is no guarantee of calm conditions an hour later.

The U.S. National Weather Service wind chill index is the standard reference for this effect in North America. Environment and Climate Change Canada uses the same formula. The index assumes no sunshine, as though skin were exposed under a clear night sky. Bright sun on the face can make conditions feel somewhat milder than the index indicates. Overcast days and workouts before sunrise or after sunset get no such help.

Many weather apps show a "feels like" reading next to the actual temperature. In cold weather, that number usually reflects wind chill, but providers calculate it in different ways. Checking the wind speed itself shows what the reading is based on.

Wind chill describes heat loss from skin. It does not lower the actual temperature of anything. A water bottle left outside on a windy day will not get colder than the surrounding air. Exposed skin, though, cools toward that air temperature much faster when the wind is blowing.

Exercise adds its own wind. A runner moving into a headwind faces the forecast wind plus the air created by their own speed. A cyclist usually faces even more, because riding is typically faster than running. A day that feels manageable on a slow walk can feel very different on a fast bike descent.

Route planning can reduce exposure. On an out-and-back course, heading into the wind first means the return leg comes with the wind at your back. That puts the harshest stretch at the start, while you are fresh, rather than at the end, when fatigue sets in. Sheltered routes through trees, between buildings or in valleys can also cut the wind compared with open fields, waterfronts or ridgelines.

Covered skin is far less affected than bare skin. The cheeks, nose and ears take the brunt of a cold wind. A windy forecast is a reason to cover more skin, shorten the session or move the workout indoors.

Frostbite is the freezing of skin and the tissue beneath it. It usually strikes the fingers, toes, ears and nose first. Its early signs are numbness, tingling or stinging, and skin that turns pale, gray or waxy. Spotting those changes early gives an exerciser time to get inside before lasting damage sets in.

The extremities are vulnerable for a simple reason. When the body gets cold, it narrows blood vessels near the surface to protect the heart, lungs and other vital organs. Less warm blood reaches the hands and feet as a result. The ears and nose sit out in the open with little fat or muscle to hold heat.

The mildest form of cold injury is frostnip. Skin feels very cold and may sting, then goes numb and looks red or pale. Frostnip does not cause permanent harm, and the skin recovers once it is rewarmed. It is still a sign that conditions are cold enough for more serious injury.

Frostbite that goes further changes how skin looks and feels. Skin can turn white, grayish-yellow or bluish and take on a waxy appearance. It may feel hard or unusually firm to the touch. Blisters can form after rewarming. In the deepest cases, tissue can turn black and die, and the muscles or joints underneath may stop working normally.

Numbness makes frostbite easy to miss during a workout. A runner focused on pace may not feel a toe going cold inside a shoe. A training partner can help by checking for pale patches on the cheeks, nose and ears. Anyone exercising alone can stop briefly to wiggle fingers and toes and check whether feeling has returned.

The response to suspected frostbite is to get indoors and out of wet clothing. Rewarm the affected area gently in warm water, not hot water. Avoid rubbing the skin, which can damage frozen tissue. Heating pads, stoves and fires are also risky. Numb skin cannot sense heat. It burns easily.

Rewarming should not begin if the area could freeze again before reaching shelter. Thawing followed by refreezing causes worse damage than staying frozen a little longer. Hard skin, blisters, darkened tissue or numbness that lingers after rewarming call for prompt medical care.

Hypothermia is a dangerous drop in the body's core temperature. It can set in during exercise when cold combines with wind or wet conditions. Early signs include strong shivering, fumbling hands and a loss of coordination. Later signs include confusion and slurred speech.

Frostbite damages specific patches of skin and tissue. Hypothermia affects the whole body. The body normally produces enough heat to keep its vital organs within a narrow temperature range. When it loses heat faster than it can make it, that balance breaks down. The heart, nervous system and other organs then begin to work poorly.

Shivering is usually the first signal. It is the body's attempt to generate heat through rapid muscle contractions. A runner or hiker may also notice that their hands have become clumsy. Zipping a jacket or opening a snack can suddenly feel difficult. Stumbling, slowed movement and unusual fatigue often follow.

As the condition worsens, the brain is affected. Confusion, memory lapses, drowsiness and slurred or mumbled speech are common warning signs. This creates a specific danger. A person with hypothermia often cannot recognize what is happening to them. They may insist they feel fine or decide to press on when they should stop. In severe cases, shivering can stop altogether. That is a sign of deepening hypothermia, not recovery.

Several workout conditions raise the risk. Rain, sleet or wet snow can soak through outer layers and leave clothing wet against the skin. Long efforts drain the energy the body uses to stay warm. An injury, a wrong turn or a broken-down bike can leave someone standing still far from shelter. Their heat output then drops sharply. Hypothermia can also develop at temperatures above freezing, especially when a person is wet and exposed for a long time.

Anyone showing signs of hypothermia needs emergency care. Call emergency services, then move the person somewhere warm and dry if possible. Replace wet clothing with dry layers or blankets. Warm the chest, neck, head and groin first. Warm, nonalcoholic drinks can help if the person is fully alert. Handle them gently, and do not rub their arms and legs.

Exercising with a partner, or telling someone the route and expected return time, means help can arrive sooner if something goes wrong far from home.

Dress for cold-weather exercise in three layers: a moisture-wicking base layer against the skin, an insulating mid layer and a wind- and water-resistant outer shell. Each layer does a separate job. Together they hold in heat while letting sweat move away from the body.

The base layer manages moisture. Exercise produces sweat even on a frigid morning, and this layer's job is to move it off the skin. Fabrics such as polyester, polypropylene and merino wool pull moisture away from the skin and toward the outer surface of the garment. There it can evaporate. A base layer works best when it fits close to the body without restricting movement.

Cotton does not belong in this system. It absorbs water readily and holds it against the skin. It also dries slowly. A cotton T-shirt that soaks through early in a run tends to stay wet for the rest of it. Under a jacket, that shirt can leave a runner damp and chilled partway through a workout.

The mid layer provides insulation. Fleece and wool are common choices because they trap warm air close to the body. How thick this layer should be depends on the conditions and the activity. On a milder day or during a hard interval session, some people skip it entirely. A brisk walk or a slow hike produces less body heat than a tempo run. Lower-intensity outings may call for a heavier mid layer.

The outer shell blocks wind and light precipitation. A wind-resistant jacket keeps gusts from cutting through to the warm layers underneath. A shell that is also breathable lets water vapor from sweat escape instead of trapping it inside. Zippers at the chest and vents under the arms release excess heat without the jacket coming off.

Starting slightly cool is a standard rule of thumb for cold-weather running. The body warms up within the first minutes of steady effort. Someone who feels comfortable standing still at the door is likely to overheat once moving. Overheating leads to heavy sweating, which works against the base layer.

The same principles apply below the waist. Running tights or wind-resistant pants cover the legs. On colder days, some exercisers add a thermal base layer underneath.

Conditions should shape the combination every time. A calm, dry day may need only a base layer and a light shell. Rain, sleet or a strong headwind calls for a more protective outer layer. The value of layering is flexibility — pieces can be added, removed or unzipped as the weather and the workout change.

The hands, feet, head and face need their own coverage on a cold-weather workout. A warm jacket does little for them. Mittens or gloves, wool or synthetic socks, a hat or headband, and a neck gaiter or balaclava close the gaps a good outer layer leaves open.

Mittens hold the fingers together in one compartment. That lets them share warmth and leaves less fabric exposed to the air. Mittens generally run warmer than gloves made of similar material. Gloves give more dexterity for working a zipper, using a phone or gripping ski poles.

Some exercisers wear a thin liner glove under a mitten. The liner stays on when the mitten comes off for a quick task. The pair can also be adjusted as the hands warm up. Convertible styles add a fold-over mitten flap to a fingerless or full glove.

Socks made of merino wool or synthetic fibers such as polyester pull sweat away from the skin. They keep insulating when damp. Cotton socks soak up moisture and stay wet, which chills the feet. Thicker socks add warmth. A sock that makes a shoe tight, though, can squeeze the foot and restrict circulation. Mesh running shoes let wind and slush through. Shoes with a water-resistant upper help on wet or snowy days.

A hat or fleece headband covers the ears, which stick out from the head and have little fatty tissue to insulate them. The head loses heat like any other uncovered skin. A hat matters most when the rest of the body is already dressed for the weather. A thin hat can be tucked into a pocket if it gets too warm partway through a run.

A neck gaiter or balaclava shields the neck, cheeks, chin and nose from wind. A gaiter can be pulled up over the face on an exposed stretch and pushed down once the route is sheltered. Moisture from breathing can leave the fabric damp or icy. A spare gaiter helps on longer outings. Sunglasses or sport goggles protect the eyes from wind and from glare off snow.

A dynamic warm-up done indoors before a cold-weather workout loosens muscles and joints that the cold makes stiffer. It also means stepping outside with blood already flowing to working muscles, rather than asking a chilled body to go from standstill to full effort.

Muscle tissue performs best when it is warm. Cold muscles contract more slowly and stretch less readily. Tendons and the connective tissue around joints also lose some of their give as they cool. A hard effort started in that state asks more of tissue that is not ready for it.

A warm-up raises heart rate gradually and increases blood flow to the legs, hips and core. Breathing deepens. Joints move through a fuller range of motion. These changes take time. Outdoors in winter, the cold air works against them from the first step.

Doing the warm-up inside avoids that problem. A hallway, living room or garage offers enough space. The goal is to leave the door already warm. The first minutes outdoors then go toward holding onto heat rather than trying to generate it.

Dynamic movements suit this job better than long, held stretches. Leg swings, walking lunges, high knees, butt kicks, arm circles and bodyweight squats all move the joints while gradually raising effort. Skipping in place or jumping jacks can bring the heart rate up further. Runners can add hip openers and ankle circles. Cyclists can focus on the hips, knees and lower back. Static stretches held for long periods can wait until after the session, once the body is warm and back indoors.

The warm-up should be thorough but short enough to avoid heavy sweating. Arriving at the door damp sets up heat loss that clothing then has to fight. The target is to feel warm and loose, not soaked. Pulling on outer layers just before stepping out helps keep the heat the warm-up built.

Once outside, the first several minutes should still be easy. An easy jog, a brisk walk or a low-gear spin lets the body adjust to the cold air before pace or power climbs. Picking up speed after that adjustment period avoids an abrupt jump from a warm room straight to full intensity.

The same approach applies to strength or interval work done outdoors in winter. Explosive efforts such as sprints, hill repeats or plyometric jumps place the highest demands on muscles and tendons. Those efforts belong later in the session. By then the body has had time to warm fully in the conditions it is actually working in.

Cold, dry air can make the airways narrow during or shortly after a workout. This condition is called exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. Covering the mouth and nose and getting a treatment plan from a doctor are two practical ways to keep it from cutting a winter session short.

The trigger comes from how the body prepares incoming air. Before air reaches the deeper parts of the lungs, the airways warm it and add moisture to it. At rest, the nose does much of that work. During hard exercise, breathing speeds up and shifts toward the mouth. That bypasses much of the nose's conditioning.

Winter air makes the job harder. Cold air holds little moisture. The lining of the airways loses water and heat as it works to bring each breath up to body temperature. That drying and cooling can prompt the smooth muscle around the airways to tighten.

The symptoms resemble asthma. Coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and shortness of breath are common. Some people notice an unusual drop in stamina or a lingering cough after a cold run rather than obvious wheezing. Symptoms often peak shortly after exercise stops, not at the hardest point of the effort.

The condition is closely linked with asthma. It can also affect people who have never been diagnosed with asthma. Anyone who regularly struggles to breathe during or after cold-weather exercise has a reason to get checked rather than assume a lack of fitness is to blame.

A doctor can confirm the problem with breathing tests, such as spirometry measured before and after exercise. Treatment often includes a short-acting inhaler taken before a workout. The right plan depends on the individual. People who already have a rescue inhaler should carry it on outdoor winter workouts.

A loose scarf, neck gaiter or balaclava over the mouth and nose traps some warmth and moisture from each exhaled breath. The next breath picks some of that back up before it reaches the airways. Breathing through the nose at easier paces does similar work. Keeping intensity lower on the coldest, driest days also reduces how much air the lungs must condition.

Breathing trouble that does not ease with rest or a rescue inhaler is a medical emergency and calls for immediate care.

Slippery footing and poor visibility are winter running hazards that have little to do with the temperature itself. Better traction, a shorter and slower stride and gear that makes a runner visible to drivers address both problems directly.

Black ice is difficult to spot. It forms as a thin, clear glaze that lets dark pavement show through. A frozen road can look merely wet as a result. Bridges and overpasses tend to freeze before other roads. Cold air reaches them from above and below. Shaded stretches, low spots where meltwater pools and patches that thaw by day and refreeze overnight deserve the same caution.

Footwear changes how much grip a runner has. Trail shoes with deep lugs bite into packed snow better than smooth road soles. On icy routes, slip-on traction devices stretch over a shoe and add metal studs, coils or small spikes. Yaktrax and Kahtoola Microspikes are common examples. These devices can feel unstable on bare, dry pavement. They suit routes that stay frozen from start to finish.

Stride mechanics also affect footing. A shorter stride keeps each foot landing closer to the body's center of mass. That lowers the chance of a foot sliding out on contact. Slowing down, keeping the knees slightly bent and taking corners gradually all give more time to react. Icy days suit easy efforts, with faster sessions moved to clear pavement, an indoor track or a treadmill.

Snow also changes the shape of a route. Plowed banks narrow road shoulders and sidewalks, pushing runners closer to traffic. Fresh snow can hide curbs, potholes and storm drains. A route the runner already knows well is easier to judge when its surface is buried.

Darkness makes each of these hazards harder to see. In the Northern Hemisphere, days are shortest around the December solstice. In the Southern Hemisphere, the shortest days fall around the June solstice. The farther a city sits from the equator, the less daylight it gets in winter. Morning and evening workouts often fall in full dark as a result.

Visibility gear works in two directions. A headlamp or handheld light shows the runner the ground ahead, including ice and broken pavement. Reflective material and blinking lights help drivers see the runner. A white light facing forward and a red light facing back match the pattern drivers expect from vehicles. Reflective bands on the ankles and wrists move with each stride. That motion helps drivers recognize a person rather than a fixed object.

Route choice ties these measures together. Well-lit streets make both ice and runners easier to see. Sidewalks keep runners off road shoulders and away from passing cars. Where no sidewalk exists, facing oncoming traffic lets a runner see approaching cars. Drivers in winter may be contending with frosted windshields, low-angle glare and longer stopping distances on slick roads. Telling someone the planned route and expected return time means help can be sent if a fall leaves a runner unable to get home.

Some health conditions make outdoor exercise in cold weather riskier, including heart disease, Raynaud's phenomenon, diabetes and asthma. Anyone with one of these conditions should talk to a doctor before starting or continuing an outdoor winter workout routine.

Heart disease is a central concern. Cold air causes blood vessels near the skin to narrow. That response helps the body hold on to heat, but it also raises blood pressure. The heart then has to work harder to move blood through the body. Physical exertion adds to that demand.

For people with heart conditions, heavy effort in the cold carries added strain. Snow shoveling is a familiar example. It pairs cold exposure with sudden, intense upper-body work, often for people who are not otherwise active. A doctor can advise on safe intensity levels and on which symptoms mean it is time to stop. Chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, dizziness or pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back all call for halting activity and seeking emergency care.

Raynaud's phenomenon affects circulation in a different way. In people with the condition, small blood vessels in the fingers and toes narrow sharply in response to cold or stress. The affected skin can go pale or bluish and lose feeling. As blood flow returns, the area may turn red and throb or tingle. Some people also notice it in the ears, nose or lips. Raynaud's can occur on its own or alongside another condition, such as an autoimmune disease. For outdoor exercisers, keeping the whole body warm — not only the hands and feet — helps limit attacks.

Diabetes can raise cold-weather risk through nerve damage and reduced circulation, particularly in the feet. Reduced sensation means a person may not notice cold injury, blisters or wet socks until harm has already occurred. Checking the feet after a winter workout is a practical habit for anyone with the condition.

Asthma rounds out the list. Breathing cold air can be a particular trigger for people with the condition. Anyone with asthma should raise winter training with their doctor specifically rather than assume a warm-weather routine carries over unchanged.

Get out of damp clothing as soon as a cold-weather workout ends. While you move, working muscles produce enough heat to offset the moisture on your skin. Once you stop, that heat source drops off, and wet fabric keeps pulling warmth away from the body.

A shirt soaked with sweat draws heat from the skin faster than the same shirt does when dry. Sweat also keeps evaporating after the effort ends, and evaporation cools the skin. That cooling is exactly what sweat is for during exercise. After exercise, in cold air, it works against you.

The result is a familiar post-workout chill. Someone can finish the final stretch feeling comfortable, then start shivering a few minutes after stopping. Shivering is the body's attempt to generate heat through rapid muscle contractions. It signals that heat loss has started to outpace heat production.

The riskiest window is the gap between finishing and getting indoors. Standing in a parking lot to stretch, chat or check a fitness watch extends that gap. So does a long walk back to the car after a cooldown. A route that ends at the front door, a parked car or a heated building shortens the exposure.

A dry change of clothes helps when the finish line is not at home. A fresh top, dry socks and a dry hat replace the items that tend to be wettest. A warm jacket thrown over the top blocks the wind while you change. Wet hair keeps cooling the head long after the workout is over. A small towel in the bag helps with that.

Indoors, a warm shower and a hot, nonalcoholic drink help bring body temperature back up. Alcohol widens blood vessels near the skin. That can make a person feel warmer while actually increasing heat loss. A snack also gives the body fuel to keep producing its own heat.

Washing gear and letting it dry completely before the next session prevents starting out in fabric that is still damp. Gloves or a jacket left balled up in a gym bag overnight often stay wet. Putting them back on means beginning the next cold workout already chilled.

#5499. AWS growth hits 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, as Amazon misses on earnings

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 1:37 pmOctober 30, 2026 at 10:35 am

Amazon Web Services revenue grew 39% to $46 billion in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said he expects the cloud unit to top 40% growth in both 2027 and 2028.

That wasn’t enough for investors. Amazon posted earnings of $1.89 per share, well short of the $1.97 analysts expected, as higher interest costs on its growing debt and other losses ate into its profit.

Operating income beat expectations at $28.1 billion, above the high end of Amazon’s own guidance, and the 13.9% operating margin for the quarter was the highest in the company’s history.

Revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12%, came in just under analyst estimates but at the top of Amazon’s forecast range. Shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading, after closing down 4% during the regular session.

Update: On the earnings call, Jassy said AWS has a backlog of $578 billion in contracted future revenue, more than double a year earlier. He also said Amazon expects to spend “meaningfully more” on capital projects in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion it plans for this year.

Amazon may need to count on its legendary willingness to be “misunderstood for long periods of time,” as it asks investors to look past the costs to where its biggest businesses are headed.

In the company’s earnings release, Jassy said Amazon’s retail business is gaining market share with improving margins. Retail sales, including online stores, physical stores and third-party seller services, totaled nearly $500 billion over the past 12 months, and AWS is now at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate.

“There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years,” he said.

On the earnings call, Jassy said those two businesses are AWS and Amazon’s stores business.

Advertising grew 11% to $19.6 billion, or 12% excluding currency changes, down from 22% on that basis a year earlier. Amazon blamed the timing of Prime Day and a few other factors, and said it expects ad growth to return to the high teens in the fourth quarter.

Online stores grew 2% to $68.5 billion, held back by Prime Day moving into the second quarter this year. Amazon said overall revenue growth would have been about 4 percentage points higher without the shift.

Third-party seller services, the fees Amazon collects from merchants on its site, grew 9% to $46.5 billion. AWS came within about $500 million of it.

Subscription services, which includes Prime memberships, grew 11% to $14 billion.

Physical stores, mostly Whole Foods, grew 2% to $5.7 billion.

Outlook: Amazon expects fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion, up 12% to 16%, and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion.

Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky said on the earnings call that costs for Amazon Leo, the company’s satellite internet service, are weighing on its fourth-quarter profit forecast as the service gets ready to launch later this year.

Wall Street had expected fourth-quarter operating income of $33.2 billion, near the top of that range, according to analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives. It still expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year.

Amazon’s free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier, mostly because of its AI investments.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

The Company provides non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP operating margin, non-GAAP net income and non-GAAP EPS financial measures as supplemental information regarding the Company's operational performance and believes providing this additional information allows investors to see Company results through the eyes of management, to evaluate more clearly and consistently the Company's core operational performance and expenses and evaluate the efficacy of the methodology used by management to measure such performance. The Company uses the measures disclosed in this release to evaluate the Company's historical and prospective financial performance, as well as its performance relative to its competitors. Specifically, management uses these items to further its own understanding of the Company's core operating performance, which the Company believes represents its performance in the ordinary, ongoing and customary course of its operations. Cost of revenues, costs of research and development and costs of selling, general and administrative: The Company's GAAP presentation of gross margin and operating expenses may include (i) additional depreciation and amortization from changes in estimated useful life and the write-down of certain property, plant and equipment and intangibles, (ii) charges such as severance, benefits and outplacement costs related to restructuring plans with a specific and defined term, (iii) costs for facilities not required for ongoing operations, and costs related to the relocation of certain equipment from these facilities and/or contract manufacturer facilities, (iv) stock-based compensation, including related employer payroll taxes, (v) amortization expense related to acquired intangibles, (vi) amortization expense related to acquisition related inventory step-up, (vii) changes in fair value of contingent consideration liabilities, (viii) acquisition related transaction and integration costs related to acquired entities, (ix) significant legal settlements and other contingencies and (x) other charges unrelated to our core operating performance comprised mainly of other costs and contingencies unrelated to current and future operations, including transformational initiatives such as the implementation of simplified automated processes, site consolidations, and reorganizations. The Company excludes these items in calculating non-GAAP operating margin, non-GAAP net income and non-GAAP EPS.

Non-cash interest expense and other expense: The Company excludes certain non-cash interest and other expenses, including loss on debt extinguishment, accretion of debt discount, and other non-cash activities that management believes are not reflective of such ordinary, ongoing and core operating activities, when calculating non-GAAP net income and non-GAAP EPS.

Income tax expense or benefit: The Company excludes certain non-cash tax expense or benefit items, such as (i) the utilization of net operating losses (NOLs) where valuation allowances were released, (ii) intra-period tax allocation benefit and (iii) the tax effect for amortization of non-tax deductible intangible assets, in calculating non-GAAP net income and non-GAAP EPS.

Non-GAAP financial measures are not in accordance with, preferable to, or an alternative for, generally accepted accounting principles in the United States. The GAAP measure most directly comparable to non-GAAP operating income is operating income. The GAAP measure most directly comparable to non-GAAP operating margin is operating margin. The GAAP measure most directly comparable to non-GAAP net income is net income. The GAAP measure most directly comparable to non-GAAP EPS is earnings per share.
