#5497. Hottest years on record: 10 topics, from 2016 to 2024 and what 2027 would need

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The hottest years on record, including 2016, 2023 and 2024, explained in 10 topics, plus why 2027 could join them if long-term warming and El Niño line up

For the first time in the Copernicus Climate Change Service record, a full calendar year ran more than 1.5°C warmer than the pre-industrial era. Copernicus put 2024 at 1.55°C above its 1850–1900 baseline. The World Meteorological Organization also reported 2024 as the warmest year in its records.

That milestone came only a year after the previous record. Copernicus put 2023 at about 1.48°C above the same baseline. Before that, 2016 held the title, helped along by a strong El Niño. The record has now changed hands twice since 2016.

The pattern raises a question for anyone tracking climate, energy markets or long-range business risk. Could another year soon join the hottest years on record? The answer depends on two forces working together. The first is long-term warming from greenhouse gases, which sets the base trend. The second is short-term natural variation, such as El Niño. El Niño adds warmth to the global average, and its effect shows up in the year after it peaks.

Both forces mattered in 2023 and 2024. El Niño helped lift those years, but it does not explain the full rise across several years. The longer climb comes from greenhouse gas warming.

The numbers also need context. The Paris Agreement's 1.5°C goal refers to warming averaged over decades, not to a single year. One year above the line, as 2024 was, does not by itself mean the goal has been breached. That distinction matters when reading each new annual figure.

This slideshow is a selection of 10 topics rather than a ranked list. It covers the record years themselves, including 2016, 2023 and 2024, and where 2025 stands while its ranking awaits confirmation. It explains the 1850–1900 baseline behind the figures, and how Copernicus and the WMO report a record year. It also walks through the mechanisms behind each record.

The final slide looks at 2027. It does not offer a forecast. Instead, it sets out what would need to line up for 2027 to join those record years. That means the steady pressure of greenhouse gas warming plus a short-term boost such as El Niño.

2024 is the warmest calendar year on record. The Copernicus Climate Change Service and the World Meteorological Organization both reported it as the warmest year in their records.

Copernicus put 2024 at 1.55°C above the 1850–1900 pre-industrial baseline. It described 2024 as the first calendar year above 1.5°C.

The figure covers a full calendar year, from January through December. That makes it a different kind of measure from a single hot month or a heat wave in one region.

The ranking does not rest on one organization. Copernicus and the WMO each placed 2024 at the top of their own records. The result appears in two separate records, not just one.

The words "so far" in the title matter. 2024 holds the record as of these reports. A later year could still overtake it, just as 2024 overtook the year before it.

2023 was the warmest year on record until 2024 overtook it. The Copernicus Climate Change Service put 2023 at about 1.48°C above the 1850–1900 pre-industrial baseline.

That left 2023 roughly 0.02°C below 1.5°C. The Paris Agreement's 1.5°C goal refers to long-term warming over decades, not to any single year.

Copernicus described 2024 as the first calendar year above 1.5°C. By the Copernicus figures, 2024 ran about 0.07°C warmer than 2023.

Before 2023, the record belonged to 2016. That mark held until 2023, seven years later. The next change came after just one year, when 2024 set a new high.

El Niño helped lift global average temperatures in 2023. Its effect on the global average shows up in the year after it peaks. It also helped lift 2024.

El Niño does not account for the full rise across those years. Long-term warming from greenhouse gases is the base trend underneath it. A short-term boost such as El Niño adds to that trend in a given year rather than replacing it.

2016 held the record for the warmest year until 2023 overtook it. A strong El Niño helped drive the heat that put 2016 at the top.

Among the years that have held the global temperature record in recent succession, 2016 is the earliest. Its mark has since been passed twice, first by 2023 and then by 2024.

The El Niño boost in 2016 came on top of the long-term warming trend from greenhouse gases. It added to that trend rather than replacing it.

The same pairing helped set the later records. El Niño also helped lift 2023 and 2024, while greenhouse gas warming supplied the base beneath them.

The ranking of 2025 among the warmest years is pending confirmation. No verified position or temperature figure for 2025 is available here, so this slideshow does not place the year on the list.

That sets 2025 apart from the record years around it. 2024 is the warmest calendar year in the records of both the Copernicus Climate Change Service and the World Meteorological Organization. 2023 held the record before 2024 overtook it. 2016 held it before 2023.

Any confirmed placement for 2025 would be judged against those years. That comparison works only when every figure is measured against the same reference period. A number built on a different baseline would not line up with the earlier results.

A ranking would also need a named record keeper behind it. Copernicus and the WMO each publish their own annual results. A position for 2025 would be credited to whichever of them reported it, not stated as a general finding.

Until one of those record keepers confirms it, where 2025 sits among the warmest years remains an open question.

A single calendar year above 1.5°C does not mean the world has missed the Paris Agreement target. The 1.5°C goal refers to long-term warming measured over decades, not the temperature of any one year.

That distinction now applies to a real case. The Copernicus Climate Change Service described 2024 as the first calendar year above 1.5°C.

The record year before it sat on the other side of the line. In the Copernicus record, 2023 came in just under 1.5°C. Two record years in a row straddled the threshold, one below and one above. That shows how close individual years now run to that line.

The Paris goal is built around a sustained level of warming. A long-term measure averages many years together. Averaging smooths out the swings that push any one year up or down.

Single years carry short-term noise. El Niño is the clearest example of that noise, and it helped lift both 2023 and 2024. A year boosted that way can sit above the long-term level.

The reverse also holds. A year without that boost can land below the long-term level while the underlying trend keeps rising. Judging the goal on one year would mean judging it partly on natural swings rather than on greenhouse gas warming.

Greenhouse gas warming is the base trend beneath those swings. That base trend is what a decades-long measure is designed to track.

For anyone reading annual climate reports, a record year and the Paris goal measure different things. A record year is a statement about one calendar year. The Paris measure is a statement about sustained warming.

A year above 1.5°C shows that annual temperatures can now reach the threshold. It cannot show, on its own, whether the long-term average has crossed it. That question can only be answered by looking at warming across decades.

El Niño adds warmth to the global average temperature in the year after it peaks, not only while the event is under way. It helped lift both 2023 and 2024, two consecutive years that each set a new high in the Copernicus record.

El Niño is the warm phase of a natural climate pattern in the tropical Pacific Ocean. During an El Niño, surface waters across a wide stretch of that ocean run warmer than usual. The pattern recurs on its own rather than being caused by greenhouse gas emissions.

The timing matters for annual temperature rankings. Records are kept by calendar year, but an El Niño event does not start in January and end in December. Its effect on a given year's average depends on when the event peaked.

That lag explains why a record-setting year can arrive after an El Niño has already passed its peak. A reader looking only at when an El Niño was strongest would miss part of the effect.

For anyone reading a list of record years, this means a year's rank reflects timing as well as the underlying climate. Two years with similar long-term warming can land in different places, depending on where an El Niño peak falls.

El Niño is a short-term boost, not the main driver of rising temperatures. It does not explain the full rise across 2023, 2024 and the years before them. El Niño adds to the long-term warming trend for a period, then fades.

That makes the El Niño share of a record year temporary and tied to a single event. The warming that remains after it fades comes from greenhouse gases.

Long-term warming from greenhouse gases is the base trend beneath the hottest years on record. El Niño can lift a single year above that trend, but it does not explain the full multi-year rise in global temperatures.

One way to picture the relationship is a rising slope with bumps on it. The slope is the greenhouse gas trend. The bumps are short-term natural variation, and El Niño is the best-known source of them. A bump can push one year above the line. Once it passes, the slope is still there.

The record years fit that shape. A strong El Niño helped drive the heat of 2016, the record holder until 2023. El Niño also helped lift 2023 and 2024, the years that took the title after it. Each of those boosts was temporary. A temporary ocean pattern cannot explain a climb that has continued across several years. That part of the rise comes from the base trend.

The distinction shapes how any new record should be read. A record year reflects both forces at once. Separating them shows which part fades when El Niño ends and which part stays in place. Short-term boosts come and go, while the level they push off from keeps rising.

The 1850–1900 baseline is the reference period Copernicus used to measure how warm recent record years were. Each annual warming figure shows how far a year's global average temperature sat above the average for those five decades.

Every warming figure needs a starting point. Without one, a number in degrees Celsius would have nothing to be measured against. The baseline supplies that reference. The period stands in for pre-industrial conditions, which gives the baseline its name.

Because it is an average across five decades, the reference is not tied to any single year. A warm or cool year inside the 1850–1900 window has little pull on the overall average.

The numbers built on it are differences, not raw temperatures. Climate reporting calls such a difference an anomaly. An anomaly shows how much warmer or cooler a year was than the reference period. It does not show what a thermometer read in any one place.

A shared baseline makes years comparable. Copernicus reports different years against the same 1850–1900 average. The gap between their figures therefore reflects a real difference in warmth, not a change in the yardstick.

The baseline stays fixed as the climate warms. Each new record is set against the same pre-industrial average, not against the year it replaced. So a rising series of anomalies tracks warming built up since the late 1800s.

The choice of baseline also shapes the size of the number. Measuring the same year against a later, warmer reference period would produce a smaller anomaly. A reading quoted against one period cannot be set beside a reading quoted against another without adjustment.

The same reference period gives the 1.5°C threshold its meaning. That line is measured from 1850–1900 conditions, not from a recent decade. A year counted as above 1.5°C sits above it relative to the pre-industrial average.

The Copernicus Climate Change Service and the World Meteorological Organization each name a record year by comparing it with their own temperature records. Both reported 2024 as the warmest calendar year in those records.

The unit being ranked is the calendar year. A record covers January through December as a whole. A single hot month or season does not earn the title.

The wording of each finding also sets its limits. The phrase "warmest in its records" refers to the period each organization's data covers. It is a statement about that record, not about every year in Earth's history.

Copernicus and the WMO reached the same conclusion about 2024. The record was reported by two organizations rather than one. When both bodies name the same year, the record does not hinge on a single organization's report.

For 2027 to join the hottest years on record, it would need two things working together. One is the long-term warming trend driven by greenhouse gases. The other is a short-term boost such as El Niño. That pairing explains how a record year forms. It is not a forecast for 2027.

Greenhouse gas warming sets the floor each new year starts from. Because that floor has kept rising, a short-term boost of a given size lands on a warmer starting point than it would have in earlier decades. El Niño on its own cannot account for the climb across several years.

The timing of El Niño is what makes it relevant to any specific year. Its added warmth shows up in the global average in the year after it peaks. Applied to 2027, the question is whether an El Niño peaks during 2026. If one does, 2027 could receive that boost. If none does, 2027 would be leaning on the base trend alone.

The record years show the pairing at work. El Niño helped lift 2023 and 2024. A strong El Niño also helped drive the heat of 2016, the record holder before them. In each case, the short-term push arrived on top of the long-term trend rather than replacing it.

Setting a new record outright and joining the hottest years are different tests. A new record would mean beating 2024, the warmest calendar year in the records of both Copernicus and the World Meteorological Organization. Ranking among the warmest years is a lower bar, and a year can clear it without passing 2024. How high 2027 might land depends partly on the size of any boost it receives.

Specific numbers for 2027 belong to named forecasters and their dated releases. The U.K. Met Office publishes an annual global temperature forecast. NOAA issues outlooks on El Niño and La Niña conditions. Any temperature or probability for 2027 should come from one of those releases, read alongside its publication date.

#5496. Tech Moves: Former Amazon execs depart Warner Bros. Discovery; Amazon leader returns to Microsoft

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 29, 2026 at 3:16 pmOctober 29, 2026 at 6:07 pm

— Two former Amazon executives who helped build Discovery’s direct-to-consumer operation in Bellevue, Wash., are stepping down from their leadership roles following the company’s acquisition by Paramount Skydance. They will remain in advisory roles during the transition.

Avi Saxena joined Discovery in 2019 as chief technology officer of its direct-to-consumer business and led its new Bellevue office. He became CTO of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) following Discovery’s 2022 merger with AT&T’s WarnerMedia business. Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of WBD on Oct. 6, with the combined company taking the name Skydance Corporation.

Before joining Discovery, Saxena was with Amazon for 19 years over two stints, most recently as vice president of technology for Amazon Marketplace. He also held leadership roles at Microsoft and internet infrastructure startups.

Tyler Whitworth is stepping down as executive vice president and chief product officer for WBD’s streaming business. He led teams working on digital products for HBO Max, discovery+, Eurosport, TNT Sports, Food Network and others. Before joining Discovery, he spent more than seven years at Amazon, leading teams developing products and services for customers and third-party sellers.

Dane Glasgow, Skydance’s chief product officer, announced the departures of Whitworth, Saxena and WBD Chief Information Officer Dave Duvall in a memo shared with GeekWire.

“Much of the strength of WBD’s product and technology organizations reflects their leadership and dedication. Please join me in thanking them and wishing them the very best,” Glasgow wrote.

The company has not responded to GeekWire’s inquiries about the future of the Bellevue office.

— Bahadir Onalan is returning to Microsoft as a vice president in its CoreAI organization, focused on responsible AI, after nearly 10 years at Amazon. Onalan first joined Microsoft in 2005 and worked on Azure teams focused on search, analytics, business intelligence and security. He left in 2017 as a principal software group engineering manager to join Amazon, where he worked on machine learning initiatives.

“This second tenure feels like a true homecoming,” Onalan wrote. “Our goal goes beyond shipping a platform or a product; we are here to define the global standards for AI safety.”

— Naria Santa Lucia is leaving Microsoft after seven years, most recently as a general manager with Microsoft Elevate. She previously served as executive director of the Washington State Opportunity Scholarship.

“I’ll carry the lessons I learned from my time at Microsoft as I continue my personal and professional mission to serve people and communities by teaching, advising nonprofits and mission driven organizations, and spreading joy and human connection,” Santa Lucia wrote.

She did not announce a specific next role.

— VertueLab, a Pacific Northwest nonprofit supporting climate tech entrepreneurs, has named Leo Ochoa executive director, promoting him from managing director for Oregon. He succeeds Aina Abiodun, who is transitioning to chair of the organization’s board after more than three years as executive director.

“Leo brings a unique blend of vision, relationships, and entrepreneurship experience,” the organization said, noting his background as a wildland firefighter, startup founder and patent holder for wearable safety gear.

Abiodun’s accomplishments include co-creating the Seattle Climate Innovation Hub, launching the Opalene Climate Challenge and helping lead the Just Future Climate Labs initiative.

— Seattle’s Pulse Space has appointed Leah Sardone as vice president of engineering. The startup is developing laser-based systems to deliver power and enable long-distance communications in low Earth orbit and beyond. In July, the company announced a $40 million U.S. Space Force contract to advance its laser-based space power technology.

Sardone brings more than 23 years of experience in hardware, sensors and embedded systems development. She joins Pulse Space from IonQ, where she most recently served as director of quantum networking and interconnects. Her previous employers include Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Honeywell Aerospace, Blue Origin and Amazon’s Project Kuiper, now known as Amazon Leo.

— Caravel Bio a Portland, Ore., startup developing technology to rapidly test newly designed proteins, has announced Michał Jastrzębski as its CTO. The company says its platform can screen millions of protein designs in parallel at low cost, helping identify promising candidates for applications in human health, pollution reduction and industrial processes.

Caravel also announced a nearly $1.25 million Small Business Innovation Research Phase II grant from the National Science Foundation to further develop the platform.

Jastrzębski previously served as a principal machine learning engineer at Ginkgo Bioworks. His past employers also include GitHub and Intel.

— Darick Baker has been appointed the director the University of Washington’s Washington Nanofabrication Facility, which the UW describes as “the largest publicly accessible nanofabrication facility and cleanroom in the Pacific Northwest.” Baker joined the facility in 2012 as a research engineer and has served as acting director since 2025. He previously worked at the Colorado School of Mines

— Technology Alliance announced that Stoke Space director of communications Kyra Jorgensen has joined its board. Jorgeson recently joined the space startup from the fusion company Helion Energy.

#5495. Arista’s record quarter shows the network has become central to AI

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The artificial intelligence buildout is well underway, with much of the focus on silicon and compute hardware. The network is treated as plumbing, something you connect after the important decisions have been made. Arista Networks Inc.’s strong third-quarter results signaled greater awareness of the network’s critical role, and Arista is well-positioned to benefit from this secular trend.

Arista reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 58.5% year over year and 20.5% sequentially. That is the fastest growth in the company’s history as a public company and well ahead of its $3.3 billion guide. Adjusted, non-GAAP earnings per share were $1.20, up from 77 cents a year ago. Gross margin was 64%, operating margin was 49.1%, and cash totaled $14.4 billion with no debt.

Management raised full-year 2026 guidance for the fourth time this year to about $13.3 billion, representing 48% growth. Fourth-quarter revenue is expected to come in between $3.9 billion and $4 billion. Arista also gave a first look at 2027, calling for 38% to 40% growth to about $18.5 billion. Within that, AI networking is expected to double from $3.5 billion to about $7 billion, and campus is expected to grow 60% to about $2 billion. The shares rose about 12% in after-hours trading, moderating to a 5% rise today.

Though investors will always gravitate toward the numbers as proof points, the commentary by Chief Executive Jayshree Ullal (pictured) was equally important. “We believe the industry is shifting from a compute-centric vertical stack to a holistic network-centric approach,” she said.

I agree, and the reason is economics. In large clusters, the network often determines how productive the AI factory is. When packets drop or a link fails, expensive accelerators sit idle, and inference makes the problem worse. Ullal described the move from “highly centralized training compute to disaggregated and distributed inference,” with prefill, decode, storage and KV cache spread across resources. “A well-designed network is becoming a foundational cornerstone for optimal token efficiency,” she said.

Buyers are getting it. Boards and chief financial officers now measure AI by cost per token and accelerator utilization, both of which depend on the network. A 5% gain in GPU utilization across a multigigawatt build is worth far more than the switches that delivered it. Once you understand that math, the network shifts from a commodity to a performance decision.

This awareness benefits every networking vendor, but it disproportionately benefits Arista for three reasons.

The first is accelerator diversity. Three years ago, Arista talked about four or five AI customers running 50,000 to 100,000 Nvidia Corp. graphics processing units, often on InfiniBand. Today, it has more than 100 Etherlink customers and expects more than 10 gigawatts of deployment across 10 or more types of accelerators by the end of 2027.

“In 2026, we are in a super cycle of AI,” Ullal said. “What a stark inflection in just three years.” Nvidia is a formidable networking competitor, and its Spectrum-X Ethernet has won over hyperscalers such as Meta Platforms Inc. and Oracle Corp. But Nvidia’s networking is optimized around its own full stack, and as customers bring Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Microsoft Corp.’s Maia, Meta MTIA, Qualcomm Corp., and Cerebras  Inc. silicon into production, many will prefer a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing accelerator.

Every new accelerator expands the share of AI networking open to an independent Ethernet vendor, and Arista leads that category. Co-design work with Cerebras and Maia means Arista is now involved in system design rather than added afterward.

The second is scale-across. Power limits are forcing AI capacity to be spread across buildings and regions, and connecting those sites requires deep buffers, large routing tables and very high reliability. Ullal said scale-across accounted for about 30% of AI demand this year and should rise in 2027, with the 7800 platform as the anchor. “There’s just no room for error when you’re connecting millions of XPUs,” she said. This is where Arista’s routing and EOS software experience matter most.

The third is scale-up. Arista showcased rack-scale Ethernet designs at OCP, built on the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking or ESUN specification, with trials in 2027 and production in 2028. Ullal compared it to the InfiniBand transition: Arista expects to move from “staring at proprietary UALink or NVLink” to “of course, it’s going to be ESUN.” If that happens, Arista’s market expands inside the rack, a segment it has never served.

Security strengthens the argument. Chief Technology Officer Ken Duda said Arista is working with Anthropic PBC, Google LLC and OpenAI Group PBC to integrate AI-driven vulnerability discovery into its software pipeline, including through Project Glasswing. As AI finds flaws faster, an operating system with process isolation and hitless patching becomes an advantage.

Ullal drew the contrast sharply: “Everybody else is dealing with a game of Whac-A-Mole where they’ve got thousands of vulnerabilities and no AVA can possibly keep track of it.” President and Chief Operating Officer Todd Nightingale said this “Glasswing and Mythos effect” is a major reason campus is growing so far ahead of the market.

The stock had fallen more than 20% in the month before the report, according to Chartmill, and analysts raised several concerns.

Deferred revenue. Total deferred revenue was flat at about $6.8 billion, which some interpret as a sign of slowing demand. CFO Chantelle Breithaupt said the balance had “the largest churn in and out” yet stayed flat while the company delivered 58.5% growth, and that the year-end balance will be higher than last year. Ullal said parsing it that way turns demand into “a physics problem,” adding, “We’re just in the best position we’ve been in a long, long time in my 18-year career at Arista.”

Spending and margins. Research and development jumped to $408.5 million from $278.1 million. Duda attributed the increase to hyperscaler prototypes and liquid cooling, and Breithaupt kept the long-term R&D range at 9% to 11% of revenue. Gross margin dipped from 65.2% a year ago, but Ullal held the long-term range at 62% to 64%, including for scale-up products.

Supply and visibility. Purchase commitments rose to $11.4 billion, and inventory to $3.2 billion. Multiyear agreements now cover silicon, circuit boards and memory. Regarding visibility, Ullal said that although Arista has two quarters of order visibility, “we have two years of work behind it.”

For several years, the debate over Arista has centered on whether Ethernet could displace InfiniBand. While InfiniBand will continue to play a key role in AI buildouts, Ethernet has much broader applicability, and its growth will outpace InfiniBand.

The new question is how much of the AI system the network will define, and this quarter suggests the answer is more than most expected. As accelerators multiply, inference spreads and AI-driven threats grow, value moves toward the layer that connects and protects everything. That is Arista’s layer.

Sebastien Naji of William Blair expressed a similar view in his earnings note. “As networking becomes a more important lever for improving performance and token output in AI data centers, Arista is well positioned to capture a growing share of spending across the most demanding AI workloads,” he wrote. “Combined with continued share gains at enterprises and neoclouds, we believe Arista’s expanding addressable market and competitive positioning support further upside in the coming quarters. We continue to view Arista as a core AI infrastructure holding and reiterate our Outperform rating.”

The biggest risk to Arista isn’t deferred revenue or market demand; it’s whether it can keep executing as crisply as it has as it gets bigger and demand accelerates But execution is something the company has excelled at under Jayshree Ullal.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5494. Dave Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results

Q3 Revenue Growth Accelerates to 31% Y/Y to $198 Million, Driven by Record New Member Acquisition as well as Continued MTM Growth and ARPU Expansion

28-DPD Rate Improves Y/Y and Q/Q to 2.09%, Falling Below 2.00% in September; Net Monetization Rate Expands to 5.2%, Its Highest Level in Five Years

Net Income of $64 Million; Adj. EBITDA Increases 39% Y/Y to $82 Million, Representing a 41% Margin

Raises 2026 Revenue, Adj. EBITDA and Adj. Diluted EPS Guidance

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Dave Inc. ("Dave" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: DAVE), one of the nation's leading neobanks, today reported its financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026.

"Q3 was another strong quarter, with revenue growth accelerating to 31% year-over-year, driven by faster MTM growth and continued ARPU expansion," said Jason Wilk, Founder and CEO of Dave. "Our 28-day past due rate improved year-over-year and sequentially to 2.09%, even as originations grew 23% from a year ago. In September, with CashAI v6.0 fully deployed, average ExtraCash size reached $225, our 28-day past due rate fell below 2.00%, and our gross monetization rate was approximately 7.0% as we relaxed legacy fee caps. Together, these changes let us responsibly extend more credit while delivering greater value to members and strengthening unit economics. Based on this momentum, we are raising our full-year 2026 guidance for Revenue, Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Diluted EPS."

Wilk added, "We are also seeing solid early traction with Dave Flex, our new Pay in Four credit card that gives members greater flexibility in managing everyday purchases. During Q3, we grew Dave Flex adoption from single- to double-digit thousand actives, through both cross-selling to existing members and direct customer acquisition at better-than-expected acquisition costs. We are additionally encouraged by strong cross product adoption with ExtraCash that suggests significant upside to baseline member lifetime value. We are excited to continue expanding access to more members ahead of a broader rollout planned for 2027."

#5493. Pump.fun Perps on Hyperliquid: How the 0.10% Builder Fee Works

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On a $10,000 Bitcoin perpetual order placed through Pump.fun, Pump.fun can charge up to $10.

Hyperliquid, the exchange that actually matches and settles the trade, charges a standard taker $4.50. Only one of those fees has a written rule sending it toward a token burn, and it's Hyperliquid's.

Most launch coverage focused on whether to buy HYPE or SOL. The more useful question for PUMP holders is where each dollar of perps fees goes. When you compare Pump.fun's fee schedule, its buyback methodology and Hyperliquid's fee documentation, then, you'll see they don't connect the way many people assume.

Pump.fun didn't build a derivatives exchange. Its perps run on Hyperliquid's order books through builder codes, a feature that lets outside apps send user orders to Hyperliquid and add their own fee on top. Hyperliquid's engine handles matching, margin and liquidations.

The product first appeared in Pump.fun's API around October 9, when Wu Blockchain spotted a /coins/perps endpoint showing prices, funding rates, open interest and maximum leverage, all pulled from Hyperliquid's mainnet. The same endpoint also listed SOL, Nvidia, Tesla, gold and crude oil contracts. Trading launched around October 16 and 17, with up to 40x leverage on BTC and 25x on ETH reported at launch.

Pump.fun updated its terms and conditions on October 17. The perps feature is blocked for users in the United States and Ontario, along with sanctioned parties.

Pump.fun's official fee schedule splits the cost of a perp trade into separate parts.

Here's the math on a $10,000 market order at entry-tier rates, assuming Pump.fun charges its full maximum:

For a maker order, the gap is wider: $1.50 to Hyperliquid and up to $10 to Pump.fun. At full rate, the app routing the trade earns more per order than the exchange that runs it. Note that 0.10% is the published maximum, not a confirmed rate for every trade.

This side of the trade has the clearest documentation. Hyperliquid says its fees are "entirely directed to the community," meaning its HLP vault, the assistance fund and market deployers.

The assistance fund converts trading fees into HYPE automatically as part of the chain's execution.

According to Hyperliquid's documentation,

So every Pump.fun perp trade feeds part of Hyperliquid's own token-burn mechanism through standard protocol rules. That share never touches Pump.fun's treasury.

There's one more possible layer. Some of the markets in Pump.fun's API, such as stocks and commodities, are the kind of contracts that third-party HIP-3 deployers usually run on Hyperliquid. Those deployers can set their own fee share. If Pump.fun lists them, another party joins the split.

Under Hyperliquid's builder code rules, the builder fee goes to the builder's address on Hyperliquid. Builders claim it through the standard referral-reward process. The fee is charged in the collateral asset, so for these markets it builds up in USDC on Hyperliquid, not in SOL on Solana.

That matters once you check Pump.fun's PUMP buyback methodology. The program puts 50% of revenue toward buying and burning PUMP. It defines revenue as income from:

Perps builder fees and bridge fees aren't on that list. The page also says buybacks aren't a commitment to future purchases, except as "deterministically programmed prior to April 29, 2026." Perps launched in October, so they weren't covered by that commitment.

To be fair to Pump.fun, the absence of a rule isn't proof that the money stays out of buybacks. Pump.fun could add perps to its revenue definition at any time. But as of today, no published Pump.fun document links a perps fee to a PUMP burn. Any connection would also need USDC moved off Hyperliquid and converted, because the buyback table records purchases in SOL.

This also changes how to read the buyback numbers I've covered before. The PUMP page shows $490.65 million in cumulative buybacks on its dashboard and $465 million in Newsletter #14. It also says the fee dashboard has misreported revenue and buyback amounts since Custom Pairs launched and that this "will be fixed soon." If perps revenue grows, Pump.fun's total income and the share that actually reaches PUMP burns could move further apart.

Hyperliquid makes the builder side of this traceable. It publishes daily fill files for each builder at:

[https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/](https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/){builder_address}/{YYYYMMDD}.csv.lz4

The builder address must be entirely lowercase. A builder's total collected fees also appear in Hyperliquid's referral info query.

Without Pump.fun's builder address in its fee schedule, terms or announcements, nobody outside the company can add up the actual perps revenue, which is the number that would show whether this product is a side feature or a real revenue line. Once that address is public, the next step is to check whether a matching amount ever shows up in the PUMP buyback table.

Until then, the honest answer is this: Hyperliquid's share has a documented path to a HYPE burn, while Pump.fun's share has a documented path into Pump.fun's own wallet.

#5492. Reno's freeze-free season grew 69.6%, the largest gain of 16 ranked U.S. locations

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Longer allergy seasons can follow longer freeze-free growing seasons — see 10 of 16 U.S. locations ranked by how much theirs grew since the 1970s

Pollen season starts where frost ends. Every night that stays above freezing gives trees, grasses and weeds more time to grow, flower and release pollen. In the places ranked below, those nights now come in longer unbroken runs than they did in the 1970s.

The measure is the freeze-free growing season: the average yearly count of consecutive days with minimum temperatures above 32°F. Climate Crisis 247 ranked 16 U.S. locations by how much that stretch has changed, using a Climate Central analysis. The readings come from station records in the Applied Climate Information System, a NOAA program. The analysis compares the 1970-79 average with the 2015-24 average. Locations are ordered by percent change, not by the number of days added.

The growing season is a stand-in for allergy season, not a direct count of pollen or symptom days. The link runs through plant biology. A year's pollen intensity rises and falls with the length of that year's growing season. Higher carbon dioxide levels can also push plants to make more pollen. Forecasts cited by Climate Crisis 247 put growing seasons in some regions more than a month longer than they were 50 years ago. Those connections tie longer allergy seasons to a warming climate.

This list covers 10 of the 16 ranked locations, presented in the ranking's countdown order from No. 10 to No. 1. They sit in eight climate regions, from the Northeast to the Southwest. Three are in Montana: Bozeman, Helena and Missoula. Their starting points differ widely. In the 1970s, Bozeman averaged 93 freeze-free days a year, while Las Cruces, New Mexico, averaged 196.

Reno, Nevada, holds the No. 1 spot. Its freeze-free season grew 69.6%, from 112 days to 190. That is the largest gain among all 16 ranked locations by a wide margin. Missoula follows at 39.4%, rising from 104 days to 145. Las Cruces now averages 253 days above freezing, the highest 2015-24 figure in this selection.

Bozeman's freeze-free growing season has grown 25.8%. It went from an average of 93 days a year in 1970-79 to 117 days in 2015-24. Local plants now have a longer window to grow and release pollen.

Bozeman sits at No. 10 in the Climate Crisis 247 ranking, which Yahoo News published.

Bozeman added 24 days to its average yearly run of consecutive days with overnight lows above 32°F. Its 1970s baseline of 93 days is the shortest among the 10 locations in this selection. Its recent average of 117 days is also the lowest of the group.

Bozeman falls in the Northern Rockies and Plains climate region. Helena and Missoula carry the same regional label.

Helena's freeze-free growing season averaged 152 days a year in 2015-24, up from 118 days in the 1970s. The 28.8% increase puts the Montana city at No. 9 among the 16 U.S. locations in the Climate Crisis 247 ranking.

That works out to 34 more days a year in an unbroken run without a freeze. For local trees, grasses and weeds, those days add time to grow, flower and release pollen before cold weather returns.

Helena shares the Northern Rockies and Plains climate region with Bozeman and Missoula. Among those three, it started with the longest 1970s baseline. It also has the longest 2015-24 average.

Its percentage gain is larger than Bozeman's 25.8% and smaller than Missoula's. Measured in days added rather than percent, Helena also lands between the two. Bozeman gained fewer days, and Missoula gained more.

Marquette, Michigan, now averages 132 consecutive days a year with daily lows above freezing, up from 106 days in 1970-79. That 24.5% expansion puts the city at No. 8 of the 16 locations ranked.

The gain works out to 26 more freeze-free days a year on average. Trees, grasses and weeds around the city have that added time to grow and shed pollen.

Marquette started from a short base. Among the 10 locations in this selection, only two averaged fewer freeze-free days in the 1970s. Both are in Montana: Bozeman and Missoula.

Marquette's season is still short by this selection's standards. Only Bozeman, Montana, posts a lower 2015-24 average among the 10. Marquette's recent figure of 132 days also falls below the 147-day average that Toledo, Ohio, recorded in 1970-79.

Marquette's 24.5% rise is the smallest percent increase among the 10 locations here. Tupelo, Mississippi, comes closest to it.

Marquette is the only Upper Midwest location in this selection.

Toledo's freeze-free growing season averaged 186 days a year in 2015-24, up from 147 days in 1970-79. That 26.5% increase places the city at No. 7 among the 16 U.S. locations Climate Crisis 247 ranked.

The gap works out to 39 more days a year. That is more than five weeks of additional time with overnight lows above freezing. The recent average now covers roughly half the calendar year.

Toledo is the only city in this selection from the Ohio Valley climate region. Its 1970s baseline of 147 days was already longer than that of any of the three Montana cities on this list.

The figures do not show whether the extra days arrived in spring, in fall or at both ends of the season. They count consecutive days above freezing, not days with pollen in the air.

That timing is relevant to ragweed. Ragweed pollen is the leading cause of allergy symptoms in late summer and early fall. The plant is most common in the Midwest, the region that includes Ohio.

The effects of warming on pollen extend beyond the calendar. Climate change can shift when pollen season starts and ends. It can also change how long the season lasts and how much pollen plants produce. Those changes increase people's exposure to pollen. They also raise the risk of allergy and asthma symptoms.

Tupelo, Mississippi, averaged 237 consecutive days a year with minimum temperatures above freezing in 2015-24, up from 190 days in 1970-79. That 24.7% increase places the city at No. 6 in the source's countdown of 16 ranked U.S. locations.

In raw terms, the change adds up to 47 more frost-free days in an average year. Each of those days pushes back the point at which a freeze cuts off the season for local trees, grasses and weeds.

Tupelo is the only location from the South climate region among the 10 covered here. It also entered the comparison with a long season already in place. Among these 10, only Las Cruces, New Mexico, started the 1970s with a longer average freeze-free stretch. The same order holds in the recent decade. Tupelo's 2015-24 average is the second-longest in this selection, again behind Las Cruces.

That high starting point shapes how the percentage reads. A moderate percent gain on a 190-day base translates into a large number of added days. Only Marquette, Michigan, posted a smaller percent increase among these 10.

Concord, New Hampshire, posted a 36.3% increase, yet it gained 41 days. That is six fewer than Tupelo added. Because the ranking runs on percent change, Concord sits two places above Tupelo despite adding fewer days.

Tupelo's 1970s average is the same figure Reno, Nevada, the No. 1 location in the ranking, reached in 2015-24.

At 237 days, Tupelo's average freeze-free period now spans roughly 65% of the calendar year.

Las Cruces, New Mexico, now averages 253 consecutive days a year with minimum temperatures above 32°F, up from 196 days in the 1970s. That 29.1% increase places the city at No. 5 among the 16 U.S. locations in the ranking.

Measured in days rather than percent, the city's typical freeze-free run grew by 57 days between 1970-79 and 2015-24.

No other city in this selection started from a higher baseline. Its 1970s average already exceeded the 2015-24 average in seven of the other nine cities covered here. Only Tupelo, Mississippi, and Medford, Oregon, now average more than 196 days.

That high starting point shapes the percentage. When a season is already long, each added day makes up a smaller share of the total. The same number of added days would produce a larger percent change in a city with a short 1970s season.

The city sits in the Southwest climate region. It is the only Southwest location among the 10 cities in this selection.

A freeze-free stretch of 253 days leaves most of the calendar open for trees, grasses and weeds to grow and release pollen.

Concord, New Hampshire's freeze-free growing season has expanded 36.3%. It averaged 113 days a year in 1970-79 and 154 days a year in 2015-24.

That change places Concord at No. 4 in Climate Crisis 247's countdown of 16 U.S. locations. It is the only location from the Northeast climate region among the 10 covered here.

Measured in days, Concord now averages 41 more consecutive days a year with minimum temperatures above 32°F than it did in the 1970s. That is nearly six more weeks a year in which local plants can grow and release pollen.

Missoula, Montana, added the same 41 days. Its percent gain was larger, at 39.4%. The difference comes from the starting point. Missoula began with a shorter season, so the same number of added days made up a bigger share of it.

Medford, Oregon, shows the reverse pattern. Its percent change of 36.5% is close to Concord's. Medford started at 156 days and added 57, which is 16 more days than Concord gained. Its longer baseline means those extra days amount to a similar share of the season. The two sit side by side in the countdown, at No. 4 and No. 3.

Reno, Nevada, offers a third comparison. It began the 1970s with almost the same freeze-free season as Concord. Its percent gain, however, was nearly twice as large. Two locations with nearly matching baselines ended up far apart. In this selection, a similar starting length did not produce a similar gain.

Concord's 113-day baseline falls in the lower half of the 10 locations in this selection. Its current average of 154 days sits just above that of Helena, Montana, which now averages 152 days.

Medford, Oregon's freeze-free growing season averaged 213 days a year in 2015-24, up from 156 days in 1970-79. That 36.5% increase puts Medford at No. 3 in the countdown of 16 ranked U.S. locations.

Counted in days, the change comes to 57 more consecutive days a year with overnight lows above freezing. The measure tracks the longest unbroken run of nights that stay above 32°F. In Medford, that run now lasts nearly two months longer than it did in the 1970s.

Medford is the only location in this selection from the Northwest climate region. Its percent gain edges past Concord, New Hampshire's 36.3% by 0.2 percentage points. Only Missoula, Montana, and Reno, Nevada, rank higher in the source's list.

Medford also started from a longer baseline than Concord. Its 1970s average of 156 days was 43 days longer than Concord's 113. Even from that higher starting point, Medford's season grew by more than a third.

The gap between the two cities has widened in absolute terms. In 2015-24, Medford's 213-day average ran 59 days longer than Concord's 154. A similar percentage gain adds more days to a season that was already longer at the start.

Missoula's freeze-free growing season grew from an average of 104 days a year in 1970-79 to 145 days in 2015-24, an increase of 39.4%. That is the second-largest percentage gain among the 16 U.S. locations in the ranking.

That works out to 41 more consecutive days a year with overnight lows above 32°F than in the 1970s. Only Reno, Nevada, posted a larger percentage increase. Missoula trails it by 30.2 percentage points. Medford, Oregon, follows Missoula at No. 3 with 36.5%, starting from a longer 1970s baseline of 156 days. That leaves 2.9 percentage points between the No. 2 and No. 3 spots.

The ranking places Missoula in the Northern Rockies and Plains climate region. It gives the same label to Helena and Bozeman, the other Montana cities in this selection. Missoula's gain is larger than either of theirs. Helena's season rose 28.8%, and Bozeman's rose 25.8%. Missoula's 1970s baseline of 104 days was shorter than Helena's 118 days but longer than Bozeman's. By 2015-24, Missoula's 145-day average still trailed Helena's 152 days but exceeded Bozeman's 117.

Missoula lies in western Montana, in the area that separates the Sapphire range from the Bitterroot range. No other U.S. municipality fully ringed by the Rocky Mountains is larger.

The city's predominant pollen types span trees, grasses and weeds. Tree pollen comes from alder, maple, elm, juniper, poplar, pine, birch, willow, larch and ash. Grasses, sedge and cattail also contribute. Weed sources include ragweed, pigweed, goose-foot and wormwood/mugwort.

Plant growth in Missoula's ecosystem depends on winter snow. Snowmelt waters vegetation in spring. Runoff from that melt then supplies most of the moisture for plants along rivers and on upland ground through summer and early autumn.

The 145-day average measures frost-free time, not pollen. It does not show when Missoula's allergy season begins, how long symptoms last or how high pollen counts climb.

Reno, Nevada's freeze-free growing season expanded 69.6% between 1970-79 and 2015-24, rising from an average of 112 days a year to 190. No other location among the 16 in the ranking posted a larger percent gain.

That works out to 78 more days a year in Reno's average run of consecutive days with lows above 32°F. Those added days give trees, grasses and weeds in the West climate region a longer stretch to grow and release pollen. Reno is the only location from that region in this selection.

Reno started from a modest base. In the 1970s, its 112-day average sat close to those of colder northern locations in the ranking. Concord, New Hampshire, averaged 113 days in that decade, and Helena, Montana, averaged 118.

Those two places have gained less since then. Concord now averages 154 days and Helena 152. Reno's 190-day average runs 36 days longer than Concord's and 38 days longer than Helena's.

Reno has also overtaken Toledo, Ohio. In the 1970s, Toledo's season averaged 147 days, well ahead of Reno's. By 2015-24, Toledo averaged 186 days, a few days short of Reno's 190.

Reno has narrowed the gap with Medford, Oregon, too. In the 1970s, Medford's freeze-free season averaged 156 days, 44 days longer than Reno's. By 2015-24, Medford's 213-day average led Reno's by 23 days.

The largest percent gain is not the same as the longest season. Tupelo, Mississippi, averaged 190 days in the 1970s, the same length as Reno's current average. Tupelo has since climbed to 237 days. A location that starts with a long season needs far more added days to post a large percentage increase.

Summer heat in Reno is uneven. Neighborhoods near the airport run much hotter than the tree-shaded homes close to the Truckee River. Downtown, heavily paved sidewalks around casinos and shopping centers offer little relief.

#5491. Andy Jassy’s prediction: Amazon could have two $1 trillion businesses within a decade

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 6:08 pmOctober 31, 2026 at 8:51 am

No company has ever had a business with $1 trillion in annual revenue. Andy Jassy says Amazon is on a path to have two.

Amazon Web Services and the company’s stores business could both reach that milestone in the next five to 10 years, the Amazon CEO said Thursday in the company’s third-quarter earnings release and on its call with analysts.

It’s “pretty rare” for Jassy to make a projection that far out, Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak observed on the call, asking how he gets there.

Jassy’s answer started with AWS, which is at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate after growing 39% in the third quarter. He expects growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, and pointed to a $578 billion backlog of contracted AWS revenue.

The largest customers reserve capacity in huge blocks, sometimes as much as a gigawatt at a time, giving Amazon “very good visibility” into 2027, 2028 and part of 2029, he said.

Beyond that, he said, businesses are still early in using AI, the cost of running AI models keeps falling, and new uses keep emerging, such as AI models finding and fixing security flaws.

“You can’t predict with any certainty five to 10 years from now, especially at these types of growth rates,” Jassy said of AWS. “But it’s not a stretch for us to imagine that this could be over a trillion dollar business.”

Jassy’s forecast is a big jump from seven months ago. In March, Jassy told employees that AWS had a chance to reach at least $600 billion in annual revenue within about a decade, double his earlier expectation, according to Reuters.

Amazon’s stores business is bigger than AWS. Sales from Amazon’s online and physical stores totaled $309 billion over the past 12 months, or about $575 billion if Jassy is including third-party seller services and advertising in his trillion-dollar projection. We’ve asked Amazon to clarify.

For comparison, Walmart, the world’s largest retailer, had $713 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year.

Whichever numbers he’s using, Jassy said “some folks are sleeping a bit” on how much progress the stores business has made.

Jassy argued that Amazon’s stores business is gaining ground on competitors. Amazon added more than $90 billion in gross sales over the past 12 months, he said, and is adding about twice as much per quarter as its next-largest U.S. competitor.

Units sold are up nearly 15% so far this year, Jassy said. He noted that nearly 80% of retail sales still happen in physical stores, which he expects to shift online over time.

The bold prediction came on a rough day for the company. Amazon shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading after its profit fell short of Wall Street’s expectations.

It’s not going to be cheap to get there. Amazon expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year, mostly for AWS, and Jassy said the company will spend “meaningfully more” in 2027. He said Amazon has “a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns” and is earning back its capital spending faster than before.

The impact is showing up in Amazon’s finances. Its free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier.

With its spending running ahead of the cash its businesses bring in, Amazon has raised $115 billion through long-term debt this year. Its interest expense more than tripled in the third quarter to $1.7 billion, cutting into its profit.

“We’re in the very early days of this inflection,” Jassy said. “Our strategy is working, and I expect it will for the foreseeable future.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5490. Unisys Announces 3Q26 Results

Unisys Continues Strong New Business Signings and Raises Full-Year Revenue Guidance

Revenue of $471.5 million, up 2.5% year over year (YoY), up 0.6% in constant currency(1)

Technology Solutions & Services(13) (TS&S) revenue of $387.1 million, up 2.6% YoY, up 0.9% in constant currency

Unisys increases 2026 full-year constant currency revenue guidance; reaffirms full-year non-GAAP operating profit(6) margin guidance

Gross profit margin of 26.7%, up 120 basis points (bps) YoY

Operating profit margin of 5.0% improved YoY; non-GAAP operating profit margin of 7.2%, improved 180 bps YoY

New Business(5) Total Contract Value (TCV)(3) of $221 million, an increase of 78% YoY

Purchased group annuity contract to transfer approximately $200 million of projected U.S. defined benefit pension liabilities to a third-party insurer, funded with plan assets

BLUE BELL, Pa., Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Unisys Corporation (NYSE: UIS) reported financial results for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26).

"The year continues to gain momentum, with the third quarter building on a solid first half," said Michael Thomson, Unisys CEO and President. "New business signings once again were strong, and client interest continues to deepen across the portfolio. Our AI-First execution is transforming our delivery, opening new markets in agentic services, AI infrastructure and the ClearPath ecosystem."

Unisys Chief Financial Officer Deb McCann said, "We are pleased with our third quarter results. Revenue came in ahead of our expectations, led by TS&S, and our non-GAAP operating profit margin of 7.2% was above what we had guided. Together with our fourth quarter visibility, this supports the increase to our full-year revenue guidance and our reaffirmed profitability guidance."

Financial HighlightsPlease refer to the accompanying financial tables for a reconciliation of the GAAP to non-GAAP measures presented, except for financial guidance since such a reconciliation is not practicable without unreasonable effort.

(In millions, except numbers presented as percentages)

Net loss attributable to Unisys Corporation

Non-GAAP net (loss) income attributable to Unisys Corporation(8)

Adjusted EBITDA as a percentage of revenue

Revenue increased 2.5% YoY, up 0.6% in constant currency. Gross profit margin improved 120 bps YoY, primarily driven by a higher mix of software licenses relative to hardware within ClearPath renewals, partially offset by higher cost reduction charges.

TS&S revenue increased 2.6% YoY, or up 0.9% in constant currency. TS&S gross profit margin decreased 200 bps YoY, primarily driven by higher cost reduction charges.

During the third quarter of 2026, gross profit margin and TS&S gross profit margin benefited by approximately 50 and 70 bps, respectively, from a first quarter transaction within the company's United Kingdom business process outsourcing consolidated joint venture. This transaction is expected to generate gross profit benefit of approximately $3 million quarterly and $12 million for full-year 2026. The financial impact of this transaction will be fully recognized by year end.

For the third quarter of 2026, net loss attributable to Unisys Corporation included a non-cash pension settlement loss of $151 million, net of tax, as a result of the purchase of a group annuity contract to transfer approximately $200 million of projected U.S. defined benefit pension liabilities to a third-party insurer, funded with plan assets. Including this transaction, the company has reduced approximately $520 million of U.S. qualified defined benefit pension plan liabilities since July 2025, working towards its approximately $600 million reduction target. The company expects to complete an additional pension settlement in the first half of 2027 to substantially achieve this objective.

(In millions, except numbers presented as percentages)

Cloud, Applications & Infrastructure Solutions (CA&I):

DWS revenue increased 3.9% YoY, or up 1.7% in constant currency, primarily driven by higher hardware revenue. DWS gross profit margin was 9.5%, a decrease of 670 bps YoY, primarily due to known client attrition, and increased implementation and delivery costs.

CA&I revenue declined 0.1% YoY, down 1.2% in constant currency. CA&I gross profit margin was 20.6%, an increase of 100 bps YoY, primarily driven by delivery improvements.

ECS revenue increased 5.6% YoY, up 2.7% in constant currency, primarily driven by higher specialized project work in the business processing solutions. (1) Constant currency â A significant amount of the company's revenue is derived from international operations. As a result, the company's revenue has been and will continue to be affected by changes in the U.S. dollar against major international currencies. The company refers to revenue growth rates in constant currency or on a constant currency basis so that the business results can be viewed without the impact of fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates to facilitate comparisons of the company's business performance from one period to another. Constant currency is calculated by retranslating current and prior-period revenue at a consistent exchange rate rather than the actual exchange rates in effect during the respective periods.

(2) Backlog â Represents the estimated amount of future revenue to be recognized under contracted work, which has not yet been delivered or performed. The company believes that actual revenue reflects the most relevant measure necessary to understand the company's results of operations, but backlog can be a useful metric and indicator of the company's estimate of contracted revenue to be realized in the future, subject to certain inherent limitations. The timing of conversion of backlog to revenue may be impacted by, among other factors, the timing of execution, the extension, nullification or early termination of existing contracts with or without penalty, adjustments to estimates in pricing or volumes for previously included contracts, seasonality and foreign currency exchange rates. Investors are cautioned that backlog should not be relied upon as a substitute for, or considered in isolation from, measures in accordance with GAAP.

(3) Total Contract Value (TCV) â Represents the initial estimated revenue related to contracts signed in the period without regard for early termination or revenue recognition rules. Changes to contracts and scope are treated as TCV only to the extent of the incremental new value. New Business TCV represents TCV attributable to expansion and new scope for existing clients and new logo contracts. ClearPath TCV is driven by software license renewals, and as such, changes in timing or terms of renewals can lead to fluctuations from period to period. The company believes that actual revenue reflects the most relevant measure necessary to understand the company's results of operations, but TCV can be a useful leading indicator of the company's ability to generate future revenue over time, subject to certain inherent limitations. Measuring TCV involves the use of estimates and judgments and the extent and timing of conversion of TCV to revenue may be impacted by, among other factors, the types of services and solutions sold, contract duration, the pace of client spending, actual volumes of services delivered as compared to the volumes anticipated at the time of contract signing, and contract modifications, including, without limitation, contract nullification and termination, over the lifetime of a contract. Investors are cautioned that TCV should not be relied upon as a substitute for, or considered in isolation from, measures in accordance with GAAP.

(4) Book-to-bill â Represents total contract value booked divided by revenue in a given period.

(5) New Business â Represents expansion and new scope for existing clients and new logo contracts.

(6) Non-GAAP operating profit â This measure excludes pretax pension and postretirement expense, pretax goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges and pretax charges or gains associated with certain legal matters related to settlements, professional services and legal fees, including legal defense costs, associated with certain legal proceedings, and cost-reduction activities and other expenses.

(7) EBITDA & adjusted EBITDA â Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) is calculated by starting with net income (loss) attributable to Unisys Corporation common shareholders and adding or subtracting the following items: net income (loss) attributable to noncontrolling interests, interest expense (net of interest income), provision for (benefit from) income taxes, depreciation and amortization. Adjusted EBITDA further excludes pension and postretirement expense; goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges, foreign exchange (gains) losses, debt extinguishment, certain legal matters related to settlements, professional services and legal fees, including legal defense costs, associated with certain legal proceedings; environmental matters related to previously disposed businesses; cost reduction activities including workforce reduction actions, lease abandonment costs, asset impairment charges and other costs associated with exited operations and facilities; non-cash share-based expense; and other (income) expense adjustments.

(8) Non-GAAP net income (loss) and non-GAAP diluted earnings (loss) per share â These measures exclude pension and postretirement expense and charges or (credits) in connection with goodwill and intangible asset impairment; foreign exchange (gains) losses, debt extinguishment, certain legal matters related to settlements, professional services and legal fees, including legal defense costs, associated with certain legal proceedings; environmental matters related to previously disposed businesses; and cost reduction activities including workforce reduction actions, lease abandonment costs, asset impairment charges and other costs associated with exited operations and facilities. The tax amounts related to these items for the calculation of non-GAAP diluted earnings (loss) per share include the current and deferred tax expense and benefits recognized under GAAP for these items.

(9) Free cash flow â Represents cash flow from operations less capital expenditures.

#5489. Certinia brings AI into professional services workflows

Certinia Inc. is bringing AI into the software firms use to sell projects, assign staff, deliver work and bill clients.

AI’s ability to instantaneously draw from a deep well of information and provide guidance in practically any field of expertise has changed the paradigm for professional services. For Certinia Inc., whose business facilitates 7.1 billion professional services operations per month, AI represents a significant opportunity for its clients.

“I think the only industry that’s probably been more disrupted by AI than the technology industry has probably been the services industry,” Robert Cesafsky, chief operating officer of Certinia, told theCUBE. “Whether you are a software company, a hardware company, a tax and accounting firm [or] management consulting … all of these industries are being directly targeted or impacted by AI. Whatever your strategy is, you need to be able to have the right tools. You need to be able to have control of that services business, and that’s what Certinia provides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s coverage of the Certinia at Dreamforce event. (* Disclosure below.)

Certinia launched in 2009 as FinancialForce.com Inc., a cloud-based accounting and enterprise resource planning provider built natively on the Salesforce Inc. platform. It rebranded in 2023 as it broadened from accounting and ERP to managing services businesses.

Certinia’s Salesforce-native platform connects a wide range of processes spanning sales, project delivery, financial management and customer success. The company’s approach helps clients transform cost centers into profit centers by improving visibility into customer activities, optimizing resource deployment and maintaining connectivity throughout the customer lifecycle.

“We can take away all the administrative tasks and outsource that to AI in order to help them deliver faster time outcomes, but it also helps them deliver a lower cost to serve that project,” said Mimi Spier, chief marketing officer of Certinia, in an interview with theCUBE. “We can identify expansion opportunities, [and] at-risk customers where we need to optimize renewals. Everything we’re doing is ultimately affecting the bottom line.”

Certinia’s long-time relationship with Salesforce is a key element in the company’s overall strategy. Certinia is featured under the AI agents and tools category for Salesforce’s AgentExchange and has provided AI-powered sales and delivery for Salesforce’s consulting partner network.

“We have a deep partnership with Salesforce,” said Raju Malhotra, chief product and technology officer of Certinia. “I spend personally a lot of time with the Salesforce executives on business and engineering, and we collaborate. We bring our customer use cases, they tell us about what’s coming up from a capability perspective and we work very well together. They’re led by a founder [chief executive officer] who’s very much in tune with the market, and they want to stay ahead.”

Certinia has sought to stay ahead in its own right by introducing Veda, an enterprise-grade intelligent operations engine that functions as the company’s suite of AI specialist agents and intelligent actions. The solution delivers rules-bound, trusted and ROI-focused autonomous workflows, combining Certinia’s years of institutional memory with advanced AI reasoning. Certinia’s goal with Veda is to provide customers with enough flexibility so that agents integrated into existing business workflows can drive immediate and measurable value.

“We’ve infused Veda throughout the experience for users to be more productive,” Malhotra said. “We have package agents, which are Veda agents. We launched Veda with 10 packages. Now we have 24, and we will finish the year with more than 40 package agents. Those agents are very much persona based, and they help our customers.”

Veda is not simply a layer of generic automation; it represents a key shift in how AI is being used in the enterprise. Certinia’s focus on serving the professional services market motivated the company to ground its AI offering in operational reality, where context, coordination and control matter as much as speed, according to Scott Hebner, principal AI analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Certinia’s recent announcement of Veda is more profound than it may appear on the surface,” he said. “Veda is notable not simply because it introduces a new suite of AI agents and intelligent workflow-based actions, but because it offers a glimpse into what the future of enterprise AI is likely to look like: AI that works alongside humans in consequential workflows, helps people make better decisions and earns trust by being grounded in business context, governance and real operational outcomes.”

Since the launch of Veda in April, Certinia has taken several actions to enhance its AI capabilities. In July, the firm acquired Moonnox, an AI-native services delivery platform purpose-built for the professional services sector.

This acquisition added a contextual layer to Veda through knowledge graphs, persistent project memory and services-specific agents. The combined platform can now connect a new client request with approved scope, staffing requirements and financial impact, then recommend governed actions for professional review, according to Hebner.

“Certinia provides the deep, structured foundation of professional services, customer success and financial management; Moonnox brings the missing half: capturing the unstructured reality — the emails, chats, and calls — where delivery actually happens,” he explained. “Together, they fuse everything a services business knows with everything their teams do, moving Veda beyond orchestration toward context-aware, AI-native services delivery.”

The context graph can also draw on structured records such as timecard entries and utilization figures. Moonnox helps bring that information into the graph for client-facing teams managing projects, according to Cesafsky.

“That’s been where Moonnox has really showed up for us over the last couple of months,” he said. “It’s those capabilities to help the client-facing services [and] delivery teams run and operate their projects. [Moonnox] is effectively an intake machine for a lot of that structured data to bring that into the context graph as well.”

In September, Certinia unveiled its System of Action for services businesses. The offering significantly expanded the Veda AI suite with new agents and more than doubled the Veda Intelligent Actions library from 64 to 135.

Certinia’s System of Action uses a three-tier architecture to bring AI agents into services workflows. The first tier brings together structured records and unstructured project data. The second draws on more than 17 years of Certinia’s experience in services to inform decisions. The third lets agents act within existing workflows.

“We want to accelerate the delivery for our customers,” Malhotra said. “Our customers are solving some specific problems in the professional services world. We don’t want to just give you a project plan. If you choose to execute that project plan with some agents, we’ll give you that. If you want to really think about agentic capabilities to help you in making money, in expanding your time [and] in terms of delivery, we will help you with that.”

For professional services firms, adopting AI agents means deciding which parts of project delivery to delegate to them.

“We view professional services as a leading indicator of where enterprise AI is heading because it combines knowledge-intensive work, dynamic context, collaborative decisions, measurable economics and human accountability,” Hebner said. “If Certinia executes well, Veda could become an important blueprint for translating digital labor into economic outcomes.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Certinia Signal interview series. Neither Certinia, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)
